The hymn beginning with “mahāṃ asi,” consisting of five verses and eleven ṛcs, is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and is addressed to Agni.
It is introduced by the word “mahān.
Its application (viniyoga) is prescribed for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra.

Great art thou, the herald of the sacrifice; indeed, without thee the immortals do not rejoice. Come hither on one chariot with all the gods, O Agni; sit down as the first invoker (hotṛ). Great art thou, the herald of the sacrifice; indeed, without thee the immortals do not rejoice. Come hither on one chariot with all the gods, O Agni; sit down as the first invoker (hotṛ). 1.
O Agni, you are great as the one who makes known—that is, the indicator—of the sacrifice.
Without you, the immortal gods do not rejoice; they find no delight.
Come hither together with all the Viśve Devas upon one chariot;
being the foremost and principal invoker, sit down here upon the strewn sacrificial grass.
The invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the Bārhaspatya oblation at the Vājapeya sacrifice is prescribed in the Sūtra:
“They praise you, the agile one, for the mission of a messenger, while singing hymns to the one who is easy to invoke and fair to behold” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.9).
The human beings, possessing oblations, ever invoke you, the agile one, for the office of messenger— O Agni,
upon whose sacrificial grass the gods sit, for him the days become auspicious.

The human beings, possessing oblations, ever invoke you, the swift one, for the office of messenger; O Agni, he upon whose sacred grass you sit together with the gods—for him the days become auspicious. 2.

O Agni, human beings—those who offer oblations and perform sacrifices—constantly, at all times, invoke you, the swift one who advances, for the office of a messenger, that is, for the task of carrying the oblation.
For what purpose? He says:
for that sacrificer whose *barhis* grass you occupy together with the gods, for that sacrificer the days become auspicious, truly fair days.
The thirty [gods] have declared that treasures are within you for the mortal who offers oblations.
Like a man among men, sacrifice here to the gods; be our messenger, the protector against curses.

Three times, indeed, the wise one has distributed treasures from the unshakable one; within you, O Agni, lord of men, dwell riches for the mortal who offers oblations. Sacrifice here to the gods, O Agni, and be our messenger, the protector against curses.
O Agni, within you— in the midst of the day (though *akuh* is a name for night,
here it refers to the day because in this [day] forms and other qualities are manifested)—
three times, at the three libations (*savana*), bestow riches, that is, the oblations, upon the mortal, the human being who offers the sacrifice.
The meaning is "for that purpose.
The officiating priests (ṛtvijas) make it known or proclaim it.
Or else:

Then Agni and Śramaja have perceived the threefold [sacrifice] and what is contained within you; that is to say, they have found it. Moreover, O Manu-pat, like Manu, do thou, as a messenger, worship the gods here in this sacrifice of mine.
Be for us a protector against imprecation; be our guardian, protecting us from the curse and from the enemy.
O Agni, Lord of the great sacrifice, Agni, may they take pleasure in the ritual power and the splendor of every oblation prepared; then the gods established you as the bearer of the offerings.

Agni rules over the great sacrifice; Agni [rules] over every oblation that has been prepared. For they delight in his ritual wisdom and his splendor; thus the gods have established him as the bearer of the oblation. 4.
Agni rules over the vast, great, and unswerving sacrifice;
Agni alone rules over every prepared oblation.
For the Vasus, the gods, delight in and attend to his ritual act.
Moreover, the gods have established Agni as the bearer of oblations; that is to say, they have made him the carrier of their sacrificial offerings.
1. Śa causes exhilaration; 2. Jha becomes likewise; 3. Kha-bha is the name of night.
O Agni, bring the gods here to partake of the oblation; let them, with Indra as their chief, rejoice here.
Place this sacrifice among the gods in heaven. Do you all protect us always with your blessings.
O Agni, bring the gods to the offering; may they, with Indra as their chief, rejoice here. Place this sacrifice among the gods in heaven. Do you all protect us always with blessings. 5.
O Agni, bring the gods here for the placing of the oblation and for the consumption of the offerings.
To the question "For what purpose?", he says:
so that in this sacrifice the gods, with Indra as their chief (*indrajyeṣṭhāsaḥ*), may rejoice.
Place this sacrifice and this sacrificial oblation among the gods who abide in heaven; establish it there.
The sense is: "Bring the gods here" or "lead this oblation to the gods.
The final quarter-verse has already been explained.
The twelfth hymn, consisting of the verse beginning with “agnama mahā,” is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to Agni.
Thus it is enumerated: “agnama [consists of] three verses. Its application has been stated for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina Śastra.

In the Daśarātra sacrifice, during the ninth day of the Vyūha, this hymn serves as the Ājya-śastra. It is stated in the Sūtra: "The Ājya [hymn] for the third [day] is the *agna ā yāhi* [hymn]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.11).
I have praised with great reverence the most youthful one, who has shone forth when kindled in his own dwelling;
him of wondrous luster between the two wide worlds, well-invoked, facing every direction.

We have brought [oblations] with great reverence to the youngest [Agni], who, kindled in his own dwelling, has shone forth with wondrous luster between the two wide worlds, heaven and earth; he is well-invoked and faces every direction.

That Agni who, kindled with wood in his own dwelling, in his own place—the Āhavanīya fire—having been kindled, shines forth; him, this most youthful (yaviṣṭha) one, the youngest, between the two wide and expansive worlds (rodasī), heaven and earth, in the midst of the intermediate space, the one of brilliant luster (citrabhānu), whose flames are manifold, who is well-invoked with excellent oblations, and who moves toward us from every side—that great Agni we approach with great reverence (namas).
May he, Jātavedas, who overcomes all great misfortunes, be praised with hymns in our home;
may he protect us from evil and from reproach, and likewise protect us and our patrons who sing his praises.
He, Agni Jātavedas, the great conqueror of all misfortunes, is praised within the home. May he protect us from distress and from reproach—both us who sing his praises and our wealthy patrons.

That Agni—who, by his greatness, overcomes and conquers all misfortunes; who is Jātavedas, whose wealth is born or whose wisdom is born—and who is praised by us in the *dama*, the sacrificial hall—that Agni shall protect us from misfortune, from sin, and from blameworthy action. He shall protect us even as we sing praises. Moreover, that Agni shall protect our patrons who offer oblations.
O Agni, you are Varuṇa and Mitra; the Vasiṣṭhas magnify you with their hymns.
May there be excellent riches in you; do you all protect us always with your blessings.
You, O Agni, are Varuṇa and you are Mitra; the Vasiṣṭhas magnify you with their hymns. May all treasures of gain be yours. Do you protect us always with your blessings. 3.
1. Bring this! O Agni, you are Varuṇa;
and furthermore, you are Mitra, the protector of the world from injury.
The Vasiṣṭhas magnify you with their thoughts—that is, with hymns of praise.
May the treasures existing within you be well-enjoyed by us.
The rest is clear.
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with “*prāgnaye*,” is the *ṛṣi*-seer Vasiṣṭha’s; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and has Vaiśvānara as its deity.
Thus it is enumerated: “‘*prāgnaye*’: [this is] addressed to Vaiśvānara.”
The application [of the mantra] is indicated by its internal characteristics (*laiṅgika*).

"O Agni, who purifies all, who bestows wisdom; O divine Agni, bring forth our prayer and our devotion! Like an oblation upon the sacred grass, we offer it, pleasing Vaiśvānara, the director of our thoughts. (1) *pra agnaye viśvaśuce dhiyamdhe asuragne manma dhītiṃ bharadhvam | bhare haviḥ na barhiṣi prīṇāno vaiśvānarāya yataye matīnām || 1 ||*

O friends, bring forth a prayerful thought (*manma*) and a ritual act (*dhīti*) to that Agni—the friend, the all-illuminating one who kindles everything, the ordainer of thoughts and deeds, the slayer of the Asuras.
To Vaiśvānara, the specific form of Agni who belongs to all men and is the giver of desired objects, I, being gratified, offer praise like an oblation upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Or rather: [the same].
Pleasing the oblation and making it pleasing, I gather the oblation upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). "Na" is used here in the sense of "now.

O Agni, blazing with your flame as you were being born, you filled the two worlds (*rodasī*). O Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas, by your greatness, you released the gods from their curse. 2. You, O Agni, blazing with your flame, as you were being born, filled the two worlds. O Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas, by your greatness, you released the gods from their curse.
O Agni, you, shining intensely with your flame as you are being born, have filled the two worlds, heaven and earth.
Furthermore, O Jātavedas—possessor of innate wisdom or innate wealth—O Vaiśvānara, O Agni who belongs to all men, by your greatness you have liberated the gods from the curse of the enemy.

When you were born, O Agni, you looked out upon all beings like a watchful guardian of cattle, moving everywhere. O Vaiśvānara, find a path for our sacred prayer. And do you all protect us always with your blessings. 3. When you were born, O Agni, you looked out upon all beings like a watchful guardian of cattle, moving everywhere. O Vaiśvānara, find a path for our sacred prayer. And do you all protect us always with your blessings. 3.

O Agni, you who are born from the Sun as its very self—you, the lord or the impeller, being the one who moves all around (*parijmā*), are the guardian of cattle (*paśūn gopāḥ*). Just as a protector of cows beholds his cattle, so do you;
whenever (*yat*) you have looked upon (*vyakhyaḥ*) the worlds (*bhuvanā*), that is, all beings.

1. In the *kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* recensions, the word "vardhanti" is absent. 2. [The verses] are well-worshipful (*susaṃbhajanīyāni*). Then, for the sake of protection, you behold the *brahman*; *brahman* here means a hymn of praise. For that purpose, find the way (*gātu*), that is, the path or the attainment of the fruit. Or alternatively: find the way for the sake of the *brahman*, that is, for the sake of the Brahmins. The meaning is: find that way by which the Brahmins go away from calamities. The rest is clear. 16.
The hymn beginning with “samidhā jātavedase” is the fourteenth [hymn] in the [Maṇḍala], consisting of fourteen verses; it is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Vasiṣṭha and is addressed to Agni.
The first verse is a Bṛhatī, while the second and third are Triṣṭubhs.
Thus it is enumerated in the Anukramaṇī: “samidhā, beginning with a Bṛhatī.”
The application is inferential.
With fuel, with invocations to the gods, and with oblations, let us, full of reverence, worship Agni Jātavedas, the divine one of bright luster.
With fuel-sticks, with invocations to the gods, and with oblations, may we, full of reverence, worship Agni Jātavedas, the divine one whose radiance is bright. 1.

To Jātavedas, to Agni who is Jātavedas—the one whose wisdom is born—we, the Vasiṣṭhas, would offer with fuel; we would serve the god Agni, who is worthy of praise, with invocations to the gods, that is, with praises to the gods. To him of bright radiance, to Agni of bright radiance, the one of pure luster, we, being humble and possessing oblations, would offer with our sacrificial gifts.
Here, the fourth case is used for the object due to its connection with the root *dāś* (to offer).
Generally, in almost all instances, the fourth case is seen for the object when connected with *dāś*.
O Agni, may we worship you with fuel; may we offer to you, O holy one, with excellent praise.
O Hotṛ of the sacrifice, O god of auspicious luster, may we serve you with clarified butter and with the oblation.

O Agni, may we honor you with fuel; may we worship you, O Holy One, with beautiful hymns. O Priest of the sacrifice, may we worship you with clarified butter; O God of auspicious luster, may we worship you with the oblation. 2.
O Agni, we, the Vasiṣṭhas, shall worship you with fuel;
we shall serve you, O adorable one worthy of sacrifice. O Agni, with a beautiful hymn of praise we shall honor you;
we shall serve you, O Hotṛ of the sacrifice. O Agni, with clarified butter we shall honor you.
O you of auspicious luster, O fair-flaming one, O shining god Agni, may we worship you with an oblation.
O Agni, come with the gods to our invocation of the deities, taking pleasure in the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.
May we be those who offer gifts to you, the god; and do you, O gods, protect us always with your blessings.

O Agni, come with the gods to our invocation of the deities, enjoying the offering of the *vaṣaṭ* call. May we be those who give to you, the god; and do you, O gods, protect us always with your blessings. 3.

O Agni, come near to us, enjoying and partaking of our invocation of the gods, our hymn of praise, and our sacrifice, along with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance and the oblation, together with the gods. May we be those who offer service and attend upon you, the radiant one; may we remain so.
The rest is self-evident.
The hymn beginning with “*upasadyāya*” consists of fifteen verses; it is the *ṛṣi*-seer Vasiṣṭha’s composition, in the *gāyatrī* meter, and addressed to Agni.
Thus it is stated in the *Anukramaṇī*: “*upasadyāya*: [it has] five fewer [verses]; it is in *gāyatrī*.
This hymn is used in the *prātaranuvāka* (morning litany) during the *āgneya-kratu* (rite for Agni), in the *gāyatra-chandas*, and in the *āśvina-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “Having approached [the fire], one should omit the last three verses beginning with ‘O Agni, you of all sacrifices’” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
1. In the manuscripts kha, bha, the word ‘taṃ’ is absent. 2. In the manuscripts jha, na, bha, śa, the reading is ‘śubhradīptim’.
In the Upasad rite, during the morning session, the three verses beginning with "upasadyāya" are the *sāmidhenīs*.
As it is stated in the Sūtra: "The three verses beginning with 'upasadyāya mīḍhuṣe', reciting each one three times without pausing" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.8).
In the Pavitreṣṭi, the verse "agnī rakṣāṃsi" is the first *anuvākyā* for the butter-portion (*ājyabhāga*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Accompanied by the two Ājyabhāgas, one drives away the Rākṣasas" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.12).
In the Anvārambhaṇīyā [iṣṭi], there is a Yājyā for Agni as a recipient of a share.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'Like the impulse of Savitṛ, bring to us wealth'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.8).
In the *iṣṭi* sacrifice for well-being (*svasti*), "svastyanyān" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the first portion of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*).
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "svastyanyāṃ rakṣatvantābhre rakṣā ṇo aṃhasaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.10).

Offer the oblation into the mouth of the one who is to be approached, the bountiful one—he who is our nearest kin. O Adhvaryus, offer the oblation into the very mouth of Agni, who is to be approached (upasadya), the showerer of desires (mīḷahuṣ), for his pleasure. He, Agni, is our nearest (nediṣṭha) kinsman (āpya). The word *āpya* here is a derivative used in its own sense to mean "one who is close."

He who, as a seer, a master of the house, and a youth, has settled down in every dwelling facing the five tribes of men. (2) *Yaḥ*, Agni, the *kaviḥ*—the wise one; the *gṛhapatiḥ*—the protector of the household; the *yuvā*—the eternally youthful—being thus, he has *niṣasāda*, settled down, *abhi*, facing toward, the *pañca carṣaṇīḥ*, the five tribes of men, *dame-dame*, in every single house. The completion of the sentence occurs with the following verse.

May that Agni protect our domestic wealth on every side; and may he also guard us from distress. (3) May that Agni protect our domestic wealth (*vedaḥ*)—that which is near to us or shared with us—from all sides against any oppressor. And furthermore, may he protect us, the Vasiṣṭhas, from distress (*aṃhasaḥ*), that is, from sin. (3)

I have generated a new hymn for Agni, the falcon of heaven; will he not surely grant us wealth? (4) I have generated a new hymn for Agni, the falcon of heaven—the swift-moving one—to whom I produce this fresh praise. Will that Agni not surely grant (*kuvit*) much wealth (*vasvaḥ*) to us? (The genitive *vasvaḥ* is used here in the sense of the accusative. He shall give it; such is the meaning.

Desirable are his splendors to behold, like the wealth of one possessing heroic sons—O Agni, of you who shine at the forefront of the sacrifice. (5) The splendors (*śriyaḥ*) of that Agni, who shines (*śocataḥ*) in the eastern portion of the sacrifice (*yajñasya*), are desirable (*spārhāḥ*) to behold (*dṛśe*), just as the wealth (*rayiḥ*) of one who possesses heroic sons (*vīravataḥ*) is desirable. To him, I have generated a new hymn (*stoma*); this is the ellipsis to be supplied, or it connects with what follows. (18)
1. Kha, bha, and upasad [are used] in the Saumikī [rite].
2. Jha, ta, śa, jī, jana, and marjana.

May Agni accept this most excellent offering; may he, the best of sacrificers and the bearer of oblations, graciously receive our hymns. (6) May that Agni, the most worthy of worship or the greatest of sacrificers, the carrier of the oblations, accept this most excellent creation—the oblation being offered by us—and graciously enjoy our songs of praise. (6) *Yajiṣṭhaḥ*: most worthy of sacrifice or the best at sacrificing; *havyavāhanaḥ*: the carrier of the oblations (*havya*) and offerings (*havis*). May that Agni accept (*vetu*)—that is, desire or consume—this most excellent creation (*varṣṭakṛti*), the oblation given by us; and may he graciously enjoy (*jupata*)—that is, attend to—our songs (*giraḥ*), our praises. (6)

O Agni, worthy of being reached, Lord of the people, radiant one, God, we have established you—the possessor of heroic sons—within ourselves, O you who are invoked by all sacrificers. (7) *ni tvā nakṣya viśapate dyumantaṃ deva dhīmahi suvīram agne āhuta.* *nakṣya*: "to be approached" (*nakṣ* is a verb meaning "to pervade" or "to reach"). *Viśapate*: "Lord of the people. *Devā*: "O shining one. *Āhuta*: "O you who are invoked by all sacrificers. *Agne*: "O Agni. *Dyumantam*: "radiant," "possessing splendor. *Suvīram*: "having excellent heroes" (i.e., "having good singers/stewards"). *Tvā*: "you. *Ni dhīmahi*: "we have established" or "we have placed within. [We have established] you, the radiant one, the possessor of heroic sons, within ourselves, O Agni, worthy of being reached, Lord of the people, shining God, you who are invoked by all sacrificers. (7)

O Agni, shine throughout the nights and the days—indeed, at all times. Through you, may we, the Vasiṣṭhas, possess beautiful fires. May you be one who loves us and be rich in heroic sons. *kṣapaḥ* (nights), *uta* (and), *ca* (also), *dīdihi* (shine), *svagnayaḥ* (possessing beautiful fires), *tvayā* (through you), *vayam* (we), *suvīraḥ* (rich in heroic sons), *tvam* (you), *asmayuḥ* (loving us). O Agni, you—throughout the *kṣapaḥ* (nights) and *uta* (and) *ca* (also) *ahāni* (days)—that is to say, at all times—*dīdihi* (shine). By you, shining brightly, *vayam* (we) Vasiṣṭhas become *svagnayaḥ* (possessors of beautiful fires). *Asmayuḥ*: loving us. Having applied the suffix *kyac* according to the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, the suffix *up* is added by the rule *kyācchandasi*, and the letter *d* is elided by Vedic license. Thus Yāska says: "Asmayuḥ means loving us" (Nirukta 6.21). *Tvaṃ* (you) be *suvīraḥ* (rich in heroic sons), that is, possessed of excellent praisers.

The leaders, the inspired sages, approach you with their prayers for the sake of gain; our thousandfold, imperishable speech approaches you. O Agni, the *naraḥ*—the leaders, the sacrificers—and the *viprāsaḥ*—the inspired, wise ones—approach (*upa yanti*) you with their *dhītibhiḥ*—their ritual acts—for the sake of *sātaye*—gain, that is, for the acquisition of wealth or the fulfillment of desires. Furthermore, our thousandfold (*sahasriṇī*), imperishable (*akṣarā*) speech, consisting of hymns of praise, also approaches you.

Agni, with his bright luster, the immortal, the pure, the purifier, the one worthy of praise, drives away the demons. 10. Agni; the demons; he drives away; bright-lustered; immortal; pure; purifier; worthy of praise. 10. *Śukraśociḥ* (bright-lustered) means having a brilliant flame; *amartyaḥ* (immortal) means the divine essence free from death; *śuciḥ* (pure) means himself pure; *pāvakaḥ* (purifier) means the cleanser of others as well; *īḍyaḥ* (worthy of praise) means to be lauded; *agniḥ* (Agni); *rakṣāṃsi* (the demons)—that is, the Rākṣasas—he *sedhati* (drives away), that is, repels. 10.

May he, the lord of strength, O young son of power, bring to us riches; and may Bhaga grant us what is desirable. (11) O Agni, son of strength (*sahasaḥ yaho*), you who are the renowned lord (*īśānaḥ*) and master of the entire world, bring (*ā bhara*) to us (*naḥ*) riches (*rādhāṃsi*)—for "wealth" (*rādhaḥ*) is listed among the names for riches—and may Bhaga also grant (*dātu*) that which is desirable (*vāryam*). (11)
1. *kha-na-bha-śa-arhāna*; 2. *gha-jha-ta-dīdihi ca*; 3. *kha-na-bha-sarvajagataḥ*; 4. *kha-jha-ta-na-bha-śa-no'smabhyamā*.
May the divine Bhaga also grant us, to us, the desirable wealth (*vāryaṃ dhanaṃ*).
The elision of the following vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
In this hymn, Bhaga is the deity who shares in the portion.

O Agni, you [grant] glory accompanied by heroic sons; and may the god Savitṛ, Bhaga, and Diti bestow what is desirable. 12. You, O Agni, [grant] glory accompanied by heroic sons; and the god Savitṛ, Bhaga, and Diti bestow what is desirable. 12.
"O Agni, you [grant] glory—meaning, grant food accompanied by heroes, i.e., endowed with sons and grandsons.
And may the god Savitṛ, the impeller, also bestow desirable wealth;
and may the god Bhaga likewise grant it."
"May Diti and also the goddess Diti grant [it];
she is the deity who receives the invocation in the Sāvitrī hymn."

O Agni, protect us from distress; O God, burn against those who seek to harm us with your most scorching flames, for you are ageless. 13. Agni! Protect us from evil; O God, strike back at those who wish us ill; burn them with your hottest fires, for you are undecaying. 13.
O Agni, protect—meaning, guard—us from distress, that is, from sin.
The long vowel in the *saṃhitā* is a Vedic archaism.
Furthermore, O radiant Deva Agni, you who are ageless (*ajara*), devoid of decay, burn up—the enemies who seek to harm us—with your most scorching, intensely heating splendors; reduce them to ashes.

Now, O Agni, you who are unassailable (*anādhṛṣṭe*), for our protection (*nṛpītaye*)—that is, for the sake of guarding men—be our great (*mahī*), iron-made (*āyasī*), hundredfold (*śatabhuji*) fortress (*pūḥ*). By "fortress" is meant either a city or the ramparts and other defensive structures that serve as its means of protection.
Be such a one.

Just as a city constructed by an artisan, or its protective means such as walls and so forth, protects those who are afraid of enemies, so too, protect us who are afraid of those who would harm us—this is the meaning.

Do you, O invincible one, protect us from distress at evening and at dawn from the one who seeks to harm us, by day and by night. 15. You; us; protect; from distress; O dweller in the evening; from the malevolent; by day; by night; O invincible one. 15.

O Agni, you who are "unassailable" (adābhya), meaning non-violent, and "clothing in darkness" (doṣāvastaḥ)— that is, the dispeller of darkness— protect (pāhi) us (naḥ) from distress (aṃhasaḥ) and from the enemy (aghāyataḥ) who desires evil, both by day (divā) and by night (naktam), at all times.
The sixteenth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with “enā vaḥ,” is the seer Vasiṣṭha’s composition addressed to Agni.
The odd-numbered verses are Bṛhatīs and the even-numbered verses are Satobṛhatīs.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: “enā vaḥ—twelve verses; [this is] a Prāgātha.”
This hymn is used in the Prātaranuvāka during the Āgneya rite, in the Bārhata metre, and in the Āśvina Śastra.
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: “*enā vo agni pra vo yaham*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
In the Āgnimāruta Śastra, the Pragātha beginning with “*devo vo draviṇodāḥ*” serves as the *anurūpa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two Pragāthas, 'devo vaḥ' and 'draviṇodāḥ', are the Stotriya and Anurūpa [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.20).
With this homage, I invoke for you Agni, the Son of Strength— the beloved,
most perceptive messenger, the immortal who attends to the sacrifice and is the envoy of all.
1. *ta-ya-vārya* means that which is to be chosen (*varaṇīya*).
2. In the case of *kha-jha-ta-na-bha-śa*, the term *anṛpītaye* does not exist.
3. In *kha₁*, it is said to be *tha-purī*; in *ja*, it is said to be *pūrī*.
With this reverence, I invoke for you Agni, the Son of Strength—the beloved, most wise, the steward of the fair sacrifice, the immortal messenger of all. 1.

With this homage— this hymn of praise— we [approach] Agni, the son of strength (the grandson of power), our beloved, the most perceptive knower or instructor, the one who goes forth as a steward or master, the performer of excellent sacrifices, the immortal messenger of every sacrificer.
Although there is no subsequent reference (anvādeśa), nevertheless, due to its Vedic character, the word *idam* takes the substitute *enā*.
Alternatively,
*enanam* is a qualifier of *abhi*.
Because the same *ṛṣi* as the previous hymns has been indicated, the *sisena* formula is applied here by way of reference.

O Son of Strength (*sahasaḥ sūno*), for your sake—O you who are most glorious, exceedingly renowned—we make you our messenger; as such, bring the gods here for the enjoyment (*bīti*) of the oblations.
Furthermore, whenever we entreat you, grant us at that very moment all the auspicious riches that are the enjoyments of mortals—that is, the wealth to be enjoyed by human beings. Give them to us.

O Agni, you are the lord of the house; you are our Hotṛ at the sacrifice. You are the Potṛ, O possessor of all boons, the wise one; you worship and you bestow that which is desirable. 5. You, O Agni, are the lord of the house; you are our Hotṛ at the sacrifice. You are the Potṛ, O possessor of all boons, the wise one; you worship and you bestow that which is desirable. 5.
O Agni, possessor of all boons, worthy of praise by all, you are the master of the house (gṛhapati) at our sacrifice (adhvara); you are the sacrificer (yajamāna).
You alone are the invoker (hotṛ) of the gods;
you yourself are the purifier (potṛ).
Therefore, O Pracetā, you of preeminent intellect, sacrifice—that is, worship—with the desirable oblation;
and tremble, that is, desire it, or consume it.

Bestow wealth upon the sacrificer, O you of noble wisdom, for you indeed are the bestower of treasures. Sharpen us at the rite; sharpen every priest who is well-praised and who is skillful. 6. Bestow. Wealth. Upon the sacrificer. O you of noble wisdom. For. You. Indeed. Are the bestower of treasures. Be. Toward us. At the rite. Sharpen. Every. Priest. He who is well-praised. And. Who. Is skillful. 6.
O Agni of noble deeds (*sukrato*), bestow (*kṛdhi*) wealth (*ratnam*)— for "wealth" is listed among the names for riches in the lexicon— as a treasure (*ratnam*) for me, the sacrificer.
The meaning is "give. For indeed, you are the bestower of jewels (*ratnadhāḥ*).
Without us, at the sacrifice, sharpen (*ā-śiśīhi*) the entire assembly of priests.
Furthermore, [the meaning is]: "O you who are well-praised, cause that son of ours who is well-extolled to prosper and grow.
Or else:
"He who is the well-praised Hotṛ-priest prospers; cause him to grow"—this is the sense.
Let it be so; the separate mention is for the sake of showing respect.

In thee, O Agni, well-invoked, let there be dear refreshments, O Surya; those liberal patrons who lead men and bestow wide pastures of cattle. 7. In thee, O Agni, well-invoked, let there be dear refreshments, O Surya; those liberal patrons who lead men and bestow wide pastures of cattle. 7.
O Agni, well-invoked by the sacrificers—O you who are excellently worshipped—let the Sun, the impellers, or the praisers, be dear, let them become beloved.
Furthermore, those wealthy ones, the masters and givers of our people, who bestow vast herds of cattle, let them also be dear to you; this is the connection with the preceding [verse].
Those for whom the libation, with ghee in hand, is poured out and sits down within the dwelling— protect them from malice and reproach, O Victorious One, and grant us long-renowned shelter.

1. *gha*, *ma*, *ta* are [the substitutes for] *bhojanā*; *ya*, *ma*, *ta* are [the substitutes for] *bhojanā*. 2. *kha*, *na*, *bha*, *tvaṃ*, *na*: [these are the substitutes]. 3. *kha*, *na*, *bha*, *'ye'* do not exist.

Those for whom Iḷā, with butter in her hand, sits down within the dwelling as she is invited—protect them, O Victorious One, from the malicious, from the reviler; grant us peace, O you of far-reaching fame. 8.
In whose house— in whose dwelling— she is *ghṛtahastā*,
that is, one whose hand is joined with clarified butter;
the meaning is that she is sprinkled with clarified butter.
Iḷā is the goddess whose form is food, characterized as an oblation,
since "irā" and "iḷā" are listed among the names for food.
Filled, she sits down— that is, she settles— upon [the altar].
The word *api* is used for completion.
O *sahasya*, [Agni] who is beneficial for strength (*sahasa*), protect those sacrificers who possess oblations (*haviṣmant*) from the harm (*duhaḥ*) and the revilers (*nidaḥ*) of the enemy.
And, O you of far-reaching fame (*dīrghaśrut*), grant us—that is, bestow upon us—*śarma*, which is happiness or a home, that is worthy of being heard of for a long time.
May he, the bearer, most skilled with his tongue and mouth, utter a low-toned sound;
bring wealth to us and to our patrons at the outset, and prepare the offering of the oblation.
He, the bearer, with his tongue and mouth, sweet-toned and most wise, shall first bring wealth to us and to our patrons; and he shall prepare the offering of the oblation. 9.

He, the most wise one, the bearer of oblations, with his tongue— which is like the mouth of the gods— gladdening the delightful [gods], that renowned one, bring wealth to us, to us who are liberal patrons of the sacrifice;
and [bring] the giver of oblations,
the sacrificer who bestows the offerings.
And thus the Vājasaneyins declare: "The sacrificer is indeed the giver of the oblation" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.4.1.24).
[O Agni,] prepare [the sacrifice] and impel it toward the ritual acts.
Those who bestow gifts of wealth, horses, and bounties out of a desire for great renown—
protect them from distress, O youngest one, with a hundredfold fortifications.
Those who bestow gifts of wealth, horses, and bounties out of a desire for great renown—deliver them from distress through thy battles, O most youthful one, with a hundredfold fortresses! 10.
O most youthful one, you who are the youngest—those sacrificers who, desiring great and glorious fame (meaning:

being seekers of renown), give gifts that bring success, consisting of horses and wealth; protect those givers from distress, from evil, or from the enemy, with your hundredfold, limitless protections and fortified cities that serve as means of defense.
The god who bestows wealth desires from you a full ladle;
pour it out or fill it up, for the gods take notice of this.
The god who bestows wealth upon you desires a full pouring; pour out or fill it up, for then the god takes heed of you. 11.
The divine Agni, the giver of riches, desires your full ladle poured with oblation;
therefore, pour it out with Soma,
or fill the vessel with Soma.
1. *kha-na-bha-śa-mā-diyā*.
2. *kha-na-ma* does not contain the word *‘haviṣmadbhyaḥ’*.
The two words *vā* have the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The meaning is: "Fill the *hotṛ*’s cup with the *dhruva* vessel and offer the *soma* to Agni.
Immediately thereafter (*ādita*), the divine Agni carries you (*vaḥ*) forward (*ohate*).

The gods made him the Hotṛ of the sacrifice, the wise one, the bearer; Agni bestows treasure and heroic strength upon the person who worships and serves him. 12. Him | as the Hotṛ | of the sacrifice | the wise one | the bearer | the gods | made | he bestows | treasure | upon the worshiper | heroic strength | Agni | for the person | who gives. 12.
The gods made Agni the carrier of the sacrifice, the hotṛ-priest, and the one of supreme intelligence (pracetasaṃ).
To what end? It is said:

may that Agni bestow upon the person who serves him and offers oblations—a giver of sacrificial gifts—wealth that is delightful and endowed with excellent heroic power (suvīrya). This is the intended meaning.
The hymn beginning with “agne bhava susamidhā” consists of seven verses; it is the seventeenth hymn, composed by Vasiṣṭha, addressed to Agni.
All seven verses are *dvipadā-triṣṭubh*.
It is accordingly enumerated thus: “agne bhava: seven [verses], *dvipadā*, in the *triṣṭubh* meter.”
On the sixth day of the Atirātra, during the third pressing, in the Maitrāvaruṇa’s Śastra, the triplet beginning with “O Agni, be [our friend]” (agne bhava) is the anurūpa.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘O Agni, you are our closest [friend]’ and ‘O Agni, be well-kindled with good fuel’ are the stotriya and the anurūpa” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.2).
O Agni, be well-kindled with excellent fuel; and let the sacrificial grass be spread out widely for heroic deeds. || 1 ||
O Agni, being well-kindled with a beautiful fuel-stick, become fully inflamed;
and furthermore, let the Adhvaryu spread out the sacrificial grass (barhis) extensively.
And let the longing doors open wide; and bring hither the longing gods. 2. And let the longing doors open wide; and bring hither the longing gods. 2.
Moreover, let the doors—the divine ones of the sacrificial hall, desiring the gods—open wide;
for thus says Yāska: "The word *dvār* [is derived] from the root *ju*, or from *dru*, or from *vṛ*" (Nirukta 8.9).
Let them open wide.
And furthermore, bring hither to this sacrifice the gods who desire the sacrifice.
O Agni, partake of the oblation; worship the gods; perform well the sacrifice, O Jātavedas! 3. O Agni, partake; with the oblation, worship the gods; make the sacrifices successful, O Jātavedas! 3.
O Agni Jātavedas, whose wealth is born, go toward the gods; worship the gods with the oblation and perform the sacrifice;
and make the sacrifices beautiful.

May Jātavedas make the sacrifice well-performed; may he worship the immortal gods and offer them gifts. 4. May Jātavedas make the sacrifice well-performed; may he worship the immortal gods and offer them gifts. 4.
Let Agni Jātavedas—the knower of all beings, whose wealth is born—make the gods immortal, free from death, and perform excellent sacrifices (*svadhvarān*);
let him worship with oblations while consuming them, and let him also gladden them with hymns of praise.

Bestow upon us all desirable things, O wise one; may our prayers be fulfilled this day. 5. Bestow! All! Desirable things! O wise one! May our prayers be true! Today! 5. va̭sva | viśvā̭ | vāryā̭ṇi | pracḙtaḥ | satyā̭ | bhava̭ntu | ā॒śiṣa̭ḥ | naḥ | a॒dya || 5 || va̭sva | viśvā̭ | vāryā̭ṇi | pracḙtaḥ iti॒ pra'cḙtaḥ | satyā̭ | bhava̭ntu | ā॒śiṣa̭ḥ | naḥ | a॒dya ||5|| Grant us all things worthy of choice, O most wise one; let our aspirations be realized today. 5. Grant! All! Things to be desired! O highly intelligent one! Let [our] blessings be true! For us! Today! 5.
O Agni, most wise one of preeminent intellect, bestow upon us all desirable riches; grant them to us.
May our prayers today become true and according to the facts.

Thee indeed, O Agni, those gods have established as the bearer of oblations, the son of strength (ūrjaḥ). || 6 || Thee indeed, O Agni, those gods have established as the bearer of oblations, the son of strength. || 6 ||

The gods, those well-known deities, have established you alone as the bearer of the oblation—the one who carries the sacrificial offering—[you] the son of Vṛtra, the consumer of strength and power; for the term *sunu-napāt* is also listed among the names [of Agni]. You, indeed, they have established as the carrier of the oblation.
The meaning is "not doing."
May we be those who offer gifts to you, O God; bestowing great treasures upon us, do you distribute them as you are entreated.
O Agni, may we—the Vasiṣṭhas, well-known to you—be those who offer oblations to you, the radiant god.
Therefore, O Great One, being approached or entreated by us, do you bestow upon us great and delightful treasures. Grant them to us!
In the second anuvāka, there are sixteen hymns (*sūktas*).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of twenty-five verses beginning with "tve ha yat pitaraḥ," is composed by Vasiṣṭha, is in the *triṣṭubh* meter, and has Indra as its deity.
With the four verses beginning from the twenty-second, the gift of the king named Sudās is praised.
Therefore, they have those deities.
For it is stated in sequence: "In this [hymn], there are fifteen verses addressed to Indra; four others are praises of the gifts of Sudās Paijavana.
In the Mahāvrata rite, these fifteen verses are to be recited from the beginning.
Likewise, it is stated in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: "The fifteen [verses] beginning with 'tve ha yat pitaraś ca indra'. (AiĀ 5.2.2).

For in you alone, O Indra, our ancestors, even as singers, have found all desirable things; with you are the cows that yield milk well, and with you the horses; you are the most bountiful bestower of wealth upon the one who seeks the gods. In you indeed, O Indra, our ancestors, even as singers, have found all desirable things; with you are the cows that yield milk well, and with you the horses; you are the most bountiful bestower of wealth upon the one who seeks the gods.

O Indra, truly, all our fathers—even those who were our ancestors—were indeed your praisers and singers because, for that reason, they obtained all desirable riches (*vāmāni*). As Yāska says: "The word *vāma* means 'desirable'" (*Nirukta* 6.31). Dwell among us; therefore, we too, desiring wealth, praise you.
As it has been said:

For because of this reason, in you the cows are easy to milk; in you all things exist; and you are the most excellent giver (*vaniṣṭhaḥ*) to the sacrificer who desires you as a god, bestowing wealth (*vasu*) upon him.
1. Kha-bha read *prīyayati*. 2. Kha-bha read *haviṣām*. 3. Kha-bha do not have the word *ataḥ*. 4. Kha-bha do not have the word *dhanāni*. 5. Jha reads *sudānāmno*. 6. Jha reads *antyāścastro*.

For like a king with his subjects, like a dwelling with its days, you are the wise seer who knows all. O Maghavan, adorn our songs with cattle and horses; as one who seeks you, sharpen us for the sake of wealth. Like a king indeed, with his subjects; like a dwelling, truly, with its days; being a wise seer who knows all—O Maghavan, adorn our songs with cattle and horses; as one who seeks you, sharpen us for the sake of wealth.
O Indra, you dwell with your wives as with your people, like a king with his days, or like one who dwells with splendors;
"iva" and "hi" are particles used for emphasis.

Furthermore, O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, being wise, a seer, and one whose deeds or wisdom are far-reaching, protect us, the singers, from all sides with your forms, with gold and other riches, and with cattle and horses.
Sharpen us, who long for you and desire you, for the sake of wealth; and prepare us for the purpose of acquiring riches.

These joyful songs, contending here and seeking the gods, have approached you. May your broad wealth come hither; O Indra, may we abide in your favor and protection. imāḥ | ūm | tvā | paspṛdhānāsaḥ | atra | mandrāḥ | giraḥ | devayantīḥ | upa | sthuḥ | arvācīm | te | pṛthvī | rāyaḥ | etu | syāma | te | sumatau | indra | śarman || 3 ||

O Indra, these delightful and joyous songs of praise, proceeding toward you here at this sacrifice while competing with one another, wait upon you. Therefore, may the path of your wealth—the way to riches—come hither toward us. O Indra, may we abide in your favor, established in your excellent praise and within your protection, your auspicious shelter.

Like a cow in a field of good pasture, Vasiṣṭha has released his prayers toward you, the one who yields milk. All men call you my lord of cattle; may Indra come toward us with his favor. 4 dhenum | na | tvā | suyavase | dugdhan | upa | brahmāṇi | sasṛje | vasiṣṭhaḥ | tvām | it | me | gopatim | viśvaḥ | āha | ā | naḥ | indraḥ | sumatim | gantu | accha || 4 ||
O Indra, [we have milked] you who are present in the sacrificial hall where offerings are well-made, like a cow staying in a stall with excellent pasture and good grass;
by the force of the illustration, the application to the subject is obtained.
We have milked you as you abide there.
In the *saṃhitā*, the letter *da* occurs by way of metrical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
Desiring to milk out his desires, Vasiṣṭha has released—or releases—the *brahmans*, which stand in the place of calves, namely the hymns of praise.
All people, every single person, calls you alone, O Lord of Cows (*gopati*), the owner of cattle.
Now follows the indirect praise: May Indra come toward, that is, approach, our good thought—that is, our excellent hymn of praise.

Even the spreading floods Indra made shallow and easy to cross for Sudās; he, and no other, turned the curse of the rivers—the defiant Śimyu—into blessings for the sake of the noble man. *Arṇāṃsi cit prathānā sudāse indro gādhāny akṛṇot supārā | śardhantaṃ śimyum acarthasya nanyo śāpaṃ sindhūnām akṛṇod aśastīḥ || 5 ||* Even the spreading floods Indra made shallow and easy to cross for Sudās; he, and no other, turned the curse of the rivers—the defiant Śimyu—into blessings for the sake of the noble man.
1. O Khamakuru! 2. These [women] who desire you, the god—those who are *devayantīḥ*, desiring the gods.
(Ṛgveda 3.20)

Indra, worthy of praise from the center [of the sacrifice], made the waters of the Paruṣṇī—though they were being torn apart by enemies—into shallow fords for King Sudās, even though they were spreading out and swelling; he made them easy to cross and fit to be traversed. Furthermore, he rendered the defiant, harassing curse of Śiśu, arising from Viśvarūpa, as well as the invectives and imprecations of the singer Uvatha, into rivers.
Puroḷāsa was the offering for Turvaśa; the Matsyas were eager for wealth like fish in shallow water.
The Bhṛgus and Druhyus made their departure; a friend rescued his friend from the two who were hostile.

Puroḷāḥ, Turvaśa, and Yakṣu were there for the sake of wealth; like fish in a net, they were driven together. The Bhṛgus and the Duhyavas made their escape. The friend rescued his friend from the two who were spreading out. 6.
Yakṣu was skilled in sacrifice.
The suffix *san* is applied to the root *yaj*, but it is not a form ending in *san*;
therefore, there is no reduplication.
Puroḷāḥ is one who goes before, or perhaps one who offers first;
*in* is a filler particle;
there was a king named Turvaśa.

Turvaśa went for the sake of wealth and the acquisition of riches to Sudās, the friend of Indra. Like fish cast into water, even though they were sharpened and restrained, the Bhṛgus and the Duhyus—the warriors of Sudās and Turvaśa—brought about their swift arrival.
Between the two widely scattered peoples, Indra, the friend of Sudās, crossed over and delivered his friend Sudās.
The meaning is that he killed Turvaśa as well.
Or alternatively:
there was a king named Turvaśa who was *yakṣu*—meaning habitually performing sacrifices—and *puroḷāḥ*, meaning a giver of oblations.
Because of him, the Matsyas and the people of the Matsya kingdom were sharpened and oppressed;
yet the Bhṛgus and the Druhyus brought prosperity and happiness to Turvaśa.
Between Viṣpūcī and Viṣvagjana, both of whom were spreading abroad, Indra—friend of Turvaśa—acted as a friend and caused his royal comrade to cross over.
The Pakthas, Bhalānasas, Bhanuntas, Alinas, Viṣāṇins, and Śivasas have come;
he who brought the good man has driven the secret men of the Ārya by battle against the Tṛtsus.

The Pakthas, the Bhalānas, have broken; the Alinas, the Viṣāṇins, and the Śivas have broken. He who, as a leader, led the secret treasures of the Ārya to the Tṛtsus, has come through battle to the men.
The *pakthas* are the cooks who prepare the oblations; the *bhalānasas* are those with auspicious faces—*bhala* being a word signifying "auspicious";
the *alināsas* are those with bee-like noses.
The meaning is that they have not increased through austerities (*tapas*).
"Horned" (*viṣāṇinaḥ*) means having black antelope horns in their hands for the purpose of scratching;
the meaning is that they are consecrated (*dīkṣita*).

The *śivāsas* are auspicious; through sacrifice and other rites, they bring about the welfare (*śiva*) of the entire world, for by means of sacrifice the world attains well-being (*śiva*). The *ābhanantas* address that Indra.
He speaks; for he is included among those whose action is speech in the rule "he speaks, he sounds" (*bhanati*, *śabdakarmasu*).
Indra is the one who rejoices in the company of the good; he is called *sadhamāda* because he intoxicates himself together with the drinking of Soma.
The *sadhamā* are indeed those who rejoice together (*sadhamāda*).
He brought the secret herds of cattle from the *tṛtsus*, the violent ones, for the sake of the noble one whose conduct is virtuous.
He has come; he has truly come, and he himself obtained the herds of cattle.
And he slew those men, the enemies, by means of *yudh*—that is, by battle; this is the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).
From afar, the ill-minded and thoughtless ones, seeking their own welfare, have shattered the Paruṣṇī;
digging deep, they have dug up the earth, while the cattle lie scattered about as they are driven away.
1. *Gha*: deep, touching the bottom. 2.
*Kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*: possessing energy and pride.
3. *Kha*: sharpened and unrestrained; *jha*, *na*, *bha*: sharpened and not unrestrained; *ta*: sharpened and restrained.
4. The people are like fish in a pond; the country is like a fish in a pond.
5. [The vowels] from *jha* to *na*, *śa*, and *va* are the limiters. 6. They have increased by means of *gha*, *śa*, *ta*, and *pa*.
7. Kha, na, bha—more auspicious. 8. Kha, jha, ta, na, bha, śa; ‘anṛn’ does not exist.
Duḥ’ādhyaḥ. Aditim. Sevyantaḥ. Acetasaḥ. Vi. Jagṛbhe. Paruṣṇīm. Mahā. Avinyak. Pṛthivīm. Patyamānaḥ. Paśuḥ. Kaviḥ. Aśayat. Cāyamānaḥ. || 8 ||
The enemies of Sudās— evil-minded, harboring wicked intentions, senseless, and dull-witted— while resorting to the Aditi, the undepressed Paruṣṇī river, were caught in a conflict;
"vigraha" means the breaking of the bank,
and they brought that about.
The meaning is that they broke through the bank of the Paruṣṇī river.
That Sudās, by means of his greatness obtained through the great favor of Indra, pervaded the earth;
he was not, however, oppressed by the water.

Then Sudās’s enemy, Cayamāna—the son of Cayamāna—being a seer (Kavi) by name, fled; like a sacrificial animal consecrated for the rite, he lay down, he fell prostrate. The meaning is that he was slain by Sudās.

They went to their purpose, not to ruin, to the Paruṣṇī; even the swift one did not overtake him in his course. For Sudās, Indra subdued the well-impelling enemies, those of emasculated speech among men. They went to their purpose, not to ruin, to the Paruṣṇī; even the swift one did not overtake him in his course. For Sudās, Indra subdued the well-impelling enemies, those of emasculated speech among men.
Then Indra joined together the severed joints of the Paruṣṇī;
thereupon the waters of the Paruṣṇī flowed toward the downward slope as they had done before, and they reached their destination.
From the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going," with the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it, the form *īyuḥ* is derived in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
Therefore, this verb is transitive with two objects (*dvikarmaka*).
They went to the other side; they did not go toward the Paruṣṇī river, but toward the low-lying land situated on both banks of the Paruṣṇī.
Even the swift horse of King Sudās went straight toward the *abhipitva*, the place of slaughter.
And Indra [gave] to King Sudās in the world of men enemies who speak like eunuchs (*vadhrivācaḥ*), chatterers, and who are well-disposed toward [his] offspring (*sutukān* / *sutokān*).
Because "tuku tokam" is listed among the names for offspring; "arandhayat" means he brought [them] under his control.

They have gone forth like cattle from the pasture without a herdsman, gathering toward their friend as they were wont; with spotted cows, sent forth by the spotted one, the *niyut* teams and the *rantayaḥ* have performed their service. 10. They have gone forth; like cattle; from the pasture; without a herdsman; toward what was done; toward their friend; gathering together; with spotted cows; sent forth by the spotted one; they have performed; their service; the *niyut* teams; and the *rantayaḥ*. 10.

Just as Indra comes for the sake of protecting Sudās, then the *pṛśnigāvaḥ*— those whose spotted cows (or horses) are *pṛśnipreṣitāsaḥ*, sent forth by their mother Pṛśni, or thoroughly dispatched by her, being conscious and united— the Maruts, having transgressed that previous agreement made [with the thought], "Let us perform assistance for Indra according to his deed," [depart] from Indra, their friend, from the pasture (*yavasāt*). The fifth case ending is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*).
Taking the pasture as their sign, the cows—though without a cowherd and unguarded by herdsmen—came toward [the Maruts] like cows [to their stalls];
so too did the *rantayaḥ*, the delighting *niyutaḥ*, the horses of the Maruts.
They performed *śruṣṭi*, that is, they achieved swift arrival.
The meaning is that in that battle, the Maruts approached Indra for the purpose of providing assistance.
He who, as the commander of the Vaikarṇas, laid low one and twenty [foes] at a single hearing;
like a wild beast that does not spare the sacrificial grass, the hero Indra made a discharge of them.

1. Kha-bha-saḥ does not exist. 2. Kha-jha-ta-na-bha-śa is being protected. 3. Kha-gha-bha is a sloping region. 4. Kha is the form. 5. Kha-jha-ta-na-bha-śa is to be approached. One and also he who—thirty [men] of the two Vaikarṇas, the people, the king has laid low. Like a mower, he mows down the sacrificial grass; the hero Indra has made their release. ekaṃ ca yaḥ triṃśatiṃ ca śravasyā vaikarṇayoḥ janān rājā ni asto duṣmā na sabhraṃ ni śiśāti barhiḥ śūraḥ sargam akṛtot indra eṣām || 11 || And he who, for the sake of glory, the king laid low the thirty-one people of the two Vaikarṇas; like a mower, he mows down the sacrificial grass as if it were a cloud; the hero Indra has made their release.

The king who, out of a desire for renown, glory, or food, struck down twenty-one men belonging to the two neighboring peoples of the Vaikarṇas—those situated on the flanks—himself casting them down; that king was as wondrous to behold as a youthful Adhvaryu priest in the sacrificial hall when he spreads the *barhis* grass. In that battle where he utterly cuts down his rivals, the heroic Indra brought forth the onset, the mobilization, of these Maruts to provide assistance to Sudās.
Hearing half, making it whole, grown in the waters;
and for *duvoyu*, [the form] *duvoyuve* [occurs],
with the elision of the dative case ending.
For Sudās, who desires to serve him—
since the roots *namas* and *duvas* are listed among the verbs signifying acts of service— he "has laid himself down well" (*ni suṣupuḥ*), meaning he lies down completely.
The meaning is "slain.
These very deeds, all of them performed, are indeed the heroic exploits of Indra alone.

With Indra, these Tṛtsus, performing service, flowed downward like released waters. The ill-disposed enemies, measuring out their strength, abandoned all their provisions to Sudās. With Indra: these; the Tṛtsus; performing service; like waters; released; they flowed; downward. The ill-disposed; measuring out their power; they abandoned; all; their enjoyments; for Sudās. 15.
Sometimes protected by Indra, they are at other times oppressed by him.

These *Tṛtsus*, having evil friends (*durmitrāsaḥ*), being ignorant (*aprakalavit*), and though incited by Indra (*indreṇa veviṣāṇāḥ*) to come together for battle, were driven away and fled like downward-flowing waters (*nīcīr apo na*).
Then, being measured out and oppressed by Sudās, they abandoned all their enjoyments and wealth (*viśvāni bhojanā*) to King Sudās.

Indra cast down to the earth the defiant one who drank the cooked [soma] but was not Indra; he measured out his fury against those full of fury, and being the lord, he took possession of the paths and the tracks. 16. Half. Of the hero. Drinker of the cooked [soma]. Not-Indra. Away. The defiant one. He pushed down. Toward. The earth. Indra. His fury. Against those full of fury. He measured out. He took possession of. The paths. The track. Being the lord. 16. Half. Of the hero. Drinker of the cooked [soma]. Not-Indra. Away. The defiant one. He pushed down. Toward. The earth. Indra. His fury. Against those full of fury. He measured out. He took possession of. The paths. The track. Being the lord. 16.
"Indra [overcame] the earth— the ground; that is, upon the earth—
[the army] of Sudās, who was possessed of heroism, [and] his *ardha*, the one who harms."
The word *ardha* is derived from the root *hiṃs* (to injure) with the prefix *ā*.
"Anindram":
he in whose intellect Indra does not exist is "anindra"; [the word refers to] him.
The meaning is that he disregarded Indra.
He pushed back the one who is "śrutapāṃ"—the drinker of the "śruta," such as milk and other pressed juices (*vipas*)—and who is "śardhantaṃ," exerting himself with vigor.
Furthermore, regarding "manyumyaḥ," from the enemy who intends to act with wrath or who harms with wrath, he "mimāya," that is, he suppressed his "manyuṃ," his anger.
Then Sudās’s enemy, falling away from the paths—that is, traveling along them—resorted to, or reached, the path of flight on the road.

With a mere glance he made that one [his own]; with a mere bird he slew even the lion. Indra cut down the bonds of the courtesan; he bestowed all provisions for sustenance upon Sudās. 17. With a mere glance—indeed—he made that his own; with a mere bird he slew even the lion. He cut down the fetters of the courtesan; Indra bestowed all means of enjoyment upon Sudās. 17.
Indra then caused even Sudās, though he was *āghena*— that is, poor— to perform that one principal act of giving; indeed, like a lion,
for a lion is one who is full of vigor (*pravayas*).
He also killed—that is, caused to be killed—that goat by means of a *peṭu* (a small animal).
A *veśyā* is a prostitute; a *veśī* is a needle.
With that [power], he "cut down" (*ava-avṛścat*) the three sacrificial posts at their base;
the meaning is that he performed the task of a commoner and so forth as if with a mere needle.
These three deeds, though seemingly impossible, are not to be doubted in the case of Indra.

1. [The syllables] *kha*, *jña*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* are placed [therein]. 2. *Ta* and *na* do not obstruct. 3. Merchants (*vaṇijaḥ*) who know the *prakala*; Yāska says that a merchant is one who knows the *kala*, as well as the *kalā* and the *prakalā*. 4. [This applies] to one endowed with *kha*, *śa*, and *vīra*. 5. *Kha*, *gha*, *jña*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* signify "possessing energy" (*utsāhamānam*), because of the excellence of his greatness.
He bestowed and granted all (*viśvā*)—that is, all—the enjoyments (*bhojanā*), meaning objects of enjoyment, riches, to King Sudās.
For eternal enemies have indeed submitted; find the way to subdue even the defiant Bheda.
O Indra, strike with your thunderbolt against that mortal who does harm to the one who flows like a stream.

For your enemies have constantly yielded to you; find the weak point even of the defiant Bheda. Strike down with your thunderbolt, O Indra, that mortal who harms the innocent and wields a sharp weapon against us.

O Indra, those many and numerous enemies and adversaries of yours have always yielded; they have come under your control—even those who were defiant and arrogant. "Bheda" refers to one who breaks the boundaries of propriety; thus, "bheda" is a nihilist (*nāstika*).
Or rather, "Bheda" was a certain enemy of Sudāsa.
The meaning is "of him" (tasya).
O Randhi, find and obtain subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
Regarding that partisan who commits sin or evil against the mortals who praise you—against those very mortals who offer hymns—in him [is] the sharp, whetted warrior who incites others to battle.
And thus Yāska says: "Tigma [is derived] from the root *tij*, meaning 'to exert' or 'to incite' (Nirukta 10.6).
As for *vajra*: it is called *vajra* because it goes (*vajati*) toward the enemy and does not turn back.
To him.
The word *vajra* [is derived] from the root *vraj*; by the rule beginning with "ṛjendrāgravajravipra," it is established as a conventional form (*nipātita*) ending in the suffix *ran*.
"Destroy it! means "Strike it with a thunderbolt so that it is shattered."
The Tṛtsus, with their spirit uplifted, increased Indra; at dawn they overcame Bheda in every battle.
The Ajas, the Śigrus, and the Yakṣus brought tribute and offered up their own heads.

The Tṛtsus, with Indra at their head, turned back the assault; there, in the total conflict, they overcame Bheda. Both the Ajas and the Śigrus, as well as the Yakṣus, brought tribute and surrendered their heads. || 19 ||
In this very battle for total victory, Indra—who struck down Bheda, the nihilist or the one named Bheda, the enemy of Sudās—overcame him;
that is, he slew him. It was Yamunā who favored that Indra, meaning she gratified him.

The meaning is that all the people living on its banks satisfied [him]. Regarding the word *tṛtsavaḥ*: they heard of the men of Tṛtsu. The singular form *āvat* is here connected by being transformed into a plural form.
Furthermore, the Ajāsas are the Ajā people;
the Śigrus are the Śigru people, and the Yakṣus are the Yakṣu people;
and the *abhvyāni* are heads (*śīrṣāṇi*) belonging to horses.
The meaning is "the heads of horses slain in battle. They brought, that is, they offered, a tribute—an oblation—to that Indra.
Or alternatively:
The meaning is that they offered the heads of those slain in battle and the horses captured with their bridles as a sacrificial oblation to Indra.
Neither thy favors, O Indra, nor thy riches are to be fully perceived, like the many dawns of former times or those of now.
Having struck down even the god-like one who deemed himself great, thou didst shatter Śambara from his lofty height.

Not so, O Indra; those well-disposed intentions are not like riches, nor are the many dawns past and present equal for comparison. Having slain even the godlike Mānya, you swiftly shattered Śambara from his lofty fortress.
O Indra, those many ancient *sumatayaḥ* (benevolent thoughts) of yours, as well as the riches (*rāyaḥ*), are like the dawns; both the new *sumatayaḥ* and the riches are not for me to behold.
1. *gha-śa*: of one who is exerting effort. 2. *ya*: by that. 3. *kha-na-bha*: for strength. 4. *kha-jha-ta-na-bha-śa*: "na" is absent.
Furthermore, you yourself (*tmanā*) struck down—that is, you killed—the enemy Devaka, the son of Mānyamāna;
and from the great mountain (*bṛhataḥ śailāt*), you caused Śambara to fall.

Those who, led by Parāśara, Śatayātu, and Vasiṣṭha, have come forth from their homes to you with praise—they do not forget the friendship of Bhoja. May fair days dawn for these patrons. pra | ye | gṛhāt | armadamuḥ | tvā | parāśaraḥ | śatayātuḥ | vasiṣṭhaḥ | na | te | bhojasya | sakhyam | mṛṣante | adha | sūrībhyaḥ | sudinā | vi | ucchān || 21 ||

O Indra, Parāśara, Śatayātu, Bahurakṣas— the latter being one whom many desire to afflict with many *rakṣas* demons, or one who is the destroyer (*śātayitṛ*) of many *rakṣas*— Śakti, Vasiṣṭha, and other such sages, through their devotion to you (*tvāyā*), that is, by their desire for you, having reached house after house...
In the case of *lyap* and *lope*, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of the second case (*dvitīyārthe*). (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.28.1)
Or rather, "from house to house" (*gṛhād gṛhe*);
here the ablative case is used in the sense of the locative.

They—Parāśara and the others—have gladdened you (*pra amamaduḥ*), meaning they have thoroughly satisfied you. They do not forget (*na mṛṣante*) the friendship (*sakhyaṃ*) of you, the protector (*bhojasya pālakasya*), that is, the friend's duty, whether it be hymn-singing or sacrifice.
‘Mṛṣā marṣe’:
*marṣaṇa* means forbearance;
the meaning is that they do not practice it.
Because they do not forget this, for that reason, may auspicious days dawn—meaning they shine forth—for the wise ones, that is, for the wise ones who are the singers [of hymns].
Here there is a change of case endings (*vibhaktivyatyaya*). May they dwell [in these days].
The meaning is "they approach."

Two hundred horses, two chariots with brides—these were from Sudās, the grandson of Devavrata. Deserving the gift of Paijavana, I have come around, sitting like a Hotṛ-priest, chanting aloud. Two hundred, of the grandson, of Devavrata; two hundred, of cattle; two chariots, accompanied by brides, from Sudās. Deserving, at the forefront, the gift of Paijavana; like a seated Hotṛ-priest, I have gone around, chanting.

From King Sudās, the grandson of Devavat, the great-grandson of Paijavana, and the son of Pivana—two hundred cows accompanied by brides, and two chariots, as a gift to be given—I, Vasiṣṭha, worthy and fit, singing praises to Indra, approach the sacrificial hall like a Hotṛ priest through my beauty. Here, the address to Agni is for the purpose of establishing his preeminence among all the gods, and not for the purpose of indicating him as the deity of this hymn, which belongs to the *ahavattāka* class.

The four gifts of Paijavana, accompanied by well-offered oblations, [flow] for me alone; the straight-moving ones, established upon the earth, carry the offspring of Sudās for the sake of his progeny and for glory. 23. The four | mā (me) | paijavanasya (of Paijavana) | dānāḥ (gifts) | smadiṣṭayaḥ (with well-offered oblations) | kṛśininaḥ (belonging to Kṛśīnu) | nireke (for my exclusive possession) | ṛjāsaḥ (the straight-moving ones) | mā (me) | pṛthiviṣṭhāḥ (standing upon the earth) | sudāsaḥ (of Sudās) | tokam (offspring) | tokāya (for the sake of progeny) | śravase (for glory) | vahanti (they carry). 23.

The four horses—belonging to King Sudās, the son of Pijavana and grandson of Paijavana; urged by us, granted by his command, endowed with faith and the impulse for giving; adorned with golden ornaments, belonging to the Kr̥śinis; upright in their course, standing firm upon the earth, worthy of being given as gifts—carry me, Vasiṣṭha, who am like a child to be protected, seated upon the chariot, for the sake of my offspring (the fourth case used in the sense of the sixth), for the sake of fame, food, or sacrifice.
Furthermore, "mā" is a filler word.
1. Established in the space-like samādhi.

Whose fame lies between the two wide worlds (Heaven and Earth), who has distributed wealth head by head as a dispenser; him indeed, like Indra, the flowing rivers praise; he struck down Yudhyāmadhi in close combat. Whose fame lies between the two wide worlds—meaning his glory resides within the vast Heaven and Earth—and who, as a distributor, bestowed wealth head by head upon each most excellent person, that Sudās the people praise just as they praise Indra. Furthermore, the flowing rivers struck down the rival named Yudhyāmadhi in the encounter of battle.
As such, you are the bestower, the one who grants wealth to the people who perform the Soma-pressing with the greatest excellence.
Because it ends in a suffix marked with *tṛ*, there is an absence of the genitive case here.

Since the verb *asi* is unaccented (*anudātta*), it is impossible for it to be unaccented due to connection with a relative pronoun (*yadvṛtta*); therefore, a construction has been made by joining it with another verb ending in a suffix marked with *tṛ* that is connected with a relative pronoun.
O Indra, you indeed protected Kutsa, lending him your body as you listened in the battle; when you subdued the Dāsa Śuṣṇa for Ārjuneya Kurva, you were providing aid to him.
O Indra, you indeed protected Kutsa there; listening with your own body in the conflict, you subdued the Dāsa Śuṣṇa for him, bestowing favor upon the son of Arjuni.
O Indra, indeed it was you who then, with your own body, served and attended upon him for the sake of battle.

O wielder of the thunderbolt, those nine great deeds of yours—when you shattered the ninety-nine fortresses and shook them down at their dwelling place—you struck Vṛtra and Namuci as well. You slew them both. 5.
O Vajrahasta, such were those exploits and powers of yours:
that when you instantly and simultaneously shattered the ninety-nine cities of Śambara— this is the sense of the verse—
then you pervaded the hundredth city for the sake of entering it.
He slew Vṛtra,
and he also slew Namuci.
Everlasting are those enjoyments of yours, O Indra, for the liberal donor Sudās who offers oblations.
For you, the bull, I yoke the two bay steeds; may our prayers reach you, O most powerful one, and bring us strength.

O Indra, those enjoyments of yours have been eternal for the liberal donor Sudās, who has offered oblations. For you, the bull, I yoke the two vigorous bay steeds; may our sacred prayers reach you, O most powerful one, and attain strength. O Indra, O performer of many deeds, for you—the showerer of desires—those enjoyments and riches bestowed by you have indeed become eternal for the liberal donor Sudās, who has presented the oblation. O Indra, for you, the bull, I yoke the two vigorous bay horses to the chariot so that you may come. May our sacred hymns reach you, the mighty one, and attain strength.
O powerful Lord of the bay horses, let us not fall into your grasp or be delivered over to the wicked in this world;
protect us with your wolf-averting defenses, and may we remain dear to you among the patrons.

O powerful one, O possessor of bay horses, Indra, let us not be subject to harm or destruction in this search performed by us through our hymns; let us not fall into misfortune. Furthermore, protect us with your unassailable defenses—those protections which ward off calamities—and may we be dear to you among the patrons who offer praise.
O Maghavan, these men, your dear friends, shall indeed rejoice in your protection during the exhilaration of the Soma;
you, who are worthy of praise, will bring low Turvaśa and Yadu when you intend to perform a glorious deed for Atithigva.

O Maghavan, in your protection, may we men—your friends and beloved ones—rejoice indeed in your shelter. Subdue Turvaśa and Yadva; you shall perform a praiseworthy deed for Atithigva. O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, in that protection of yours, in your favor, may we men—the leaders of hymns, your friends and beloved ones—rejoice and be glad even within your very home. Furthermore, for Atithigva—for Sudās or Divodāsa, our king, whom one approaches as a guest—you shall perform a praiseworthy deed.
1. In the manuscripts kha, jha, ta, na, bha, and śa, the word "tā" is absent. 2. In manuscript kha, it reads "aghāya"; in gha, jha, ta, na, bha, and śa, it reads "aghāya ahantre.
3. In jha, ta, na, bha, and śa, it reads "vā madīyāya."
Bestowing praiseworthy happiness, while acting and performing [this], sharpen down King Turvaśa; bring him under control.
And as for the meaning of "sharpen down the king," it is as follows: [he should be brought under control].
O Maghavan, even now the men who recite hymns proclaim their praises for you to shatter;
those who, with their invocations, did not honor the Paṇis—choose us for that very alliance.
Even now, O Maghavan, men who recite hymns proclaim your praises at the place of assembly; those who, with their invocations, have scattered the Paṇis—choose us for that very alliance. ||9||

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, now indeed, for you— those men who are reciters of hymns (*uktha-śāsaḥ*), the chanters of *ukthas*, those who at once, even this very day, recite *ukthas*— that is, ritual hymns; furthermore,
by means of their invocations and praises, they have caused even the *paṇis*, the stingy merchants, to give away— that is, they have made them bestow wealth in abundance.
Choose us for that worthy friendship; accept us in order to follow after that which is capable of being endured together.
These hymns of men, O most heroic one, are for you; may they grant us riches that bring us aid.
For them, O Indra, be auspicious in the slaying of Vṛtra—be the friend, the hero, and the protector of these men.

These hymns of men, O most heroic one—O you who favor us, may they grant you riches. For them, O Indra, be auspicious in the slaying of Vṛtra; be the friend, the hero, and the protector of these men. 10.

O most heroic leader, O Indra, for you—those men who are leaders, these hymns of praise, these congregations, giving and bestowing great and worshipful oblations, have become turned toward us (as our protectors).
For those men, in the battle against Vṛtra, be auspicious, a bringer of welfare;
and be their friend.
He is the protector and the guardian of the earth.
Now, O heroic Indra, being praised for your aid, strengthened by our prayer, increase yourself in body.
Bestow upon us strengths and dwellings; protect us always with your blessings.

Now, O Indra, hero, being praised for your aid, impelled by our prayer, grow strong in your body. Bestow upon us strengths and bestow upon us heroes. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 11.
O heroic Indra, now being praised by us, being extolled, impelled by sacred prayer (*brahman*), urged on by our hymn of praise, increase yourself through your own body and through your protection;
furthermore, mete out to us, for our sake, strengths— that is, grant us food.
Measure out the three houses;
the rest is clear.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of the heart,
may Vidyātīrtha Maheśvara bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the second chapter of the Fifth Aṣṭaka in the Commentary on the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabuka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.
1. *Jha*: "The hero" (*śūraḥ*) means one endowed with valor, a protector (*avitā*).
2. *Kha*, *Jha*, *Ta*, *Na*, *Bha*, *Jhā*: the phrase "by protection" (*ūtyā rakṣaṇena*) is absent.
Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the third chapter begins.
The third hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “*ugro jajñe*,” is the *ṛṣi*-seer Vasiṣṭha’s composition; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and is addressed to Indra.
Thus it is enumerated: “*ugro daśa*” (ten verses on *ugra*).
On the fourth day of the Ābhiplavika period, this hymn is the Nivid-insertion place in the Niṣkevalya Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "For the fourth [day], 'ugro jajñe' is the Niṣkevalya" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).
This hymn is also [used] in the Niṣkevalya at the Mahāvrata.
Likewise, it is stated in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: "The fierce one, self-dependent, was born for valor; the Brahmins have risen up, desiring glory" (Ai. Ā. 5.2.2).
In the Soma-related Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the first Pṛṣṭhya day occurs in place of the Vaiśvadeva [parvan];
there too, this hymn is the locus for the Nivid in the Niṣkevalya [śastra].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘Thou hast been born fierce; the fierce one was born’—this is for the midday [pressing]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.2).
The self-reliant and fierce one was born for heroic power; he is the manly doer of deeds that he intends to perform.
The youthful Indra has come with his aids to the one who dwells among men; may he be our protector even from great sin.

The fierce one was born for heroic power, self-sustaining, capable, active, and manly; he who, intending to act, goes forth as a youth with his aids to the one who sits among men. Indra is our protector even from great sin. 1.
Indra—self-dependent, powerful, fierce, and full of vigor, or perhaps one who has raised himself up—was born (*jajñe*) for the sake of heroic deed (*vīryāya*), that is, to perform a heroic act.

Being beneficial to men (*naryaḥ*), whatever deed he was about to do, he performed that work (*apaḥ*) like a craftsman (*cakriḥ*). In the word *cakriḥ*, the suffix *kin* is used; because it is treated as an optative (*liṅvad-bhāvaḥ*), the genitive case is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām*.
Moreover, being ever-youthful, may he go to the sacrificial hall of Nṛṣadanta together with his protections; may he be our savior and protector even from great sin.
Slaying Vṛtra, Indra, hearing our call, has now protected the singer with his aid;
he is indeed the maker of space for Sudās and has repeatedly become the giver of wealth to the donor.

Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, hearing [our call], has come forward to aid us; may the hero now protect the singer with his help. Truly, he is the maker of space for Sudās; may he be the giver of wealth, ever present to the donor.
Indra, being strengthened and listening, becomes the slayer of the Asura Vṛtra.
In the case of "tubhyam tvā adya," there is an absence of the sixth case ending.
Being himself a hero, the hero has swiftly protected and continues to protect the singer, the praiser, with his aid— his saving help—
and he shall also create a realm, a settlement, for King Sudās.
Or alternatively:
And he becomes a creator of the world for Sudās, the sacrificer who bestows auspicious gifts.
In this case as well as in the subsequent one, there is an absence of the genitive case because [the word] belongs to you.
The three particles *ā*, *vā*, and *u* are used for filling the meter.

[O Indra,] you have repeatedly (*muhuḥ*) and ever more abundantly (*bhūyo bhūyaḥ*) become (*abhūta*) a giver (*dātā*) of wealth (*vasu*) to the donor (*dāśuṣe*), that is, the sacrificer (*yajamānāya*).
The particle *ā* is used in the sense of "and" (*ca*).
Armed with the mace, the stirrer of battle, the equaling one, the hero, the ever-conquering, invincible from birth—
Indra, self-powerful, has scattered the hostile armies and struck down every enemy.

The wielder of the mace, the follower, the stirrer of the battle-churn, the victor in combat, the hero, the ever-conquering—Indra, the subduer of all from his very birth, has spread himself abroad; he of mighty strength has struck down all those who raise up enemies in battle. 3.
1. *na-śa-atha* belongs to the fifth [class]. 2. *kha-jha-na-bha-śa* is there. 3. *kha-jha-bha-śa* is the *mādhyaṃdina*. 4. *jha-bhavati*.

*Vyudhmaḥ* means a warrior (*yoddhā*), one who does not retreat from battles, or one who acts as a champion (*vanarvā*). He is a maker of conflict (*vkhajakṛt*) or a maker of war (*yuddhakṛt*), because the word *khale khaje* is listed among the names for battle.
He is one who completely overcomes;
he is one for whom strife has been leveled.

Such a hero, endowed with valor, is by birth—by his very nature—a conqueror of many, one who is unsubdued by anyone himself, and one who is self-born with great strength. This Indra indeed scatters the armies of his enemies.
Moreover, he slew—that is, he kills—all that is hostile, namely, one who acts with enmity toward his enemies.
O Indra, you who are exceedingly powerful, you have indeed surpassed both worlds with your greatness;
the tawny-hued Indra, possessing the thunderbolt, has struck down [the enemy] with his strength, or he has uttered his roar in the exhilaration of the soma-draughts.

O Indra, you have filled the two worlds with your greatness; O mighty one, you have pervaded them with your powers. Indra, the lord of the bay horses, brandishing his thunderbolt, has uttered his voice in the exhilaration of the soma-juice.
O Indra, you who are most powerful, by your greatness (*mahitva*) and your vastness, and by your many forces (*tarvi*), you have filled both the *rodasī*—both heaven and earth.
Now follows a praise in the third person:

Indra, the possessor of bay horses (*hari-vān*), the possessor of steeds (*aśva-vān*), brandishing his thunderbolt (*vajram ni mimikṣan*) and directing it against the enemies, has spoken together with Soma during the exhilarations (*madeṣu*), at the sacrifices (*yajñeṣu*), or in the dwellings (*nivitsu*). He is united or comes into contact with it.
The verbal root is *uc* in the sense of "assemblage" (*samavāya*);
*vai* is an expletive.
The Bull has procreated the Bull for the sake of battle; even the woman has given birth to him, the manly one.
He who stands as the leader of armies for men, the unassailable warrior, the seeker of cattle—he is the bold one.

The bull has procreated the bull for the sake of battle; even the woman has given birth to him, the manly one. He who is the leader of armies, the lord over half of men, the powerful warrior seeking cattle—he is the bold one. ||5||

The bull, the sower, the father Kaśyapa, begot for battle—that is, for the sake of combat—the bull Indra, the showerer of desires. The verbal root *jan* means "to beget. Even the woman Aditi gave birth to that very same Indra, who is beneficial to men.

Moreover, Indra is the one who slays; he is the leader of men among men, the commander of armies, and as their guide, he prevails and exercises sovereign power. Indeed, Indra is the lord of the entire moving world—for the term *niyutvān inaḥ* is listed among the names for the Lord (*īśvara*).
Furthermore, he is the subduer of enemies, the seeker of cattle, and the bold one who overcomes his foes; this is the sense of the remaining words.
Never does that person falter, nor does he suffer loss, who seeks to win his formidable spirit;
he who offers worship with sacrifices and pays homage to Indra shall dwell in wealth—he who guards the Truth and is born of the Truth.

Never does that person stumble, nor does he falter in mind, who seeks to win his terrible power; he who, with sacrifices, offers worship to Indra—he, the protector of Truth and born of Truth, shall rule over wealth.
That person who, through sacrifices, seeks to win over the terrible mind of Indra—which is the subduer of enemies—serves him; that person indeed [is the one].
