*Nu* functions as a particle of negation (*pratiṣedha*);
*cit* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.
He does not falter at all, nor does he fall from his station;
he does not tremble, nor does he waste away.

Moreover, for that person who bestows—that is, deposits—praises and recitations (*stotra-śastra*), which are the means of service, upon Indra, for that person Indra—the protector of the rite (*vṛtapāḥ*), the drinker of the sacrifice, and the one born of the rite (*vṛtejāḥ*)—dwells and abides for the sake of the prize and for wealth.
The meaning is "it would be."
1. It perishes at Kha-Gha-Ta-Bha-Ya.

O Indra, if the elder, bestowing gifts, should give to the younger, let the immortal remain far away; bring to us wonderful, variegated wealth. yat | indra | pūrvaḥ | arpāya | śikṣan | aryan | jyāyān | kanīyasaḥ | deṣṇam | amṛtaḥ | it | pari | āsīta | dūram | ā | citram | cicyam | bhara | rayim | naḥ ||7|| If, O Indra, the elder, seeking to bestow, should grant a gift to the younger, let the immortal one indeed remain far off; bring to us wonderful, variegated wealth.
O Indra, that wonderful and praiseworthy wealth which a father, being the elder, or an elder brother, bestows as a gift upon a younger son;
for the root *śikṣ* is taught among the verbs meaning "to give" in the sense of "he gives" or "he pleases.
The word "it becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied [at the end of the sentence].
And whatever portion or wealth is due to the elder, may the senior obtain it from the junior.

Even if a son, having received wealth from his father, were to leave the father’s house and dwell far away as one who is truly immortal (*amṛta*), O wonderful Indra— O you, grant us sustenance and maintain us so that we may enjoy the food given by you yourself.
And those liberal patrons (*maghavant*) who, possessing oblations, themselves impel the offerings—that is, send them forth toward you—place them also in the nourishment (*iṣ*) that comes from you.
Moreover, let there be for me, your singer and praiser, power and capability (*śakti*) in the three most excellent hymns of praise;
or alternatively: [let there be power for me].
May that excellent and praiseworthy power of yours be manifest for me, your singer;
the rest is clear.
The fourth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “asāvi deva,” is the ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Indra.
Thus it is enumerated: “asāvi.
This hymn is recited by the Maitrāvaruṇa priest at the midday pressing while the soma is being poured.
Regarding the rule, “*asāvi devaṃ ihopayāte* at each pressing” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.5),

for the animal sacrifice of Indra Vṛtrahan, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*) is “*abhi katvendra bhūradha oṃstvaṃ mahā~ indra tumyaṃ ha kṣāḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8). This is also stated in the Sūtra.
The bull-strengthening Soma-juice has been pressed; Indra has taken pleasure in it from his very birth.
We awaken you with sacrifices, O Lord of the bay horses; awaken our hymn of praise in the exhilaration of the juice.

The Soma, the draught that wins the cattle, has been pressed for the god. By his very birth, Indra has taken pleasure in it. We awaken you with sacrifices, O Lord of the Bay Horses; take heed of our hymn in the exhilaration of the soma-juice.
The blazing god, *go-ṛjīka*— meaning refined with cows,
that is, mixed with products of the cow—
the food in the form of Soma, has been pressed (*asāvi*).
In this pressed soma-juice, Indra, by his very birth—by his inherent nature—is deeply attached; he remains closely united with it.
Now follows a direct praise:
O Lord of the bay horses (Haryaśva), we awaken you with sacrifices, with hymns, or with oblations.
And in the exhilarations of the pressed soma, be mindful of our hymn of praise; awaken to it.
They go forward to the sacrifice; they spread the sacrificial grass; at the beginning of the assembly, those of fierce speech take hold of the Soma.
The glorious, far-resounding, bull-like heroes are brought down from their grasp for the protection of men.

They go forth to the sacrifice; they spread the sacred grass at the beginning of the Soma rite, shouting loudly in the assembly. The glorious ones, the bulls who protect men, take their place from afar, holding fast with a firm grasp.

The sacrificers go forth to the sacrifice and spread out the sacrificial grass (barhis)—*vipi* being a word for the act of spreading. At the *vidatha*, that is, at the sacrifice, the Soma-drinking pressing-stones (*prāvāṇaḥ*) become "loud-voiced" (*dudhravācaḥ*), meaning their voices are difficult to restrain. Moreover, they are glorious (*yaśasaḥ*), possessing renown, and "far-resounding" (*dūraupabdaḥ*), meaning those whose sound is heard from afar. They are "protectors of men" (*nṛpācaḥ*); because they accompany the priests (*nṛ* = priests), they are called *nṛpācaḥ*. The "bulls," the pressing-stones, are held fast (*gṛbhāt*)—that is, from the house; for the pressing-stone is within the house. From there (*ā* being used in the sense of "from"), they are fixed down (*ni dhriyante*), held firmly at the time of the libation. The particle *u* is a filler.
O Indra, you, the hero, have set free the many waters that were obstructed by the serpent;
at your roar, O charioteer, all artificial fortifications tremble in fear like lowing cows.

O Indra, you must release the waters; O Hero, you shall make the many rivers that were obstructed by the serpent flow again. At your roar, all artificial fortifications tremble with fear, like cows fleeing from a chariot.
1. The Jha-hymn.
And it is stated in the Sūtra:
2. "The Jha-cup belongs to the Madhyamagrāvan; or, the Śa-cup belongs to the Madhyamagrāma."
O heroic Indra, you made the many ancient waters flow forth to stream—that which had been obstructed and overwhelmed by the serpent Vṛtra.
And the rivers, like chariot-drivers on their way, have come forth from you; for "vavrre" means they have emerged, according to the root *vaki* in the sense of "to go crookedly."
All beings, every single one created by artifice, tremble and shake out of fear of you.
Bhīma has clothed himself in their weapons; he, the knower, knows all their manly deeds.
Indra, exulting, shattered their fortresses; with thunderbolt in hand, he struck them down by his greatness.
Bhīma has pervaded their deeds with his weapons; "he has not pervaded" means he has encompassed all their labors. (Maṇḍala 7, Anuvāka 2, Sūkta 21) Fifth Aṣṭaka, 321.
For with your own inherent power and strength, you indeed struck down Vṛtra;
and your enemy, through battle, could not find or obtain an end—that is, an injury—to you.
The ancient gods fashioned powers for thee, O Asura, for dominion and for strength.
Indra distributes riches to the people; they invoke Indra at the winning of booty.
Even the ancient gods measured out their powers for your divine dominion; Indra, the subduer, distributes riches. They call upon Indra repeatedly for the winning of booty.
Even the ancient gods, the Asuras, [struggled] for *asurya*—that is, for power (*bala*) and for dominion (*kṣatra*).
The root *kṣad* has the sense of injury;
thus, the meaning is that they desired to perform both power and injury.
O Indra, they have measured themselves after (*anu*) your powers (*sahāṃsi*), that is, your strengths.
By the rule *hīne* (Pāṇini 1.4.86), *anu* is a *karmapravacanīya*.
The meaning is: "they measured themselves as inferior to your strengths."
And so says another Vedic verse: "The great heaven has measured up to your heroic power" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.57.5).
Now follows the indirect praise:
Indra, having struck down his enemies, bestows—that is, grants to his devotees—the *maghāni*, the great and venerable riches.
Moreover, the singers invoke or praise Indra for the sake of winning, that is, obtaining, booty—that is, food.
For even a lowly man has indeed invoked you for protection, O Indra, the ruler of abundant prosperity.
You have become a helper to this man, O lord of a hundred aids; you are the protector of one who praises you.

For indeed, the singer has invoked you for protection, O Indra, you who are the lord of abundant prosperity. You have become a protector for this man of a hundred aids; you are the defender of one like you who overcomes his enemies. 8.
O Indra, the singer—
the term *kīriḥ* being listed among the names for a praiser in the glossary of hymns (*stotra-nāmasu*) as synonymous with *kāruḥ*—
namely Vasiṣṭha, has indeed invoked you, the sovereign lord, for protection; that is, he praises you or implores you.
The particle *cit* is a filler.

Furthermore, O *śatamūti*, you who possess many protections, O Indra, you have become (*babhūtha*) the protector (*acaḥ*)—that is, the guardian—of our abundant (*bhūreḥ*) good fortune (*saubhagasya*), that is, of wealth. And be the warder-off (*varūtā*) of one like you (*tvāvataḥ*), of an assailant (*abhikṣattuḥ*).
O Indra, may we be your friends forever, increasing our reverence through your greatness, O Deliverer.
May they indeed overcome the hostilities of the enemy in battle by your protection; may they subdue the strength of those who desire to conquer us.

O Indra, may we always be your friends, increasing your glory through our homage, O Deliverer! May we, by your protection, prevail in the encounter against the onset of the enemy and the strength of those who strive against us.
O Indra, may we—your increasers through homage (*namas*), through praise, or through oblation—be your friends forever, at all times.
O Deliverer, by your greatness, through your protection, in the encounter of battle, let the singers overcome the assault of the enemy and the strength of the assailants.
1. He is the protector. RV 3.21.10:

O Indra, grant us that strengthening food which comes swiftly, and those wealthy patrons who urge us on. May there be a powerful and effective strength for your singer; protect us always with your blessings. He, O Indra, bestow upon us that food which comes quickly, and [those] bountiful ones who themselves incite us. May your power be truly effective for your singer; do you all protect us evermore with your auspicious blessings.
This [verse] has already been explained in the section on the seasons (*ṛtu*).

"Drink the Soma, O Indra; let it exhilarate you"—this is the fifth hymn, consisting of nine verses. It is enumerated thus: "Piba [is the first]; nine verses; in the Vairāja meter; except for the last [verse]. The seer is Vasiṣṭha.
The first eight verses are *virāj*, the ninth is *triṣṭubh*.
Indra is the deity.
In the *niṣkevalya* śastra on the fourth day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), the six verses beginning with "Drink the soma, O Indra" constitute the *stotriya* and *anurūpa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “If the *pṛṣṭha* is the *vairāja*, then ‘pibā somam indra mandatu tvā’ constitutes the six *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.11).
In the *mahāvrata* as well, the first six [verses] belong to the *niṣkevalya*. And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘pibā somam indra mandatu tvā’, etc., are the six” (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5.3.1).
The first [verse] is the *yājyā* for the *niṣkevalya-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Drink the Soma, O Indra; let it exhilarate thee’ is the *yājyā*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.15).

On the fourth day, during the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), among the recitations of the *hotraka* priests, seven *virāj* verses are to be formed into three-verse hymns (*ṛcas*), and each such *ṛca* is to be recited.
In that context, there are four ṛcs beginning with "na te giraḥ.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "na te giro api mapye turasya pra vo mahe mahivṛdhe bharadhvam" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.11).

Drink the Soma, O Indra; let it exhilarate you—the Soma which the stone, pressed by the arms of the presser, has well-poured for you like a well-guided steed by its reins. Drink the Soma, O Indra; let it exhilarate you. O Lord of the Bay Horses (Haryaśva), that Soma which the stone—well-guided by the arms of the presser like a horse by its reins—has well-poured for you.

That exhilarating draught of yours which is worthy of union and beautiful, by which you, O Lord of the Bay Horses, slay the Vṛtras—that, O Indra, Lord of abundant wealth, may it intoxicate you! That exhilarating draught of yours which is worthy of union and beautiful, by which you, O Lord of the Bay Horses, slay the Vṛtras—that, O Indra, Lord of abundant wealth, may it intoxicate you! O Lord of the Bay Horses, that exhilarating draught of yours which is worthy of union, beautiful, and excellent—existent as a soma that causes intoxication—and by drinking which you slay the Vṛtras, O Indra, Lord of abundant wealth, may that soma intoxicate you!
O Maghavan, graciously accept this hymn of praise which Vasiṣṭha recites for you;
enjoy these sacred prayers at our common feast.
There is no one like Kha-ta-na-bha-jñā-yaḥ.
O Bountiful One, understand this speech of mine well; this hymn of praise which Vasiṣṭha recites for you—O you who drink the sweet Soma, graciously accept these prayers. 3.

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, that speech which Vasiṣṭha utters as praise for you—be well-attentive to this word of mine belonging to Vasiṣṭha; understand it thoroughly. Furthermore, graciously accept and enjoy these sacred prayers (brahmāṇi) at the communal feast of the sacrifice.
Hear the call of the one who has drunk deeply from the stone; take note of the prayer of the inspired singer who offers praise. Accept these most intimate acts of devotion and be present with them.
Hear the call of the pressing-stone as it crushes; take notice of the inspired singer’s hymn of praise. Accept these offerings most intimately; be present here with them.
O Indra, hear my call—the invocation from the pressing-stone and the pressing-presser who has drunk deeply and is exhilarated by the soma.
And thus another Vedic passage says: "O eloquent one, speak your word to the pressing-stones" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.94.1).
Furthermore, take note of and understand the prayerful hymn of the wise Vasiṣṭha as he offers praise.
These very deeds and services being performed—those that are most ultimate and most proximate, present before the mind—do thou perform them together with me, acting as my companion.
I do not forget the songs of you, the swift one, nor the well-spoken praise of you, O Sūrya; knowing them, I ever proclaim your name, which is its own glory.
No, I do not forget those words of the swift one, nor his well-spoken praise; being wise, I ever proclaim your name, O self-glorious Asura. 5.

O Indra, knowing your power—your divine strength (*asurya*) which destroys enemies—I do not forget your songs of praise. (The genitive case *te* is used in the sense of the accusative; thus, "I do not forget your divine power.")
The activity of cleansing the sage means:
"I do not cleanse," which signifies that I do not abandon [it].
Nor do I tolerate even a beautiful hymn of praise (*suṣṭuti*).
Here, the root *mṛṣ* is seen to have the sense of "rubbing away" or "cleansing," as for example in: "O Agni, do not rub away our forms like oil-cakes" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.71.10).
But I always speak—that is, I utter—the hymn of praise for your own name, which is your unique glory.
For great indeed is your healing power among men; the wise one calls upon you abundantly. O Maghavan, do not let our life-span be shortened.
For abundant indeed is your wealth among men; as one rich in wisdom, he invokes you alone. O Maghavan, do not keep us far away from this for long. 6.
O Maghavan, your pressings—your many, numerous soma-pressings—abound among us humans; this is the sense of the remainder.
The wise singer calls upon you alone, repeatedly invoking and praising you.
Therefore, do not make yourself distant from us for a long time.
Quickly make yourself our servant; this is the purpose.

For you alone, O Hero, are all these libations; for you I perform the strengthening prayers. You are to be invoked in every way by men with their offerings. (7) O Hero, for you alone are all these libations (*savana*)—the pressing of Soma—[performed] by me; this is the sense. For you alone do I perform the strengthening prayers (*brahmāṇi*), the hymns of praise that cause increase. You alone are to be invoked (*havyaḥ*)—to be summoned or praised—in every way (*viśvadhā*) by men (*nṛbhiḥ*), the leaders of the sacrifices. (7)

Never indeed, O fierce Indra, do they reach the limit of your greatness as you are being praised; nor your heroic power, O Indra, nor your bounty. Never indeed, never indeed—O fierce one, as you are being praised, no one at all reaches the limit of your greatness, O powerful one; neither your heroism, O Indra, nor your wealth. O beautiful one, as you are being praised, no one ever quickly reaches the limit of your greatness; O fierce one, they do not reach your wealth.

Those seers of old and those who are new, O Indra—the wise ones who have generated sacred hymns—may your auspicious friendships be with us. And may you all protect us always with blessings. (9) Those seers of old and those who are new—the wise ones who have generated sacred hymns—may your auspicious friendships be with us. The rest is clear.
The sixth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “udu brahmāṇi,” is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is dedicated to Indra.
It is cataloged as “udu pad.
This hymn is recited by the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest during the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana) at the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Udu brahmāṇy ujjīṣī vajrī vṛṣabhas turāpāḷ* is the *yājyā* mantra” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 5.16).
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), this hymn is recited by the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest; it is known as the daily-recitation hymn (*aharahaḥśasya*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Udu brahmāṇy abhi taṣṭeva* and so forth are the two daily-recitation hymns” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.4).
This very hymn is used on the second and subsequent days of the *ahargaṇa* sacrifices;
it is also used as the *niṣkevalya* hymn at the *mahāvrata*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘udu brahmāṇi’, ‘eta śravasyā’, ‘te maha indrotyudyu’—these are the five hymns” (Ai. Ā. 5.2.2).

O Vasiṣṭha, come forth with your sacred prayers for the sake of glory; magnify Indra in the great battle. He who by his might overcomes all those [enemies] shall listen to my piercing words. ut | ūm iti | brahmāṇi | aitā | śravasyā | indram | sumūrye | mahaya | vasiṣṭha | ā | yaḥ | viśvāni | śavasā | tān | upaśrotā | me | īrvataḥ | vacāṃsi || 1 ||
With the desire for renown, through prayer, hymns, and oblations, all paths have been opened for Indra;
*vu* is a filler particle.
O Vasiṣṭha, you too, in this sacrificial assembly, magnify Indra with praise and with the offering.

Moreover, may Indra, who by his power (*vīśvasā*) or strength (*balena*) has pervaded (*vyatāna*) all beings (*viśvāni bhuvanāni*), listen attentively (*upaśrotā bhavatu*) to my words (*vacāṃsi*)—these utterances in the form of hymns (*stuti-rūpāṇi vākyāni*) that approach him from all sides (*vīvataḥ*).
The cry has gone forth, O Indra, born of the gods, as the bounties rise up in the contest for praise.
No one among men perceives his own life-span; may you carry us across these days.

I have come. O Indra, kinsman of the gods, when you rule over the spoils in the conflict, do not hide your own life-span from among the people; for those very sins, carry us across. ghoṣaḥ | indra | deva-jāmiḥ | irajyanta | yat | śurudhaḥ | vi-vāci | mā | nuhi | svam | āyuḥ | cikite | janeṣu | tāni | it | aṃhasi | ati | parṣi | asmān ||2||
When the *śurudhaḥ*—
the plants so called because they "obstruct suffering" (*śucaṃ rudhanti*)—
are distinguished and flourish, then, O Indra, for your sake, among the singers of praise, there arises a cry that is kin to the gods (*devajāmi*), a bond of the gods (*devānāṃ bandhuḥ*).
Sound is the resonance in the form of praise;
it has been produced.
Furthermore, among living beings, no one knows—nor is it perceived—what their own lifespan or their own life truly is.
Whatever sins have been committed by us, all those you indeed carry away; O Vāyu, protect us and carry us across.
I have yoked the two bay steeds to the chariot that seeks cattle; my prayers have reached him who delights in them.
Indra, having struck down the Vritras without opposition, has forced apart these two worlds by his greatness.

I yoke the gold-hued chariot with the two bay horses; my prayers have reached him who delights in them. Indra, having struck down the Vritras without opposition, has forced asunder those two worlds by his greatness. ||3||
I yoke with hymns the two bay steeds, Indra’s carriers, for the purpose of seeking out and bringing the cattle, and for the sake of the slow-moving [Indra].
The prayers and praises approached Indra, who delights in them and is served by his attendants.
By his greatness, this very Indra has pervaded and filled the two worlds, heaven and earth.
Moreover, O Indra, you have struck down—that is, slain—the Vṛtras, the enemies who were without rival.
Seeking you with songs like lowing cows, your singers have approached the sacred Law, O Indra. Come toward us as Vāyu comes with his teams; for by your insights you distribute spoils of war.

Like a swift arrow, like a cow longing for her calf, let our singers reach the sacred Law (*ṛta*). O Indra, come toward us as Vāyu comes with his teams; for through our prayers you distribute spoils of war. 4.
O Indra, by your own grace, may these waters, these barren cows, these barren female goats, and these barren female cattle increase.
Indeed, the cows that have not yet calved become well-fleshed.
May those singers and praisers of yours reach—that is, pervade—the chosen water.
Moreover, you are like Vāyu; like Vāyu, drive us forward and advance.
For through your insights—whether by wisdom or by deeds—you distribute and bestow food and strength upon those who praise you.

1. *Jha*: they have impelled [thee]. 2. *Ta*: he has pervaded. 3. *Ta-na-bha-śa*: thy own life. 4. *Kha-bha*: Indra, who is to be served. 5. *Kha*: those without rivals; *Jha*: those without rivals; *Na-bha*: thus the pairs.
May those exhilarating draughts, O Indra, intoxicate thee—the powerful one, the giver of much bounty—for the singer.
For thou alone among the gods hast compassion for mortals; O Hero, rejoice at this libation!

O Indra, let these exhilarating draughts intoxicate you, the impetuous one who bestows abundant wealth upon the singer; for alone among the gods you take pity on mortals. O Hero, rejoice yourself at this libation!
O Indra, may these exhilarating Soma juices, which intoxicate, gladden you.
Furthermore, [he] bestows upon the singer—the one who praises—a powerful son, one who is mighty and possesses abundant wealth; this is the ellipsis.
O Hero, for you alone among the gods (devatrā) show compassion toward mortals (martyān).
The root *day* has the sense of compassion.
"Rejoice in this libation, in this sacrifice!
Thus do the Vasiṣṭhas honor Indra, the bull whose arm wields the thunderbolt, with their hymns.
May he, being praised by us, grant us wealth consisting of heroes and cattle; protect us always with your blessings. 6.

Thus indeed do the Vasiṣṭhas praise with hymns Indra, the bull, whose arm wields the thunderbolt. May he, being praised by us, grant us wealth consisting of heroes and cattle; protect us always with your blessings. 6.

The most excellent ones, the Vasiṣṭhas, with hymns worthy of praise—songs that are to be honored—worship and glorify Indra, who has arms like a thunderbolt, whose arms are like the thunderbolt itself, and who is the showerer of desires.
Thus praised, may that Indra bestow upon us wealth consisting of heroes, such as sons, and wealth consisting of cattle;
the rest is clear.
The seventh hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "yoniṣṭa indra sadane akāri," is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Indra.
It is cataloged as "yoniḥ."
This hymn is recited at the Niṣkevalya of the Mahāvrata.

"A seat has been prepared for thee, O Indra; come hither to it, O thou who art much-invoked, accompanied by the heroes."

O Puruhūta, come hither to that seat together with the Maruts,
so that you may be our protector and our strengthener for our prosperity.
And so: "O Vasu, give us wealth; grant it to us!
Rejoice with our Soma offerings and gladden yourself!
O Indra of double strength, your mind has been captured; the Soma is pressed and the sweet juices are poured out."
The well-fashioned hymn, accompanied by the released voice, brings [the gift] to him whom the inspired thought repeatedly invokes—Indra.

O Indra, of double might, your mind has been captured by us; the Soma has been pressed, and the sweet juices have been poured out into the vessels. This hymn of praise, uttered with a released tongue and a melodious voice, bearing a perfect conclusion, brings forth Indra, calling upon him repeatedly. O Indra, of double might—the first case used here in the sense of the genitive—your mind, belonging to you who are powerful in both places, has been seized by us. And the Soma has been pressed; and the sweet juices have been poured out into the cups. This hymn of praise, with its released tongue—meaning uttered in the middle register—and its beautiful completion, bringing forth Indra, calling upon him intensely, is being brought forward.

From heaven and from earth, O possessor of the *ṛjīṣa*, come to this sacred grass (*barhis*) for the drinking of Soma. Let your bay horses carry you toward the exhilarating draught, toward the *āṅgūṣa* hymn, toward the powerful one, for the sake of intoxication. O Indra, O possessor of the *ṛjīṣa*, come from heaven—our [heaven]—and from earth (the intermediate space, as "earth" is listed among the names for the intermediate space), come to this sacred grass, that is, to this sacrifice, for the drinking of Soma. Furthermore, let your bay horses carry you toward the powerful one, who is increasing or strong, who is directed toward the exhilaration, toward the *āṅgūṣa* hymn, for the sake of intoxication.

Crushing the enemies intensely with your steadfast [days], O fair-cheeked one, granting us a virile, powerful son, and enjoying our prayer, come to us!

1. Regarding the two places of *śa*: likewise, the *Nighaṇṭu* states, "The word *parivṛḍha* occurs in the middle place and the highest place" (*Nighaṇṭu* 6.17). 2. *Śa-prayacchaṃs tvam*.
Thus, O Indra, fill us with what is desirable; may we find for you great favor.
Swell the nourishment rich in heroes for our patrons; and do you all protect us always with blessings.
Thus, O Indra, fill us with what is desirable. May we find for ourselves your great favor. Send down nourishment rich in heroes upon our patrons. Do you all protect us always with blessings. 6.
O Indra, thus indeed, with such desirable wealth— the genitive case here used in the sense of the instrumental— fill us, satisfy us.
We thoroughly obtain—that is, we may fully receive—your great and excellent favor, your benevolent intention.
For us, who are like Maghavans (givers) possessing oblations, swell—that is, bestow—the nourishment (*iṣ*) consisting of excellent sons and other blessings.
The rest is clear.
The eighth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "ā te maha indra," is the seer Vasiṣṭha’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Indra.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry "ā te.
In the Niṣkevalya section of the Mahāvrata rite, these five hymns beginning with this one are recited.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘Ā te maha indrotyum’ and so forth constitute five hymns” (Ai. Ā. 5.2.2).
Hither toward thee, O Great Indra, let the fierce hosts, sharing one common purpose, advance together when they encounter;
let the lightning of the hero fall upon the strength of the foe, and let not thy all-seeing mind stray elsewhere.
Come to us with your great aid, O mighty Indra, for when the armies of equal fury clash together, the lightning shall fall from the arms of the hero; let not your all-seeing mind wander elsewhere.
O fierce, preeminent, and powerful Indra! When—
those armies whose minds are unified (samanyavaḥ)—
meet, fight, or encounter one another, then the double-flash of weapons stands within the two arms of you, the great one, who belongs to men (narya).
Because "the double-edged weapon" (*dvidyut heti*) is listed among the names of the thunderbolt (*vajra*), may it fly hither for our protection (*ūtī ūthai*).
And let your all-seeing mind (*viśvadṛk manaḥ*) not wander away; may it remain firm within this field.
O Indra, loosen our enemies in their strongholds—those mortals who assail us. Drive far away the curse of the reviler; bring to us the gathered wealth of those who are bound.
O Indra, loosen our enemies in their distress—those mortals who assail us. Drive far away the curse of the reviler; bring to us an abundance of riches! 2.
O Indra, those mortals who, facing us in a difficult battle, assail and overcome us—bind fast and slay those enemies and foes.
Furthermore, cast far away the praise and the hope of the man who desires to revile us.
Moreover, bring to us the gathering and accumulation of riches and treasures.
A hundred are your forms, O Śipiviṣṭa; let there be a thousand praises for Sudās, and let there be delight.
Strike down the increasing hostility of the mortal; bestow upon us resplendent wealth and treasure.
1. They gather for battle with the *jha*; they gather for battle with the *ta* and *śa*. 2.
O Śiprin, a hundred aids are yours, and a thousand blessings for Sudās; let there also be bounty. Strike down the weapon of the mortal who seeks to harm us; bestow upon us splendor and wealth. (3)
O Indra, may those hundred of your many protections— those who wear turbans and head-coverings— be for my sake, for Sudās of noble gifts;
may there be a thousand praiseworthy desires,
and furthermore, let there be wealth as a gift.
Slay the forest-dwelling assailant, the mortal, and his weapon—the instrument of violence.
Furthermore, bestow upon us (asme adhi) resplendent food, glory, or treasure.
Thus Yāska says: "Dyumna is derived from the root *dyut* (to shine); it is either glory or food."
"Bestow upon us splendor and treasure;
bestow upon us both splendor and treasure" (Nirukta 5.5).
O Indra, I am yours for the sake of wisdom; O Hero, I am yours for the gift of the Protector.
O Mighty One, fierce with power throughout all days, display your strength, O Lord of Bay Horses, and do not neglect us.

For I am yours for the sake of wisdom, O Indra; I am yours for the sake of protection, O Hero, at the time of your bounty. O Lord of power, O Fierce One, throughout all days, O Lord of the bay horses, manifest your strength and do not neglect us.
O Indra, I am indeed present for the sake of the wisdom and the action of one such as you, equal to you;
O Hero, protector and guardian of all, I am likewise present for the granting and the giving of one such as you, equal to you.
O powerful, fierce, and mighty Indra, make our dwelling-place—our very home—for all days.
O Lord of the bay steeds, O possessor of bay steeds, do not neglect us; do not harm us.
These songs of praise go forth to the bay-horsed Indra for strength and victory, impelled by the gods.
O Hero, make the enemies easy to slay; may we, as conquerors, win the prize.

These Kutsas have come seeking strength and conquering power from Indra, the lord of bay horses, impelled by the gods. O Hero, make our enemies easy to slay; may we, as conquerors, win the prize. ||5||

We, the Vasiṣṭhas—known as Kutsas—performing a strengthening hymn that brings happiness for Indra, whose horses are bay (haryaśva), [we do so] while seeking from Indra a conquering force impelled by the gods; having crossed over difficulties, may we win and obtain strength (*vāja*). (Note on etymology: the word *kutsāḥ* is derived from the root *karoti* [to do/make]). (Note on etymology: the word *tarutrāḥ* means those who have crossed over [difficulties]).
Moreover, O Hero, make the Vṛtras—the enemies—always easy to slay; that is, make them always capable of being killed.
Thus, O Indra, grant us a portion of the strengthening food; may we find for you great favor.
Swell the nourishment rich in heroes for our patrons; and do you all protect us ever with blessings.

Thus, O Indra, grant us a portion of the *vāyrya* draught. May we find for ourselves your great favor. Cause nourishment rich in heroes to swell for our patrons. Do you all protect us always with blessings. 6.
This has already been explained.
‘Na soma indram’ is the fifth hymn, the ninth [in the collection], composed by Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and addressed to Indra.
Thus it is enumerated: ‘Na somaḥ pañca’.
Its application (viniyoga) has been stated for the Mahāvrata rite.

1. O Indra, the unpressed *soma* has not exhilarated you; nor have the pressed juices, though sweet, exhilarated the Bounteous Lord (*maghavan*) who is without prayer (*abrahmaṇaḥ*). For him I generate a hymn (*uktha*) which he may enjoy—a newer one, like that of men—so that he may hear us. 1. Not the *soma*, when unpressed, has exhilarated Indra; nor have the pressed juices [exhilarated] the Bounteous Lord who is without prayer. For him I generate a hymn which he may enjoy—a newer one, like that of men—so that he may hear us.

The unpressed Soma, not pressed [properly], has not exhilarated nor satisfied Indra, the possessor of wealth (Maghavan). Even the pressed and well-pressed Somas have not exhilarated one who lacks *brahman*—that is, one devoid of hymns of praise.
The verb "has exhilarated" (*mamāda*), having been modified from its singular form into a plural ending, is connected here [to the subject].
For this very reason, at all three pressings (*savana*), only those *soma* juices that have been praised with the *pāvamāna* hymns are offered.

Furthermore, so that Indra may enjoy (*jujoṣat*) our own hymn (*uktha*) and listen to it with care, like a king among men (*nṛvat*), I generate—that is, I recite—for that Indra a newer, more recent hymn, a liturgical chant (*śastra*). This is the meaning.

At every hymn, Soma has exhilarated Indra; at every song, the pressed juices have gladdened the Bountiful One. When they, striving together with one accord, call upon him for aid as sons call upon a father. At every hymn, Soma has exhilarated Indra; at every song, the pressed juices have gladdened the Bountiful One. When they, striving together with one accord, call upon him for aid as sons call upon a father.

Since Soma gladdens Maghavan Indra at every hymn (*uktha*) and at every recitation (*śastra*), and since the pressed juices of Soma exhilarate him at every chant (*nītha*) and at every praise (*stotra*), therefore the officiating priests—united with one another, possessing equal skill and equal zeal—invoke this very Indra for protection or for self-preservation, just as sons call upon their father;
they praise him with recitations and hymns.

He has indeed performed those many deeds which the wise proclaim at the libations. Like a single common husband with his wives, Indra has thoroughly adorned all the fortresses. 3. He has performed; those; he shall perform; now; others; which; they proclaim; the wise; at the pressed juices; like wives; a husband; one; common; he has adorned; the fortresses; Indra; well; all. 3.
Indra performed those deeds, such as the slaying of Vṛtra and others, in former times—deeds which the ordainers of hymns proclaim when the Soma juices have been pressed.
Surely even now he would perform other, further deeds.
Moreover, that Indra, being equal in conduct, alone and without companion, would thoroughly cleanse all the strongholds of his enemies, like a husband his wives.
Thus have they called thee, O Indra, the one who hears, the distributor of treasures, the swift victor;
whose many aids come one after another, and from whom auspicious and beloved blessings flow like rays.
1. Kha na bha na vam | 2.

Kha jha ta na bha śa—‘One’ means ‘without a companion’; there is none. Thus: they call him Indra. Moreover, he is heard of as the one who distributes treasures, the overcomer of enemies, whose aids are manifold. May auspicious and beloved things be ever with us. 4.

Of that Indra, whose many ancient protections (*ūtayaḥ*)—whether pressing against one another or closely united—are ever-present, him indeed, endowed with such qualities, the ancient seers have proclaimed.
Moreover, this very Indra is heard of as the distributor and giver of desirable riches (*maghānām*), as the one who carries us across, the deliverer from distress;
and by his grace, may dear and auspicious blessings attend us continually.
Thus, O Vasiṣṭha, praise Indra at the pressing for the protection of men—the bull of the peoples.
Bestow upon us thousandfold strengths; and do you all protect us evermore with blessings.
Vasiṣṭha praises Indra for his aid—the bull of the peoples—at the pressing of the juice. Grant us thousandfold nourishment and strength. And do you all protect us evermore with blessings. 5.

Vasiṣṭha praises—praises in the manner previously described—Indra alone, the bull of desires, the showerer [of benefits], for the sake of protection (*ūtaye*) and for the sake of the lordship over men (*nṝṇām patyarthe*), that is, for the protection of the people (*kṛṣṭīnām*). The accusative case here is used in the sense of "for the sake of. He lauds Indra in this very way.
Now follows the direct praise:
O Indra, bestow upon us, for our sake, thousands—meaning foodstuffs numbering in the thousands.
The sense is: "Grant them."
The rest is clear.
The tenth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “indraṃ naraḥ,” is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and addressed to Indra.
It is cataloged as “indraṃ naraḥ. In the Mahāvrata ritual, this hymn is recited as the third in the Niṣkevalya litany.

For the animal sacrifice dedicated to Indra, the first three verses in their respective order serve as the *anuvākyās* for the omentum (*vapā*), the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and the oblation (*havis*).
This is stated in the Sūtra: ‘“Indraṃ naro nemadhitā havante” and “Uhaṃ no lokamanu nepi vidvān”’ (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
The two leaders call upon Indra at the distribution of the spoils, so that he may harness those prayers of ours.
O Hero, protector of men, who delights in strength, grant us a share in the stall full of cattle.
Men invoke Indra in the contest for booty, when the sons of Pṛthu yoke their prayers. May you, O Hero, desiring strength in the battle for men, grant us a share in the stall filled with cattle.

Whenever the sons of Pṛthā employ those well-known thoughts—that is, their ritual actions—motivated by the burden of battle, then men, as leaders, invoke that Indra in the *nemadhit* (the encounter of armies), in the midst of combat; you, being such a hero, a protector of men, and a distributor of strength, desiring power for yourself, grant us a share in the cattle-pen, in the fold, in the multitude of cows.

1. *Jha-iti*—three *uk* [syllables]. 2. *Kha-jha-na-bha-śa*: "Then men, the leaders, call upon Indra whom they invoke. *Ta-ya-nemadhitā*: "In battle, at the place of conflict (*nemadhitau*), men—the leaders of actions—call upon Indra; the meaning is that they invoke him.
[The phrase] "whom Indra they invoke" [is repeated].

3. In the *kha*, *jha*, *bha*, and *śa* recensions, the phrase "gomati...prāpaya" is absent. In the *gha* recension: "O most excellent protector (*goptamā*), bestow (*ābhaja*) [us] upon our *gomati*—that is, upon the cow-pen (*vraja*) or cattle-shed (*goṣṭha*) containing cows (*go-yukte*); protect us. In the *jha* recension: "In that *gomat*—meaning 'that in which cows exist'—cow-pen, cattle-shed, or assembly (*samūha*), bestow (*ābhaja*) us; lead us there. In the *tara* recension: "In that *gomat*—meaning 'that in which cows exist'—cow-pen, cattle-shed, or assembly, bestow (*ābhaja*) upon us; the meaning is 'give [us] that.'"

O Indra, O Maghavan, whatever strength (*śuṣma*) you possess, bestow it upon your friends, the men, O much-invoked one! For you, O Maghavan, are the discerning one who has shattered the firm [fortresses]; therefore, as one of distinct wisdom, open up for us the wealth that is enclosed, as if it were hidden. *Ya indra śuṣmo maghavante asti śikṣa sakhibhyaḥ puruhūta nṛbhyaḥ | tvaṃ hi dṛlhā maghavannicaitā apā vṛdhi parivṛtaṃ na rādhaḥ || 2 ||* O Indra, O Maghavan, whatever strength you possess, bestow it upon your friends, the men, O much-invoked one! For you, O Maghavan, are the discerning one who has shattered the firm [fortresses]—the words "you have broken down the gates of the cities" being understood. Therefore, being one of distinct wisdom, open up for us the wealth that is enclosed, as if it were hidden. The particle *na* is used here in the sense of "as if."

Indra is the king of the moving world and of the peoples; whatever exists in manifold forms upon the earth, from that he bestows riches upon the donor. May he, being praised by us, impel wealth toward us. Indra is the king of the moving world and of the peoples; whatever exists in manifold forms upon the earth, from that he bestows riches upon the donor. May he, being praised by us, impel wealth toward us. That Indra is the sovereign lord of the moving world—that which moves, such as cattle and so forth—and he is the king of the peoples, of human beings. Upon the earth, he is the ruler even of that wealth which exists in various forms. From that, he gives riches to the donor, to the sacrificer. That Indra, being praised by us, shall impel wealth toward us, hitherward.

May Indra Maghavan, when invoked together with the great, surely grant us food for our aid; he whose perfect and abundant gift flows forth as desirable wealth for the men, his friends. May Indra Maghavan, the bounteous giver, through our joint invocation, quickly bestow upon us strength for our protection. He whose perfect and abundant gift flows forth as desirable wealth for the men, his friends. Maghavan, the wealthy one, the giver—may that Indra, through our joint invocation (sahūtī), by means of a great collective call, grant us food (vāja) for our aid (ūtī)—that is, for our protection—quickly indeed. Of that Indra, the perfect and abundant gift (dakṣiṇā), having reached (abhīvītā) his friends, the singers, yields (pīpāya) desirable wealth for the men.

O Indra, now grant us wide space for the sake of wealth! May we turn your mind toward us for the gift of riches—toward wealth consisting of cattle, horses, and chariots—as we increase [in prosperity]. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 5. Now, O Indra, make wide room for us for the sake of wealth! May we turn your mind toward us for the gift of riches—toward wealth consisting of cattle, horses, and chariots—as we increase [in prosperity]. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 5.
1. Kha-bha: the city gates.
2. Kha-kṣa-tajña-na-ma-śa-yaḥ.
O Indra, for us—namely, for our attainment of wealth (*rāye*)—grant (*nu*) quickly (*kṣipram*) prosperity (*varivaḥ*), that is, wealth.

Because "veda varivaḥ" is listed among the names for wealth, [the meaning is] "do"—that is, grant—it. We, having praised your mind for the sake of *magha*, that which is to be honored, shall bring it hither; we shall cause it to turn toward us.
The rest is clear.
The hymn beginning with "brahmaṇa indra" consists of five verses; it is the eleventh hymn, composed by Vasiṣṭha, in the Triṣṭubh meter, and addressed to Indra.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry "brahmaṇaḥ.
Its application is stated as being for the fifth position in the Niṣkevalya section of the Mahāvrata rite.
On the eighth day, in the Prauga-śastra, the first verse is addressed to Indra (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.10).

O Indra, come to our prayer as one who knows; let your bay steeds be harnessed and turned hitherward. For all mortals indeed invoke you; hear us alone, O you who impel all things! *brahma na indropayāhi vidvān arvāñcaste harayaḥ santu yuktāḥ | viśve ciddhi tvā vihavantamartā asmākamicchṛṇuhi viśvaminva || 1 ||* O Indra, come to our prayer as one who knows; let your bay steeds be harnessed and turned hitherward. For all mortals indeed invoke you; hear us alone, O you who impel all things!
O Indra, you who are all-knowing, come toward our prayer and hymn of praise.
Let your bay horses be harnessed and turned hither toward us.
O Indra, you who satisfy all, although all mortals indeed invoke you individually, nevertheless hear—listen!—to our invocation alone.

O Indra, your greatness has extended far when you, O powerful one, protect the sacred word (*brahman*) of the seers. When you, O fierce one, take the thunderbolt in your hand, though being terrible, you are born through your own will as one who is invincible. Your call, O Indra, your greatness has spread abroad when you, O powerful one, protect the sacred word of the seers. When you, O fierce one, take the thunderbolt in your hand, though being terrible, you are born through your own will as one who is invincible.
O powerful and mighty Indra, whenever you protect the *brahman*— the hymn of praise—
of the seers (for the protection of a hymn consists in the granting of its fruit),
then let your greatness pervade that invocation; "invocation" (*hava*) here means the singer.

O Indra, when you hold the thunderbolt in your hand—that is, when you grasp it in your paw—then, through your power consisting of deeds such as the slaying of enemies, you became fierce, invincible, and unconquered by foes. You were born; you came into being.

O Indra, by your guidance, you brought together the two worlds for those who invoked you repeatedly; for you were born for great dominion and power, and the swift one has strengthened even the slow. O Indra, when you, by your guidance, brought together the two worlds as if they were men who repeatedly invoke you; for you were born for great dominion and power, and the swift one has strengthened even the slow.
O Indra, when you, by your guidance—that is, by leading—bring together the two worlds, Heaven and Earth, for the men who cry out to you with fervent praise, you cause them to meet;
the meaning is that you establish the worshippers both in heaven and on earth.
Such as you are, [you lead them] to great dominion and wealth.
Because “rathiḥ kṣatram” is listed among the names for wealth; and for the sake of *śavas*, that is, strength. [Note: 1.
kha-na-bha read "pradānam" (bestowal).]

2. He pervades the sky (kha). 3. The meaning is that he establishes (pratiṣṭhāpayati) the letters kha, kṣa, ta, na, and bha; or the meaning is that he establishes the letter śa. The meaning is that he bestows great wealth and strength upon the sacrificers (yajamāna). "You were born at the sacrifice" (yajñe jajñiṣe). The particle "hi" is used in the sense of a reason. Because this is so, for that reason, the non-giver sacrificer (atūtajim yajamānam), being struck with fear by the giver sacrificer (tūtajiḥ yajamānaḥ), "perishes" (aśibhat). The root *śibh* has the senses of fear and injury. Therefore, the form is used in the sense of the aorist (luḍ). He injures. The particle "cit" has the sense of emphasis (evakāra).
O Indra, with these [songs] show me favor; for the peoples are hostile.
Whatever falsehood the guileless one has observed, may the wondrous Varuṇa grant us a double portion of it.
With these days, O Indra, show us favor; for the people with evil friends are hostile. When the sinless one perceives their falsehood, may Varuṇa, the master of wondrous power, protect us from harm.
O Indra, the *durmitrāsaḥ*—those who have become evil friends, the hostile *kṣitayaḥ*, the people—*pavante*; that is, they attack (*pavati* being a verb meaning "to go" or "to assail").
Having seized wealth from them, bestow it *naḥ*, upon us, with these *sāttvikaiḥ ahabhiḥ*, through these auspicious days; *daśasya*, grant it!

Furthermore, may Varuṇa—the sinless destroyer of transgressions, the wise one—whatever falsehood he perceives against us, that falsehood, O Indra, by your grace, may he release doubly; that is, in two ways. Thus says Yāska: "The root *syati*, when preceded by a prefix, signifies releasing" (Nirukta 1.17).
Let us call upon this Indra, the dispeller of enemies, who bestows great wealth and bounty;
he who is most intent upon the prayerful work of the singer. Do you all protect us always with your blessings.

Call upon Indra, this one who wards off enemies, so that he may grant us great wealth and bounty. May he, who has accepted the prayerful work of the singer, protect us. And you, O gods, protect us always with your blessings. 5.
That Indra who gave to us— that is, bestowed upon us— a great gift of wealth, a source of success;
and that Indra who is the most excellent protector and goer toward the prayer (*brahman*) being performed by the one who praises him— that wealthy Indra we would indeed praise.
The rest is clear.
The twelfth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “atha soma indra,” is the seerly work of Vasiṣṭha, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and addressed to Indra.
It is cataloged under the heading “ayaṃ somaḥ.
In the expanded ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), on the ninth day, the triplet addressed to Indra used for the *prauga-śastra* is “atha soma indra.”
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Now, O Soma, for you, O Indra, [the juice] is pressed; come then, O Brahmins" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.11).
In the Ṣoḍaśin-śastra, this Triṣṭubh verse beginning with "O Hero, O Brahmin" is used.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "'O Hero, O Brahmin, enjoying the performance of the Brahman,' this is the Triṣṭubh" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.2).
This Soma, O Indra, is pressed for you; come hither, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, longing for it. Drink of this well-prepared, pleasant draught, bestowing gifts as a bountiful giver.
This Soma, O Indra, is pressed for you. Come hither, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, seeking that goal! Drink of this well-pressed, lovely juice; bestowing riches, O Maghavan, as we entreat you. 1.

1. Those who are evil spirits (duṣṭabhūta) are like the letter *kha*; those who are evil friends (duṣṭamitra) are like the letter *ya*; those who are evil in the form of friends (duṣṭamitrabhūta) are like the letter *śa*.
O Indra, for you, for your sake, this Soma has been pressed—purified by the stones.
O Lord of Bay Horses (Harivaḥ), O Indra, you whose dwelling is that [Soma].
He for whom this [Soma] is to be pressed is "tadokaḥ" (having that as his abode).
Or rather, it means "quickly.
Proclaim [the praise] of that beautiful Soma, which is well-pressed, thoroughly poured out, and moving.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative;
"well-pressed" means "beautifully.
[O Indra,] drink quickly indeed!
Moreover, O Maghavan, whether you are being approached with knowledge, or being approached, or being entreated, do you, as the giver of riches, grant us wealth.
O Great Hero, enjoying the creation of the sacred word (*brahman*), come hither swiftly with your bay steeds;
rejoice at this libation, and listen closely to these our prayers.
O Great One, O Hero, enjoying our sacred formulation, come hither swiftly with your bay steeds; rejoice well at this libation, and listen to these our prayers. 2.
O Indra, sovereign hero, lover of prayer, taking pleasure in and enjoying the hymn being performed, come hither toward us with your bay horses; come swiftly and quickly.
At this very pressing of the sacrifice, rejoice well, and listen closely to these our prayers and hymns. Listen!
What preparation for your hymn do you have? When indeed, O Maghavan, shall we offer to you?
I have spread out all my prayers out of devotion to you; therefore, O Indra, hear these invocations of mine.
What preparation do you have for my well-spoken hymn? When indeed, O Maghavan, shall we serve you? I have extended all my prayers toward you; O Indra, hear these my invocations here and now. 3.
O Indra, what kind of adornment—what sort of embellishment—is there for you through our hymns, the praises being performed by us?
O Maghavan, when indeed, at last, shall we satisfy you and produce delight in you?
By my own desire for you alone, I extend all these prayers and hymns of praise toward you.
For this reason, O Indra, hear—listen to these my calls, these my invocations and hymns of praise.
Moreover, you have indeed heard of those many men—the ancient seers—among others;
therefore, O Maghavan, I invoke you with fervor: you, O Indra, are our providence, like a father.
Moreover, indeed, those men were truly many, of whom, the ancient seers, you heard; therefore, O Maghavan, I invoke you repeatedly. You, O Indra, are our providence, like a father. 4.
Moreover:
*vgha* is a filler particle.
O *vmaghavan*, you who heard the praises (*vaśṛṇoḥ*) of those *vpūrveṣām vṛṣīṇām*—those ancient seers were *vpuruṣpāḥ*, that is, indeed beneficial (*hitā*) to men.
Therefore, having chosen you for slaughter, I invoke you and praise you fervently.
Moreover, O Indra, may you be our protector and kinsman, like a father to his son.

Let us call upon this Indra, the Maghavan, so that the god may grant us sudden wealth and bounty; he who, being present, accepts the prayerful work of the singer. Do you all protect us ever with your blessings.

1. *kha* is to be cultivated; *gha*, *jha*, *taña*, and *śa* are to be cultivated; *jha*, *ta*, and *sa* are to be cultivated; *ta₁* and *ta₂* are to be cultivated by him; *ya* is to be cultivated; that very thing is *sa*.

Let us speak here of this Indra, the Maghavan, so that he may grant us great wealth and bounty—he who favors the prayerful act of the one who praises you. Do you all protect us always with blessings. (5) This [verse] has already been explained. (13) The hymn beginning with “ā no deva” consists of five verses; it is the thirteenth hymn, composed by Vasiṣṭha, in the Triṣṭubh meter, dedicated to Indra. It is introduced in the Anukramaṇī as “ā no deva. In the Prauga-śastra of the first Chandoma, this is the Indra-hymn of eight verses beginning with “ā naḥ. For it is prescribed: “ā no deva śavasā yāhi śuṣmin... pra vo yajñeṣu devayanto arcan” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.9). O God, come to us with power, O impetuous one! Be the increaser, O Indra, of this wealth—for the sake of great manliness, O Lord of men, wielder of the good thunderbolt, for the sake of great dominion and manly strength, O Hero. (1) Come to us, O God, with power, O impetuous one! Be the increaser, O Indra, of this wealth—for the sake of great manliness, O Lord of men... (1)
O Indra, O God, we are yours, as are those who praise you, O Hero, while bestowing riches. Grant to our patrons the highest protection; may we, possessing horses, reach old age in well-being.

We are yours, O Indra; and those gods who praise you, O Hero, as they bestow riches—grant to our patrons that most excellent protection. May they, being well-supported and possessed of horses, reach old age.
O divine hero Indra, those Vasiṣṭhas who are your own people,
and those men— my sons, grandsons, and others— who offer and present the *maghāni*, the magnificent oblations, and praise you, they too are your own people.
To both these groups of patrons (*sūri*) and singers (*stotṛ*), grant and bestow the most excellent protection (*varūtha*) and home (*gṛha*).
Moreover, let both of you, being self-existent and perfectly prosperous, reach old age, O possessors of horses.

Let us invoke this Indra, the Maghavan, who bestows great wealth and bounty; he who is most attentive to the one who offers praise and composes sacred hymns. And may you all protect us evermore with your blessings.

Let us speak thus: [we call] upon this Indra, the Maghavan, so that he may bestow great wealth and bounty upon us. May he, who has favored the prayerful act of the singer, protect us. And do you all protect us evermore with blessings. 5.
This is established.
The fourteenth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with “pra va indrāya,” is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and is addressed to Indra.
The last three verses, starting from the tenth, are in the Virāj meter, while the remaining verses are in Gāyatrī.
Thus it has been cataloged: “‘pra vaṃ’: twelve verses, in Gāyatrī, ending with three Virājs.”
The application of the hymn (*sūktaviniyoga*) is based on its indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).
In the first round of the night (*prathame rātriparyāye*), in the *maitrāvaruṇa* litany (*śastra*), the triplet beginning with “*pra va indrāya*” is the *stotriya*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*pra va indrāya mādanam pra kṛtānmṛjīpiṇaḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).
In the first *anirā* section, during the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* recitation, the verse for the *anurūpa* is "vatham indra tvāyavo 'bhi.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "One should extract the last verses [of the *stotriya*] with 'vatham indra tvāyavo 'bhi vātrahatyāya' etc. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).

On the fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), in the recitation of the *hotraka*, following the *ārambhaṇīyā* verses, there is one *tṛca* of the Vairāja [Sāman] to be offered in the *āhavanīya* fire.
Namely: the three [verses] beginning with “pra vo mahe mahivr̥dhe bharadhvam” and so forth.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘pra vo mahe mahivr̥dhe bharadhvam’—these three [verses] are for the Trirātra sacrifice” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.11).
Sing forth a gladdening song for Indra, the lord of tawny steeds,
O friends, at the Soma-vessel.
Sing forth for you a gladdening song for Indra, the lord of the bay horses, O friends, at the Soma-vessel. 1.
O friends, you who possess tawny horses, sing forth a gladdening hymn for Indra—the exhilarating song that produces intoxication—at the Soma-vessel, at the vessel of the pressed juices.
One should recite the hymn of praise for the one who bestows good gifts, just as men have performed it for him whose wealth is true.
Recite a hymn for the one who gives good gifts; even as men have prepared a chariot-yoke for him whose bounty is true. 2.

Moreover, O singer, recite—just as other men, the singers, recite a hymn that is a means for kindling—the hymn of praise for Indra, who possesses beautiful gifts, whose wealth is true, and who is worthy of our offerings;
we too shall perform this hymn. (The word *iti* is a filler. We shall indeed compose the song of praise.
Ṛgveda 3.22

O Indra, you are our seeker of strength; O Śatakratu, you are our seeker of cattle; O Vasu, you are our seeker of gold. (3) O Indra, you are our seeker of strength (*vājyu*); O Śatakratu, you are our seeker of cattle (*gavyu*); O Vasu, you are our seeker of gold (*hiraṇyayu*). O Indra, may you be our seeker of strength—that is, desirous of food—for us. O Śatakratu, may you be our seeker of cattle—that is, desirous of cows—for us. O Vasu, O Indra, the dweller or bestower, may you also be our seeker of gold—that is, desirous of gold. The suffix *kyac* is applied here according to the rule: "In Vedic usage, the suffix *kyac* is seen even when expressing the desire of another."

O Indra, we who long for you, O Bull, praise you aloud; know this of us, O Vasu. O Indra, O showerer of desires, we the Vasiṣṭhas, longing for you, praise you aloud with excellence. O Vasu, O Indra, the dweller, quickly know—that is, take note of—this our hymn of praise.

Do not deliver us over to the reviler, nor to the speaker of evil, nor to the one who finds our flaws, O Indra; for my heart’s resolve is fixed upon you alone. (5) O Indra, Lord, do not subject us to the reviler, the speaker of wicked words, or the one who seeks out our vulnerabilities. Furthermore, let my mental resolve—my hymn of praise—be directed toward you alone; that is, let our hymn of praise enter into your mind.

You are our armor, O wide-extending one, and the warrior in the van, O slayer of Vṛtra; with you as my ally, I speak back [against the enemies]. 6. O Vṛtrahan—O Indra, destroyer of foes—you are our *varma*, our armor; that is to say, you are a protector like a suit of mail. You are *saprathaḥ*, broad on all sides; and you are the *puroyodhaḥ*, the warrior who fights from the front. With you as my ally (*yujā*), I speak back against the enemies; that is to say, I strike them down. 6.

Great indeed art thou, O Indra, whose conquering power the two worlds, rich in self-sustenance, acknowledge. Great indeed art thou, O Indra; whose conquering power (*sahas*) the two worlds—Heaven and Earth, which possess self-sustaining nourishment (*svadhāvarī*)—acknowledge and approve. The meaning is that both worlds, intending that thy power is supreme over all, do not contradict one another.

May the Marut-filled voice, moving along with its own course and reaching toward you, encompass you together with the days of light. 8. [Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 7, Adhyāya 2, Sūkta 31] Fifth Aṣṭaka, 339. May that voice, accompanied by the Maruts, moving on its own path and reaching toward you, encompass you together with the days of light. 8.
O Indra, [we call upon] you who are distinguished by those aforementioned qualities; "sayāvarī" means she who goes with you—meaning she goes wherever you go.
"Dyubhiḥ" means with splendors; "nakṣamāṇā" means pervading; "vyāmuvatī" means expansive; and "marutvatī" means accompanied by the Maruts.
The Maruts are the praisers;
may the voice consisting of that [praise], the hymn, encompass them—
here, the verb *pari-bhū* has the sense of "accepting" or "embracing."
The meaning is "may he accept."

The drops have followed you upward, O wondrous one, toward the sky; all the people bow down before you. 9. Upward, O wondrous one, the drops have followed you toward the sky; all the people bow down before you. 9.
O Indra, directed toward you—the wondrous and beautiful one—standing near the sky (*upa dyavi*), our *indavas*, our Soma drops, rise upward;
and the people (*kṛṣṭayaḥ*) bow down in homage to you. On earth, the Somas are born solely for your sake, and the creatures likewise prostrate themselves before you; such is the praise of Indra.

Bring forth [your song] to the great one, the upholder of greatness; offer your devotion to the wise one. O you who fill the people, go forth unto the many clans. 10. Bring forth [your song] to the great one, the upholder of greatness; offer your devotion to the wise one. O you who fill the people, go forth unto the many clans. 10.
O my men, you who are here, bring forth and present the Soma juices to Indra—the great one, the increaser of vast riches—for the sake of the great.
And for Indra, the one of preeminent wisdom, offer your excellent devotion and well-wishing thoughts. Now follows the direct praise:
O Indra, you who fill the people, fulfill the desires of all creatures; O fulfiller of many oblations, proceed toward and approach the various clans and progeny.

For the wide-extending one, the great-minded Indra, the inspired poets have generated a well-fashioned prayer; the wise do not violate his ordinances. 11. For the wide-extending one, for the great-minded one, a well-fashioned hymn—for Indra, they have generated the sacred word, the inspired ones; his ordinances the wise do not violate. 11.

For that Indra of vast extent and wide pervasion—for him who is great—the wise ones generate and offer forth well-fashioned praise, prayer, food, and oblation; even the sagacious gods do not violate nor harm his protective ordinances and deeds.

The voices have established Indra alone as the unassailable king, ever to be victorious; they have brought together strengthening allies for the sake of the Lord of the Bay Horses. 12. Indra. Voices. Unassailable. Truly. Ever. King. They have established. To be victorious. For the Lord of the Bay Horses. Strengthening. Together. Allies. 12.
"The hymns (vāṇīs) have established that very Indra— the king, the lord of the entire world, the unsurpassed and final one,
whose wrath (manyu) is unassailable by anyone—
in order to overcome the enemies of the worshippers."
Therefore, O singer, you too should rouse the prayer for Indra, the lord of the bay horses—
to praise Indra, that is the meaning—
for those who are kinsmen by kinship.

The hymn beginning with "mo ṣu tvā" consists of twenty-seven verses and is the fifteenth [hymn] in the [Maṇḍala]. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "The [hymn] beginning with 'mo ṣu' has twenty-seven verses; it is a *pragātha* [of seventeen syllables], and the third [verse] is a *dvipadā*. While being thrown into the fire by the Saudāsas, Śakti took up another *pragātha*; when he had uttered half of the verse, he was consumed by fire.
Vasiṣṭha completed that verse which had been spoken by his son—so says the Śāṭyāyanaka. According to the Tāṇḍaka, however, it was the curse of Vasiṣṭha himself whose sons had been slain."
Vasiṣṭha, the seer, is the observer of the maṇḍala.
For the pragātha beginning with "indra kratuṃ naḥ" and for the half-verse, [the seers are] Śakti, the son of Vasiṣṭha, or Vasiṣṭha himself.
Indra.

[Maṇḍala 7, Anuvāka 2, Sūkta 32] Thus [it is stated]. On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (mādhyandina-savana), this *trya* *pragātha* is an optional *stotriya* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Indra, bring us wisdom; O Indra, bring us the highest [wisdom]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
O Indra, do not delight in the enemy even if the priests call upon you; come to our communal feast from afar, or if you are already here, listen to us.

O Indra, let not even the priests turn you away from us; do not let us be far removed from you. Even from afar, come to our exhilarating draught of Soma; or if you are here, listen well to our prayer.
O Indra, let not even the priests who offer sacrifices turn you away from us; let them not cause you to rest far off, nor let them make you dwell in lowliness.
Therefore, even though you are far away, come to our exhilarating sacrifice. Whether you are here or elsewhere, being mindful, listen closely to our hymn of praise.
For these, created by Brahmā, sit with him at the pressed juice like bees upon honey;
desiring wealth, the two singers have placed their desire in Indra as one places a foot upon a chariot.
For these, the makers of prayer, sit beside the pressed juice like flies at honey; the singers, seeking wealth, have placed their desire upon Indra as one places a foot upon a chariot. || 2 ||

O Indra, when the Soma is pressed for you, those who have composed sacred hymns (*brahmakṛtaḥ*) and those who have offered praise (*stotrakṛtaḥ*) sit together with it, like bees upon honey; that is, they settle down together with the sweet juice.
Now follows an indirect praise (*parokṣastuti*):
the singers (*jaritāraḥ*), the praisers desiring wealth, place their desired wish in Indra, just as one places a foot upon a chariot; that is, they entrust it to him.
Desiring wealth, I call upon the one with the thunderbolt in his hand, the very skillful one, as a son calls upon his father.
Desiring wealth, I call upon him who holds the thunderbolt in his hand, the one most skilled in giving, as a son calls upon his father. 3.
Desiring kingship and desiring wealth, I call upon Indra, who possesses a beautiful hand for giving and holds the thunderbolt; I invoke him as a son calls upon his father.
These Soma juices, mixed with curds, have been pressed for Indra;
come hither with thy two bay steeds, O wielder of the thunderbolt, to these for exhilaration and for thy draught.
These Soma juices, mixed with curds, have been pressed for Indra; O wielder of the thunderbolt, come with your two bay horses to our home, to these drinks for exhilaration and for you to drink. 4.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, these Soma juices mixed with curd—these Somas have been pressed for you, O Indra; they have become prepared for you.
Come toward them, toward this dwelling place, the seat of sacrifice, with your two bay horses, for the sake of exhilaration, for the purpose of intoxication, so that you may drink these Somas.
1. [The letters] kha, jha, ta, na, bha, and ña are also [present]; jha is also because of ya-ta. 2.
[The letter] 'ma' does not exist after kha, bha, and ta³; [the letters] jha, ta⁴, śa, and mā [follow]; na and jā [are present]. 3.
'na' does not exist after kha, bha, and ta³.
He whose ears are attentive to wealth approaches; he is truly wonderful and most bountiful.
He who instantly bestows hundreds and thousands—no one can restrain him when he wishes to give.

He hears; he whose ears are attentive listens. He is implored for wealth. Now indeed, may he take pleasure in our songs—he who at once bestows hundreds and thousands. No one can restrain him when he desires to give. 5.
Śrutkarṇaḥ:
Indra, whose ears consist of hearing supplications, is entreated for riches (*vasūni*).
May he hear (*śravat*) our songs (*giraḥ*), that is, our words of supplication.
May he never indeed cause me harm;
that is to say, may he not render my words of supplication fruitless through non-hearing.
Moreover, Indra, immediately—even at once—following the very act of supplication, shall bestow and grant hundreds and thousands.
No one shall harm or injure that Indra who desires to give, who wishes to bestow [wealth]. O my men, press out the Soma for Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, into the Soma-vessel.
Cook the *paktīḥ*—the cooked offerings such as the *puroḍāśa* cakes—to satisfy Indra for his protection (*avase*).
Indeed, perform those very actions that are dear to Indra.
For Indra, bestowing happiness (*mayaḥ*) upon the sacrificer, approaches the oblations (*havīṃṣi*), as is understood from the context.
Do not obstruct the Soma-presser; bestow skill for the sake of greatness. Make riches easy to win.
The one who crosses over conquers, dwells in peace, and prospers; the gods do not grant such things to the one who lacks wisdom.

Do not obstruct the Soma-pressers! Be skillful; prepare for the great wealth; impel yourselves forward! Only the one who crosses over conquers; he dwells in peace and prospers; the gods do not favor the stingy. 9.
O my people who possess Soma, do not obstruct— do not harm— the Soma-offerings;
exert yourselves and be capable of performing the sacrifice and other rites for the sake of great booty.
*Tur* has the sense of "injuring" or "giving. For Indra—who is the injurer of enemies or the bestower of wealth—perform rites for the sake of *rāye*, that is, for the acquisition of riches;
and do so, acting with speed like one who is swift (*taraṇiḥ*) in his deeds, for he conquers his enemies.
He dwells in the house and resides there;
he prospers, becoming nourished with offspring and cattle;
[this is] for the sake of evil deeds, for vile actions.
The form *kavattanūḥ* is derived from the root *at*, meaning "continuous movement," with the prefix *upa*.
The phrase *devāmo na* means "they do not become gods"; the intended sense is that they become those who are well-disposed toward the sacrifice (*suvaprāsaya*).
No one has overturned Sudās’s chariot, nor has anyone brought it to a halt;
he for whom Indra is the protector and the Maruts are his helpers shall go to a stall full of cattle.
No one has obstructed the chariot of Sudās; Indra has not let it rest, he for whom Indra is the protector and the Maruts are his allies—he shall reach the stall filled with cattle. 10.
No one at all overturns the chariot of Sudās, the sacrificer of beautiful gifts; nor does anyone cause it to stop—
meaning that no one seizes it for their own sake.
Moreover, he whose protector and guardian is Indra, and whose protectors are the Maruts—he shall go to the cow-filled enclosure, to the pen abounding in cattle.
O Indra, may the mortal whose protector you have become win the prize through his steeds;
be the protector of our chariots and of our men, O Hero.
May he go to the prize; may he win the prize through our prayers, O Indra, you whose protector we have become. Be the protector of our chariots, O Hero, and the protector of our men. 11.
O Indra, that mortal man of whom you become the protector and guardian—he, striving for strength by making you powerful through his hymn of praise, shall attain *vāja*, that is, food.
Moreover, O Hero, be the protector and guardian of our chariots, which are most beloved to us. (The form *bodhi* is the imperative of the root *bhū*).
The substitution of *ba* for *bha* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
Be the protector of us, our men—our sons and others.
The portion of one who has risen up is not diminished, nor the wealth of the victor;
Indra, the lord of the bay horses, bestows skill upon the Soma-presser whom his enemies seek to harm.
1. Kha-bha-karma.
2. Ta-kuphata; śa-ca kuphata.
3. Kha-gha-ta-na-bha-ātmānaṃ.

And indeed, his portion remains superior, like the wealth of a victor; Indra, the lord of the two bay steeds, does not fail the Soma-presser, for he bestows skill upon him so that no enemy may harm him.
The lineage of that Indra is such that his portion of the Soma in the sacrifice exceeds even that of the other gods;
for Indra has the drinking of Soma in all three pressings, since the entire midday pressing belongs to Indra.
He is like the wealth of one who has conquered, as if it were actual riches.

The three words *vudiṣu* are fillers. Moreover, when there is a Soma-offering sacrificer, Indra, the possessor of wealth (*vharivān*), bestows (*dadhati*) power (*dakṣam*) and exhilaration (*mandati*) upon him; the enemies (*ripaḥ*) do not shake him (*na dabhrānta*) nor do they harm him (*na hiṃsanti*).
Bestow upon those worthy of sacrifice a mantra that is not deficient, well-placed, and beautiful;
even many snares cannot overcome him who stands by Indra through his ritual action.

The mantra: Place it—unfailing, well-established, and beautiful—among those worthy of sacrifice. Even many [enemies] cannot prevail against it. O Indra, the lowest wealth is yours; you nourish the middle wealth.
You are the sovereign ruler of the entire universe; no one can restrain you when you are among the cattle.
Thine, O Indra, is the lowest wealth; thou nourishest the middle; as the threader [of all], thou rulest over the highest of all; no one holds thee back from the cattle. 16.
O Indra, [give] the lowest, most base wealth such as tin, lead, and so forth;
or rather, the lowest earthly wealth—
[all this] belongs to you alone.
You alone nourish the middle wealth— such as silver, gold, and the like— or that which belongs to the intermediate space;
you reign over and rule all supreme and most excellent wealth, whether it be jewels or celestial riches,
wherever you so intend.
Moreover, having [attained] you, no one at all—none whatsoever—can obstruct you when the cows are the cause.
You are renowned as the giver of wealth to all; those who become victorious are yours.
O you who are invoked by many, this entire earthly world begs for your protection.
You are the wealth of the universe.
To him who is perceived in some place,
who exists somewhere, and who is the knower in some place.
The meaning is: "to whomever [the gift] may exist.
For the person who honors [me], that is, worships me, I shall grant—meaning, I will surely give—riches, that is, wealth, day after day.
The vowel *ā* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).
Having heard these words of Indra, the sage spoke with satisfaction:
"O Maghavan, there is nothing else to be attained or known by us apart from you.
Even our father, the most excellent and praiseworthy protector, is none other than you. This is the meaning.
The swift one indeed desires booty with the aid of wisdom;
I bend Indra, who is invoked by many, with my song, as a carpenter fashions the rim of a wheel from good wood.

The deliverer, the fulfiller of desires, the possessor of many riches—him we invoke with our song for strength, even as a carpenter fashions the felly of a well-made wheel; I bend Indra, who is invoked by many, toward us. 20.

A man who is swift in actions such as praise and the like, desiring to win (*sipāsati*) food (*vāja*) through his great, wise intellect acting as a companion (*yujā*), seeks to enjoy it. With my song (*girā*), I bend you, Indra—who are invoked by many (*puruhūta*)—toward me with my speech, just as a carpenter bends the felloe (*nemi*) of a wheel made of fine wood; that is to say, just as a builder shapes the wooden rim of a wheel, so do I.
A mortal finds no wealth through ill-praise; he who falters does not obtain riches.
O Maghavan, may this well-performed hymn be for you, O Marut, as a warding off of enmity from the one who protects us.

A mortal does not find wealth through ill-praise; riches do not reach one who is wearying himself. O Maghavan, you alone possess great power; for you, the impeller, is that which is hateful to the enemy. || 21 ||
A mortal man does not obtain wealth through ill-praise;
the meaning is that only by praising Indra does one obtain wealth.
[He obtains wealth] from one who is *sredhantam*, i.e., harming.

The meaning is: [the wealth] does not reach one who performs actions such as praising Indra and his domain. O Maghavan, that which is to be given as a gift by you on the next day, in heaven, to one like me—that wealth which exists—belongs to you; it is indeed a good deed (suśakti) coming from you.
The word "vindata" (you find) is supplied even though it is distant, because an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) involves proximity.
"We praise you, O Hero, like unmilked cows,
you who are the lord of this moving world, the beholder of heaven, the lord, O Indra, of all that stands still."
We cry out to you, O Hero, like unmilked cows; to you, O Indra, the lord of this moving world, the beholder of heaven, the lord of all that stands still. 22.

O heroic Indra, we praise you intensely—we who exist as those filled with the highest essence, just as milk-filled cows exist with udders full of milk—praising you, the beholder of heaven, the all-seeing one, the sovereign lord of this moving world and the lord of that which is stationary; the repetition of the word "lord" (*īśāna*) is for the sake of emphasis. We praise you most fervently.

None other like you exists—neither celestial nor terrestrial; none has been born, nor shall be born. O Maghavan Indra, desiring horses, seeking booty, and longing for cattle, we invoke you. (23) O Maghavan Indra, no other like you—whether celestial (*divya*), existing in heaven, or terrestrial (*pārthiva*), existing on earth—has been born. Neither a celestial nor a terrestrial being like you has ever been born, nor will one ever be born. The meaning is that there is no one equal to you in all three worlds, whether on earth or in heaven. Desiring horses (*aśvāyantaḥ*)—those who wish for horses—and *vājinaḥ*, those seeking booty (*vāja*); the suffix *-in* is used here in the sense of desire. Or, possessing oblations (*haviṣmantaḥ*), and *gavyantaḥ*, longing for cattle, we invoke you; we call upon you.

O Indra, bring that [wealth] from the younger [to the] elder; for you, O Maghavan, have been the possessor of many riches from of old, and you are to be invoked in every battle. O elder Indra, bring toward me—that which is well-known—those riches from the younger one. O Maghavan, you have indeed been the possessor of abundant wealth from time immemorial; and in every battle, or at every sacrifice, you are the one to be invoked with oblations.

Drive away our enemies, O Maghavan; make wealth easy for us to find.
