Be our protector in the great battle; be the increaser of our friends. 25 O Maghavan, drive away—push back—the enemies, the adversaries. Make wealth easy for us to obtain. In the great battle—for "great battle" is listed among the names for combat—be the protector and guardian of us, your friends, the Vasiṣṭhas who offer praise. And be their prosperer. 25

O Indra, bring us wisdom, just as a father provides for his sons. Teach us, O much-invoked one, on this path; living, may we attain the light. 26. Indra | wisdom | us | hither | bring | father | sons | as | teach | us | in this | much-invoked | journey | living | light | may we attain. 26.
1. O Indra, bring to us—*naḥ* meaning "to us"—*kratum*, which means action or wisdom; bring it!
Furthermore, just as a father bestows wealth upon his sons, so do you *śikṣa*, that is, give wealth to us.
O Puruhūta, invoked by many, may we, being alive, attain—the very light—Sūrya at every journey, that is, at every sacrifice, day after day.
Let not unknown, malevolent powers overcome us; let not the barking dogs leap upon us.
With you, O Hero, we shall cross over the eternal downward-flowing waters.
Let not unknown, malevolent, and evil-minded men overcome us; let not the snorting, leaping steed overcome us. O Hero, with your help may we cross over the eternal downward-flowing waters.
O Indra, let not the unknown ones—those whose ways are unknown, the obstructors, the harmful, and those of evil intent—trample upon us or overcome us.
O Hero, through you we, being most excellent and swift-flowing like waters down a slope, cross over and pass beyond the many, eternal waters.
The sixteenth hymn, consisting of fourteen verses, begins with "śrityaśvaḥ.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: "śrityaśvaḥ: a praise by Palūta of Vasiṣṭha along with his sons, or a dialogue with Indra.
For the first nine verses, Vasiṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi).
Because he is being praised by the sons of Vasiṣṭha, Vasiṣṭha himself is the deity.
Vasiṣṭha is praised by his own sons, beginning with Bhadraśarman, in the verses starting with "The light of the lightning" (*vidyuto jyotiḥ*).
Therefore, Vasiṣṭha is the deity.
Nor can it be the *ṛṣis*,
according to the maxim "that which is stated by him [the seer]";
for they did not state that it was a *triṣṭubh*.
Relying on you, O Aśva, may those with braided hair on the right, who stir our devotion, be joyful toward us.
Rising from the sacrificial grass, I have addressed the men; O Vasiṣṭhas, you are not far from helping me.

Relying on the horse, do not [turn] to the right; O Kapardas, quicken our prayer! For you have gladdened us; standing here, I speak around the men of the sacrificial grass. O Vasiṣṭhas, you are not for me to protect against ill-fortune. 1.
*Śrityaśva*:
those who resort to *śrī*, which is the white color, are called *śrityaśva*;
the meaning is that they are white-colored.
"Invigorating the intellect" means those who fulfill ritual actions;
"with braided hair on the right" means those whose braids are on the right side of their heads.
It is recorded in the Smṛti that "for the Vasiṣṭhas, [the braid] is on the right during the tonsure ceremony."
"Do not overwhelm me," meaning "do not strike me down by means of the power of knowledge.
For they overwhelmed me from the *barhis* sacrifice;
the word "from" (*pari*) is a restatement of the sense of the ablative case.
Rising up, I speak—I declare—to men who lead the sacrifice:
"O Vasiṣṭhas, my sons, you are difficult to overcome; they cannot be harmed," so it remains, [meaning] they are unable to go away for the sake of protecting me.
From afar they brought Indra with pressed juice, past the Vaiśanta pool, beyond the fierce one who drinks;
from the pressed soma of Pāśadyumna Vāyata, Indra chose the Vasiṣṭhas.
From afar they brought Indra hither with the pressed juice, past the Vaiśanta lake, past the fierce one who was drinking. From the pressed Soma of Pāśadyumna Vāyata, Indra chose the Vasiṣṭhas. 2.
1. kha-eṣā | 2. kha-bha-anuvādī | 3. jha-putrāḥ sudāsaṃ rājānam; ta1-putrāḥ sudāsarājānaḥ; tara-putrāḥ mudāmarājāna | 4. kha-ta-na-bha-śa—'na' is not present.
[Ma. 7 A. 2 Sū. 33] Fifth Aṣṭaka, 349:
When the sons of Vasiṣṭha officiated as priests for King Sudās, at that very time the king of the Pāśadyumna clan also made an effort to sacrifice with Soma.

Then those sons of Vasiṣṭha, having set aside the pair of nooses, by the power of the mantra snatched Indra away from him as he was drinking the Soma at that sacrifice and established him at the sacrifice of Sudās.
Reciting this very account, Vasiṣṭha praises his own sons with this mantra:
"Vaiśāntam."
*Veśāntaḥ* means a pool.

Here, by the word *veśānta*, the *śarman* (refuge) which is the vessel for the Soma is indicated. Having crossed through the pair of bonds, the Vasiṣṭhas brought—by the power of their mantras—the fierce (*ugram*), exalted (*udvarṇam*) Indra, who was drinking (*pāntam*) the Soma situated there, to the sacrifice of Sudās, using the pressed Soma as the means; they brought him swiftly.
Indra, having bypassed the pair of snares belonging to Vāyata, the son of Naya— that is, the second pair of snares—
chose the Vasiṣṭhas, the sons of Vasiṣṭha, for the sake of the Soma at the sacrifice of Sudās.

The meaning is that while Indra was drinking the Soma situated in the *camasa* vessels during the Soma sacrifice, he disregarded those two nooses and, by the power of the efficacy of the mantra, arrived at Sudās’s sacrifice at the time of the invocation, accompanied by the Vasiṣṭhas.
With these [hymns], he crossed the river Sindhu; with these, he struck down Bheda.
With these, O Vasiṣṭhas, Indra protected Sudās in the battle of the ten kings through your sacred prayer (brahman).

Truly, indeed, with these he crossed the Sindhu; truly, indeed, with these he struck down Bheda; truly, indeed, for the sake of Sudās in the battle of the ten kings, Indra protected him through your prayer, O Vasiṣṭhas. ||3||

Just as Sudās obtained Indra—even though he was drinking the Soma situated in the *camasa* cups during the first Soma-sacrifice of the twin pair of *pāśas*—so too did he, by means of these Vasiṣṭhas, easily cross over (*tantāra*) the river Sindhu; thus his self was delivered.
The particle *nu* is a filler.
And so there is another scriptural citation: "He [Indra] spread out the waters for Sudās" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 7.18.5).
In this very way, he slew even his enemy named Bheda by means of these very Vasiṣṭhas. Now follows a direct praise:
in this very way, O Vasiṣṭhas, through your *brahman*—that is, your hymn of praise—Indra protected King Sudās when a battle had commenced with ten kings.

And likewise, another Vedic passage states: "Ten kings assembled together, non-sacrificers; O Indra and Varuṇa, you did not fight against Sudās" (Ṛgveda Maṇḍala 7, Sūkta 83, Verse 7), and also: "Against him who was surrounded on all sides by the ten kings" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 7, 83, 8).
O heroes, through the prayer of our fathers you have been pleased; indeed, you do not fail us with malice.
Since you, O Vasiṣṭhas, have established power within Indra by means of the great roar in the Śakvarī verses.

O men, through the prayer of your fathers, you have taken pleasure [in us]; indeed, you do not harm our unaging eye. Since, with a great roar over the pebbles, O Vasiṣṭhas, you have infused strength into Indra. 4.
O heroes, by means of your *brahman*—your hymn of praise—the ancestors become pleased.
By the word "ancestors," Vasiṣṭha himself is being praised indirectly;
the meaning is: "I myself become pleased."

Now, as I am preparing to go to my own hermitage, I shall "vyāyāmi"— that is, I shall exert myself with the axle (akṣa) of the chariot; the verb is in the present tense (laṭ) used in the sense of the future (laṅ),
meaning "I shall set it in motion."
O Vasiṣṭhas, you truly do not harm us, nor do you become exhausted, because with the best, lofty sound in the Śakvarī verses, you have bestowed strength and power upon Indra.

1. In the version designated as Kha-na-bha-saṃsavākhye; [in the version] designated as Jha, the term ‘savākhye’ is absent; in Jha-ta-śa-maṃvākhye; in Ta₁-gakhye; and in Ta₂-khye. 2. In Śa-pravṛddhe. 3. In Jha-tara-parokṣeṇa; in Ta₄-parokṣeṇa.

Like those parched with thirst looking up toward the sun, the Vasiṣṭhas, besieged and imploring for rain during the battle of the ten kings, meditated upon Indra. Hearing the praise of the lauding Vasiṣṭha, Indra granted wide space to the Tṛtsus. Like those parched with thirst, the imploring ones, besieged in the battle of the ten kings, looked upward toward Indra as if toward the sun. Hearing the hymn of the praising Vasiṣṭha, Indra gave ear; he made wide room for the Tṛtsu kings—he indeed created and bestowed it.

Like sticks used for driving cattle, the Bharatas were cut down; they were small and few. Yet Vasiṣṭha became their leader from the very beginning, and then the subjects of the Tṛtsus spread abroad. Like sticks (*daṇḍāḥ*) used for driving cattle (*go-arjanāsaḥ*), the Bharatas were severed like branches with trimmed leaves. The Bharatas are mentioned here as another name for the kings of the Tṛtsus. They were indeed cut down by their enemies and were small (*arbhakāsaḥ*), insignificant. From that moment of being cut down, Vasiṣṭha became the leader (*purastā*) and domestic priest (*purohita*) of those Tṛtsus. Because of his priesthood, the subjects (*viśaḥ*) and progeny of the Tṛtsus expanded and increased.
Three create the seed within the worlds; three are the noble progeny, whose forefront is light.
Three are the heats that attend the highest [heaven]; all these indeed the Vasiṣṭhas know.
Three perform [their work] among the worlds.
Semen;
three; progeny.
The noble ones; having light as their foremost; three.
The hot libations attend upon the highest.
All of them indeed.
The Vasiṣṭhas have understood it.
In the worlds—earth, the intermediate space, and heaven—the three, namely Fire, Wind, and Sun, produce in due order the seed, that is, water, which sustains the universe.
Of these three, there are three noble and preeminent offspring, headed by the Āditya, whose light is foremost.
And those three—Fire, Wind, and Sun—as radiant heats, attend to and unite with the Supreme.
The Vasiṣṭhas alone know and fully recognize all those things that are difficult to understand;
even their knowledge of the secret doctrines is a praise for the Vasiṣṭhas alone.

And likewise, the Jñātyāyanaka states: "Three create seed in the worlds"—Agni creates seed on earth, Vāyu in the intermediate space, and Āditya in heaven; "the three noble progenies have light as their head"—these are the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas; "their light is that which is called yonder Āditya"; "the *gharmas* attend upon them"—Agni attends upon them, Vāyu attends upon them, and Āditya attends upon them.
1. In manuscripts Kha, Jha, Ta³, Ta⁴, Na, Bha, and Śa, "udadīdhayuḥ" is absent; in Jha, Ta¹, and Ta², it is "adīdhayuḥ. 2.
In manuscripts Kha, Na, and Bha, it is "yatpaurauhityam"; in Jha, it is "tatpaurauhityam"; in Ta³, it is "yatpaurauhityam. 3.
In manuscript Kha and Bha, it is "sevante."
Like a tree for the sun, their light is manifest; like the ocean, their greatness is profound.
Like the speed of the wind, your hymns cannot be followed by anyone else, O Vasiṣṭhas.
Like the light of the sun upon the tree, the greatness of these [Maruts] is as profound as the ocean; like the rushing wind, your hymn of praise, O Vasiṣṭhas, cannot be followed by another. 8.
O Vasiṣṭhas, this hymn of praise (*stoma*) of yours, or even your greatness (*mahiman*), is manifest like the light of the sun, O Vasiṣṭhas;

your greatness, or even your hymn of praise, is deep like the ocean, O Vasiṣṭhas. Likewise, O Vasiṣṭhas, this hymn of praise of yours—a collection of *ṛc* verses—or even your greatness, is as swift as the wind; just as the impulse of the wind cannot be followed by another, so too it cannot be followed by another.
Following the signs of the heart, they move toward that thousand-branched *iṇṇiyā*.
Spinning the thread stretched out by Yama, the Vasiṣṭhas, the sages, have settled upon the essence of the waters.

They have come together from here with the intimations of the heart, toward the great branch; weaving the outspread enclosure by means of Yama, the Vasiṣṭhas, possessing the essence of the waters, have sat upon the bull. 9.

They, the Vasiṣṭhas, indeed [know] that which is hidden and difficult to discern; for "niyam" is read among the names for the hidden in the list of secret names (*antarhitanāman*). With the perceptions of the heart—that is, with their insights—they traverse the great, thousand-branched cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

Thus, acting according to their own will, those Vasiṣṭhas approached the waters as their mother—those waters which, by Yama, the causal self and universal controller, constitute a spread-out and extended garment. By the term "garment" (*paridhi*), the continuous flow of birth and so forth is intended. Weaving that [garment], they settled near the waters.
In this context, the plural form "Vasiṣṭhāḥ" is used for the sake of honor.
The sense is that Vasiṣṭha formerly formed the intention: "Having cast off my body from the lap of Prajāpati, may I be born among the Apsarases."
When Mitra and Varuṇa beheld you emerging from the lightning’s light,
that was your first birth, O Vasiṣṭha, when Agastya brought you to the people.

From the lightning, from the light, you were completely gathered together when Mitra and Varuṇa beheld you; that was one of your births, O Vasiṣṭha, and [the other] when Agastya brought you to the people. 10.
In these verses, the assumption of a body by Vasiṣṭha himself is set forth.
Regarding these, some describe them as the words of Indra, while others [describe them] as the words of Vasiṣṭha’s sons.
"O Vasiṣṭha," [it means] when—just as lightning—you, who possess your own light, were about to abandon [your former state] for the sake of assuming another body (*parisaṃjihānam* = *parityajantam*).
This is a Vedic middle-voice form (ātmanepada).
Alternatively,
it means "enveloping its own light for the sake of the body it intends to assume."
The meaning is "desiring to seize.
In this interpretation, since the root *jahāti* has the sense of "going," the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is not a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
Mitrāvaruṇā, i.e., Mitra and Varuṇa, beheld him.
The meaning is that they both resolved, "Let this be born from us two.
That was then your first birth.

Furthermore (*uta*), when Agastya brought you forth (*ājabhāra*)—that is, he took you—from that prior state [of being] as Mitra and Varuṇa intended, "We two shall give birth to the people (*viśaḥ*)," that was your second birth.
1. O Knower, Your majesty is to be followed; O Ta, Ta, Ta, Your majesty is to be followed.

2. O Knower, by Your own will (svacchanda). 3. To the one who desires to assume a body (jighṛkṣitadehāya); O Knower, for the sake of the body desired [to be assumed]; O Na, to the one who does not desire to assume a body.
4. And when?

"And you, O Vasiṣṭha, are the son of Mitra and Varuṇa, born from the mind of Urvaśī, O Brahman. All the gods received you in the lotus-leaf as a fallen drop by means of divine prayer. (11) And you are, O Vasiṣṭha, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa; born from the mind of Urvaśī, O Brahman. All the gods received you in the lotus-leaf as a fallen drop by means of divine prayer. (11)
Moreover, O Vasiṣṭha, you are the son of Mitra and Varuṇa.
O Brahmin Vasiṣṭha, from such a mental resolve as "May there be a son born of my mind," the seminal drop (drapsa) was spilled by Urvaśī upon seeing Mitra and Varuṇa;
from that you were born.
And so it will be stated in the *Ṛgveda* hymn: "Born in the *sattra*.

Thus, you who were born, I—endowed with the divine *brahman*, that is, the mass of the Veda—[invoke] you in the lotus (*puṣkara*) during the *sattra*, a sacrifice performed by many agents, [where] all the gods [were present].
The particle *ha* is for filling the meter.

Mitra and Varuṇa, who were consecrated (*dīkṣitau*) by birth, being impelled (*iṣitā*)—that is, requested—by other people with salutations (*namobhiḥ*) and hymns of praise, poured forth (*asisicatām*) their common (*samānam*) seed simultaneously (*ekadā*) into the *vāsatīvara* jar.
Then, from the midst of that *vāsatīvara* jar, Agastya emerged (*udiyāya*), appearing as a *māna* in size, measuring the span of a *śamī* tree.
From that very jar, they say that even Vasiṣṭha was born as a seer.
He bears the bearer of the *uktha*, he bears the bearer of the *sāman*; bearing the pressing-stone, O Agni, he praises you.
Approach him with a well-disposed mind; let Vasiṣṭha, the piercer, come to you.
Bearing the hymn, bearing the Sāman, he bears the pressing-stone. Bearing it, let him speak forth, O Agni! Approach him with well-disposed minds; Vasiṣṭha shall come to you, O Pratr̥das. 14.
The *pratṛdas*—by the name *pratṛda*, the *nṛt-savas* themselves are designated—are being addressed. *Vasiṣṭha* comes toward you; he approaches you.
With well-disposed minds, being yourselves well-disposed, approach and attend upon this Vasiṣṭha.
Having arrived at the sacrifice as Agni’s domestic priest (*purohita*) and acting as the Brahman priest, he supports the one who bears the *ukthas*—the reciter of the *śastras*;
he supports the one who bears the *sāmans*—the *udgātṛ* singer.

Indra speaks to the men: "He who bears the pressing-stone and bears the Adhvaryu priest shall proclaim at the sacrifice whatever is to be proclaimed—that which must be performed on account of the eating [of the Soma]. Thus he speaks.

In the third Anuvāka there are twenty-two Sūktas. Among them, the first Sūkta, beginning with "pra śukrā," consists of twenty-five Ṛcas. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "Pra śukrā; [it has] five more [than twenty]; it is addressed to the Viśvedevas; the first twenty-one verses are Dvipadās; the lower half-verse of the last verse belongs to Abjāmahi, and the latter [half-verse] is for Ahivṛndhya."
The seer is Vasiṣṭha.
The first twenty-one verses are *virāj* meters consisting of twenty syllables with two lines; the last four are *triṣṭubh* meters consisting of twenty-two syllables.
The deities are the Viśvedevas.
In the *vyūḍha-daśarātra* sacrifice, on the fourth day, this hymn is the *vaiśvadeva-nividdāna* within the *vaiśvadeva-śastra*.
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The *vaiśvadeva* [śastra] begins with *pra śukra*... (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 8.8).
Furthermore, regarding the *ṣoḍaśin* [sacrifice], it is stated: "'*ā dhūrvasmā*' is the two-footed verse" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.2).
This same [dvipadā] occurs also in the Mahāvrata;
likewise, it is stated in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: "‘ā dhūrvasmai’ is one [verse], the Sūddohās" (AiĀ 5.2.2).
May the divine inspired thought go forth from us, like a well-fashioned, prize-winning chariot.
May the bright goddess of inspired thought go forth from us, like a well-fashioned, prize-winning chariot. 1.

May the bright, radiant goddess Manīṣā, the bestower of all desires, proceed forth like a chariot—well-fashioned and well-prepared—that is praised by us; may she go forward toward the gods who are being extolled in this hymn. May the swift, impetuous one, like a chariot, advance.
The wise know the birthplace of earth and heaven; they hear the waters as they flow.
They know him as the birthplace of the earth and of heaven; even the flowing waters listen. 2.
In this ṛc, the waters are praised:
"the flowing waters [flow] from heaven and from earth"—
that is to say, from both worlds.
They know—that is, they understand—the *janitra*, which means the place of origin;
moreover, they listen to the hymns of praise—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

1. jha-vāsatīvarī; 2. jha-sisicatuḥ; 3. jha-abhiṣavapāṣāṇam; 4. kha-gha-jha-tara-na-bha-śa-bibhratam; 5. kha-kartavye sati; na-bha-kartavyasati; 6. ta-gacchatu; śa-āgacchatu. Ṛgveda 3.23.354 (Aṣṭaka 5, Adhyāya 3, Varga 25).

Even the waters swell for him; the earths expand; even in the midst of obstacles (vṛtras), the fierce ones consider themselves heroes. Even the waters swell for him; the earths expand; even in the midst of obstacles (vṛtras), the fierce ones consider themselves heroes. In this hymn, Indra is praised: "The earths," meaning the expansive regions, and "even the waters" swell and overflow for this Indra. Even when obstacles or calamities arise, those who are "fierce"—meaning exalted or radiant—and "heroes," meaning warriors, likewise "consider themselves" as praising this very Indra.

"Yoke the horses for him; like Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, with golden arms. (4) *Ā dhurṣv asmai dadhādaśvān indro na vajrī hiraṇyabāhuḥ.* (4) The dative case *asmai* is used here in the sense of the genitive (*asya*). For the arrival of this [Indra], "yoke the horses" (*ā dadhāt*) to the poles (*dhurṣu*) of the chariot. "*Indro na*"—the particle *na* has the sense of *ca* (and). Indra is the "wielder of the thunderbolt" (*vajrī*) and possesses "golden arms" (*hiraṇyabāhuḥ*), that is, golden hands. Because this verse is recited during the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, it is understood to belong to Indra. In the phrase "*ā dhurṣv asmai*," the word *asmai* is unaccented because Indra was the subject of the preceding verse. For this very reason, it is recognized that the preceding verse also belongs to Indra. In the preceding *ṛc* as well, the word *asmai* is unaccented; however, the unaccented form is used when the meaning is less significant. Thus Yāska says: "The pronoun *asya* is accented when it is a nominative substitute; it is unaccented when it is a substitute for other cases. When the accent is close to a sharp tone, the unaccented form is closer to the accented one" (*Nirukta* 4.25). This "lesser degree" (*alpīyastva*) should be understood as the proximity of the cause for the application of the word *veva*, which is situated at a distance.

Set forth toward the sacrifice like one setting out; like a traveler on his path, urge yourselves forward by your own power. (5) This is a praise of the sacrifice: O people, set forth toward the sacrifice; advance toward it. "Like one setting out" (*aha iva*) completes the comparison. Furthermore, on the path (*patman*), that is, on the path of sacrifice, "like a traveler," that is, like one who goes, "by your own power" (*tmanā*), "urge yourselves forward"—that is, go. The root *hi* means "to go."

By yourselves, go forth in battles; establish the sacrifice, set up the banner for the people—the hero. (6) This is an elaboration of what was already stated. O my people, in battles (*samatsu*), by yourselves (*tmanā*) go forth (*hinota*). Furthermore, for the sake of the people (*janāya*), establish (*dadhāta*) the sacrifice (*yajñam*)—that is, for their protection—setting up the banner (*ketum*), the hero (*vīram*), meaning the destroyer of evils. Set it up; ordain it.

From his vigor the light has risen; he bears the burden as the earth bears the world. (7) From his vigor (*śuṣma*), the light (*bhānu*)—the sun—has risen (*ud-ārta*). And like the earth bearing the multitude of beings (*bhūma*), this sacrifice of his bears the burden of the world.

I invoke the gods, O Agni, who are free from disease; with the *ṛta* as my companion, I fix my thought upon them. (8) I invoke the gods, O Agni, who are free from disease; with the *ṛta* as my companion, I fix my thought upon them. (8)
1. śa—It increases.
2. jña ta1-2—The earth is not like the earth.
3. gha jña ta1-2 ca—And it is not full.
In this triplet of verses, the gods are praised.
O Agni, I invoke the gods with *ṛta*—the sacrifice characterized by non-violence and other such restraints—accomplishing desires and bringing them to fulfillment.
Moreover, I perform the *dhi*, the ritual activity consisting of the service of the gods.
The meaning is "I perform."
Direct your divine thought toward us; send forth your speech to the gods.
Direct your divine thought toward us; raise your voice toward the gods. 9.
O people, you all, directed toward the gods, should establish—that is, perform—the radiant *dhi* (inspired action);
moreover, you all should offer forth—that is, produce excellently—the speech in the form of praise among the gods.
The mighty Varuṇa, the thousand-eyed, has surveyed the course of these rivers as they move toward their destination.
Varuṇa, the fierce one with a thousand eyes, ordains the course of these rivers. 10.
Varuṇa, the thousand-eyed one with many eyes, observes—that is, beholds—the path, that is, the water, of these rivers.
Of what nature is Varuṇa?
He is fierce, impetuous, or powerful.
The king is the form of the realms, the leader of the rivers; to him belongs supreme sovereignty for all life.
The king [is] the ornament of kingdoms; [he is] the foremost of rivers. To him belongs sovereignty, all-encompassing life. 11.
Of kingdoms, of kingdoms.
The absence of the *natva* (the substitution of *n* for *ṇ*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
Varuṇa is the sovereign king even of the lords;
he is the beauty of the rivers—that is to say, he is also the fashioner of forms.
To him.
The dative case is used here in the sense of the genitive.
This Varuṇa’s sovereignty (*kṣatra*)—his power—is "unconquered" (*anuttama*), meaning unopposed by others; it is "all-pervading" (*viśvāyu*), meaning it extends everywhere.
May he, pervading us in all our dwellings, render the curse of the reviler ineffective.
"Having entered us, at all times, make the praise of the one who seeks to revile us insignificant. 12.
This is a verse addressed to the gods:
"O gods, protect us (*aviṣṭana*) in all our various offspring.
*Aviṣṭa* and *u* are combined as *aviṣṭo*.
Protect him;
and against the curse of the enemy who desires to revile him, make it [your own] lack of luster—render it powerless.
May the hostility of our enemies depart; may he separate all those who incite us to strife.
May it go away from us; drive far away the malice of our enemies and the affliction of our bodies. 13.
May the weapon of the hating enemies—the one that brings misfortune—depart and vanish from every side.
O gods, remove and separate from us the evil and sin of our bodies and our ignorance.
The beloved Agni has been established for him with oblations; a hymn of praise has been offered to him.
Agni has been invoked by us with reverent salutations; the most beloved hymn has been offered to him. 14.
May Agni, the eater of oblations, being most beloved through our reverential salutations (*namas*), protect us;
for this Agni, a hymn of praise has been offered by us.
1. *Jha-śaṃsaṃ* means praise. 2. *Kha-kṣā-asukhakarā* means that which causes unhappiness.

Making him our friend together with the gods, may the Son of the Waters be auspicious to us. (15) Together with the gods, making the Son of the Waters our friend, may he be auspicious to us. (15) O worshippers, make Abhimanyu—the Son of the Waters, that is, the Son of the waters—your friend and ally through your hymns, together with the gods. And may that Son of the Waters be auspicious, a bringer of happiness, unto us.

With hymns, you praise Aja, the Dragon, who sits at the bottom of the rivers in the mid-air regions. "With hymns, you praise Aja, the Dragon, who sits at the bottom of the rivers in the mid-air regions. Aja is the slayer of the clouds (ahiṃ meghānām āhantāram). He sits at the "bottom" (budhne), that is, in the place of the waters of the rivers; for the etymology of *budhna* is "the atmosphere (*antarikṣa*) in which the waters are bound and held. Sitting there in those "mid-air regions" (*rajaḥsu*), which means in the waters, you praise with hymns—that is, with songs of praise—this Aja, who is born in the waters (*ap-jām*). As it is said in the Nirukta (10.44): "At the bottom of the rivers, sitting in the mid-air regions, that is, in the waters; 'budhna' is the atmosphere, so called because the waters are bound and held therein."

May Ahibudhnya not deliver us over to harm; may his sacrifice of the one seeking the *ṛta* be successful. (17) May Ahibudhnya not give us up to injury (*riṣe*). May the sacrifice of this seeker of *ṛta* (*ṛtāyoḥ*)—the sacrificer who desires the sacrifice—not fail. *Ahibudhnya*: "Budhnya" means that which exists in the *budhna*, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); he is both a serpent (*ahi*) and Budhnya, thus Ahibudhnya. May he not deliver us to injury—that is, may he not hand us over to the harmful one. And may the sacrifice of this seeker of *ṛta*—of the sacrificer desiring the sacrifice—not perish. Or alternatively: the meaning is that the sacrifice of this seeker of *ṛta* directed toward this Ahibudhnya—that is, the sacrifice performed for the sake of Ahibudhnya—shall not be exhausted.

And may they bestow renown upon these men of ours; may the noble ones, exulting, advance toward wealth. (18) And indeed, may the gods or the Maruts bestow *śravaḥ*—food or fame—upon these men of ours. May the noble ones (*aryaḥ*), exulting (*śṛdhantaḥ*)—meaning either exerting themselves or rejoicing—for the sake of wealth (*rāye*), go forth (*pra yantu*). That is to say, may they attain prosperity.

They satisfy the enemy, like the sun the earth; these great-armied ones [afflict] them with their onslaughts. (19) They satisfy the enemy, like the sun the earth; these great-armied kings, by means of the *ama*s—i.e., the powers—of these Maruts, the gods, afflict (*tapanti*) and oppress the enemy, just as the sun [afflicts] the worlds. Even great kings oppress enemies by means of their *ama*s, i.e., their forces; those forces are of divine nature—this is the meaning.
From whence our wives come hither, may Tvaṣṭṛ, the fair-handed, bestow upon us heroic sons. || 20 ||
1. *jha-gṛṇīṣe* means "I praise. 2. *jha-yāskaḥ*. 3. *kha-jha-śa-yaiḥ*.
In this [hymn], Tvaṣṭṛ is the deity and the wives of the gods are the deities.
When the wives of the gods come toward us, then may the god Tvaṣṭṛ, with beautiful hands, grant us heroic sons.
May Tvaṣṭṛ accept our hymn of praise; may Aramati, who seeks wealth, be present with us.
May Tvaṣṭṛ accept our hymn of praise; may Aramati, who seeks wealth, be present among us. 21.
May Tvaṣṭṛ accept—that is, favor—our hymn of praise;
moreover, may Tvaṣṭṛ, who possesses sufficient wisdom or whose intellect pervades all objects, become one who desires wealth for us.
May they both grant us riches; may Rodasī and Varuṇānī hear us.
With the Varūtrīs as our protectors, may Tvaṣṭṛ be a secure refuge for us; may he, the bounteous giver, bestow wealth upon us.

May she, the giver of wealth, the mistress of the sacrifice, grant us riches; may Rodasī and Varuṇānī hear us. May he who provides excellent refuge be with us through the protectresses; may Tvaṣṭṛ, the bounteous giver, bestow upon us riches. 22.
May those *vasūni*, the desired riches that are accompanied by gifts (*rātipācaḥ*), the wives of the gods (*devapatnyaḥ*), grant them to us—*naḥ*, to us—*rāsan*, may they bestow them.
Furthermore, may *Varuṇānī*, the wife of Varuṇa, listen to our hymn; may she hear it.
And may *Rodasī*, Heaven and Earth, both hear it.
May Tvaṣṭṛ, the giver of auspicious gifts, together with the Varūtrīs—the wives of the gods who ward off calamities—be a good refuge for us, a bestower of secure protection;
may he also distribute riches and wealth unto us.
Then let the mountains, the waters, the nights, and the plants, as well as the sky, the trees,
and the earth with her pleasant companions— may both worlds protect us on every side.

May that wealth come to us from the mountains; may that come to us from the waters, that from the gods who delight in giving, and from the plants. May the sky with its forest trees and the earth, well-disposed, and may both heaven and earth, protect us on every side. 23.
ᵛnaḥ: for us. ᵛtat: this is an indeclinable particle.
ᵛtāḥ: those. ᵛrāyaḥ: riches or wealth. ᵛparvatāḥ: mountains. ᵛparipām: [of] protection.
May those riches of ours and the waters protect us;
may the divine wives, accompanied by gifts, protect us;
and may the medicinal herbs also protect us.
Moreover, may Heaven protect that;
and may Earth and the Mid-region, joined together with the lords of the forest (*vanaspati*), protect that—
since "the waters" and "the earth" are recited among the names for the mid-region.
May even both *rodasī*, heaven and earth, protect us on every side.
May the two vast worlds, heaven and earth, yield to this; may the celestial Varuṇa, with Indra as his friend, yield to it;
and may all the Maruts who possess great power yield to it. May we be the sustainers of wealth for the sake of meditative thought.

1. jña-ta1-2-asyā; 2. jña-śa-anuparatiḥ vā tvaṣṭā; 3. jña-tā tāni; ya-tāni; 4. jña-ta1-4-ya-’tāni does not exist; 5. jña-ya-dānena sametāḥ; ta1-dāninaḥ sametāḥ; ta2-4-dāninaḥ sametāḥ; 6. kha-na-bha-abhiśṛṇoti.

May the two vast worlds, Heaven and Earth, grant their assent to that; may Varuṇa, the friend of Indra, grant his assent; and may all the Maruts, who are powerful, grant their assent. May we become the support for the bestowing of wealth. May the two vast worlds, Heaven and Earth (*urvī rodasī*), grant their assent to that which is about to be spoken of; that is, may they follow it or give their approval. *Dhukṣaḥ* means the dwelling place of light; *Indra-sakha* (the friend of Indra)—where "Indra" is the companion—forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound. May Varuṇa also grant his assent to that. The dual ending is changed here to a singular. And those Maruts who are *sahasaḥ*, meaning conquerors of enemies—they too shall grant their assent. Here, the plural ending is changed. He states what is to be approved: *dhiyadhyai* (to be supported), in order to maintain and sustain *rāyaḥ* (wealth), may we become *dharuṇam* (the support, the foundation, the place). May Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Agni, the Waters, and the Plants take pleasure in that. May we abide in the protection of the Maruts in their lap. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. *That... naḥ* (that... for us).

May Bhaga be for our peace; may the praise (of Narāśaṃsa) be for our well-being; may Purandhi be for our peace; may riches be for our well-being. May the word of Truth, which is well-guided, be for our peace; may Aryaman, born in many places, be for our peace. May the god Bhaga be for our peace—that is, for our tranquility. May the praise (śaṃsa), namely Narāśaṃsa, be for our well-being—indeed, for our peace. May Purandhi, the one of great wisdom, be for our peace—that is, for our tranquility. May riches also be for our well-being—indeed, for our peace. May even the word (śaṃsa) of Truth, which is well-restrained, be for our peace. May Aryaman, who is manifested in many forms, be for our peace—that is, for our tranquility.
May the medicinal herbs also be auspicious;
may the forest trees be a source of well-being;
and may Indra, the victorious lord of the world (rajas), also be for our peace and tranquility.
May the god Indra with the Vasus be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa, the one of fair praise, with the Ādityas be auspicious;
may Rudra, the healer, with the Rudras be auspicious to us; and may Tvaṣṭṛ with the Bhāmis hear us here for our well-being.

May the god Indra with the Vasus be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa, the one of fair praise, with the Ādityas be auspicious; may Rudra, the healer, with the Rudras be auspicious to us; and may Tvaṣṭṛ with his radiance hear us here for our well-being. 6.
May the god Indra, endowed with qualities such as radiance, together with the Vasu deities, be for our peace and well-being.
May the god Varuṇa, of excellent praise, together with the Āditya deities, be for our peace.

May Aditi be auspicious to us through her sacred observances; may the Maruts, who are praised with beautiful hymns, be auspicious to us. May Viṣṇu be auspicious to us, and may Pūṣan be a source of peace for us. May the world (or the waters) be auspicious to us, and may Vāyu be a source of peace for us. Aditi, the goddess, together with her *vratas*—her sacred rites and actions—may she be for our peace (*śam*). May the Maruts, who are praised with beautiful hymns (*su-arkāḥ*), also be for our peace. May Viṣṇu, the all-pervading one, be for our peace. May the god Pūṣan also be for our peace alone. May the *bhavitra*—the world, the intermediate space, or the waters—be for our peace. And may Vāyu also be for our peace alone.

May the divine Savitṛ, the protector, be auspicious to us; may the radiant dawns be auspicious to us. May Parjanya be auspicious to our offspring; may the Lord of the Field, the source of well-being, be auspicious to us. May the divine Savitṛ, endowed with qualities such as playfulness and the like, being the protector who guards us, be for our peace. May the dawns, shining brightly, also be for our peace. May Parjanya also be for the peace of our progeny. May the Lord of the Field, the bringer of happiness, be for our peace.

May the gods, the Viśvedevas, be auspicious to us; may Sarasvatī be auspicious along with our prayers and deeds. May those who attend the sacrifice be auspicious, and may those who accept our offerings be auspicious. May the celestial beings be auspicious to us, the terrestrial beings be auspicious to us, and the beings of the waters be auspicious to us. May the Viśvedevas—the gods who receive many hymns—be for our peace and well-being. And may Sarasvatī, together with our *dhīs* (prayers or ritual acts), be for our peace. May the *abhiṣācas* (those who attend to the sacrifice from all sides) be for our peace, and may the *rātiṣācas* (those who partake of our gifts) also be for our peace alone. May the celestial (*divya*) beings, existing in heaven, be for our peace; may the terrestrial (*pārthiva*) beings, born upon the earth, be for our peace; and may the aquatic (*apya*) beings, existing within the waters—that is, in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), since "the waters" are listed among the names for the atmosphere—be for our peace. May they all be for our peace and well-being.

May the Lords of Truth be auspicious to us; may the coursers be auspicious to us, and may the bulls be full of peace. May the Ṛbhus, the doers of good deeds with skillful hands, be auspicious to us; may the Fathers be auspicious to us in our invocations. 12. śam | naḥ | satyasya | patayaḥ | bhavantu | śam | naḥ | arvantaḥ | śam | u | santu | gāvaḥ | śam | naḥ | ṛbhavaḥ | su-kṛtaḥ | su-hastāḥ | śam | naḥ | bhavantu | pitaraḥ | haveṣu || 12 ||

May the gods, the lords and protectors of Truth, who are themselves of truthful character, be for our peace (*śam*). May the swift horses be for our peace; may the cows also be for our peace. May the *Ṛbhus*, who are well-performing, of good deeds, and of beautiful hands, be for our peace. And may the Fathers, rejoicing in our invocations and hymns, be for our peace. May the god Aja Ekapāt be for our peace; may Ahi Budhnya be for our peace; may the ocean be for our peace. May the distant protector, Apāṃ Napāt, be for our peace; may Pṛśni, whose guardians are the gods, be for our peace. May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus enjoy this prayer being performed, O newest ones. May the celestial and the terrestrial, those born of the Cow, and those who are worthy of sacrifice, hear us. The Ādityas—the celestial ones (for the Śruti says, "the thirty [deities]"); the Rudras—the atmospheric ones; and the Vasus—the terrestrial ones—may they enjoy this newest prayer being composed by us. Furthermore, may the other celestial ones, the terrestrial ones, and those born of the Cow (Pṛśni)—since "Cow" is listed among the common names for heaven—and those who are worthy of sacrifice, all of them hear our invocation. Those who are worthy of sacrifice among the gods worthy of sacrifice, who are worshipful to Manu, immortal, and knowers of Truth (*ṛta*); may they grant us wide-striding progeny. And do you, O gods, protect us always with blessings. May those gods who are worthy of sacrifice among the gods worthy of sacrifice, who are worshipful to Manu Prajāpati, who are immortal and knowers of Truth—they all grant us wide-striding progeny. (The final quarter-verse has already been explained. By illuminating the meaning of the Veda and dispelling the darkness of the heart, may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara bestow the four aims of human life. Thus ends the third chapter of the Fifth Book in the *Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa*, a commentary on the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the minister of the sovereign King Vīrabukka, the promoter of the Vedic path under the supreme lordship of the Emperor. 1. *Jha-ta-śa*: others. 2. *Ta3-śa2*: by Sāyaṇācārya.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now begins the fourth chapter of the fifth Aṣṭaka.
Therein, in the third Anuvāka of the seventh Maṇḍala composed by Vasiṣṭha—which consists of six Anuvākas—there are twenty-two Sūktas.
Among these, the third Sūkta, consisting of nine verses beginning with "pra brahma," is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and, as before, is dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
And it has been recited: "pra brahma nava.
The application [of the mantra] is based on its indicative mark (liṅga).
From the seat of the sacrifice, Sūrya has sent forth his prayers; with his rays, he has released the cows.
The broad earth has spread out with its ridges; Agni stands in the midst with his wide face.

Let the sacred prayer proceed from the seat of Cosmic Order; Sūrya has released the cows with his rays. The broad earth has spread out with her ridges; Agni has been kindled upon his wide-extending face.

From the seat, the place of the sacrifice of Truth (*ṛta*), from the region of the gods, let the sacred hymn (*brahman*)—the praise—go forth preeminently toward those worthy of praise, such as the Sun and others. How so? He says: "The Sun," the god who impels all or possesses a beautiful color, [goes] with his own rays, his beams.
He has released, he releases, and he lets loose the rays—the waters, that is, the waters of rain;
he pours them down.
For it is heard [in scripture]: "With those very rays by which the sun shines, with those Parjanya rains" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.63).
And there is a traditional teaching (smṛti): "From the sun rain is born; from rain, food; and from that, living beings.
Therefore, by this quarter-verse, the sun is praised, for such majesty belongs to the sun alone and to no other.
Furthermore, the earth—the well-known ground—being vast and wide, along with its elevated mountains and the like, spreads out and pervades everywhere.
Likewise, upon (*adhi*) this broad (*pṛthu*), extensive (*vistīrṇa*) surface (*pratīka*) of the earth—that is, the place characterized by the assembly of gods—the fire is kindled (*edhe*).

Since *adhi* and *pari* are designated as *anarthaka* (meaningless/without specific semantic weight), they receive the technical designation of *karmapravacanīya*; consequently, by the rule "when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*," the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative.
It is kindled in such a place.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, O Asuras, I fashion for you this newest well-spoken hymn like nourishing food.
No other is more powerful than you; he who speaks as a friend among the people exerts himself as your messenger.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, O Asuras, I fashion this new, well-spoken hymn for you like strengthening food. One of you is a powerful, infallible pathfinder; the other, Mitra, watches over the people as he speaks.
O powerful Asuras, O Mitra and Varuna, I, the singer, offer this newest hymn of praise—like fresh food consisting of oblations—to you both.
Of you two, one is the lord, Varuna, who is invincible, unharmed by enemies, and the progenitor of the station (padavīḥ);
for Varuna is called "the progenitor of the station" because he is the upholder of dharma and adharma.
Speaking thus and being praised by us, Mitra impels—that is, he moves and sets in motion—the entire people, the whole multitude of living beings.
And so it is heard in the Veda: "Mitra, speaking, impels the people" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.59.1).
The streams of the rushing wind have sped hither; like milch-cows they have swelled with milk.
Born at the seat of heaven, the steed, being groomed, has neighed loudly upon this summit.
Of the one who moves swiftly, as he flows, the streams have swelled like milch-cows. Born at the seat of the great heaven, the bull has bellowed in this place of abundance.
The movements (*ityāḥ*) of the wind (*vātasya*), as it moves (*vrajataḥ*), rest (*ā rante*) all around;
likewise, the *sūdāḥ*.
The root is *sūda* in the sense of "impelling."
They shall cause the milk to flow like milch-cows;
and in the sense of "not," the cows also swell, they become full, and they flourish.

Moreover, the great bull Parjanya, characterized by his habit of raining, being born—that is, arising—in that seat or place of the great, shining sun, namely the intermediate space (antarikṣa), has bellowed within that very intermediate space.
With this speech, O Indra, I yoke for you these two swift, beloved, and powerful steeds that carry you, O Hero.
May I turn toward you, the one of excellent wisdom, who thwarts death as it seeks to strike and who brings the sun to a halt.

O Indra, O Hero, with this song may I bring hither Aryaman, the one of noble will, who yokes for you these two beloved bay horses, well-yoked and swift; he who destroys the death that seeks to strike us down. (4)
Of this [verse], the first half-verse is a praise of Indra, and the latter half is a praise of Aryaman.

O *śūra*, O valiant *indra*, *te*—of you—*priyā*, the two beloved ones; *surathā*, having excellent chariots; *dhāyū*, the two sustainers; *etā*, these two; *harī*, your two bay horses—whatever person *girā*, with speech in the form of praise, *yunajat*, should yoke them to the chariot, O Indra, you [should come to his sacrifice]—this is the ellipsis.
May I turn toward Aryaman—the one of excellent deeds—with praise, he who utterly destroys the wrath and anger of the enemy who desires to harm us.
The reverent ones worship his swift vigor in the very abode of Truth; he, being praised by men, has driven away the two enemies. This most beloved homage is for Rudra.

They sacrifice to him, the one who hears us, the one to whom we pay homage, in his own abode of Truth. He has spread abroad nourishments, being praised by men. This most beloved homage is for Rudra. 5.
By this [verse], Rudra is praised.
Those who possess reverence (*namasvin*) and are endowed with oblations (*havirlakṣaṇānvantaḥ*), standing in each respective place (*dhāmani dhāmani*) of the *ṛta*—
that is, the sacrifice— meaning they are situated within their own sacrificial hall.
And we, the sacrificers performing rituals, worship—that is, honor—this Rudra, aiming for his renowned friendship.
Being praised by men, the leaders, Rudra bestows—that is, firmly grants—*pṛkṣaḥ*, food, upon the singers.
The meaning is that he gives it.
This most beloved salutation is performed by me for that Rudra, the most dear to Rudra.
When the two glorious ones come together lowing, Sarasvatī, the mother of rivers, is the seventh;
they who flow forth, well-yielding with good streams, swelling with their own milk.
When the glorious ones lowed together, Sarasvatī, the seventh, mother of the rivers—those who flow forth well, yielding milk, with beautiful streams, swelling with their own milk—[they came]. 6.

1. *śa*—it swells (*āpyāyate*). 2. *jha-ya*—in all [manuscripts]; *ta1-4*—in that (*tasmin*); *ta3*—in this (*sismin*). 3. *jha*—he made sound (*acikadat śabdāyate*). 4. *kha-sa-ta3-4-na-bha-śa*—of which (*yasya*); *jha*—of that (*tasya*). 5. *jha*—he strikes him down (*hinasti tam*).

Among those rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others, the river named Sarasvatī—who is the mother of the waters (*apām mātṛbhūtā*) and the mother of the Sindhu—is the seventh (*sasathī saptamī*). She is "well-milking" (*sudughāḥ*), meaning she is easily able to yield one's desires; she is "possessing beautiful streams" (*sudhārāḥ*); and these rivers "flow beautifully" (*suṣyavanta*). This is a verb meaning "to go."
Let the rivers flow forth; swelling with their own waters, increasing [the crops], glorious, and lowing—that is, desiring—let them come together at once.
(The verb "come" is to be supplied in connection with the prefix *ā*.)
And may those Maruts, being exhilarated, protect our prayer, our offspring, and our strength;
may they not overlook us as they move through the imperishable [spaces], and may they increase for us enduring wealth.

And may those Maruts, rejoicing, protect our prayer and our offspring, O possessors of strength! May Viṣṇu and Akṣarā not overlook us; may they bestow upon me, who sings and praises, progeny in the form of sons and vital food. May they grant it! May they bestow it! May they grant it!
O Maruts, O Viṣṇu, may you all always—through blessings that are non-destructive—protect and guard us.
The verse beginning with “ā vo vāhiṣṭhaḥ” is found in the fourth hymn; it belongs to Vasiṣṭha, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is addressed to the Viśvedevas.
It is enumerated as “ā vo’ṣṭau.
Its application is indicated by its internal characteristics (liṅga).
O Vājās, O R̥bhukṣans, let your most swift and inviolable chariot bring you hither to be praised.
At the libations, with triple draughts of Soma, fill yourselves with great joy, O fair-cheeked ones!

May your most swift chariot bring you hither to be praised, O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans—uninjured. At the libations, fill yourselves with the triple-backed Soma-juices for exhilaration, O fair-jawed ones, with great [splendors].
By this verse, the Ṛbhus are praised:

O Ṛbhukṣans, you who are the abodes of vast splendor; O Vājas, O Ṛbhus! May your chariot—the most excellent carrier (*vāhiṣṭha*), worthy of praise (*stavadhyai*), and unimpaired (*amṛkta*) by any [enemy]—bring you hither (*vahatu*) and carry you all around to our sacrifice.

O you of beautiful jaws (*suśiprāḥ*), having arrived with that chariot at our sacrifices during the *savanas*, for the sake of exhilaration (*made*), fill (*abhipṛṇadhvam*) your own bellies with the great Soma juices—those which are "three-backed" (*tripṛṣṭhaiḥ*), consisting of milk, curd, and parched barley flour (*saktubhiḥ*). The connection with the preceding verse is: "May that chariot carry you [to us]."
You indeed bestow treasure upon the bounteous patrons, O R̥bhukṣans, you who behold the light of heaven, an unimpaired gift.
Drink together at the sacrifices, O self-dependent ones; distribute riches to us through our prayers.

You indeed bestow treasure upon the bounteous patrons; O R̥bhukṣans, you who behold the light of heaven, drink together at the sacrifices, you who possess self-sustaining power; and through our prayers, grant us riches. 2.

O Vṛbhukṣans, O Ṛbhus, you who behold the light of heaven (*svardarśaḥ*), seeing the celestial realm— you yourselves indeed, for our sake— bestow upon us, who possess the sacrificial offerings characterized by oblations, that which is unimpaired (*amṛktam*),
meaning it has not been stolen by thieves or others;
you hold fast that delightful treasure (*ratnam*).
Immediately thereafter, O you who possess inherent power and strength, drink together—drink the Soma properly—at our sacrifices;
moreover, with your insights for the sake of wealth, bestow upon us riches; grant them to us abundantly.
For you have granted a gift, O Maghavan, at the distribution of wealth, both great and small;
both your arms are full of riches, and your hand does not withhold the abundance of treasure.
For you have bestowed, O Maghavan, a gift of wealth, both great and small, at its distribution. Both your hands are full of riches; indeed, the one who bestows wealth does not withhold it. 3.
The [hymns] beginning with ‘uvocitha’ have Indra as their deity.

O *maghavan*, O wealthy Indra, you indeed (*hi*) *uvocitha*—that is, you attend to or bestow—*deṣṇam*, wealth, for the purpose of giving, which is conducive to service, in the distribution of *mahaḥ*, great, and *arbhásya*, small, *vasunaḥ*, wealth.
The root *ucati* signifies the act of serving.
Likewise, both your two arms are filled with wealth;
your lofty speech bestows riches.
1. [He is] joined with *jha*, *kṣa*, *ta*, *la*, *4*, *saṃ*, and *ṣi*. 2. By means of the causes of wealth (*dhana-hetubhiḥ*), which are to be meditated upon through hymns (*mananīyaiḥ stotraiḥ*).

He neither blows away (*na ni dhamate*) nor restrains (*na niyacchati*). Or rather: she who is excellent (*sādhuḥ*) among the treasures (*vasuṣu*) worthy of being dwelt in (*vasadhyā*), whose speech is truthful and pleasant (*sūnṛtā vāk*), and who is full of breath (*dhamena saṃpūrṇā*), does not restrain her two arms (*bāhū na niyacchati*). The meaning is that she does not cause the price to be paid.
O Indra, you of resounding fame, R̥bhukṣan, like Vāja the successful, come home with our hymns.
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, may we, the Vasiṣṭhas, now be those who offer you choice gifts while performing sacred prayer.

O Indra, you who possess glorious fame, lord of the *Ṛbhus*, you go toward our home like one skilled in battle; we, the Vasiṣṭhas, now desire to offer to you, making prayers for you, O Lord of the Bay Horses. 4.

O Indra, you who are self-glorious, possessing unique renown, the lord of the Ṛbhus (Ṛbhukṣan)—whether as the one who dwells among the Ṛbhus or the master of those named Ṛbhus—you, being virtuous and effective like food (vāja), come to our home, which is worthy of praise; reach it!
Now, therefore, O Lord of Bay Horses (Harivan), O Indra, for your sake, we, the sages known as the Vasiṣṭhas, [pray].

Even the goddess Nirṛti herself rules over him; the beautiful autumns reach Indra. With three kinships, he approaches the power that wears out old age—the power which mortals make for themselves so that he has no dwelling place. The shining goddess Nirṛti, the Earth, indeed rules over him. [The suffix -ya denotes "that which is to be ruled over. Being her own, she reaches—that is, pervades—Indra. The beautiful autumns, those years of excellent form, also reach and pervade Indra. Mortals, we singers subject to death, make Indra one who has no dwelling place, one who does not settle in his own station. He, Indra, the binder and sustainer of the three worlds, approaches with that power whose cause is the wearing away of old age—that power by which food is consumed.

May bounties come to us from you, O Savitṛ, for our praise; may riches come from the gift of Parvata. May the divine protector always attend to us. Do you all protect us always with blessings. (8) O Savitṛ, impeller of all, may wealth worthy of being praised come to us from you. Upon the giving of the god named Parvata—a friend of Indra—may riches come to us. May the divine protector, the guardian of all who dwells in heaven—that Indra—always attend to us with his protection. O all you gods set forth in this hymn, do you all protect us always with well-being. (8)
The fifth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "udu tyad devaḥ," is the Ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and has Savitṛ as its deity.
The seventh and eighth verses have the Vājins as their deities.
The half-verse beginning with "bhagam ugro 'vase" has Bhaga as its deity, or alternatively, Savitṛ.

And thus the table of contents (anukramaṇikā) states: "Then follows the Sāvitra; at the end are the two [verses] beginning with 'vājini' and 'bhaga'; the portion consists of one or two verses. The application of the hymn (sūkta-viniyoga) has been explained.

God Savitar has extended that golden form which he has sent forth. Truly, Bhaga is to be invoked by men—he who, possessing abundant wealth, bestows jewels. Savitar, the impeller of all—that very god—has extended that golden *amati* (form or radiance) which he has sent forth; he raises it aloft, he lifts it up. (*Ut* is used here as a metrical filler. Truly, today, Bhaga—the one worthy of being shared—is to be invoked by men, by the worshippers; he is to be called upon for praise. He, the possessor of much wealth, the god who distributes (*vidadhāti*) jewels, delightful riches, to those who praise him—that god Savitar has raised that *amati* aloft; this is the connection with what precedes.
Arise, O Savitṛ, and hear this man, O golden-handed one, as you extend your bounty.
Casting forth your wide and broad thought, bestow nourishment upon the mortal men.
1. Those which are expressed by the syllables *kha*, *jña*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*.

2. O Śaraksata! Ut! Ūm! Stand up, O Savitṛ! Listen to this! O golden-handed one, at the impulse of the cosmic Order (*ṛta*), releasing wide space and broad earth, free from decay, bestowing upon men the food that sustains mortals. ||2||
O Savitṛ, O God who impels all things, do thou arise and go upward.
Then, O Hiraṇyapāṇi, O Golden-handed One, for the sake of granting our desired objects, at the offering and commencement of the *ṛta*—the sacrifice—do thou hear (*śṛdhi*) this our hymn of praise.
The particle *u* is a filler.
What kind of person are you?

You who emit—that is, radiate—your immortal form and splendor across the vast, wide, and renowned earth; you who impel toward the leaders, the singers, and the mortals that food which is suitable for human enjoyment, namely wealth;
being such as this, you should hear this hymn—this is the connection of the words.
May Savitṛ, the praised god, be present—he whom all the Vasus and even the Aśvins extol.
May he accept our hymns of praise; may he protect us and our patrons with all his guardians.
May Savitṛ, the god, be praised—he whom all the Vasus indeed extol. May he, who is worthy of homage, find pleasure in our hymns; with all his protections, may he guard the patrons.
Moreover, may the god Savitṛ be praised by us;
the meaning is that he should listen to our hymns.

Even all the Vasus—indeed, all the gods—who praise and extol that Savitṛ, that god who is worthy of homage and to be revered by all—he, the god, shall bestow *canaḥ*, food, upon our *stomān*, our hymns of praise.
May he grant us the fruits of our food;
with all protections, with every means of preservation, may he guard us—the patrons and us who offer praise—most excellently.
Whom the goddess Aditi praises, rejoicing in the impulse of the god Savitṛ;
whom Varuṇa, the sovereign, praises, and whom Mitra and Aryaman praise in unison.
Him whom the goddess Aditi praises, taking pleasure in the impulse of the god Savitṛ; him the sovereign Varuṇa praises, and Mitra and Aryaman in unison. 4.

The goddess Aditi, shining and undepressed, the mother of the gods, praises—that is, extols—the god Savitṛ. Of what nature is she? She is one who delights in—that is, accepts and serves—the *sava*, the impulse or permission, of the god Savitṛ himself.
The sovereigns— meaning those who shine perfectly, such as Varuṇa (this being an elliptical expression including Varuṇa and the other gods)—
those deities who praise and extol that Savitṛ.

May the Mitrāsas and those beginning with Mitra, as well as Aryaman—the god so named—being of one accord and equal affection, bestow these upon us; this connects with the preceding verse: "May he place our hymns within his mind."
May those who move together, vying with one another—the guardians of the gift from heaven and earth—hear us;
may Ahibudhnya and Varuṇa hear us, and may he protect us with his many fires.
Those who move together in mutual rivalry, the givers of heaven and the followers of bounty upon earth—may Ahi Budhnya hear us, and may Varuṇa protect us with his single-cow herds. 5.
The *rātiṣāc*—those who bestow gifts, the seekers, the sharers—who, as sacrificers, having united with one another, worship and attend upon Savitṛ. Of what sort?
[They worship him] who is the gift (*rāti*) of heaven (*divaḥ*), the celestial world, and of earth (*pṛthivyāḥ*).
It is a friend;
and moreover, Ahirbudhnya—
the one dwelling in the intermediate space (antarīkṣa) is Budhnya.
The passage beginning with "etīti" and so forth:
that which is designated by these two words, situated in the middle, is called Abhirahirbudhnya.
Being a friend of Savitṛ, may he too hear our hymn directed toward Savitṛ.
Likewise, may the goddess of speech, Varutrī, being accompanied by Savitṛ, protect us thoroughly with the "Ekadhenu" cows—that is, with the most excellent cattle.
May the Lord of the House favor this our prayer, seeking the treasure of the divine Savitar.
The fierce one calls aloud for Bharga for the sake of protection; the non-fierce one likewise approaches for the sake of Bharga and for treasure.
May Jāspati grant us that treasure of the god Savitṛ, when he is entreated. The fierce one repeatedly invokes Bhaga for protection; the mild one likewise attains Bhaga and half the treasure. 6.
Being entreated by us, Savitṛ—the Lord of Creatures (jāspati), the protector of all beings—may he graciously grant us that well-known and delightful wealth belonging to himself, the god Savitṛ.
The powerful worshipper loudly invokes Bhaga—the adorable one, or the god named Bhaga—for our protection.
Moreover, even if the praiser is incapable of favoring him, he approaches Bhaga—so named—or Savitṛ, to beg for *ralam*, that well-known and delightful wealth.
At the Vaiśvadeva parvan, there are two invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) for the *vājina* oblation, beginning with "May they be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no bhavantu*).

This is stated in the Sūtra: "‘May the Vājins be auspicious to us in our invocations; protect us in every contest,’ [this] is the uninterrupted offering verse (*yājyā*) recited straight upward" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.16).
May the Vājins be auspicious to us in our invocations—those who protect among the gods, who move with measured pace, and who possess beautiful voices;
may they crush the serpent, the wolf, and the demons, and drive away all maladies far from us.

May the steeds be auspicious for us in our invocations—those divine protectors who run with measured pace, who are worthy of praise, and who crush the serpent, the wolf, and the demons; may they drive away all maladies far from us. 7.
May the gods who protect among the gods, who come swiftly at our invocations and hymns, who move with measured pace, whose paths are measured, and who are beautiful singers—
may these deities called Vājins be for our well-being and happiness. Moreover, may they be the slayers of the serpent and the seizers of the wolf that carries away our riches.
The word "openly" (*coram*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
And the *vājins*, the gods, who are "crushing" (*jambhayantaḥ*), that is, harming, the *rākṣasas*, [drive them] "without end" (*sanemi*).
This is an ancient name.
May they drive away from us, from each of us, the ancient diseases.
O swift ones, protect us in every contest for booty; O wise, immortal, and truth-knowing ones, drink of this honeyed draught and rejoice; being satisfied, go to the earth with divine songs.

In every contest for booty, O Vājins, protect us in the battles for wealth! O inspired ones, immortal, knowers of the Eternal Law (Ṛta), drink of this honeyed mead and rejoice! Satisfied, go forth upon the paths that traverse the earth, the ways traveled by the gods.
1. Kha, bha, and savitrī are honored; gha, jha, śa, and savitr-prahitā. 2.
Kha, na, bha, and those ending with śobhana; gha, śobhanāga; śa, śobhamāna. 3.
Kha, jha, jña, t (twice), 2, 4, bha, and pṛthakkurvati.
O Vājins—gods of this name, wise, immortal, possessing the nature of the immortals, and knowers of Truth—you who are such, protect us in every battle (vāja-vāje) and for the sake of wealth (dhaneṣu).
Then drink this honeyed Soma;
after drinking the Soma, rejoice and become the saviors of men.
Therefore, O thirsty ones, go forth by way of the paths that serve as the means for traveling to the gods.
The sixth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "ūrdhvo abhiḥ," is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to the Viśvedevas.
The table of contents (Anukramaṇikā) states: "‘Ūrdhvaḥ sa sa vaiśvadevam tu’.
The application of the hymn is based on its internal characteristics (laiṅgika).
In the second Chandoma, in the Prauga-śastra, the triplet beginning with ‘ūrdhvo agniḥ’ belongs to the Viśvedevas.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘The Vasus have sent their benevolence upward; may Sarasvatī also be pleased with us’—this is the Prauga hymn” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.10).
“May the Vasus—the gods known as Vasus—be delighted here, in this sacrifice, on the earth (*jmyāḥ*), being present upon the ground.”
Abiding in the wide, expansive mid-air, the auspicious and radiant Maruts perform their purification;
they are being served. O Vasus and Maruts of vast power and great movement, you who are urugrāyaḥ, make your paths turn hither, toward us.
Furthermore, listen—yea, hear—the call of this our messenger who has come to you.
The meaning is that, acting as a messenger for the sacrificers, he calls upon the gods.
For they, the worshipful ones, the helpers at the sacrifices—all the gods—occupy their common dwelling place.
Worship them first at the sacrifice, you who desire it: Bhaga, the Nāsatyas, and Purandhi, with ready hearing.

For they, the worshipful ones, the helpers at the sacrifices—all the gods—occupy their common dwelling together. Sacrifice to them, O Agni, as they desire at the rite: to Bhaga, to the Nāsatyas, and to Purandhi, with readiness to hear. 4.

In the sacrifices and rites, they indeed are those well-known ones, the *yājñiyāsas*, worthy of sacrifice; the *ūmas*, protectors; all the *devās*, gods; they occupy and overcome the *sadhastham*, the common dwelling place.
O Agni, in our sacrificial rite (*adhvara*), worship—perform the sacrifice for—those gods who desire [it].
Likewise, with readiness (*śruṣṭī*).
Quickly worship this one called Bhaga, the gods Nāsatyas— the two Aśvins— and Purandhi, as well as Indra, the thinker of many thoughts.
From the mountain, from heaven, and from the earth, bring hither Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, and Agni; bring Aryaman, Aditi, and Viṣṇu. May Sarasvatī and the Maruts rejoice among them.
O Agni, from heaven and from earth, bring hither our songs—Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Agni, Aryaman, Aditi, and Viṣṇu. May Sarasvatī and the Maruts rejoice among them. 5.
O Agni, from the sky, bring hither—the gods who are worthy of praise and to be celebrated—to our sacrifice; perform the invocation.
Bring them also from the earth and from the intermediate space.
As for which gods, it is said as follows:

Bring hither for the sake of us, these sacrificers, Mitra by name, Varuṇa, Indra, and Agni who abides among the gods in his divine form; Aryaman by name, Aditi the mother of the gods, the Earth, and Viṣṇu—bring these deities so constituted. And may Sarasvatī, the goddess of speech, and the Maruts rejoice.
And let them rejoice, being distinguished by our hymns of praise.
May the oblation of the worshipful ones reach their desire through our prayers, never failing for mortals; may the Giver bestow inexhaustible wealth, and may we ever be united with the yoked gods.

O Agni, come with the prayers of those worthy of sacrifice; reach the desire of mortals, being unsatiated. Bestow wealth that is never-failing and ever-present. May we now prevail through our allied gods. 6.

The genitive case is used in the sense of the dative. To the gods who are worthy of sacrifice, the oblation (*havyam*) is offered by us, together with our mental offerings (*matibhiḥ*), that is, our hymns of praise. *Re* is a particle used for emphasis.
May [Agni], not withholding our desire—the longing of us mortals, of human beings—reach our sacrifice with unimpeded [flames].
O gods, you who are never failing, always be present.
1. jha-gantumicchati | 2. jñāta-1-2-4 'te' nāsti | 3. ta-mu-pṛthvī | 4 na-vyāpnoti |
O Lord of the chariot, grant us wealth that is always to be honored by all;
indeed, may we now prevail here at this sacrifice together with the gods who have assembled as our worthy allies.
May it be abundant!
*nu* is used in the sense of comparison. May we be joined with the gods as if with kinsmen; may we be united.

Now, may Rodasī (Heaven and Earth), Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni—the upholders of *ṛta*—who are praised by the Vasiṣṭhas, grant us a most excellent hymn, O radiant ones. Do you all protect us always with blessings. || 7 || *nu*: now. *Rodasī*: Heaven and Earth. *Abhiṣṭute*: praised. *Vasiṣṭhaiḥ*: by the Vasiṣṭhas. *Ṛtāvānaḥ*: upholders of *ṛta*. *Varuṇaḥ*: Varuṇa. *Mitraḥ*: Mitra. *Agniḥ*: Agni. *Yacchantu*: may they grant. *Candrāḥ*: O radiant ones. *Upamam*: most excellent. *Naḥ*: to us. *Arkam*: a hymn. *Yūyam*: you all. *Pāta*: protect. *Svastibhiḥ*: with blessings. *Sadā*: always. *Naḥ*: us. || 7 ||

Now, the two worlds, Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), have been praised on all sides by us, the Vasiṣṭhas— the plural being used for the sake of honor. They have become [the objects] of praise everywhere.
Likewise, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni—these gods who are accompanied by us through the sacrifices performed by us and who possess the quality of truth (ṛtāvānaḥ)—have been praised by us.
May all these gods, who are radiant (candrāḥ) and delightful, grant us excellent food (arka) that is supreme and worthy of comparison.
O you gods who have been described in this hymn, may you all protect us always with blessings (svastibhiḥ) that lead to non-destruction.
6 | "O śruṣṭiḥ" (O, listen!)— with these words he recited the seventh hymn, which is the seer-verse of Vasiṣṭha, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
This is indicated by the introductory heading "O śruṣṭiḥ."
The application [of the mantra] is indicated by its characteristic marks.

O! May [our] readiness [to hear] be established; may it come together; we shall offer a hymn of praise in response to the swift ones. Whatever the god Savitṛ shall impel today, may we be his delight in the distribution [of wealth]. (1) O! Readiness. May it be established. Together. May it come. In response. Hymn of praise. We shall offer. To the swift ones. Whatever. Today. The god. Savitṛ. Shall impel. May we be. His. Delight. For us. In the distribution. (1)
O gods, may the accomplishment (*śruṣṭi*) brought about by your attentive mind (*vidadhyā*) come to us;
or rather, let the swift accomplishment (*śruṣṭi*)—the praise being performed in the sacrifice—come toward you.
We shall offer up (*pratidadhīmahi*), that is, perform, the hymn of praise (*stoma*) for the swift gods.
Now, at this very moment, whatever wealth the divine Savitṛ may impel toward us—may we be present for the distribution and the granting of that wealth of his, which is delightful and full of riches.

May Mitra, Varuṇa, the two worlds (Heaven and Earth), Indra, and Aryaman grant us that which is their allotted portion. May the goddess Aditi bestow wealth upon us, as well as Vāyu and Bhaga, who yoke [their steeds] for this purpose. Mitra, Varuṇa, and the two worlds—may Indra and Aryaman grant us that which is their allotted portion. May the goddess Aditi bestow wealth; and may Vāyu and Bhaga, who yoke [their steeds], grant it as well.
May the god Mitra grant—that is, bestow upon us—that well-known wealth;
likewise may Varuṇa grant it;
and may Rodasī, heaven and earth, both grant it.
Likewise, may Indra grant that wealth which is shared by heaven and purified by auspicious hymns, and served by those who offer praise;
and may Aryaman grant it as well.
Likewise, may the goddess Aditi bestow *rekṇas*, wealth; may she point out that wealth to us.
"Vāyu and Bhaga, both these gods, shall bestow that wealth; may they yoke it more closely for us"—this is the connection with what precedes.
"jha-sakṣīmahe" means "may we be united."

O Maruts, let that mortal be fierce and powerful whom you, O lords of spotted horses, protect; and whom Sarasvatī impels with these [aiding powers]—for him there is no one who can obstruct his wealth. O Maruts, sons of Rudra, you whose steeds are the spotted deer—let that mortal whom you protect be indeed fierce and full of vigor. Moreover, those whom Sarasvatī impels with her aids—for him there is no one who can encompass his riches.

O Mātarisvan, O Pūṣan, O Āghṛṇi, be free from envy; may Varūtrī and the Rātisācas grant us boons. May our steeds, increasing in strength, protect us; may Vāta, the wind that traverses the earth, bestow rain upon us. 6.
O Pūṣan, O God, who has thus come to this sacrifice through our arrival, do not be envious here; do not cause an obstacle to this gift.
Varūtrī, Sarasvatī—who is most worthy of being chosen by all—and Rāti (the Giver) [are present]. Rāti means "giving."
From their shared enjoyment, let the wives of the gods give us that wealth which they have spread out;
"do not withhold it from us"—this is the connection with the preceding [verse]. Furthermore, may the swift-moving gods, who bring about happiness (*mayobhuvaḥ*), protect us thoroughly.
May Vāta, the wind that moves all around, the one who goes everywhere, grant—that is, bestow upon us—vṛṣṭi, water characterized by rain.

Now may Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni—the upholders of Ṛta—be praised by the Vasiṣṭhas, O Heaven and Earth. May these radiant ones grant us the highest splendor; and do you all protect us evermore with blessings.

Now, O Heaven and Earth, praised by the Vasiṣṭhas—may the upholders of Truth, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni, the radiant ones, grant us this our highest hymn. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 7.
This has been explained previously.
As for the literal meaning:
Heaven and Earth, as well as Varuṇa and the other gods, have been offered oblations by us, the Vasiṣṭhas.
May such gladdening gods grant us the most excellent [boon].
O all you gods set forth in this hymn, protect us always with auspicious blessings.
‘Prātarabhīma’ is a hymn consisting of seven verses.

Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “‘Prātarbhāgam’: the first [verse] is in the Jagatī meter; the deities are indicated by their characteristic marks; the last [verse] is addressed to Uṣas. Vasiṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi).
The first [verse] is in the *jagatī* meter; the remaining ones are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.

The first has Indra and other deities as its divinity; the second through the fifth have Bhaga as their deity; the seventh has Uṣas as its deity. Regarding this, some say: "One who desires marriage or one afflicted by disease should always mutter the *bhaga-sūkta*."
"He quickly enters his dwelling and is completely freed from diseases" (Ṛgvidhāna 2.25).
At dawn we invoke Agni; at dawn Indra; at dawn Mitra and Varuṇa; at dawn the Aśvins;
at dawn Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Brahmaṇaspati; at dawn we shall call upon Soma and Rudra.
At dawn we invoke Agni; at dawn Indra; at dawn Mitra and Varuṇa; at dawn the two Aśvins; at dawn Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Brahmaṇaspati; at dawn let us call upon Soma and Rudra. 1.
In the morning, at the time of dawn, we, the worshippers, invoke the god Agni;
likewise, in the morning, we invoke Indra;
and likewise, in the morning, we invoke Mitra and Varuṇa, the two gods presiding over day and night.
Likewise, we invoke the two Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, at dawn.

Likewise, at dawn, we call upon the god Bhaga, the god Pūṣan, and Brahmaṇaspati—known as the presiding deity of the sacred hymns. Likewise, at dawn, we invoke the god named Soma and also the god Rudra.
Let us invoke the fierce Bhaga, the winner in the morning, the son of Aditi who is the distributor;
him whom even the poor man, even the swift one, and even the king, thinking "may I partake of Bhaga," addresses.
1. [The word] "devāḥ" is not present in kha-sa-ta-na-bha-śa.

In the morning, we invoke Bharga, the fierce conqueror, the son of Aditi; he who is the sustainer, whom even one who is sluggish calls upon, and whom even a king, when being exhilarated, says, "May I partake of Bharga. 2.

May we invoke at the very break of dawn the god Bhaga—the ordainer, the sustainer of the entire world, the victorious, the one of conquering nature, the fierce, the uplifted son of Aditi. Even the poor man, having taken refuge in him, thinking of the god Bhaga while praising him, says: "O Bhaga, the one worthy of being enjoyed, grant me wealth; divide it for me; give it to me! Thus speaks the one who has taken refuge in the swift one.
The root *turati* has the sense of "going.
Even a king who has acquired wealth, or even a person who is capable, says to that god Bhaga—the worshipful wealth—"Give me food!
The connection is: "We would invoke that Bhaga at the very break of dawn."
O Bhaga, leader; O Bhaga, whose gifts are true; O Bhaga, grant us this prayer by raising it up. O Bhaga, further us with cattle and horses; O Bhaga, may we be rich in men through our heroes.

O Bhaga, you have led us forward; O Bhaga, you are the one who grants true wealth. O Bhaga, favor this prayer of ours and grant it fulfillment. O Bhaga, cause us to prosper with cattle and horses; O Bhaga, may we be preeminent among men through our heroic sons. 3.
O Bhaga, you are the leader; you lead us forth preeminently.
O such a leader, Bhaga, you are one whose wealth is truth (*satyarādhas*).
O such a Bhaga whose wealth is truth, granting—that is, bestowing—our desires upon us, protect (*udava*) this our prayer (*dhi*), that is, our hymn of praise, and make it fruitful.
O Bhaga, do you cause us to be procreated with cattle and horses; make us worthy of being sprinkled [with blessings].
O Bhaga, through your grace, may we prevail and flourish, possessed of men—by leaders, sons, and other kin.
May we now be in the favor of the Blessed Ones—at the beginning, at the journey’s end, and in the midst of the days;
and at the rising of the sun, O Maghavan, may we abide in the benevolent thought of the gods.
And now, O Blessed Ones, may we be yours; and at the onset of day, and at the midday of the days; and when the sun has risen, O Maghavan, may we abide in the good favor of the gods. 4.
Moreover, may we now become possessors of fortune (bhagavantaḥ);
O Bhaga, may we be endowed with you as our Lord (bhaga).
Or else:
May we be fortunate at the beginning of the days; and furthermore, may we be fortunate at the onset of the days, in the forenoon;
and furthermore, may we be fortunate in the midst of the days, at midday.
Moreover, O bountiful Maghavan, when the god Sūrya—the impeller of all—has risen, may we, through your grace, abide in the benevolent favor (sumati) of the gods, Indra and the others.
May Bhaga alone be the Blessed One, O gods; through him may we become possessed of fortune. To you, O Bhaga, everyone indeed cries out; as such, O Bhaga, be our leader here.
Bhaga! May you indeed be the blessed one, O gods. Through him may we become blessed. You, Bhaga, everyone indeed calls upon; as such, O Bhaga, be our leader here. 5.
1. O eater of space, share with me; O eater of flesh, give to me!
O gods, may the god Bhaga alone be the blessed one, the possessor of wealth. Through that god Bhaga, or through that wealth, may we become blessed—may we become wealthy.
O Bhaga, all people indeed call upon you, the well-known one, repeatedly and intensely;
O divine Bhaga, may you become our leader, going before us here in this sacrifice.
Let the Dawns bow down for the sake of the sacrifice, like Dadhikrāvan for the sake of the pure station.
May they bring hither to us Bhaga, the finder of wealth, as swift horses draw a chariot.

Let the dawns bow down for the sacrifice; like Dadhikrāvan, let them come toward us for the sake of the pure path. Like swift horses bringing a chariot, let them bring hither to us Bhaga, the finder of wealth. 6.
