To the pure, the stainless, the foot [or step] fit for movement, to the station—just like a horse that is *dadhikrāvā*—may the Dawns, the deities of the dawn (*upas*), bow together and assemble for our sacrifice (*adhvara*).
Like swift horses carrying a chariot, may the Dawns bring toward us, facing this way, the god Bhaga, the finder of wealth and the bestower of riches. May they lead him hither to us.
May the auspicious Dawns, rich in horses, rich in cattle, and rich in heroes, ever shine upon us;
yielding clarified butter and overflowing on every side—do you protect us always with your blessings.

May the auspicious Dawns, rich in horses, rich in cattle, and rich in heroes, shine upon us evermore—yielding clarified butter, overflowing on every side. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 7.

May the auspicious and worshipful Dawns—the deities of the morning—shining forth for us at all times, dispel the darkness of night. May they, who possess horses, who are accompanied by horses, who are true, who possess cattle, and who are endowed with heroes and progeny, shine upon us.
Of what nature are they? They are those who milk out water (ghṛta), sprinkling it from every side, and who are swollen and increased by all excellent qualities.
May such dawns shine upon us.
O all you gods, as set forth in this hymn, do you always—forever—protect us with blessings and auspiciousness.
The ninth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "pra brahmaṇaḥ," is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to the Viśvedevas.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Pra brahmaṇaḥ: six [verses], addressed to the Viśvedevas. The application of the hymn is determined by its internal characteristics (liṅga).
In the third *chandoma*, in the *prauga-śastra*, there is the triplet dedicated to the Viśvedevas beginning with "pra brahmaṇaḥ.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "pra brahmāṇo aṅgiraso nakṣanta sarasvatīṃ devayanto havante" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.11).
Let the Brahmans and the Aṅgirases come forward; let the roar of the celestial cloud resound.
Let the milch-cows lead the way toward the waters; let the two pressing-stones be yoked, the ornament of the sacrifice.

Let the Brahmins, the Aṅgirases, come forward; let the roar of the celestial cloud resound; let the lowing cows flow forth with their milk. Let the two pressing-stones be yoked, the ornament of the sacrifice. 1.
May the Brahman-sages, the seers known by that name, pervade everywhere.
May Parjanya roar; may our hymn of praise for the celestial song proceed with excellence.
May the milch-cows—the rivers to be gratified—flow forth like a horse.
Sprinkling the waters, let them roar;
let the two fires, being honored like wives, take their places as the ornament—the very form—of the sacrifice.

O Agni, may your path be easy to traverse for us; you who have been obtained from of old, yoke your horses at the pressing of the juice—the tawny ones and the ruddy ones—or those which are indeed ruddy, carrying heroes. Seated here, I invoke the generations of the gods. O Agni, may your path be easy to traverse for us—you who have been obtained from of old—yoke your horses at the pressing of the juice: both the tawny-colored and the ruddy-colored ones, or those which are indeed ruddy, carrying heroes. Seated here, I invoke the generations of the gods.

O Agni, enjoy this our sacrifice; together with the Maruts and Indra, make us glorious. Let Night and Dawn sit upon the sacred grass; worship Mitra and Varuṇa here, they who desire it. This, O Agni, do thou accept as our sacrifice; among the Maruts and with Indra, make us illustrious. Let Night and Dawn sit upon the sacrificial grass; worship Mitra and Varuṇa here, they who are eager for it.
O Agni, you, do you enjoy—that is, accept—our *adhvara*, our sacrifice.
Furthermore, O Agni, among the Maruts—the gods who are Indra’s friends—and in Indra himself, make our sacrifice, which is characterized by oblations and endowed with glory (*yaśas*), glorious;
that is to say, establish it.

Likewise, let Night and Dawn—the night and the day—sit down together upon the sacrificial grass (barhis), that is, upon the seat made of kuśa grass. This means: let them sit together for the duration of day and night.
Moreover, O Agni, worship—honor—in this sacrifice Mitra and Varuna, the two gods who, desiring [you], desire the sacrifice.

Thus, O Vasiṣṭha, let the sacrifice go forth toward the victorious one, like a swift horse toward its goal. Lift up the ladles filled with ghee with one mind; spread the sacrificial grass well for the rite. The flames, longing for the gods, have stood upright. 2.
May the sacrifice belonging to the venerable one proceed toward the gods; let it go to them.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
it is like a swift-moving horse that does not falter when urged by its driver.
O all you officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), being of one mind and like-minded, lift up the *ghṛtācī* ladles in your hands and hold them aloft.
Likewise, for the sake of the sacrifice (*adhvara*), spread the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) made of *kuśa*, which is effective and auspicious, covering the altar.
O Agni, may your flames (*śocis*), which desire the gods (*devayu*), stand upright and directed upwards.

Like sons borne upon their mother’s lap, may the gods sit upon the ridge of the sacrificial grass. In the contest for the gods (*devatātā*), that is, in the battle for the gods, O Agni, do not (*mā kaḥ*) let our enemies (*mṛdhaḥ*), those who harm us, prevail.
In this context, the word *devatāt* refers to the sacrifice and is used in the sense of battle.

You too, being of one mind and equal intellect, come hither;

O Agni, even so, thus for this pressed [Soma], among all creatures, bestow wealth upon us.
O powerful, mighty Agni, through you as our constant companion (*yujā*), may we, rejoicing together with wealth (*rāyā sadhamādaḥ*), remain unharmed and uninjured.
May all the gods propounded in this hymn always protect us with blessings.
The hymn beginning with “*dadhikrāṃ vaḥ*,” the fifth in the collection, consists of eleven verses; it is the *ṛṣi*-seer Vasiṣṭha’s composition and has Dadhikrāvan as its deity.

The first verse is a *jagatī*, and its deity is indicated by the characteristic marks (*liṅga*) of Dadhikrā and others; the remaining verses are *triṣṭubhs*. For it is stated in the index: “*dadhikrāṃ*: [the hymn] *dadhikrāṃ*; the first is a *jagatī*, and its deity is indicated by the characteristic marks.”
The application is concluded.
I invoke for your protection Dadhikrā, the first Aśvin, Uṣas, the kindled Agni, and Bhaga;
Indra, Viṣṇu, Pūṣan, Brahmaṇaspati, the Ādityas, Heaven and Earth, the Waters, and the Sun.
Awakening with my hymn the god Agni, who is the swift runner (*adhikrāvāṇam*)— a specific kind of horse— I praise him. Likewise, I praise the subordinate deity Sūrya, the impeller of all,
as well as Gā (the Earth), or the goddess Vāk.

I worship such gods with mantras. A *mantratuḥ* is so called because he "causes people who think and praise to perceive [the truth]," or alternatively, because he "causes those who attack him to perish."
I invoke for the sake of attaining that great, vast, and tawny-hued splendor of Varuṇa.
May those gods, being with us, drive away and separate all, every single, evil misfortune.
Dadhikrāvan, the first prize-winner, becomes the leader of the chariots, knowing the way;
he is in harmony with the Dawn, with Sūrya, with the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Aṅgirases.
Dadhikrāvan, the first prize-winning steed, comes at the head of the chariots, knowing the way and being in harmony with the Dawn, with Sūrya, with the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Aṅgirases. 4.

The foremost of all horses, the chief steed, swift-moving, ever-advancing, the divine *Dadhikrāvan*—knowing well those various places to be occupied for the yoking of the chariot, he stands at the head of the chariots. What kind of horse is he? He is one who is in perfect accord with *Upasā* (the goddess Dawn), with *Sūrya* (the Sun), the god who impels all, with the *Ādityas*, with the *Vasus*, with the gods the *Aṅgirases*, and with the seers worthy of praise, knowing them all thoroughly.
The meaning is that he has attained unanimity.
May Dadhikrā anoint our broad path; may he follow the track of this [sacrifice].
May Agni hear us, and may the divine host, all the mighty and wise ones, hear us.
May Dadhikrā anoint our path upon the earth so that we may follow the way of Truth (Ṛta). May the divine host hear us; may Agni and all the mighty, unerring ones hear us. || 5 ||

May the god Agni, who is of the nature of a horse and is the one authorized [to lead], follow the path—the way—of the *vṛta* sacrifice for us who have set out; may he tread our path and drench it with water.
The particle *u* is a filler.
May Agni, being of such a form, hear our invocation, which is the divine host (*śardhaḥ*) belonging to the gods.
May the powerful ones, the unconfused, the mighty, the great—all the gods together—hear our invocation.
The twelfth hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with “ā devo yātu,” is the Ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha’s composition; it has Savitṛ as its deity and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.

It is cataloged in the Anukramaṇī under the heading: “The group of four beginning with ā devaḥ is dedicated to Savitṛ. In the ten-night *vyūha* sacrifice, on the fourth day, this hymn serves as the insertion (*nivid-vāna*) for the *sāvitra* section of the Vaiśvadeva Śastra.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "On the fourth day, 'May the god go...
(Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.8)—this is the *vapā-anuvākyā*.
And it is also formulated in the Sūtra: 'May the god Savitṛ, rich in jewels, come; he indeed is our god Savitṛ, the powerful one' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.7)."
In the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha), there are three offerings to Savitṛ at each pressing.
Among them, this is the invitatory verse (yājyā) for the second offering.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “He who [created] all these beings; may the god come” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 10.6).
May the divine Savitṛ, possessor of excellent jewels, come hither, borne through the mid-air by his horses;
holding in his hand many benefits for men, he establishes both the waters and the earth in their places.

Let the god come hither with his chariot, which is swift, rich in treasures, filling the mid-air, borne by coursers, and holding in his hands many gifts; establishing men in their dwellings and procreating the world of beings. 1.

Possessed of excellent jewels (*su-ratnaḥ*), endowed with beautiful gems; filling the mid-air (*antarikṣa-prāḥ*) by means of his own splendor; being carried along (*vaha-mānaḥ*) by his own steeds (*athaiḥ*); Savitṛ, the impeller of all, the God—let him come (*ā yātu*). Of what sort? Holding in his hands (*hastaiḥ*) many (*purūṇi*) riches (*nayāṃsi*)—beneficial to men—to bestow; settling (*niveśayan*) beings (*bhūma*) in their own places during the nights; and impelling (*prasuvan*) them during the days.
May the god Savitṛ, being thus, come hither.
The two broad, golden arms of Urdasī have reached out to the ends of heaven;
surely his greatness shall be celebrated, for even a hero yields to him in the pursuit of waters.
The two arms of this Savitṛ—loose, relaxed, extended for the sake of giving, vast, great, and golden—are reaching upward and pervading the very limits of heaven, that is, the atmosphere.
Now, indeed, the majesty—the greatness—of such a Savitṛ is being praised by us.
Even Sūrya, having resorted to him, has granted to this Savitṛ the desire for action (*apasyā*).
For the cake offering (*puroḍāśa*) in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Savitṛ, there are two invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*), namely "asa gha naḥ" and the following;
the sūtra has been cited previously.
In the third *iṣṭi* among those belonging to the Aśvamedha dedicated to Savitṛ, these same two serve as the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "He recites the two [verses] beginning with 'sa ghā no devaḥ savitā sahāvā' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 10.6)."
May the god Savitṛ, the powerful one, the lord, impel us toward secure dwellings;
spreading out his far-reaching radiance, may he grant us our share of the food that sustains mortals.
May he, the god who is with us, the powerful one, the lord of wealth, impel us toward prosperity; spreading out his protections, may he grant us wide-reaching wisdom and the enjoyment of mortals. 3.
Sahāvā:
he who possesses a splendor that overcomes other splendors;
Vasupati: the protector of riches; may that god Savitṛ impel (āsāviṣat) and send forth (ā samantāt prerayati) riches (vasūni) toward us (naḥ).
The syllable *gha* is for the sake of completion.
That god Savitṛ [bestows] *urucīm*, meaning wide-reaching, *amatim*, meaning form; that is to say, intense radiance.
Dwelling in us and serving us, may he now grant us mortal food—wealth suitable for the enjoyment of human beings.
With these songs, they praise Savitar, the fair-tongued one, whose womb is full, the one with beautiful hands.
May he bestow upon us wondrous and great vital strength. Do you all protect us always with your blessings.
These songs praise Savitṛ, the sweet-tongued, whose arms are full, the fair-handed; may he grant us wonderful and abundant vital strength. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 4.
1. Kha-bha: for the benefit of human beings. 2. Kha-ta: in one's own place. 3. Kha-bha: that which overcomes the interior.
"These *giraḥ*—
meaning those who sing or praise— are the subjects worthy of hymns;

These are words in the form of praise.
"Sujihvam" means having a beautiful tongue;
that is to say, one whose speech is beautiful.
They praise—that is, they extol—the god Savitṛ, who has full rays and whose hand holds complete wealth.
And may that Savitṛ bestow upon us (asme)—or rather, grant to us—wondrous, great, and abundant food (vayaḥ).
Or [the phrase] "yad vā asme" means "grant it to us."
O gods, headed by Savitṛ, may you always protect us with blessings—that is, with auspiciousness—at all times.
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with “imā rudrāya,” is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha and has Rudra as its deity.
One verse is in the Triṣṭubh meter, while the remaining ones are in the Jagatī meter.
Thus says the Anukramaṇikā: “imā [is] Raudra, ending in Triṣṭubh.”
In fierce sacrifices such as the Śūlagava, one should worship the northern direction with this hymn;
for it is stated: "With the hymn beginning 'These [offerings] for Rudra, whose bow is firm,' there is the worship of the directions in all Rudra-sacrifices" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 4.9.21).
Bring these songs to Rudra, the wielder of the firm bow, the god with swift arrows, who possesses his own inherent power;
to the unassailable, the conqueror, the wise ordainer, whose weapons are sharp—bring them, and may he hear us.

Bring these songs to Rudra, the god who possesses a firm bow, swift arrows, and self-sustaining power; to him who is invincible, all-conquering, the ordainer, and wielder of sharp weapons—bring them so that he may hear us. 1.
O our praisers, you—bear and offer these songs of praise to the god named Rudra.
To what kind of one?

To him who possesses a firm bow, whose arrows fly swiftly, who is self-sustained and rich in food, who is invincible by any, who is victorious and the overcomer of enemies, the ordainer and disposer, and whose weapons are sharp.
Offer praises to Rudra who has become thus;
and may that Rudra hear our praises.
For he, through the destruction of what is subject to decay and through the sovereignty over the celestial realm, takes heed of us;
O Rudra, come to our doors, and be harmless toward our offspring.
For he, by his dwelling, takes heed of the earthly race, and by his sovereign rule, of the divine one. O Rudra, come toward our doors with your waters; be free from malady among our people. 2.
He indeed is that god Rudra; he is the one who exists upon the earth (kṣamya), on the ground (kṣamā).
He is perceived through the sovereignty (kṣaya) over the people (jana);
he is perceived through the imperial sovereignty (sāmrājya) over the divine people as well.
The remainder is based on direct perception:
O Rudra, O God, you who protect our offspring—those who satisfy you with hymns—protecting them (*avvan*), come (*upa cara*) to our dwellings, our houses (*duraḥ*).
Furthermore, be free from disease (*anamīvaḥ*) among our offspring.
Amīvā means disease;
you made that [disease] into Bhava.
That missile of yours which, discharged from heaven, moves across the earth—may it pass us by.
O you who drink yourself, you possess a thousand remedies; do not harm our children or our descendants.

That bolt of yours which, unleashed from heaven, courses through the earth—may it pass us by. A thousand are your healing remedies, O you who are well-drunk; do not harm us among our children or grandchildren. 3.

1. O Rudra, that weapon in the form of lightning which, belonging to you whose nature is like the flash of lightning, has been released from the sky—that is, from the intermediate space—and moves upon the earth or within the earth, may it spare us; may it avoid us.

Moreover, O Svapivāta, may you grant us those many thousands of healing remedies (*bheṣajā*) that are yours—namely, the medicinal herbs (*oṣadhāni*). And do not cause harm (*rirīṣaḥ*) to our children (*tokeṣu*) or to our grandchildren (*tanayeṣu*).
Do not slay us, O Rudra, do not abandon us; let us not fall into the snare of your wrath.
Grant us a share in the sacred grass and in the praise of the living. Do you all protect us always with your blessings.

Do not strike us, O Rudra; do not abandon us. Let not our wealth fall into the snare of your wrath. Grant us a share in the sacred grass and in the praise of the living. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 4.
O Rudra, do not strike us; do not harm us.
Likewise, do not cast us away, nor abandon us.
Furthermore, may we not fall into the powerful binding grasp of you when you are provoked and enraged.
Furthermore, in this sacrifice (*barhis*) which is praised by the living and desired by the living, grant us our share;
make us partakers. O gods, headed by Rudra, protect us always with blessings.
The four-verse hymn beginning with “āpo yam vaḥ,” the fourteenth [in the collection], is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and has the Waters as its deity.
It is introduced by the words “āpo yam āpam,” and its ritual application (viniyoga) has already been explained.
O Waters, that wave of yours which those seeking the gods first made into a drink for Indra—
may we today win from you that pure, untroubled, ghee-rich, and honey-sweet wave.

O Waters, that wave of yours which those seeking the gods first made into the drinking-place of Indra—that pure, stainless wave of yours, dripping with ghee and rich in sweetness, may we win today. 1.

O Waters, O divine deities, those seekers of the gods (*devayantaḥ*)—the *Atharvans*—who in ancient times first prepared that wave called Soma, that essence produced from the earth (*ilā*), which is to be drunk by Indra (*indrapāna*) and constitutes your very purpose; even now, may we too partake of and enjoy that wave of yours.

Of what nature? Pure (*śuci*), meaning clean; faultless (*aripra*), meaning free from evil; sprinkling the "ghee-sprinkled" (*ghṛtapṛṣa*) water characterized by rain; and honeyed (*madhumant*), meaning endowed with sweetness.
The connection is: "May we win that which is thus."
May the Son of the Waters protect that most honey-sweet wave of yours, O Waters,
in which Indra rejoices with the Vasus— may we, seeking the gods, attain it from you today.

That wave of yours, O Waters, which is most rich in sweetness—may Apāṃ Napāt, the swift impeller, protect it. May we, seeking the gods, attain today that wave in which Indra rejoices with the Vasus. 2.
May the god known as Apāṃ Napāt, whose movement is swift, protect—that is, preserve—that well-known wave, the most honeyed (sweetest) essence of yours called Soma;
[and may] Indra [protect it] in which [it resides].

1. From the presence of the intermediate space (antarikṣa), denoted by *kha-śa-ta-na-śa*. 2. Those whose faces are Rudra, denoted by *kha-na-bha*. 3. With auspicious blessings (*svastibhiḥ*), denoted by *kha-gha-śa*. 4. Always (*sadā*), that is, at all times (*sarvadā*), protect us! Denoted by *gha-śa*. 5. *Kha-ta-ja-bha*: "The wave called Soma... [this phrase is absent]. Ka. 1-25:

Together with the *umāḥ*—the Vasus, the gods who provide dwelling—one rejoices (*mādyate*, i.e., *mādyet*). And on this day, we, desiring the gods (*devayantaḥ*), may we obtain (*vaśyāma*, i.e., *prāpnuyāma*) that wave belonging to you (*yuṣmadīyam tam ūrmim*).

Having a hundred purifiers, rejoicing through *svadhā*, those divine waters go toward the path of the gods. They do not violate the ordinances of Indra. Offer an oblation rich in clarified butter to the rivers. *Śatapavitrāḥ*: having a hundred purifiers—those whose forms are many purifying aspects. *Svadhayā*: through *svadhā*, by means of the food that constitutes their own function. *Madantīḥ*: rejoicing, delighting the people. *Devīḥ*: the divine ones, the shining waters. *Devānām*: of the gods, such as Indra and others. *Api yanti pārthah*: they go toward, they enter the path. *Tāḥ*: those [waters]. *Indrasya*: of Indra. *Na minanti vratāni*: they do not violate the ordinances—the sacrificial rites and other duties intended for his gratification. *Sindhubhyaḥ*: to the rivers. *Havyam*: an oblation. *Ghṛtavat*: rich in clarified butter. *Juhota*: offer [it]. *Śatapavitrāḥ*: "having a hundred purifiers"—those whose forms are many purifying aspects. *Svadhayā*: through *svadhā*, by means of the food that constitutes their own function. *Madantīḥ*: rejoicing, delighting the people. *Devīḥ*: the divine ones, the shining waters. *Devānām*: of the gods, such as Indra and others. *Pārthaḥ*: the path. *Api yanti*: they enter. *Tāḥ*: those [waters]. *Indrasya*: of Indra. *Prīṇanāni vratāni*: the ordinances intended for his gratification, such as sacrifices and other rituals.
For the sake of understanding:

now let your horses—your own steeds who are the performers of actions, all-pervading (*vibhvaḥ*), powerful, and capable—turning toward us and facing us, bring our chariot, which is for the benefit of mankind, hither; that is, they should cause it to come.
May we overcome you with skill through our skills, with power through your powers;
may Vāja aid us in the winning of booty, and with Indra as our ally, may we conquer Vṛtra.

May we be R̥bhu with the R̥bhus, and Vibhvan with the Vibhūs; through your power, may we overcome all powers. May Vāja protect us in the winning of booty; with Indra as our ally, may we overcome the enemy.

O Ṛbhus, through you who are Ṛbhus, may we become Ṛbhus; being all-pervading through you who are all-pervading, and being all-encompassing through you who are all-encompassing, may we overcome—the word *abhi syāma* meaning "may we conquer"—the *śarvasi*, the powers of our enemies, by means of your own power (*śavasā*). Likewise, in the battle for booty (*vājasātau*), may this very Ṛbhu, the winner of wealth (*vāja-sāt*), protect and preserve us.
Moreover, with Indra as our ally (*yuj*), may we overcome—that is, slay—the enemy Vṛtra;
for generally, even the Ṛbhus are praised together with Indra.

For they indeed abide by ancient commands; let him overcome all enemies with his victorious power. Indra, Vibhvan, R̥bhukṣan, and Vāja, displaying their manly strength, act against the hostile enemy in his conflict.
For they indeed surpass many with their command; Indra, Vibhvan, R̥bhukṣan, and Vāja shall conquer all enemies in the struggle for preeminence, displaying their manly prowess against the hostile foe.

Such as they were, Indra and the Ṛbhus [subdued] our many, numerous enemy armies by means of *śāsa*— that is, by their command or their own decree. The word *śāsa* denotes a weapon, for it is that by which one is struck (*viśvasyate*) or slain.
By that they rest and they overcome;
for these two [eyes] are full of consciousness.
Moreover, there is the quality of being foremost.
There is elision [of the case-ending] in the seventh [case].
*Uparatāti* refers to battle, so called because it is "stretched out" (*tāyate*) with stones above—that is, with weapons resembling rocks.
In that [battle], they "van," meaning they strike, all (*viśvān*) the "arthaḥ," that is, the enemies (*arīn*).

Viśvakṣā, Vāja, and the Ṛbhus—these companions, together with Indra, being the "aryaḥ," those who go against the enemies, [they strike] the *nṛmṇam*, the strength, of the foe through their rivalry (*mithatyā*).
This form is *mithati*;
for *mithati* means injury.
By means of that, let them fashion it, that is, let them transform it.
The meaning is "let them destroy."
O gods, all of you, being of one accord, grant us wide space for our protection!
O bounteous ones, bestow upon us nourishment; and do you protect us always with your blessings.
Now, O gods, grant us wide space; be all of you of one accord for our protection. May you pour down abundance upon us; do you ever protect us with your blessings. 4.
O divine gods, the radiant Ṛbhus, you indeed—now, for us, create, fashion, and bestow upon us wide space and wealth.
Likewise, O all you Ṛbhus, being in full accord and rejoicing together, be present for our protection and preservation.
Furthermore, O praiseworthy Vasus, the Ṛbhus, may you grant and bestow food and nourishment upon us.
O Ṛbhus, may you always protect us with auspicious blessings.

The sixteenth hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ," has Vasiṣṭha as its seer, is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and has the Waters (Āpaḥ) as its deity. Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "samudrajyeṣṭhā; [the deity is] Āpaḥ. Its ritual application (viniyoga) has been explained.
Led by the ocean, purifying themselves from the midst of the waters, they flow on without resting;
those divine waters which Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt and the bull, dug out—may they protect me here.

Led by the ocean, from the midst of the flood, they go purifying themselves, never resting. Those which Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the bull, dug out—may those divine waters protect me here. 1.
"Having the ocean as their chief":
those waters for whom the ocean—the vast sea—is the "chief," meaning the most excellent or praiseworthy;
[of] the liquid.
This is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
They go—that is, they move—from the middle of the intermediate space, from the central region.
Of what kind are they?

Purifying, cleansing the people, and never remaining still but ever-flowing—Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the bull who showers down desires, has carved out these divine waters that were obstructed; may those waters protect me, guard me, or come to me here in this place.
The waters that are celestial, or those that flow, whether dug from the earth or self-born;
those whose goal is the ocean, pure and purifying—may those divine waters protect me here.
The waters that are celestial, or those that flow in channels, or those that are self-born, which have the ocean as their goal—those pure and purifying divine waters: may they protect me here. 2.
Those waters which are celestial, belonging to the intermediate space;
and also those waters which flow—that is, move—along rivers and other such places;
and those which are excavated, produced by digging.
Moreover, those rivers which are self-born, appearing of their own accord, and whose goal is the ocean— that is,
they have the ocean as their destination—
become pure, endowed with brilliance, and purifying.
"May those waters protect me."
Those in whose midst King Varuṇa moves, beholding the truth and falsehood of men—
those dripping with sweetness, pure, and purifying— may those divine waters protect me here.
Those in whose midst King Varuṇa moves, beholding the truth and falsehood of men—those waters which drip sweetness, which are bright and purifying—may those divine waters protect me here. 3.
Varuṇa, the king and master of these waters, goes—that is, moves—into their midst, in the middle world;
doing what?
Beholding the truth and the falsehood of living beings.
The meaning is "knowing.
Those waters which distill sweetness—that is, which flow with sap—those pure ones, endowed with brilliance, those purifying ones;
may those divine waters protect me.
May those divine waters in which King Varuṇa, in which Soma, and in which all the gods delight; and into which Agni Vaiśvānara has entered—may they protect me here.
1. From the *Mādhyamikasthāna* [of the *Kha-na-bha* manuscript]. 2. [The manuscript] *kha-ma* erases [the text].
3. In *kha-sa-ta-na-bha*, the phrase "having the meaning of 'ocean'" (*samudrārthāḥ*) is absent.
In which waters King Varuṇa dwells, in which Soma, in which all the gods rejoice in strength, and into which Agni Vaiśvānara has entered—may those divine waters protect me here. 4.
In those waters wherein Varuṇa, the king of waters, dwells; in those waters wherein Soma dwells;
and in those waters wherein all the gods abide and rejoice in *ūrj*, the food.
May those divine waters, into which Agni Vaiśvānara has entered, protect me as I stand here.
"‘ā māṃ mitrāvaruṇā’—this is the fourth hymn, consisting of seventeen verses, the seer of which is Vasiṣṭha.
The fourth verse is an atijagatī; by means of *vyūha* (rearrangement), it becomes a śakvarī, while the first three are jagatīs.
The first [verse] has Mitra and Varuṇa as its deities, the second is addressed to Agni, the third to the Viśvedevas, and the fourth has the Gaṅgā and other rivers as its deities."
And likewise, the table of contents (anukramaṇikā) states: ‘ā māṃ maitrāvaruṇāgneyī vai’.

Whatever poison is in the *śalmali* tree, whatever is in the rivers, and whatever poison is born from the plants—may all the gods drive that away from here. May the shaft [of the arrow] not find me with foot-infecting disease. Whatever poison is in the *śalmali* tree (the silk-cotton tree) by name; whatever poison manifests in the rivers—that is, in the waters situated therein; and whatever poison is born or produced from the plants—the word *pari* here reiterates the sense of the ablative case—from those plants: may all the gods drive that poison away from here, from this person or place, completely. "May it not find me" (*mā mām*) and so forth has already been explained.

Those rivers which flow down slopes, those which flow into hollows, and those which flow up heights; those which are full of water and those which are waterless—may they all, swelling with milk for us, be auspicious goddesses free from the *śipada* disease; may all the rivers be free from the *śimidā* affliction. Those rivers which go down the slopes (*pravataḥ*), those which go into the hollows (*nivataḥ*), and those which go up the heights (*udvataḥ*); those which are full of water (*udanvatīḥ*) and those which are waterless (*anudakāḥ*)—may those such rivers, swelling with milk—that is, making everything overflow with water—and being goddesses (*devīḥ*), shining ones, be for us free from the *śipada* disease (a particular kind of ailment); being so, may they be auspicious (*śivāḥ*). Furthermore, may all those rivers be free from the *śimidā* affliction. Of what nature? May they be givers of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). 17.
The eighteenth hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with “ādityānām,” is the seerly work of Vasiṣṭha; it is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter and has the Ādityas as its deity.
It is enumerated thus: “ādityānāṃ tṛcamādityaṃ tu. The application of this hymn [in ritual] has already been explained.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to the deity Āditya, "ādityānām avasā" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*).
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "With a new song, [we call] with the protection of the Ādityas; [this is] for the Ādityas" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
This same verse serves as the invitatory verse for the Āditya cup (*graha*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With their newest protection, may the Hotṛ sacrifice to the Ādityas" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.10).

Through the newest protection of the Ādityas, may we be united with their most auspicious shelter. May the swift ones, listening to us, establish this sacrifice in a state of sinlessness and in the freedom of Aditi. ādityānām | avasā | nūtanena | sakṣīmahi | śarmaṇā | śaṃtamena | anāgāstve | adititve | turāsaḥ | imam | yajñam | dadhatu | śroṣamāṇāḥ || 1 ||
1. *Śapravataḥ*: flowing forth with great force; *nivataḥ*: downward slopes. 2.

Regarding *kha-sa-ta-na-bha-śa*, the phrase “*yā nivato... gacchantya unnatadeśe*” (those which go from the downward slopes to the elevated region) is absent; in *gha*, it reads: *yā nivataḥ* (those going downwards) and *udvataḥ* (those going upwards).
By the *avasā*—that is, by the protection—of the *ādityānām*, the gods known as the sons of Aditi.
The meaning is: "by that which has become its cause. By the "new" (*nūtana*), meaning by the present; by the "most auspicious" (*śaṃtama*). *Śam* means happiness (*sukha*).
By means of that which produces it in an exceeding degree, [namely] *śarman*;
for *śarman* is a name for a house. May we, by means of that house, *saṃkṣīmahi*, that is, may we come together.

May the swift Ādityas, who are themselves swift-moving, hearing our hymns and listening to them, establish this person—the performer of the sacrifice—free from sin, free from transgression, and in the state of Aditi, that is, in a state of non-deprivation.
"‘ādityāso aditiḥ’—this is the *yājyā* for the Āditya cup.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘[The verse] “ādityāso aditirmādayantām”; one should not look at this cup while it is being offered’ (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.17)."

May the Ādityas and Aditi rejoice; may Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa, the most righteous, be our guardians of the world. May they drink the Soma today for our protection. (2) Ādityāsaḥ | Aditiḥ | Mādayantām | Mitraḥ | Aryamā | Varuṇaḥ | Rajīṣṭhāḥ | Asmākam | Santu | Bhuvanasya | Gopāḥ | Pibantu | Somam | Avase | Naḥ | Adya || 2 ||
The Ādityas: the gods who are the Ādityas, and Aditi is their mother;
or alternatively, "Aditi" is an epithet for the gods themselves—Aditi, Aditis, meaning those who are undecaying (adīnāḥ).
May those known as Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa—who are most upright (*rajīṣṭhāḥ*) and exceedingly straightforward—be exhilarated; may they be satisfied.
May such gods, who are the guardians (*gopāḥ*) of the entire world (*bhuvanasya*), be ours;
that is to say, may they become our protectors.
On this day, for our protection, may they drink the Soma pressed by us.

The Ādityas, all the Maruts, all the gods, and all the Ṛbhus—Indra, Agni, and the two Aśvins, being praised—do you all protect us always with your blessings. 3. Ādityas; all; Maruts; and; all; gods; and; all; Ṛbhus; and; all; Indra; Agni; the two Aśvins; being praised; you; protect; with blessings; always; us. 3.

The Ādityas, the sons of Aditi; all the twelve Arka deities; all the Maruts, numbering forty-nine; all the Devas; all the Ṛbhus; Indra; Agni; and the two Aśvins—those gods who have been praised by us with hymns, may you all, O gods, always and forever protect us with blessings.
The nineteenth hymn, consisting of twenty-nine verses beginning with "ādityāso aditayaḥ," is the Ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha's composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and has the Ādityas as its deity.
The Anukramaṇikā states: "ādityāḥ. Its ritual application (viniyoga) has been explained.

May we be Ādityas, free from bonds; may we be protectors among the gods and benefactors among mortals. May we win, O Mitra and Varuṇa, as we come together; may we be, O Heaven and Earth, as you are. ādityāsaḥ | aditayaḥ | syāma | pūḥ | devatrā | vasavaḥ | martyatrā | sanema | mitrāvaruṇā | saraṇtaḥ | bhavema | dyāvāpṛthivī | bhavantaḥ || 1 ||
1. In manuscripts *sva*, *gha*, and *na*, the word “of the gods” (*devānām*) is absent.
2. In manuscript *kha*, the particle “and” (*ca*) is absent; in *jha*, *ta*, *na*, and *śa*, it is optionally present. 3.
In *jha*, *ta*, and *na*, [the reading is] by way of being undepressed (*adīnatvena*); in *śa*, by way of being beginningless (*adititvena*).
Those Ādityas are the divine Ādityas.
The absence of the initial udātta accent occurs due to a transposition [of the rule].
Or rather:
they are like the Ādityas among the Ādityas.
The suffix *vya* is applied according to the rule *prāgdīvyato 'ṇ* in the sense of "this belongs to him" (*tasyedam*).
We are the remnants of the Ādityas.
The Adityas are those who are not to be broken.
May we be;
may we become [prosperous]. O Vasus—those who dwell among the gods—may your protection be with us mortals among men.
O Mitra and Varuna, winning [wealth] by honoring you both, may we win; may we share in the riches bestowed by you.
O Heaven and Earth, through your grace may we become prosperous; may we possess abundance.
May Mitra, Stambha, and Varuṇa grant us protection as guardians for our children and descendants;
may we not suffer for the sin committed by others, nor commit such an act, O Vasus, for which you would punish us.
May Mitra and Varuṇa, the guardians, grant us protection for our children and descendants. May we not suffer for the sin committed by another; O Vasus, may we not perform that deed which you punish.
Mitra and Varuṇa, the two deities who preside over day and night— Āhāḥ says this— all the Ādityas should grant us that well-known *śarma*, which means happiness;
*māmaha* is a verb meaning "to give," so let them bestow it.
May those gods, the protectors of the universe, grant protection to our offspring—our sons, our grandsons, and their sons. Now follows the direct praise:
O gods, may we not suffer from the sin born of others—that evil produced by another. May we not be its partakers.
O Vasus, the gods who provide dwelling, whatever act you perform by which you conceal yourselves—that is, hide yourselves—from us, may we not perform such an act; may we not do it.
In the Vedic language (luṅ), there is the third-person plural ending for the root *kṛ*;
the suffix *cli* is elided by the rule "in a mantra, [the *cli* of] *ghas* and others [is dropped]."
The youthful Aṅgirases, approaching, have attained the treasure of the god Savitṛ;
may our father and the great, worshipful Viśve Devās, being of one mind, take pleasure in this.

Seeking wealth, the Aṅgirases have approached the treasure of the god Savitṛ, making their request. May our great father, the worshipful one, and all the gods, being of one mind, graciously accept this from us. 3.

The *turuṇyavaḥ*—those who are swift in sacrificial rites and other duties—the *Aṅgirasaḥ*, sages of that name, being *iyānāḥ*, that is, supplicating Savitṛ, reach—that is, they attain—the *ratnam*, the delightful sacrifice, belonging to Savitṛ, the impelling deity. (The relative pronoun *yat* is supplied from the word *sat* occurring in the second half of the verse. He is *yajatraḥ*, one inclined toward sacrifice; *mahān*, abundant; and *pitā*, the fatherly Varuṇa, or rather Prajāpati, the father of all. And the *viśve devāḥ*, all the gods, being *samanasaḥ*, of one mind, may they *juṣanta*, enjoy—that is, favor—such a *ratnam* for us (*naḥ*), or rather, may they grant it to us. 11.
The twentieth hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with "pra dyāvā yajñaiḥ," is the Ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha’s composition dedicated to Heaven and Earth (dyāvāpṛthivya).
It is cataloged as follows: "pra dyāvā [is] dyāvāpṛthivya.
On the fourth day, this hymn serves as the introductory portion (nirvid) for the Dyāvāpṛthivī section of the Vaiśvadeva Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Vāsiṣṭha [section] begins with *ā devo yātu prāveti* (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.8).

The twenty-first hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with “vāstoṣpate,” is the Ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and is dedicated to Vāstoṣpati.
Accordingly, it is enumerated [in the Anukramaṇī]: “vāstoṣpate... [is] dedicated to Vāstoṣpati.
During the construction of a house according to the Smṛti tradition, one should offer oblations with each of the four verses beginning with “vāstoṣpate.”
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having offered oblations verse by verse with the four [verses] beginning, 'O Lord of the Dwelling, acknowledge us' (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.9.9)."

O Lord of the Dwelling, recognize us; be easy of access and free from disease for us. Whatever we entreat of you, favor that for us. Be auspicious to our bipeds, be auspicious to our quadrupeds. O Lord of the Dwelling, O God who protects the home, acknowledge us—your own worshippers—and take heed of us. Thereafter, be well-disposed toward us, providing a pleasant habitation and freedom from sickness. Furthermore, whatever wealth we seek from you, grant that to us with favor. Moreover, be a source of well-being for our two-footed kin, such as sons and grandsons, and be a source of well-being for our four-footed livestock, such as cows and horses.

O Vāstoṣpati, be our furtherer; O Indu, increase our household with cattle and horses. May we remain unaging in your friendship; like a father his sons, favor us in return. O Vāstoṣpati, lord of the dwelling, be our promoter; be the increaser of our wealth (gaya-sphāna) through cattle and horses, O Indu. In your friendship, may we be unaging—meaning free from decay—and accompanied by cattle and horses. Just as a father cherishes his sons as protectors, so may you likewise favor and cherish us.

O Lord of the Dwelling, may we be united with you through a pleasant, delightful, and prosperous assembly. Protect our bestowal of wealth both in peace and in exertion. And you all, protect us always with blessings. O Lord of the Dwelling, may we be joined by you through an auspicious, joyous, and path-providing assembly. Protect our choice wealth in security and also in endeavor. O Lord of the Dwelling, may you all—meaning you—protect us always with well-being.
The twenty-second hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "amīvahā," has the following metrical structure:

the first verse is a *gāyatrī*; the third, fifth, and seventh are *anuṣṭubh*s; and the second, fourth, and sixth are *upariṣṭādbṛhatī*s, because they possess the defining characteristics of a *bṛhatī* as stated in the rule: "A *bṛhatī* consists of eight and fourteen syllables."
The first [verse] has Vāstoṣpati as its deity; the remaining ones have Indra as their deity.

Thus it has been enumerated: "‘Amīvahā’ is addressed to Vāstoṣpati and is in the Gāyatrī meter; the rest, beginning with the ‘Upariṣṭādbṛhatī’, are Anuṣṭubhs for the Prastāpipas, [and constitute] an Upaniṣad. The application (viniyoga) has been explained.

Through that son, may we overcome the waters—that is, the enemies—and cross over them for a secure dwelling, so that we may destroy them.

Furthermore, may we, who belong to you, reach and occupy our own dwelling, our own place.
May Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Agni, the Waters, and the Plants graciously accept that for us.

May Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Agni, the waters, and the plants take pleasure in this with the Maruts. May we be in the shelter, in the lap of the Maruts. Do you all protect us always with blessings. 25. May Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Agni, the waters, the plants, and the Maruts enjoy this. May we abide in the protection, in the lap of the Maruts. Do you all protect us evermore with your blessings. 25.

This has been explained previously. As for the literal meaning: may the gods, Indra and the others, enjoy our hymn of praise. May we abide in happiness while remaining in the presence of the Maruts. O Maruts, protect us always from destructions. 26.
The second hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with “madhvo vaḥ,” is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and has the Maruts as its deity.
It is cataloged under the heading “madhvaḥ sat.
In the Daśarātra sacrifice, on the sixth day, during the Ābhimāruta litany, this hymn serves as the locus for the insertion of the Nivid formula addressed to the Maruts.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *abhimāruta* [section] begins with 'madhvo vo nāma sa pratnathā' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.8):
'O worshipful Maruts, your name is Madhva; they rejoice with power at the sacrifices—those who cause even the two vast worlds to tremble, and who swell the spring when the gods have come forth. "

O worshipful ones, the Marut host is your name; they rejoice with power at the sacrifices, they who cause even the two wide worlds to tremble. When those fierce and noble ones swell the spring. 1. O worshipful ones, the Marut host is your name; they rejoice with power at the sacrifices, they who cause even the two wide worlds to tremble. When those fierce and noble ones swell the spring.

O worshipful Maruts, worthy of sacrifice, yours is the name "Māruta," belonging to the Maruts; O exhilarators of the sweet [Soma], the singers praise it with power at the sacrifices and rites—they praise it loudly, so the meaning is.

Those Maruts who cause even the two vast expanses, heaven and earth, to tremble, and moreover, who, being fierce and full of vigor, make the cloud well up and rain down; those Maruts who are tireless and go everywhere.
The connection with the preceding verse is: "O Maruts, you whose name is 'those who rejoice'...
For the Maruts are indeed the leaders of the one who praises them and the guides of the sacrificer's thought (*manma*).
Today, at our sacrificial assemblies (*vidatha*), sit upon the sacred grass (*barhis*) for the feast, being well-pleased.
O Maruts, you who are the leaders of those who sing your praise, the guides of the sacrificer’s thought— sit today upon our sacred grass at the assemblies for the feast, being well-pleased.
The Maruts are indeed those who seek out the person who praises and lauds them; moreover, they are the ones who lead the sacrificer’s thought toward his desired wish.
The latter half-verse is addressed directly:
O Maruts!
1. [The gods] possessing progeny through *kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *na*, and *bha*.

2. Those who possess power through *kha*—you, being beloved and well-disposed, today on this day, for our sacrificial rites (*vidatheṣu*) and for the enjoyment (*vītaye*) of the Soma, sit down, take your seats, upon the sacred grass (*barhiṣi*).
The other Maruts do not shine so much with their golden ornaments, weapons, and bodies as these do;
adorning both heaven and earth with all their beauties, they anoint themselves for glory with unguents in common.

Not so; it is not merely this much. These other Maruts, as they shine forth with golden ornaments, weapons, and their own bodies, adorning both heaven and earth, they who are adorned with every ornament, anoint themselves with a common unguent for the sake of beauty.
These Maruts are such that whatever amount of wealth and so forth they bestow, other gods besides the Maruts do not bestow even that much; this is the meaning.
And they shine—always gleaming—with *rukmas*, i.e., radiant ornaments, with *āyudhas*, their own weapons, and with *tanūs*, their own bodies, which are merely [shining] forms.
Some maintain that this constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).

Just as these Maruts shine with golden ornaments and the like, it is not that they shine while being inseparable from them; moreover, illuminating the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), making all things visible (*viśvapiśaḥ*), such are the Maruts who, for the sake of splendor (*śubhe*), adorn themselves (*ā añjate*) with a common, uniform ornament (*añji*) upon their own limbs, manifesting it.
The word *kam* is a filler (*pūraṇaḥ*).
O Maruts, your splendor is indeed far-reaching when you, O lords of many people, come forth. Let us not be caught in the snare of deceit, O worshipful ones; may your most excellent favor be with us.

May that [favor] of yours, O Maruts, be distinct and manifest, whatever we may do for you, O lords of many men; may we not fall into your wrath, O worshipful ones. May your most delightful goodwill be with us. 4.
O Maruts, may that well-known weapon of yours, your bolt, be *ṛdhak*—separate—from us.
Even if we, by our very humanity (*puruṣatā*), should commit an offense against you;
for it is easy for humans to fall into negligence—this is the meaning.
O worshipful Maruts, worthy of sacrifice, do not even slightly falter in that splendor of yours;
you are *caniṣṭhā*,
meaning most excellent as givers of food.
May your benevolent thought—your mind of grace—be directed toward us.
When the two blameless, pure, and purifying Maruts have sounded here, O worshipful ones, protect us with your favor; help us to cross over toward prosperity through your strengths and spoils of war.

When this is performed, may the Maruts take delight here—they who are blameless, pure, and purifying. O worshipful ones, protect us with your favor; further us with strengths so that we may prosper. ||5||
In this very rite of ours, let the Maruts rejoice;
how are the Maruts?
They are blameless (anavadyāsaḥ), faultless, pure (śucayaḥ), endowed with brilliance, and purifying (pāvakāḥ)—such are they.
Furthermore, O Maruts, you who are worthy of worship (*yajatrāḥ*), protect us (*naḥ*) excellently with your benevolent thoughts (*sumatibhiḥ*), whether as causes or as friends.
Likewise, further us for our nourishment (*puṣyase*) with strengths (*vājebhiḥ*), that is, with foods.
1. In manuscripts Kha, Kṣa, Ta, Na, Ma, and Śa, the word *barhiḥ* is absent.
2. In manuscripts Kha and Śa, it reads *śobhanāyai*.
3. In manuscript Ta, the word *api* is absent.
Maṇḍala 7, Anuvāka 4, Sūkta 58. Fifth Aṣṭaka: 405.

And may the Maruts, being thus praised, enjoy the oblations under all their names, O heroes! Grant us immortality for our progeny; bestow upon us wealth, true speech, and bounties. (6) And (*uta*), being praised (*stutāsaḥ*) by us in this manner, may the Maruts (*marutaḥ*) enjoy (*vyantu*) the oblations (*havīm̐ṣi*). Of what sort are they? They are the leaders (*naraḥ*) accompanied by all (*viśvebhiḥ*) names (*nāmabhiḥ*), that is, by all the waters. The remainder of the verse is a direct address. O Maruts, grant (*dadāta*) us, for our progeny (*prajāyai*) and lineage, immortality (*amṛtasya*), meaning the immortal water. Likewise, for the sacrificer who offers the oblation, pour forth (*jigata*)—that is, bestow—the bounties (*maghāni*), which are true speech (*sūnṛtā*), meaning riches worthy of beautiful praise and excellent conduct.

O Maruts, being thus praised by us, all of you, accompanied by your protection (*ūtī*), come toward the patrons (*sūrīn*) at the sacrifice where all things are provided (*sarvatātā*). Those Maruts who themselves increase us to a hundredfold—meaning, so that we may become possessed of a hundred through sons, grandsons, and the like—come hither. O you who are such, protect us always with your blessings. 7.
The third hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with *pra sākumukṣe*, is the seerly composition (*ārṣa*) of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and has the Maruts as its deity.
It is enumerated thus: “*pra sākumukṣe*—six. Its ritual application (*viniyoga*) has been explained.

Sing forth to the host that sprinkles together, which is mighty by the divine station! And they shake the two worlds with their greatness; they reach the firmament from the rootless depth of the earth. O singers, praise aloud the host that sprinkles together—the company of Maruts—who is mighty by the divine station, that is, who is exalted above all the gods. To that host, sing forth your hymns. Moreover, the Maruts, accompanied by their own greatness, shake—that is, they pervade—the two worlds, heaven and earth. Likewise, from the rootless depth of the earth (Niṛti) and from the intermediate space, they reach—that is, they encompass—the firmament, the celestial realm.
1. Gha: direct perception; Jha: that which is produced by direct perception; Jha: praise of direct perception; Bha: direct perception praised. 2. Ta: beautiful conjunctions.
3. Ta: for him.

O Maruts, your birth was through the brilliance of Rudra—O you who are terrible, of many-frenzied minds, and tireless; you who prevail with greatness and with power. At your coming, every beholder of the sun (or every observer of the sky) is struck with fear. O terrible ones, O fearsome ones, O you of many-frenzied minds (of exalted intellect), O tireless ones—these are the three vocatives. O Maruts, such as you are, your birth was through the brilliance (*tveṣya*) of the radiant Rudra (this is the ellipsis). Furthermore, those Maruts who prevail with greatness—that is, with splendors—and with power, at your coming, at your journey, every "beholder of the sun" (*svardṛk*)—every host of living beings—or alternatively, *svar* is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); one who sees that is a "beholder of the sky" (*svardṛk*), meaning one who cuts through all darkness—is struck with fear.
I, the Hotṛ-priest, worship those Maruts, the sons of Rudra, the Lord who showers down desires;
may they, the Maruts, bow down to us again and again, repeatedly and abundantly.
"May they become manifest.
Since the meaning of the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is already obtained by the word *kuvic* itself, for what purpose is the word *punaḥ* included?
It is for the sake of emphasis (*ādara*).

Whatever offense we have committed against the Maruts that they might be provoked by in secret and in obscurity, and whatever offense we have committed against them openly and in public—that twofold transgression of the swift Maruts, we entreat you to remove; we drive it away through our hymn of praise.
This well-composed hymn has been uttered for you, O Maruts; may you take pleasure in it. O Bulls, drive away our enemies even from afar! Do you protect us always with your blessings.

May this excellent praise of the liberal patrons be proclaimed; may the Maruts take pleasure in this well-spoken hymn. O Bulls, drive away enmity even from afar! Do you protect us always with your blessings. The word *mahanti* means "great"; *hṛṣaḥ* refers to sacrifices characterized by oblations. For the sake of "choosing" (*varāya*)—that is, for the purpose of exclusion, so that "you do not go elsewhere, but accept only our oblations"—he "offers" (*vi dāśati*), meaning he gives specifically in order to effect such a restriction.
Therefore, the sense is that he increases his own dwelling place.
Not even Vasiṣṭha can measure you, for you are beyond all measure.
O Maruts, drink today at our pressed juice, you who are all full of desire.
Not even Vasiṣṭha will disregard your final word; O Maruts, all of you who desire it, drink today at our pressed soma together. 3.
Vasiṣṭha, the seer, does not exclude even the last among you—he does not omit anyone from his praise;
rather, the meaning is that he praises all of you indeed.
O Maruts, today, on this day, while our Soma is being pressed, you all, desiring the Soma and longing for it, drink together, having gathered in unison.
Your aids do not fail him in battles for whom you have granted success, O heroes.
May your newest benevolence turn toward us; come quickly, O ye who desire to drink!
For your aids do not fail in battles for him to whom you have granted them, O heroes. May your newest favor turn toward us. Come quickly, O ye who desire to drink! 4.

O Maruts, your protection—your aid in battles—is indeed not failing; that is to say, it does not harm us, for it does not tolerate the injury inflicted by enemies. O leaders (naras), the person to whom you have granted desires—that person it does not harm; such is the connection.
May your newest, most recent benevolent thought turn toward us;
O you who desire to drink the Soma, come quickly!
O Maruts, you whose gifts are eager, come hither to drink these libations; for I have presented these offerings to you. Do not go elsewhere, O friends.
O Maruts, you who possess impetuous bounty, come here to drink the soma-juices; these offerings are prepared for you. For I have presented them to you alone; do not go elsewhere! 5.

O Maruts, you whose gifts are eager and whose riches are firmly compacted through mutual friction—come well indeed, come hither, for the drinking, that is, for the consumption, of the *andhas* (soma-libations).
For, O Maruts, since I offer these very oblations (*havyā*) unto you, therefore do not go elsewhere. Do not depart!
And come to our sacrificial grass, O Maruts, as our constant protectors, to bestow upon us desirable wealth. Without failing, O Maruts, rejoice here with the *svāhā* at this Soma-sweetness.
1. For the purpose of excluding *kha*.
2. [The letters] *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* are for this [purpose]. 3. The *ta*s are well-combined with *ya*.

And sit upon our sacred grass; protect us and grant us desirable riches. O Maruts, not withholding [your gifts], rejoice here with the Svāhā-call at the pressing of the sweet Soma for the sake of victory. 6.
O Maruts, you should sit down—that is, take your seats—upon our *barhis*, the sacrificial grass made of *kuśa*.

To grant us desirable (*spārhāṇi*) and longed-for riches (*vasu*), come to us and protect us. O Maruts, being unobstructive and non-violent, may you rejoice with the cry of *svāhā* at this exhilarating, purifying oblation consisting of Soma within this sacrifice; indeed, do you all revel!
Even the swans with dark-blue backs, adorning their bodies, have come hither;
the entire host has settled down all around me, like joyful men rejoicing at the libation.

Svarita accent. *cit* (hi). *tunvaḥ*. *śubhamānāḥ*. *ā*. *haṃsāsaḥ*. *nīlapṛṣṭhāḥ*. *apasan*. *viśvam*. *śardhaḥ*. *abhitaḥ*. *mā*. *ni*. *seda*. *naraḥ*. "O householders" (*gṛhamedhāsaḥ*)—this is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the *gṛhamedhīya* oblation. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O householders, come; your great splendors go forth beautifully" (*gṛhamedhāsa āgata pra sundhyā va īrate mahāṃsi*; Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.18).

O Maruts, you who are the masters of the domestic sacrifice, come hither; do not stay away, O bounteous givers, through your protection. 10. gṛhamedhāsaḥ | ā | gat | marutaḥ | mā | arpabhūtan | yuṣmāka | ūtī | sudānavaḥ || 10 ||
O Maruts, you who possess the household sacrifice performed in the home, you who bestow excellent gifts—come toward our sacrifice, accompanied by your purifying protection.
O Maruts, do not depart; do not go away.
(The root *bhū* is used here in the sense of "being" or "staying.")
At the Vaiśvadeva parvan, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the Maruts is "iheha vaḥ";
this is also stated in the Sūtra: "iheha vaḥ svatavasaḥ pra citramarkaṃ guṇate turāya" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.16).

Right here, O Maruts, you who are self-strong, poets with sun-like skins—I choose your sacrifice. 11. Right here, right here; you; self-strong; poets; sun-skins; sacrifice; O Maruts; hither; I choose. 11.

O Maruts, you who possess cattle as your own strength (*pasvatavasas*), whose power is self-dependent, who have grown by yourselves, O seekers of the cooked offering (*pakvayas*), you of far-reaching vision, you whose skins are radiant like the sun—such as you are, O Maruts, I choose for myself right here this our sacrifice; I invite you to it and prepare it for you.
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
May he deliver me from death, as a cucumber from its stem, yet not from immortality.
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
May he deliver me from death as one releases a cucumber from its stem, yet not from immortality.
Regarding this, Śaunaka says: "Having fasted for three nights while remaining self-restrained, one should cook a *caru* of milk-rice;
then, having praised his vow, he should offer a full hundred oblations with it."
"Having dedicated this hundred-fold section to Mahādeva Tryambaka with the mantra 'tryambaka',
one shall live happily for a hundred years" (Ṛgvidhāna 2.314–15).
"Vasiṣṭha, composed by his disciple, speaks thus: 'We worship the three-eyed father of the triad—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
To the question 'Of what nature is he?', he replies:
'Fragrant as a flower,' meaning one whose fame for merit has spread abroad."
Furthermore, what are its specific characteristics?
It is the nourisher of growth and the seed of the world;
that is to say, it is the power of reasoning (ūhā).
The increase of the lay devotee;
the increase of powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth. Therefore, by Your grace alone, may I be liberated—may You release me—from premature death or from *saṃsāra*.
Just as a cucumber or a karkaṭī fruit is released from its binding, so too release me from death or from saṃsāra. Having made what limit? [The limit] of immortality.
The meaning is "until liberation characterized by union (*sāyujya*).
Now, in the *Taittirīya-bhāṣya* on *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.8.6.2: "He whose bodily fragrance is beautiful, or who possesses the fragrance of flowers, is *sugandhi*.
For the Śruti says: 'Just as the fragrance of a tree in full bloom wafts from afar, even so the fragrance of meritorious action wafts from afar' (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.9)."
He is the "Increaser of Prosperity" (*puṣṭivardhana*) because he causes prosperity in the body, wealth, and other such things to increase.
We worship—that is, we honor—such a Tryambaka.
Just as in this world the fruits of the *urvāruka* gourd release themselves from their bond, the stalk, so may I, by the grace of Tryambaka, be released—that is, be liberated—from death.
"May I not be excluded from immortality, from long life, or from heaven.

Regarding the fourth quarter of the mantra, he demonstrates its profound significance: "'We worship Tryambaka,' he says; 'may I be released from death, but not from immortality'—this is indeed what he says" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.6.10.5).
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness within the heart,
may the Great Lord of the Supreme Holy Place bestow the four goals of human existence.

Thus ends the fourth chapter of the fifth book in the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā-bhāṣya*, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.
Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Having explained the fourth chapter of the fifth [book],
Sāyaṇācārya, who is proficient in the Vedas, now expounds the fifth chapter.

In this context, the fifth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "yadadya sūrye," has the following Anukramaṇī entry: "yadadya [is] addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa, but the first verse is indeed addressed to Sūrya. The seer (ṛṣi) is Vasiṣṭha, the seer of the Maṇḍala.
Because it consists of *anuṣṭubh* verses, the metre is *triṣṭubh*.

Since it is stated "tu vai," these seven hymns beginning with that one have Mitra and Varuṇa as their deities, while the first [verse] has Sūrya as its deity. The application is determined by internal indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).
O Sūrya, as you rise today sinless, speak the truth for Mitra and Varuṇa.
O Aditi, may we be dear to you among the gods, praising Aryaman with our songs.
Whatever you may declare today, O Sūrya, as sinless upon rising—truth to Mitra and Varuṇa—may we, O gods, be yours, O Aditi, dear to you and singing your praises, O Aryaman. 1.

O Sūrya, you god who consists of the impelling force of all, as you are rising— should you today, at this time of performance, O Mitra and Varuṇa, have yoked to your chariot from your common abode, from the intermediate space (antarikṣa), these many green-colored horses whose nature is to glide through the atmosphere;
for it is stated in the Nirukta that "the green ones belong to the Sun."
For example: "The green, ghee-dripping [rays] carry him, the god Sūrya. The term *ghṛtācīḥ* means "ghee-dripping," which signifies "water-bearing" or "bestowers of water.
Being such, they carry him; he has yoked them.

Then, having risen, that god— who, desiring you both (*yuvāku*), beholds thoroughly (*saṃ caṣṭe*) the abodes, the stations, the worlds, and the births— that is, living beings who possess birth— just as herd-leaders behold their herds of cattle.
Just as he clearly sees that entire herd and its subordinate herds of cattle, so too does he see the worlds and all living beings.

The strengthening foods, rich in sweetness, have stood up; Sūrya has mounted the bright ocean. For him, the Ādityas carve out the paths—Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa, acting in harmony. O Mitra and Varuṇa, for your sake the strengthening foods (*pṛkṣāsaḥ*)—the sacrificial offerings such as *caru* and *puroḍāśa*, or the sweet-scented plants used as their means—have arisen and been prepared. And Sūrya has mounted, or mounts, the bright, shining ocean—the watery firmament (*arṇaḥ*). For the sake of that Sūrya, the Ādityas—the gods who are the sons of Aditi—carve out, or prepare, the paths. Who are they? Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa; these three gods, being of one accord (*sajoṣasaḥ*), act together. That god has mounted [the sky].

These are the perceivers of falsehood; Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa are indeed many. These have grown strong in the dwelling of *ṛta*; they are the capable sons of Aditi, the undeceivable. These—Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa—all three—are indeed the perceivers and destroyers of much (bhūri) falsehood (anṛta). These, Mitra and the others, have grown strong in the house (duroṇe) of *ṛta*, that is, in the sacrifice, through oblations and hymns of praise. Of what nature are they? They are the bringers of happiness (śagmāsaḥ), the sons of Aditi, and the undeceivable (adabdhāḥ), meaning they are not to be harmed.

These two, Mitra and Varuṇa, whose splendors are difficult to attain, awaken even the mindless with their powers. They turn even the wise man toward ritual action; they lead him across even sin by a good path. These—Mitra and Varuṇa, these two being thus indicative of the Ādityas—are "of difficult splendor," that is, invincible and unassailable. They awaken even the "mindless"—one who lacks knowledge regarding the sphere of performance—with their "powers," that is, their capacities. Furthermore, they turn toward "ritual action" (*kratu*) even the "wise man," one possessed of excellent knowledge, making him a performer of rites and an executor of actions. They lead him across even "sin" (*ahaḥ*) by a "good path. (Note: Regarding the variants: *api kratum* is found in manuscripts kha, kṣa, ta, na, bha, and śa; *sāmarthyaśritārthāti* in manuscript gha; *prajñānavantaḥ* in manuscript jha; *prakṛtajñānavantaḥ* in manuscript śa; and *vatantaḥ* is absent in manuscripts kha, jha, ta, na, bha, and śa.)
Leading away our evil deeds (*duṣkṛtam*) and carrying us across, they lead us by a beautiful path (*supathā*), bringing us to our desired goal, whether it be the sacrifice or heaven and so forth.

These [Maruts], the unblinking guardians of heaven and earth, being wise, lead the mindless one. Even in the violent rush, O heroes, there is a firm footing; may they carry us across this wide-straying [torrent] to the further shore. 7. These, the unblinking ones of heaven and earth, being wise, lead the mindless one. Even in the violent rush, O heroes, there is a firm footing; may they carry us across this wide-straying [torrent] to the further shore. 7.
"These [gods], Mitra and the others, belonging to both heaven and earth, are ever-watchful— knowing through their unblinking gaze— who is the one without consciousness, the ignorant."
"Ṛbhus, you lead"—that is, you cause actions to reach their goal.
"Even in the *pravāja*, even in a steep descent, even in a place exceedingly low, there is 'depth' (*gādha*) for the river—that is, it becomes fordable—through your power.
May those great ones carry us across, may they lead us to the further shore (*pāram*) of this wide-reaching (*viṣpita*) action."

The auspicious protection which Aditi, Mitra, and Varuṇa grant to Sudās as his guardians—placing our children and descendants within that, O swift ones, let us not commit any offense against the gods. 8.

That protection (*śarma*), whether it be happiness or a home, which is endowed with guardianship (*gopāvat*), auspicious (*bhadra*) and praiseworthy—may Aditi (the non-miserly Aryaman or Aditi), Mitra, and Varuṇa, these three gods, grant and bestow it upon me, Sudās, the one of liberal gifts (*sudāsa*). In that protection, may there be *toka* (offspring) and *tanaya* (descendants)—that is, sons and their children;
or alternatively, the word *tanaya* may also denote progeny in general.

Holding and supporting from all sides a young and powerful son, we, O swift ones, hastening for our journey, must not commit an offense against the gods—that is, we must not provoke the wrath of the gods, such as Mitra and the others.

May he worship at the altar with oblations; may Aryaman ward off from us any enemies held by Varuṇa, and with his hostilities; O Bulls, grant a wide space to Sudās. 9. May he worship at the altar with oblations; may Aryaman ward off from us any enemies held by Varuṇa, and with his hostilities; O Bulls, grant a wide space to Sudās. 9.

May he— the one who hates us— along with Mitra and the others, together with the *hotrās* (the name for speech), that is, with praises consisting of words, sacrifice down upon the *vedī*, the instrument of the sacrifice.
The meaning is that while performing rituals on the sacrificial altar, one should praise the gods. The root *yaj* preceded by the prefix *ava* signifies the act of relinquishing (sacrifice).
To the question "What would he obtain?", he says:

"May he who is 'held by Varuṇa' (varuṇadhṛtaḥ)—that is, harmed by you, O Varuṇa—suffer 'certain injuries' (kāścid ripaḥ); this is the ellipsis. But may the god Aryaman keep us 'around from hatreds' (dveṣobhiḥ), that is, from hateful beings such as Rākṣasas and the like; he should exclude us from them.
O 'rainers' (vṛṣaṇā), O Mitra and Varuṇa, bestow a 'broad' (urum) and 'vast' (vistīrṇam) 'world' (lokam)—a place—upon me, the 'well-giving' (sudāse) one."

1. With that unblinking [eye], for their encounter is indeed wondrous; by their secret power they prevail with force. Trembling through fear of you, O bulls, may you grant us favor even by the greatness of Dakṣa. Sasvaḥ | cit | hi | sam’ṛtiḥ | tveṣī | eṣām | apīcyena | sahasā | sahante | yuṣmat | bhiyā | vṛṣaṇaḥ | rejamānāḥ | dakṣasya | cit | mahinā | muḷata | naḥ || 10 ||

The meeting, the association, or the gathering of these [beings], Mitra and the others, is secret—that is, hidden or concealed—and their consecration (*dīkṣā*) is likewise brilliant. Such as they are, they overcome—that is, they surpass—their enemies by means of that which is "apīcya," a term for the hidden; or rather, they overcome them by means of "sahas," which means secret power or force.
Furthermore, O showerers (*vṛṣaṇaḥ*), you who rain down desired things—Mitra and the others—the adversaries tremble and shake out of fear (*bhiyā*) of you.
Since this is so, therefore, by the greatness (*mahinā*) of your skill (*dakṣasya*) and power, grant us grace and favor (*muḷata*).

He who offers worship for the favor of the Brahman at the winning of strength and the highest wealth—those bountiful lords, seeking his fervor for their purpose, have made for him a wide dwelling-place, well-established. 11. He who... for the Brahman... the favor... has offered worship... at the winning of strength... of the highest wealth... they, the bountiful lords, seeking his fervor... for the sake... have made... wide... for the dwelling... well-established. 11.
Or that sacrificer who offers a beautiful thought— that is, an excellent understanding— to the Brahman, who is preeminent in his own duties and whose form consists of hymns of praise to you;
for here the root *yaji* means "to give," he gives or performs [the act].
For what purpose?

For the sake of *vāja*, that is, food (*anna*), on the occasion of its acquisition or bestowal; and for the sake of *rāyas*, that is, supreme or excellent wealth (*dhana*), on the occasion of its acquisition. Such is the meaning of it.

The meaning is that he is the "praiser" (stotā) because he impels hymns of praise. The "magnanimous ones" (maghavānaḥ)—namely Aryaman and others who possess bounty—desire and attend upon his "wrath" (manyu), which here means the hymn of praise.
Having served him, they have made for him a beautiful dwelling (sudhātu)—that is, a splendid abode—for his vast residence (urukṣayāya). They create it; they fashion it.

O Gods, this office of domestic priest has been performed for you both in the sacrifices, O Mitra and Varuṇa. Carry us across all difficulties; do you protect us always with your blessings. 12 This, O Gods, this office of the domestic priest, has been performed for you two in the sacrifices, O Mitra and Varuṇa. Carry us across all difficult paths; do you protect us always with your blessings. 12.
With this [verse], he concludes the hymn:
O gods—O you two gods, Mitra and Varuṇa—for you both, in the sacrifices, this "purohiti"—this service, honor, or praise consisting of a hymn—has been performed.
Having served that [praise], may you cross over—that is, cast aside—all difficulties, all calamities that are hard to traverse.
Having done so, protect us—that is, carry us across.
The rest has been explained.

‘*Udvāṃ cakṣuḥ*’: this hymn of five verses, containing the word *sasvac*, is the seerly composition (*ārṣa*) of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and is addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa (*maitrāvaruṇa*).
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: “*Udvāṃ sasva*.
The application (*viniyoga*) is established by internal indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).
"O Varuṇa, you who possess a beautiful countenance, the two gods have raised up the eye; Sūrya, extending his body, beholds all beings—he perceives their intent as if among mortals."
1. Of those [sounds] *kha*, *kṣa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*, *tā*, and *sā*, [he] considers the *manyu*.
2. *kha* joins together (*sandhatte*); *gha* serves (*sevate*); *jha* served (*sevata*). Up!
To you two, O Varuṇa, the well-beautiful eye of the two gods goes—the Sun—stretching [his light] over all beings; he who beholds them has perceived the *manyu* among mortals. 1.

O Varuṇa and Mitra, O you two radiant deities, the eye of you both—the illuminating splendor—is indeed a beautiful form; such is Sūrya, spreading his brilliance with his body, that he rises upward. And having risen, that god who beholds all beings, all living creatures, he, the god, perceives and knows the devotion, the hymn, or the ritual activity set forth among mortals.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, this inspired singer, true to the cosmic order and hearing from afar, offers up his prayers to you both— those prayers of the one whose sacred hymns you, O wise ones, favor, so that through your wisdom you may fulfill his autumns as if they were your own.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, that inspired sage, true to the cosmic order (*ṛtāvā*) and far-famed, sends forth hymns to you both—he whose prayers are for you, O ye of perfect wisdom.
May those months, the divisions of time, pass by as if they were powerless and childless;
instead, may the wise sacrificer, born for the sake of sacrifice, extend his strength and his path.
The prefix *pra-* serves here for the purpose of intensifying the sense of *tan-* (to extend).
These all [waters], O you two bulls, are yours; in them no wonder is seen, nor any mystery.
The falsehoods of men follow after you; there are no secrets that remain hidden from you two.

These [are yours], O Bulls; all these [are] yours. In them no marvel is seen, nor any secret power; they yield nothing. The falsehoods of men attend them; your secrets have not remained hidden from the unwise. 5.
O you two who are unerring, O you two who are all-pervading, O you two bulls, the showerers—these words of praise are being offered to you both.
In these praises, no marvel is seen, nor is any *yakṣa* (mystery or worship) seen.
The meaning is that even by great effort, a hymn composed for you two does not produce wonder, because of your own greatness.
The false praises of men—which have unequal objects—follow and serve the deceitful;
not so the great ones.
Even the secret, hidden praises being offered to you two do not become [useless] for the ignorant; they do not fail to reach them.
I magnify your sacrifice together with prostrations; I call upon you both, O Mitra and Varuṇa, for our great prosperity.
May these prayers, these new and heroic deeds, and these offered hymns be pleasing to you.

Together—*ūm*—I magnify your sacrifice with reverence; I invoke you both, O Mitra and Varuṇa, for our great prosperity. May these prayers, fashioned by the singer and intended for praise, and these sacred hymns, be pleasing to you. 6.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, I fully honor and worship your sacrifice with salutations—that is, with prostrations and hymns.
For that purpose, O Mitra and Varuṇa, I, being beset by afflictions, invoke you both for the removal of those afflictions.
May new songs of praise—praises worthy of being celebrated—be offered forth for the service of you two. (The word "may they arise" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.)
These hymns of praise, which were performed by me and gathered together, and those now being performed—O Brahmā, O Parivṛḍha, may they please you both.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, this domestic priest has served you both at the sacrifices; carry us across all difficulties. Do you protect us always with your blessings.
This office of priest has been performed for you both at the sacrifices, O Mitra and Varuṇa. Carry us across all difficulties; protect us always with your blessings. 7.
‘This, O King,’—thus ends the seventh [chapter].
The seventh hymn consists of six verses beginning with "utsūryaḥ.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "utsūryaḥ: six [verses]; the first three are addressed to Sūrya. Vasiṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi).
The meter is Triṣṭubh.
The first three verses have Sūrya as their deity; the remaining ones have Mitra and Varuṇa as their deities.
The application of this hymn is indicated by its internal characteristics (liṅga).
1. One who possesses great intelligence for the sake of sacrifice [is indicated by] the letters kha, jha, ta, na, bha, śa, ya.

Sūrya has risen up with great rays; he has extended his light toward all the generations of men. Shining brightly, he is seen clearly by day. Created by his power, he has become well-fashioned by the fashioners. Sūrya, the god who impels all things, has raised up (*ut-aśret*) his vast (*bṛhat*), manifold (*puru*), and many (*viśvā*) rays (*arcīṃṣi*). Toward what? Toward all (*viśvā*) the generations (*janimāni*) of men (*mānuṣāṇām*). The word *jana* here denotes a multitude; he has risen up toward them. That god, shining (*rocamānaḥ*) during the day (*divā*), is seen clearly (*sumo dadṛśe*). Being uniform and constant, he is perceived. For the Śruti says: "Therefore, the Āditya exists facing every single person" (Ai. Ā. 3.2.3). That god was created (*kr̥taḥ*) by Prajāpati through his creative power (*kratvā*), and he has become well-fashioned (*sukr̥taḥ*) by the fashioners (*kartṛbhiḥ*).

O Heaven and Earth, O Aditi, protect us—you whom those of noble birth have brought forth, O exalted ones! May we not incur the wrath of Varuṇa, nor that of Vāyu, nor that of Mitra, who is most dear to men. **Commentary:** "O Heaven and Earth" (*dyāvābhūmī*): O Heaven and Earth.
