"O Aditi" (*adite*): O indivisible one. This is an address to Heaven and Earth using the singular form. "O exalted ones" (*ṛṣve*): this means "O great ones. "O great ones, protect us" (*naḥ trāsīthām*). "We," meaning those of us who are "of noble birth" (*sujanimānaḥ*), have "known you" (*jajñuḥ*). Furthermore, may we "not be in the wrath" (*hele*) of Varuṇa; likewise, may we not be in the wrath of Vāyu; and likewise, may we not be in the wrath of Mitra, who is most dear to men—the leaders of praise among humanity. The fifth verse, beginning with "pra bāhavā," is the *yājyā* for the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "pra bāhavā sisṛtaṃ jīvase no yadaṃhihaṃ nātividhe sudānu" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).

Stretch forth your arms that we may live; sprinkle our pastures with clarified butter. O youthful ones, grant us renown among the people; hear, O Mitra and Varuṇa, these my invocations. O Mitra and Varuṇa, gods, stretch forth your arms for the acceptance of the oblation or for the bestowing of wealth. For what purpose? For our life—that we may live. Furthermore, sprinkle our pastures (*gavyūti*)—the ground where cattle roam—with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), meaning water, so that grass and other plants may grow there. Moreover, grant us fame among the people, that is, among the multitude of men equal to ourselves. O youthful ones, eternally young or all-pervading, hear these my invocations.

May Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman grant us wealth for our own welfare and for our offspring. May all our paths be easy to traverse and well-trodden. Do you protect us always with your blessings. (6) Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman—may these three gods today grant us wealth for our own benefit and for our children. May all our destinations be easy to travel and well-paved. The rest is understood. (4) The hymn beginning with "Udeti" consists of six verses; it is the eighth hymn, composed by Vasiṣṭha, in the Triṣṭubh meter. The first verse, the fifth verse, and the first half of the sixth verse have Sūrya as their deity; the remaining half-verses have Mitra and Varuṇa as their deities. Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "In the hymn beginning 'Udeti,' there are four and a half verses [of the latter category]. The application is indicated by the internal marks of the text. (1) (Note: The variants *kha-jha-ta-śa* read *mahe*.)

The fortunate one, the all-seeing, the common sun of mankind rises up—the god who is the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa, he who has rolled together the darknesses like a hide. *Ud*, *ūṃ*, *eti*, *subhagaḥ*, *viśvacakṣāḥ*, *sādhāraṇaḥ*, *sūryaḥ*, *mānuṣāṇām*, *cakṣuḥ*, *mitrasya*, *varuṇasya*, *devaḥ*, *carma-iva*, *yaḥ*, *samaviviyakta*, *tamāṃsi*. Rising up, transcending, the Sun—fortunate (*subhaga*), meaning possessing auspicious fortune or well-deserving of worship; the all-seeing (*viśvacakṣas*), the beholder of everything; the common (*sādhāraṇa*) to all human beings (the scripture establishing his commonality has been cited previously); the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa, the illuminator; the shining god (*deva*). That god who, like a hide, has rolled together (*samaviviyakta*) the darknesses—that is, he moves through them together, enveloping them—he, the deity of great majesty, rises up.

The great Sun, the progenitor of people, rises up; being a shining golden ornament (*rukma*), far-reaching (*urukṣāḥ*), and possessed of abundant splendor, he rises from the sky, that is, from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
Or rather, he is the golden ornament of the sky, serving as its very adornment.
What is this like?
"One whose object is far away" means one who goes to a distance; "object" (artha) is derived from the root *ṛ* (to go).

Whether sought from afar, the *taraṇi* (the deliverer) rises up, shining brightly as he moves. Indeed, all people— every living being— being impelled, permitted, and urged by Sūrya, the impelling deity, perform their purposes, that is, the actions and duties that must be undertaken.
Where the immortals have made a path for him, he flies like a hawk toward his goal;
at the rising of the sun, O Mitra and Varuṇa, we shall worship you both with reverences and with oblations.

Where the immortals have made a path for him, the son of Pṛthā follows like a soaring falcon. When the sun has risen, let us worship you both, Mitra and Varuṇa, with salutations and with oblations. 5.

In that atmosphere (*antarikṣa*) where the ancient gods, immortal and possessing the nature of the immortals, made a path (*gātu*) for this Sun—that path, the atmosphere, he follows; he goes along it. Like what?
Like a falcon (*śyena*)—one whose movement is praiseworthy—or like a vulture (*gṛdhra*), as it flies along.
It has been stated that this verse-quarter concerns Sūrya.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, when the sun has risen, we shall serve you both at the morning pressing with salutations—that is, with praises—and furthermore, with oblations; we shall attend upon you.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman now grant wide space for our offspring in their most excellent dwelling.
May all our paths be easy to traverse and well-trodden; do you protect us always with your blessings.
Now may Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman grant wide space for our lineage and for our offspring. May all our paths be easy to traverse and well-trodden. Do you protect us always with your blessings. 6.
The sixth [chapter], beginning with "Now Mitra," has been completed.
The fifth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “divi kṣayantā,” is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha and is dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
The Anukramaṇikā states: “In heaven, five.
In the third Chandoma, the first verse of this hymn belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest at the Prauga-śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Aśvins, who dwell in heaven and in the mid-air over the earth, you who possess all desirable things, come to us" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 8.11).
Dwelling in heaven over the expanse of the mid-air and the earth, may they present for you both the garments of clarified butter.
May Mitra, Aryaman, and the well-born King Varuṇa of noble power graciously accept our oblation.

Dwelling in heaven and upon the earth across the mid-air, may they who pour forth the clarified butter grant you their gifts. May Mitra, Aryaman, the noble-born King, and Varuṇa of excellent dominion graciously accept our oblation. 1.
"You two are the lords (kṣayantā) of the *rajas*—that is, of the water—existing in the heaven (*divi*), in the intermediate space (*antarikṣe*), and upon the earth (*pṛthivyām*).
The root *kṣi* denotes the act of ruling;
thus, you two are the masters."
O Mitra and Varuṇa, the clouds impelled by you two give forth— *dadīran*, they bestow— the forms of water, which are the "garments of ghee" (*ghṛtasya nirṇijaḥ*).
Alternatively, [the phrase] "for you two, the forms of ghee" means "the ghees."
May these [gifts] be given; they are being given.
May Mitra, Aryaman—the well-born, the king, the lord of all—and Varuṇa, the one of excellent power, take pleasure in and accept our oblation.
1. And [the hymns] beginning with *kṣata nabhaśa ghṛtasya* and *ā rājānā*. O Kings, guardians of the great Order (*ṛta*), lords of the rivers, Kṣatriyas, come hither!
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who grant quickening gifts, send down nourishment to us and rain from heaven.
O Kings, great guardians of the Cosmic Order (Ṛta), lords of the rivers, Kṣatriyas, come hither! O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who grant life-giving gifts, send us nourishment and rain down from heaven. 2.
O two Kings, lords of all; O two great guardians of the mighty *ṛta*—whether water or sacrifice;
[the vocatives are treated as] *parājñavat* according to the rule "in the case of the *parājñava* accent," whereby the entire group of vocatives receives the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent].
O two Lords of the Sindhu, protectors of the river; O two Kṣatriyas, you who are powerful, come hither, toward us, do you both approach.

Furthermore, O Mitra and Varuna, O quick-givers, you two send down from the sky, that is, from the intermediate space, nourishment for us and also prosperity, as well as rain which brings that about; impel these toward us.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, and the divine Aryaman lead us forward with their most effective and broad [guidance].
May the mountain speak for our noble purpose; may we rejoice in nourishment together with Sudās, protected by the gods.

May Mitra, Varuṇa, and the divine Aryaman lead us forward with their most effective and wide-reaching aids, so that even the enemy may speak well of us; thus, O gods, protected by you, may we rejoice together in nourishment along with Sudās. 3.
May Mitra, the god Varuṇa, and Aryaman—these three—lead us, at that very time when we have need, by the most effective paths to our destination.
Furthermore, may they act so that Aryaman, the noble one, might speak of us to Sudās, the man of excellent gifts, saying, "This person is worthy of compassion.
The repetition of the name Aryaman is for the sake of emphasis.
O divine protectors, you who are our guardians—we, together with our food provided by you, and accompanied by our sons and others, may we rejoice and be glad.

He who has fashioned this chariot-seat for you both with his mind, and who shall perform and maintain this exalted prayer—O Mitra and Varuṇa, sprinkle him with clarity; as such, O two Kings, satisfy us with secure dwellings.

He who has fashioned this chariot-seat for you with his mind, and who, performing this lofty devotion, sustains it—O Mitra and Varuṇa, sprinkle him with clarity; O two Kings, satisfy those who dwell in secure habitations. 4.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, whoever should fashion this chariot of yours with his mind and conceive it with a hymn of praise—having done so, performing an elevated, exalted *dhīti* (a work in the form of praise), he should offer it aloud; having done this, he should maintain it in the *dhāman* (the sacred abode). O Kings, O Lords Mitra and Varuṇa, you two should sprinkle that person with *ghṛta*, that is, with water.
Satisfy his subjects with excellent dwellings (*sukṣitīḥ*). Grant them satisfaction in such a way that they become well-established in their homes.
1. [The syllables] *kha-sa-tanna-bha-śa-’yaḥ* do not exist [in this context].
This hymn, O Varuṇa and Mitra, is offered to you like bright Soma to Vāyu. Favor our prayers; come to our expansive thoughts. Do you two protect us always with your blessings.
This hymn, O Varuṇa, O Mitra, is offered to you, like the bright Soma to Vāyu. Favour our prayers; come to those who meditate upon you. Do you all protect us evermore with blessings. 5.
The fifteenth hymn, beginning with “prati vāṃ sure,” is the ṛṣi-seer Vasiṣṭha’s composition; it is dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
It is indicated by the phrase “prati vām.
[It is used] in the second Chandoma [stotra].

Those two, O Mitra and Varuṇa, possess many snares; they are the barriers against falsehood, difficult for the mortal enemy to overcome. O Mitra and Varuṇa, by the path of *ṛta*—of sacrifice, or of the ritual performed for you—may we cross over misfortunes as one crosses over abundant waters with a boat. In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa, this verse, "O Mitra and Varuṇa, come to us," serves as the fourth invitatory prayer (*anuvākyā*). It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, [come] to the enjoyment of our oblation; you clothe yourselves in fat garments" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8). *Tā* (those two); *bhūripāśau* (possessing many snares); *anṛtasya* (of falsehood); *setū* (the two barriers); *duḥstyetū* (difficult to cross); *ripave martyāya* (for the mortal enemy); *ṛtasya* (of *ṛta*); *mitrāvaruṇā* (O Mitra and Varuṇa); *pathā* (by the path); *vām* (your); *apaḥ na nāvā* (like waters with a boat); *duritā tarema* (may we cross over misfortunes). *Tā* (those two), *mitrāvaruṇau* (Mitra and Varuṇa), *bhūripāśau* (endowed with many snares that serve as means of binding), *anṛtasya* (of the non-sacrificer), *setū* (the two barriers), *ripave martyāya* (for the mortal adversary), *duḥstyetū* (they are difficult to pass). O *mitrāvaruṇā*, such as you are, O Mitra and Varuṇa, *vām* (by you two), *ṛtasya* (of *ṛta*), of sacrifice, or of the ritual being performed for you, *pathā* (by the way), *duritā* (misfortunes), *tarema* (may we cross), *nāvā apaḥ na* (like abundant waters with a boat). In the animal sacrifice to Mitra and Varuṇa, "ā no mitrāvaruṇā" is the fourth invitatory prayer. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "ā no mitrāvaruṇā havyajuṣṭiṃ yuvaṃ vastrāṇi pīvasā vasāthe. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).

O Mitra and Varuṇa, come to our sacrifice which delights in the oblation; sprinkle our pasture-land with clarified butter and with nourishing foods. May one here offer you the choice gift for the sake of the people; bestow upon us the water of the divine, beautiful cloud. O Mitra and Varuṇa, come to our sacrifice which is pleased by the offerings—this is the ellipsis. Having arrived, together with nourishing foods (*iḷābhiḥ*) and waters (*ghṛtaiḥ*), sprinkle (*ukṣatam*) our earth (*gavyūtim*). Regarding you both, may someone here offer (*ā yacchet*) the excellent oblation or hymn of praise. Therefore, out of pure compassion alone, grant (*pṛṇītam*) us the water (*udraḥ*) of the divine, heavenly, and beautiful cloud. (The genitive *udraḥ* is used in the sense of the accusative object. Grant us that water characterized as described above.

This hymn, O Varuṇa and Mitra, like bright Soma for Vāyu, is offered unto you. Further our prayers; come to our sacred thoughts. Do you all protect us evermore with blessings. (5) "This hymn"—thus the fifth [verse] has been explained. The eleventh hymn, consisting of nineteen verses, beginning with "pra mitrayoḥ," is the seerly work of Vasiṣṭha. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: "Pra mitrayoḥ: one less [than twenty]; Gāyatrī; the last three are Pragāthas. The fourth through the tenth are Purauṣṇiks; the [next] ten are addressed to the Ādityas; the last three are addressed to Sūrya. The tenth is Bṛhatī, the eleventh Satobṛhatī, the twelfth Bṛhatī, the thirteenth Satobṛhatī, the fourteenth Bṛhatī, the fifteenth Satobṛhatī, the sixteenth Purauṣṇik; the remaining are Gāyatrīs. From the fourth to the thirteenth, the deities are the Ādityas; from the fourteenth to the end, the three are addressed to Sūrya. The first and last Triṣṭubhs are addressed to Mitra-Varuṇa as before. In the Mādhyandina-savana of the Agniṣṭoma, nine verses from the beginning are to be recited in the Maitrāvaruṇa-śastra, according to the rule: "'pra mitrayor varuṇayoḥ'—nine" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.10). In the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava Ṣaḍahas, the first six verses are to be employed when there is an increase in the Stomas. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'pra mitrayor varuṇayoḥ'—six" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.5).
1. kha-setubandhakau; gha-setubandhakau; jña-tara-setubandhako; na-setubandhakau | 2.
O Aśvins, seekers of the gods, you two young ones [are worshipped] with hymns (stoma).
3. O you two, [possessing] kha-sa-ta-na-śā-vāṃ, [we offer] a choice [gift] in return.

May our hymn go forth, bringing joy, toward Mitra and Varuṇa—this hymn accompanied by reverence, offered to the two gods of many manifestations. *mitrayoḥ varuṇayoḥ*: This means "of Mitra and Varuṇa. The dual number is used in both instances because they are viewed as a pair. *tuvijātayoḥ*: Of the two gods who have many manifestations. *naḥ*: Our own. *śūṣyaḥ*: Bringing happiness. *namasvān*: Accompanied by food, that is, joined with oblations (*havis*). *stomaḥ*: The hymn; the song of praise. *pra etu*: Let it go forth; let it proceed. The Śruti states: "Day and night are indeed Mitra and Varuṇa" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.4.10.1). Because these two depend upon day and night, their "many manifestations" consist in their repeated arrival and departure. Alternatively, their "many manifestations" arise from their appearance for the benefit of many.

Those two whom the gods uphold—the very skillful ones, whose father is Dakṣa, the exceedingly mighty—for the sake of divine power. Those two whom the gods uphold—the very skillful ones, whose father is Dakṣa, the exceedingly mighty—for the sake of divine power. Whom? You two. Who? The gods, the original creators. For what purpose? For *asurya*, that is, for the exercise of strength. Of what nature are you two? *Sudakṣā*: possessing excellent strength; *dakṣapitarā*: whose father is Dakṣa, meaning the protectors or masters of strength, or in other words, the bestowers of strength. *Pramahasā*: possessed of preeminent splendor. "Accomplish those [tasks]"—this is the connection with the subsequent verse.

May those two, O Varuṇa and Mitra, who protect our dwellings and protect our bodies, bring our prayers to fulfillment. (3) May those two—O Varuṇa and Mitra, you who possess the characteristics described above—protect our *stipā* (dwellings), for *stayaḥ* means houses because they stand firm; they are called *stipau* because they protect them (*pā*). And may you two, as the protectors of our bodies (*tanupā*), fulfill the *dhiyaḥ* (prayers) of us, the singers—that is, our ritual acts in the form of hymns—making them fruitful. (3)

If today, when the sun has risen, Mitra, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Bhaga shall impel us to be sinless—(4) If today, when the sun has risen, Mitra, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Bhaga shall impel us to be sinless—(4) Whatever wealth is required by us, at this time when the sun has risen, during the morning libation, may the sinless Mitra, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Bhaga each individually impel it toward us. Or rather: may Mitra and Aryaman be givers so that we are sinless; may Bhaga—the one to be shared with and Savitṛ—impel that desired wealth toward us.

May that dwelling be well-protected; may it be so, O bounteous ones, as you go forth on your journey—those of you who carry us across the day’s distress. (5) May that *kṣayaḥ* (dwelling or abode) be *suprāvīḥ* (well-protecting); let it be a good protector with excellence. The prefix *pra-* is for the sake of emphasis, implying "let it be so preeminently and quickly"—this is the sense. When [is this]? It is said: O *sudānavaḥ* (bounteous ones), when there is your *yāman* (journey or coming). On whose coming? On the coming of you who, by carrying *naḥ* (us) across *aṃhaḥ* (distress or sin), *atipiprrati* (carry us across)—on the coming of such as those. (8)
1. Let him go;
for Svarāj and Aditi, who possess unimpaired vows, are kings who rule over the great.
And also: Aditi, the self-ruling one.
Of the unerring vow,
those who...
The great kings rule over it.

Furthermore, Mitra and the other three [Varuṇa and Aryaman] are self-rulers (*svarāja*), lords of all; Aditi is their mother. They are the masters (*rājānaḥ*) of this great, unassailable vow—of this deed—and they are capable (*viśante*);
that is, they are able to grant what is desired.
This is how it should be construed with the *Atharvaveda*.
Those who—Mitra and the others, as well as Aditi—are the self-ruling lords of the unfailing vow; being the kings and masters of great wealth desired by us, they have the power to bestow it upon us.
The triplet beginning with "prati vām" serves as the *paryāsa* for the Maitrāvaruṇa at the morning pressing on the twenty-fourth day.
This is prescribed in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (7.2): "prati vāṃ sūra udite vyantarikṣamatitar."

At the rising of the sun, I praise each of you individually: Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman, the destroyer of enemies. (7) O Mitra and Varuṇa, I praise you both—Mitra and Varuṇa—and Aryaman, the devourer of foes, one by one. When? It is said: when the divine Sūrya has risen; that is to say, in the morning.

This hymn, accompanied by golden wealth, is for the sake of the unobstructed power and strength; this, O sages, is for the winning of the sacrifice. This hymn, accompanied by golden wealth—that is, by riches that are truly delightful—is for the sake of *avakāya*, meaning for the unimpeded, and for *śavase*, our strength. This very hymn being now performed is the praise [offered], such is the sense. In the word *hiraṇyayā*, the third case singular ending has been replaced by *yā* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. Furthermore, O wise ones (*viprāḥ*), may this very praise be for *medhasātaye*, that is, for the attainment of the sacrifice.

May we be yours, O God Varuṇa, may we be yours, O Mitra, together with our patrons; may we obtain nourishment and light. (9) May we be yours, O God Varuṇa; may we be yours, O Mitra, together with our patrons. Furthermore, may we obtain and hold fast to nourishment and light. In the *Aśvina-śastra*, there is the *pragātha* beginning with "Many [are they] who have the sun as their eye. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The *pragāthas* beginning with 'Many [are they] who have the sun as their eye'... (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.5). This same *pragātha* also occurs in the *prauga-śastra* on the fifth day of the ten-night sacrifice. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "'Many [are they] who have the sun as their eye,' and 'These two of yours dwelling in heaven'... (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 7.12).
Many are they, with the eyes of heroes, tongues of fire, upholders of Truth; they who by their insights have mastered the three diverse realms, and by their all-surpassing powers, all things.
1. Protector of that which is known, not sleeping, and unharmed;

2. O you who are many, possessing the splendor of the sun, having Agni as your tongue, increasing the *ṛta*, those three who have directed the three sacrificial assemblies with their insights and through all-encompassing powers. 10.
Many are the great ones with divine vision, possessing a radiance like that of the sun; or rather, those for whom the light is divine. They are fire-tongued.
Those for whom the tongue and the palate are the means of enjoyment;
the *ṛtāvṛdhaḥ*, the augmenters of the sacrifice, such as Mitra and the others;
furthermore, those who [protect] the three all-pervading sacrificial assemblies (*vidathāni*)—the locations such as the earth and so forth—by means of their encompassing powers (*paribhūtibhiḥ*).
"By their steadfastness and deeds, they have restrained themselves; they bestow sovereignty"—this is to be connected with what follows.
Alternatively, one may supply the ellipsis here itself: "May those who bestow the three stations, being endowed with many qualities such as *iyugū*, come hither."
Those who have established the autumn, the month, the day, and the night— Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman, the kings, have attained unattainable dominion.
Those who established the year, the month, and then the day, the sacrifice, the night, and then the verse—the unattainable—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman, these kings have attained sovereign power. 11.

Those [beings], Mitra and the others, who established— i.e., fashioned— the autumn, the year, and immediately thereafter the month, immediately thereafter the day, immediately thereafter the sacrifice accomplished by the day, immediately thereafter the night, and the *ṛc* verses and the mantras;
or rather, in all these instances, the particle *āt* signifies "also" (*api*),
in which case the sequence is not intended to be significant.
Those three—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—the shining kings, have attained an unattainable dominion, a power that cannot be reached by others. They have pervaded it.
Therefore, we meditate upon you today with hymns at the rising of the sun, since Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman grant [our desires]; you are the furtherers of the Eternal Order (Ṛta).
That we meditate upon for you today with well-spoken hymns, O wise ones, as the sun has risen—since Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman take heed of it—you are the furtherers of the Eternal Order (Ṛta). 12.

We invoke you—that which is well-known—today at this time of sacrifice; we entreat you with hymns (*sūkta*). At what time? When the sun has risen; that is to say, in the morning. O leaders (*radhyaḥ*) of the water of Truth (*ṛtasya*), Varuṇa and the others, that wealth which you carry (*ohate*)—since this is in grammatical apposition with "you," there is a shift of person in the verb *ohate*; thus it means "you carry" (*ohadhve*). That [wealth] we invoke.
O you who are true to the cosmic order, born of the cosmic order, increasers of the cosmic order, terrible ones who hate untruth—
within your benevolence, O heroes, may we and our wise patrons abide in that which provides the most secure protection.

O you who possess the cosmic order, born of the cosmic order, strengthened by the cosmic order, terrible ones, haters of falsehood—within your benevolence, which provides the most secure protection, O heroes, may we abide, as well as those who are our wise patrons. 13.
You who are possessors of *ṛta*, endowed with *ṛta*, possessed of sacrifice, or possessed of water—born from *ṛta*.
The meaning of the word *ṛta* has already been stated;
you are those produced for that purpose.
Alternatively, they are born from *ṛta*, that is, from Prajāpati; *ṛtāvṛdhaḥ* means those who cause the aforementioned *ṛta* to increase. 1. [Variant] kha-bha-3: *krama* is here *avi*.
2. [The suffix] *pa* after *kha-prajāti*; [the suffix] *ta3-4-na* after *jha-prajāti*; [the suffix] *śa* after *pra-jāti*.

O you who are terrible, O terrible ones, O haters of falsehood, O haters of those who do not sacrifice—to you all, may we and those other wise patrons (surayaḥ), all become possessed of your excellent shelter, that most pleasant wealth, or happiness consisting of an exceedingly delightful home. In the Mādhyandina pressing, when there is an excess of Soma, this *pragātha* beginning with "udu tyat" is the *anurūpa*. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The two *pragāthas*, 'baṇ mahān asi sūrya' and 'udu tyad darśataṃ vapuḥ', are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa*. On the twenty-fourth day, at the Mādhyandina pressing, this same triplet is the optional *stotriya*. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "'udu tyad darśataṃ vapuḥ', 'udu tye madhumattamāḥ'. **udu tyad darśataṃ vapur diva eti pratihvare | yad īm āśur vahati deva etaśo viśvasmai cakṣase aram || 14 ||** That visible, beautiful form (*vapuḥ*) of the sun rises up near the slope of heaven (*divaḥ pratihvare*). When the swift, divine horse Etaśa draws it, he is ready for the sight of all. **śīrṣṇaḥ-śīrṣṇo jagatas tasthuṣas patiṃ samayā viśvā rajaḥ | sasvasāraḥ suvitāya sūryaṃ vahanti harito rathe || 15 ||** From every head—meaning from the head of every being—they carry the Lord of the moving and the stationary across all the regions (*rajaḥ*) for the sake of prosperity. The sisters, the bay-colored mares (*haritaḥ*), draw the Sun in his chariot. **taccakṣur devahitaṃ śukram uccarat | paśyema śaradaḥ śataṃ jīvema śaradaḥ śatam || 16 ||** May that eye, established by the gods, the bright one, rise upward. May we see for a hundred autumns; may we live for a hundred autumns. *Notes:* 1. *Śīrṣṇaḥ-śīrṣṇaḥ*: The fifth case is used in the sense of the third; it means "from each respective head," connecting with "they carry the Sun. Alternatively, the word "head" (*śiras*) indicates the possessor of the head, signifying the totality of all beings. 2. *Suvitāya*: For the sake of well-being or prosperity. 3. *Devahitam*: Beneficial to the gods, because the acceptance of their oblations depends upon it; or, established by the god (the Sun). 4. *Uccarat*: Rising upward. 5. *Paśyema... jīvema*: The repetition is for the sake of emphasis. *(Note: The commentary provides various variant readings for the commentary text itself, which have been omitted here for clarity.)*
In the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* six-day periods, for the insertion (*āvāpa*) occasioned by the *stoma*, the triplet "With the poetic insights, O invincible one" (*akāvyebhir adābhyā*) is used;
for it is stated in the Sūtra: "'With the poetic insights, O invincible one'—these three [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.5).
O undeceivable Varuṇa and Mitra, come resplendently with our hymns to drink the Soma.
With our poetic hymns, O invincible Varuṇa and Mitra, come hither resplendently to drink the Soma. 17.
O you two who are unassailable and not to be deceived—O Varuṇa and Mitra—you two, radiant with splendor, come hither by means of our poetic hymns;
for what purpose? For the drinking of the Soma.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, come from heaven with your radiant powers and with your waters;
drink the Soma that gladdens you both.
O Varuṇa and Mitra, you who are free from guile, come hither with the splendors of heaven; drink the Soma, O ye who are swift. 18.

O Varuṇa and you, Mitra, who are free from malice and upholders of non-malice, come hither with your splendors or manifestations from the domains of heaven— that is, from the places belonging to the celestial world (the third case used in the sense of the fifth). Or rather, together with your powers and glories, come to our sacrifice.

O Agastya and Ātujī, you who are destroyers of enemies from all sides or rather givers of wealth—being such as these, drink the Soma! The root *tuji* is used in the senses of "injury," "strength," "giving," and "dwelling";
here it occurs in the sense of either injury or giving.
Come hither, O Mitra and Varuṇa, accepting our offering, O heroes; drink the Soma, you who increase the Truth.
Come, O Mitra and Varuṇa, enjoying the oblation, O heroes; drink the Soma, you who increase the Truth! 19.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, O leaders of the sacrifice, O heroes, being pleased and enjoying the oblation characterized by Soma, come hither to the sacrifice.
Having arrived, O you two increasers of the cosmic order (ṛta), drink the Soma.
The twelfth hymn, consisting of ten verses, begins with "prati vām ratham.
According to the Anukramaṇikā: "prati vām daśa is the Aśvin hymn.
The seer is Vasiṣṭha.
The meter is *triṣṭubh*.
According to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) beginning with "tuhyādi," these first eight hymns have the Aśvins as their deity.
In the *prātaranuvāka* performed for the *āśvina* ceremony, this set of seven hymns—excluding the second—is to be recited in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
And so says the Sūtra: "One should extract the second [verse] from the triplet beginning with *prati vām ratham*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.15).
I shall celebrate your chariot, O lords of men, with a sacrificial mind endowed with oblations— that chariot which,
like a messenger, has awakened you, O bountiful ones, as a son awakens his parents who are eager to speak.

O you two lords of men, I praise your chariot so that it may be heard, with a sacrificial mind possessing oblations—(the chariot) which, like a messenger, O you two worthy of thought, has awakened you; it calls out toward you as a son [calls] to his parents. ||1||
O Aśvins, lords of men who are being praised by kings, I go toward your chariot to praise it—
"jar" meaning praise;
the ellipsis is "I go to praise."
By what means? That is now stated: by a mind endowed with oblation (*haviṣmat*), that is, joined with the sacrificial offering, and fit for sacrifice (*yajñiya*), [that is] by a hymn of praise.
O you two who possess wisdom (*dhiṣṇyā*), that chariot which belongs to you—O you two who possess the power of inspiration (*dhiṣaṇāhī*).
Dhiṣaṇā is praise.
Like a messenger, it has awakened you two—just as a messenger awakens us—to come toward that chariot; like a son toward his parents, [it calls] to you two, the parents.
I have spoken.
1. [The forms] *kha-ta3-bha-śa-kena* and *jha-na-vena* are derived from *iti*; *ta4-vana* is derived from *iti*. I shall speak (*vivakmi*) and I speak (*āvacmi*).
This is the illustration for the awakening.
Like a son [seeks] his parents, like a son [seeks] both mother and father;
or rather, the meaning should be joined thus: "O you two who have awakened, come toward us with that chariot which has awakened you two, for I desire to speak.
Agni, being kindled, has been praised for him; even the ends of the months have looked upon him.

The banner of the Dawn has shone forth in the east, being born for the glory of the Daughter of Heaven. Agni has been made pure, being fully kindled; even the very limits of darkness have been perceived.
The banner of the Dawn has shone forth in the east, being born for the glory of the Daughter of Heaven.

2. Agni has been purified, being well-kindled; even the ends of the darkness have become visible. The banner of the Dawn moves forward in the east, being born for the splendor of the Daughter of Heaven. 2.
Being kindled—that is, being set ablaze—by us, Agni has shone; he blazes forth.
Even from out of the darkness, the ends—the boundaries and regions—are seen by all.
The banner, the signifier of all, the Sun, [stands] before the daughter of Heaven, Uṣas, in the eastern direction.

O divine Aśvins, make my straight, unimpaired, and wealth-seeking prayer effective for the sake of gain. And in battle, O lords of power, protect all our thoughts with your powers. O divine Aśvins, you two gods, make my *prācīm*—straightforward, *amṛdhram*—unimpaired, and *vasuyum*—desiring wealth—*dhiyam*—my thought, praise, or ritual act—*sātaye*—for the sake of acquisition; that is, make it fit for attainment. Furthermore, in *vāje*—in battle—protect *viśvāḥ purandhīḥ*—all our thoughts. O *śacīpatī*—lords of power, *śaktam*—be able to help us—*śacībhiḥ*—with your powers. 5.

O *bhuraṇā*, you two who are the sustainers of all—when there is a single, common, and shared *yoga* (endeavor) for our desired purpose, your chariot goes around the *sas*—the substances that are by nature mobile, or numbering seven.
The meaning is that it arrives swiftly.
Therein, the favorable, well-born horses, yoked to you two gods, do not fail; they do not wither, nor do they grow weary in their rapid course.
Those swift horses of yours that carry you—crossing over, reaching across, and traveling rapidly—do not weary.
Grant imperishable wealth to the liberal patrons who incite the giving of riches;
they who further their kin with pleasant words, bestowing gifts of cattle, spotted kine, and horses.

Grant immortality to our patrons, for they have become such; they who, with their wealth, impel the gift of bounty. They who extend their kinship through gracious words, seeking boons of cattle and horses, and bestowing riches. 9.
O you two who are never attached anywhere, become—indeed, be—for the sake of the *maghavadbhyaḥ*, that is, for the wealthy patrons who offer oblations;
be truly devoted to them alone. It is the recipients of favor who are specifically distinguished here.

Those who, by means of wealth— that is, with riches as their motive— or who are endowed with wealth, impel, bestow, or offer the *maghadeya*, the wealth to be given, namely the oblation characterized as *magha*;
and those who [bestow] the *bandhu*— so called because it binds through affection.
That which binds itself;
or alternatively, a "bandhu" is one who binds by means of the fruit [of the sacrifice], such as the Adhvaryu priest and others—
him [the sacrificer] [binds] with "sūnṛtās" (truthful and pleasant words).
With words whose essence is most dear,
they promote— that is, they cause to increase; the root *tṛ* preceded by *pra* has the meaning of increasing.
Doing what?

Bestowing upon those seekers *gavyā*—wealth in the form of cattle—and *aśvyā*—wealth in the form of horses; that is, granting riches (*maghāni*) to them, the liberal patrons (*maghavadbhyaḥ*). Thus it is said.
Now hear my invocation, O youthful ones; come, O Aśvins, on your path rich in light.
Bestow treasures and grant long life to our patrons; do you protect us always with your blessings.

Now hear my invocation, O youthful ones; come to our dwelling, O Aśvins, bringing nourishment. Bestow treasures and grant long life to our patrons. Do you all protect us evermore with your blessings. 10.
O two youths, eternally young, now indeed listen to my call, our hymn of praise!
Having heard it, O Aśvins, come to our dwelling, which is rich in offerings;
and having arrived, bestow upon us delightful treasures.
"Make the patrons—the singers—grow old [in wisdom], that is, cause them to prosper;
for the roots have a single meaning.
The rest is clear."
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “ā śubhā yātam,” is the seer Vasiṣṭha’s Āśvina hymn.
Of these, the first seven are Virāj meters, while the eighth and ninth are Triṣṭubh meters. It is recorded in the Anukramaṇī: “‘ā śubhā’: nine verses; [the first] seven are Virāj.”
The application of the hymn is based on its internal characteristics.
Come hither with your beautiful horses, O youthful lords; may you, who delight in our songs, accept our oblations and attend to us.
1. He goes by means of the sky (kha) and himself (bha).

2. By means of swift movement (śa). 3. To those who ask (arthibhyaḥ), he gives while restraining (yacchataḥ); in the variant *jha-ta1-2*, it is "to those who ask, he gives while going" (*yato*); in *ta3-4-na-śa-ya*, it is "to those who ask, he gives while restraining" (*yantor*); in *bha*, it is "to those who ask, he restrains" (*yantor*).
O Aśvins, you who possess noble horses, you have heard our songs; O Dastras, you who are youthful, having graciously accepted our oblations, partake of the offerings presented to you. 1.
O Aśvins, like two beautiful horses shining in the light, come here to our sacrifice!

O Dastrās, destroyers of enemies, may you both enjoy my songs of praise—my hymns—as I, your devotee, yearn for you; this is the sense of the verse. Not only the praise, but also consume our offered oblations that have been gathered and prepared for you.
‘pra vām andhāṃsi’ is indeed the yājyā for the Śastra of the Aśvins.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘pra vām andhāṃsi madyāny asthur ubhā pibatam aśvinā’ (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.5).
The exhilarating juices have been set forth; come quickly to enjoy my oblation!
Pass over the hostile incitements of the enemy and hear us!

The intoxicating Soma juices have been set forth for you both; come quickly to enjoy my oblation. Overpowering the invocations of the enemy, hear our call! O Aśvins, the intoxicating Soma juices—those foods that produce exhilaration—have been presented before you both. That is to say, they have been taken up. Therefore, come very swiftly and promptly to partake of my oblation, for the sake of drinking it. Having set aside the invocations of the enemy (aryaḥ)—that is, those who are hostile to us—hear our call. [In this verse, the initial accent of *śrutam* is not lost due to its following the word *ati*.]
Your chariot, swift as thought and possessing a hundredfold protection, O Aśvins, speeds across the realms toward us, seeking Sūryā and Vasu.

Your chariot, swift as thought, O Aśvins, with a hundred aids, hastens through the realms for us, O you who possess the wealth of Sūryā, as it is implored. O you two who dwell together with Sūryā upon the chariot, your chariot—implored for our sake—hastens; it comes to our sacrifice, or rather, it is urged forward for its journey. Of what nature is this chariot? Swift as thought, possessing the speed of the mind; providing a hundred aids, that is, protection for us in immeasurable measure. What does it do? It hastens, passing across and transcending the *rajāṃsi*, the worlds.
This very stone, the presser of Soma for you two gods, speaks aloud like a ruddy bird;
may it bring hither the two lovely sages with our oblations.

This [is] for you two. Ha! When this stone, the Soma-presser, raised up, speaks aloud for you two, O Gods—you who desire the gods—then may the inspired singer turn toward you two, the beautiful ones, with oblations. When, whenever, for you two, for yourselves—the two gods—the god-seeking [singer], "u" being a filler, this stone, the pressing-stone, the Soma-presser, pressing out the Soma for you two, for your sake, presses it out; such is the connection. (1.
gha = havanāni / āhvanāni).
Acting thus, standing upright and elevated, he proclaims aloud; then the wise sacrificer turns toward you both, the beautiful ones, with oblations.
For your nourishment is indeed wondrous; bestow it upon Atri, that which is full of great power, upon him who, being dear to you, maintains your measure.
It is wondrous! Indeed, that food which you have for him—bestow it upon Atri, rich in buffaloes, who, being your dear friend, maintains your protection. 5.

O Aśvins, that wonderful (*citram*) and praiseworthy (*cāyanīyam*) *bhojanam*—wealth—that belongs to you both, indeed exists (*asti ha*). The particle *nu* is a filler. The meaning is: "Give that to us. Now follows the praise of them: [for] *Atraye*, for the seer named Atri; the fourth case ending is used in the sense of the fifth.

Ye were able for the wolf even as he grew old; ye were famed for the one lying there, being urged on. Ye two bestowed water upon Adhyama, like stars upon the barren cow; O Aśvins, by your powers and your deeds. For the wolf, even as he was growing old, ye were capable; and ye were renowned for the one lying there, being urged on. Ye two bestowed water upon Adhyama, like stars upon the barren cow; O Aśvins, by your powers and your deeds.
"To Vṛka, the giver of wealth"—
the meaning is "to him who desires [it]";
*cit* is an expletive.
Or else, he bestows wealth upon others;
or rather,
[he gives it] to a wolf, that is, to one who is like a wolf in his harmfulness.
To this Ṛṣi, who is named thus and who is wasting away through his labors, [the gods] did not give the desired wealth that he was capable of receiving;
this is the form of the aorist (luṅ) of the root *śak* in the sense of "giving," with the absence of the augment (*aḍ*) being Vedic.
Moreover, O you two who are being invoked, you have heard the call of the seer named Śayu;
you two filled the cow with milk—the inviolable one—just as one fills the waters of a river like the Aṅgiras.
Just as one fills that [river] with water, so did you fill her.

Of what sort [was she]? Even in the case of a *maghnyā*—even a *stary*, that is, even a barren cow who has ceased to give birth and is aged—you two, O Aśvins, having made her capable through your power (*śakti*), that is, by endowing her with the capacity characterized by milking, [acted] through your deeds (*śacībhiḥ*).

This is illustrated by the hymn beginning: "Even for Śayu, though he was wasting away, you two, O mighty ones, by your deeds (*śacībhiḥ*) made him whole; for Jaṃsurya you made the cow swell with milk" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.22).

This singer here praises you with excellent hymns, O Agni, awakening at the dawning of the mornings, full of noble thought. May he be strengthened by food, by the cow, and by milk. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 9. eṣaḥ | syaḥ | kāruḥ | jarate | su-uktaiḥ | agne | budhānaḥ | uṣasām | su-manmā | iṣā | tam | vardhat | aghnyā | payaḥ-bhiḥ | yūyam | pāta | svasti-bhiḥ | sadā | naḥ || 9 ||
This celebrated singer, Vasiṣṭha, the poet, awakening at the morning pressing of the dawns, O Agni, being mindful and well-disposed—or possessing excellent praise—praises you with hymns.
Strengthen him with food;
there is a change of voice (the imperative is used for the present).
May the inviolable cow (*aghnī*) increase;
or rather, let it be a single sentence:
"The inviolable cow, the cow specifically assigned for Vasiṣṭha’s Agnihotra, [increases] by means of shearing."
The meaning is "with clarified butter.
And with "milk," may he cause that Vasiṣṭha to grow;
thus, he refers to himself indirectly.
The remainder is clear.
The hymn beginning with "ā vāṃ rathaḥ," consisting of eight verses, is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha and is dedicated to the Aśvins.
It is catalogued thus: "ā vāṃ rathaḥ [consists of] eight [verses].
Its application (viniyoga) has been stated for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra.

May your golden chariot, firmly fastened to heaven and earth, come hither with its stallions and horses—its path anointed with ghee, shining with its fellies, bearing nourishment, the lord of men, and full of vigor. ā vām rathaḥ rodasī baddhaghānaḥ hiraṇyayaḥ vṛṣabhaiḥ yātu aśvaiḥ | ghṛtavartaniḥ pibibhī rucānaḥ iṣāṃ voḷhā nṛpatiḥ vājinīvān || 1 || May your golden chariot, firmly fastened to heaven and earth, come hither with its stallions and horses—its path anointed with ghee, shining with its fellies, bearing nourishment, the lord of men, and full of vigor.
O Aśvins, may your chariot, yoked with young, vigorous horses, come hither to our sacrifice.
Of what kind is that chariot?

*Rodasī*: Heaven and Earth; *baddhaghānaḥ*: striking down or repelling; *hiraṇyayaḥ*: made of gold; *ghṛtavartaniḥ*: whose path has clarified butter as its water; *pivibhiḥ*: with the fellies of his chariot; *rūcānaḥ*: shining or blazing; *iṣāṃ voḷhā*: the bearer of the oblations offered by the sacrificers, or the carrier of the foods; *vājānāṃ voḷhā*: the bearer of the prizes to be given; *nṛpatiḥ*: the lord of men, the master of the sacrificers; *vājinīvān*: possessed of food.
1. [In some versions] "hiraṇmayaḥ" is absent; [in others, including] kha, jha, jha, ta1-2, na, bha, it is "hiraṇmayaḥ".
2. [In versions] kha, ta, na, bha, it is "cānnānām".
Spreading out over the five worlds, may he, the three-seated one, go forth, yoked by the mind.
By which you two go to the people who long for the gods, bestowing whatever path you choose, O Aśvins.

He, spreading himself out over the five regions of the earth, let him come hither with his mind, yoked with his triple-seated chariot, by which you two go to the people seeking the gods, O Aśvins, taking your course wherever it may be.
May that chariot, which has spread across the five worlds— meaning all living beings— and which possesses three seats (the *vandhura* being the wooden frame for the driver’s position,
high and low), come hither,
yoked by our mind through our hymn of praise.
O Aśvins, on which chariot you go toward the people— the worshiping clans who seek the gods— on whatever path you maintain your course, let that vehicle come hither.
Come hither with your own splendor, O you who possess beautiful horses; as masters, drink from the honeyed vessel.
Your chariot, yoked with a bride, strikes against the ends of heaven as it moves along its two paths.
O you two with noble horses, come hither with splendor! O Dastras, drink from the honeyed vessel; your chariot, yoked by the bride, strikes against the ends of heaven as it moves along its paths.

O two gods, come hither toward us with your beautiful horses and with glory! O destroyers of enemies, you who exhaust the foes, drink—the two of you—drink the honeyed Soma prepared as a treasure-store! Your chariot, proceeding together with the bride Sūryā, goes toward those places that are to be reached.
The meaning is "causing to go.
Acting in this way, with his two tracks—that is, his two wheels—he "presses," meaning he afflicts by means of rapid motion, the "ends" or boundary regions of heaven.
The maiden, the daughter of Sūrya, chose your splendor during the night’s departure;
when you two protect the one seeking the gods with your powers, the bird goes around the snare for you both.
The maiden, the daughter of Sūrya, chose your splendor for herself at the encounter; when you protect the one seeking the gods with your powers, the bird comes to you both for refuge and for food.
Your glory—
*śrī* being so called because it rests (*śrayate*) upon you, namely the chariot,
or perhaps that which is ever to be resorted to— that the maiden, the daughter of Sūrya, has chosen for herself, constantly mingling with it.
When?

At the *paritakmyā*, the night that encompasses [the sacrifice], or at the battle, or when one must go to the sacrifice. Furthermore, whenever (*yat*) you protect (*avathaḥ*) with your powers (*śacībhiḥ*)—that is, through your deeds characterized by going and so forth—the sacrificer who desires the gods (*devayantam*), or the sacrifice itself, then at that time, the glowing (*ghrasam*) food (*vayaḥ*) consisting of Soma and the like, comes around to you both (*vām pari gāt*) by means of your favor (*omanā*), that is, by way of protection.

O Aśvins, that chariot of yours which, yoked at dawn when the stars have faded, goes around the enclosure, with that bring us well-being and wide space at the dawning of the light; come to this sacrifice, O Aśvins.

O Aśvins, that charioteer who comes to you at dawn, having yoked his chariot with oxen, goes around the enclosure; with him, O Aśvins, bring us well-being and prosperity at the breaking of the dawn to this sacrifice. ||5||
The chariot (*ratha*)— the particle *ha* being a filler— is that well-known chariot; O two charioteers (*rathirā*), O two riders!
The suffix *ra* has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
He clothes himself in, that is, covers himself with, rays of light.
And the chariot, being yoked—that is, joined with horses—goes around, meaning it traverses, the path or the house of the sacrificer.

O Aśvins, on that chariot, come to us at this sacrifice at the dawning of the night, at the time of morning; for our well-being, bring us peace from evils and union with happiness. Bring it down upon us.
O men, like thirsty ones longing for lightning, come today to our libation;
for from many places they invoke you with their prayers—do not think of us as those who would restrain you when you are eager to come.
Like two white cows toward lightning, come today with all your powers to us who thirst for you; for many places call upon you both with hymns. Let not other seekers of the gods restrain you. 6.
O leaders, you two Aśvins, like two white cows, like a doe—thirsting for Soma that shines with special brilliance—come today to our libations, one after another.
For in many sacrifices, those who sacrifice invoke you both with hymns of praise;
therefore, let other sacrificers who desire the gods not restrain you, nor hold you back.
O Aśvins, you two brought Bhujyu out from the ocean, which was surging with waves,
by means of winged steeds that were unfailing, tireless, unwavering, and of wondrous form, carrying him across.

O Aśvins, you rescued Bhujyu from the ocean; with winged steeds that do not fail, that are unwearied and unflinching, you carried him out from the waters by means of your wondrous powers, delivering him. 7.
O Aśvins, you two rescued Bhujyu—so named—who was scattered by his companions and submerged in the midst of the ocean; from the waters, you carried him away. What did you do? That is told:

with unswerving, undecaying, unwearied, and unfaltering winged steeds yoked to your chariot, and with wondrous deeds performed by your bodies, carrying him across, you carried him across the ocean from the waters.
"The Nāsatyas rescued Bhujyu with winged [horses]," thus it is stated in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā (1.116.4).
O youthful ones, hear my invocation; come, O Aśvins, upon your path rich in light.
Bestow treasures and grant long life to our patrons; protect us always with your blessings.

Now hear my invocation, O youthful ones; come to our dwelling, O Aśvins, bringing refreshing food. Bestow treasures upon us and grant long life to our patrons. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 8.
The eighth [verse], "nū me havam," is established.
The hymn beginning with “ā viśvavārā,” consisting of seven verses, fifteen pādas, and composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, is the seer’s work of Vasiṣṭha and is dedicated to the Aśvins.
It is enumerated thus: “ā viśvavārā sapta.
Its application (viniyoga) has been stated for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra.
The first triplet is employed in the *prauga-śastra* during the third *chandoma*, because it is prescribed in the Sūtra:
“O Aśvins, you who possess all boons, come to us; this Soma is for Indra” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 8.11).
Because this [oblation] occupies the position of the head for every sacrifice;
the *gharma* which reaches you two— this is the ellipsis—
it fills the oceans and the rivers by means of its increase.
*etagvā citra*:
*cit* is an expletive.
The meaning is: "like two horses, well-yoked—that is, as if they were properly harnessed to a chariot."
"Neti" is used in the sense of comparison.

O two Gods, take pleasure in the plants and in the waters—that which is most desirable—since you have pervaded the plants and the waters belonging to the seers as is fitting for you. Bestow many jewels upon us; follow after the ancient pairs through the ages. O two Gods, you both should take pleasure (*caniṣṭam*) in the plants—that is, in the sacrificial cakes and other products of the plants—and in the waters, namely the Soma juices. "Since" (*yat*) you, being "fitting" (*yogyāḥ*), have pervaded (*abhāvethē*) the plants and the waters associated with the seers, therefore you should also desire our [offerings]. Or rather: the plural "of the seers" (*ṛṣīṇām*) is used for honorific purposes. Since you have taken pleasure in the plants and the waters and have manifested your fit praises, therefore, bestowing many delightful treasures (*ratnā*) upon us, you have followed after the ancient pairs—the couples in the form of husband and wife—through the ages, having meditated upon them for the sake of showing favor.

O Aśvins, though you have already heard [our prayers], you behold the many sacred hymns (*brahmāṇi*) of the seers (*ṛṣīṇām*). Come forth toward the choice offering for the sake of this person; may your most excellent favor be with us. O Aśvins, you who have indeed heard [our calls], you behold the many powerful hymns of the seers. Therefore, come forward toward the sacrifice, the choice of this person. May your most gracious favor be directed toward us.

Now, he concludes the praise of the locative case.
O Aśvins, this *manīṣā*—that is, this hymn of praise has been composed for you; this is the ellipsis.
For that very purpose, it is stated again:
this *gīḥ*, this hymn, has been made.
O *vṛṣaṇā*, you two showerers of desires, may you both *juṣethām*—enjoy and accept—this *suvṛktim*, this beautiful hymn composed by us.
May these *brahmāṇi*, these ritual acts in the form of praises, which are *yuvayūni*—longing for you both—*agman*, go unto you. "May you protect [us]" is the established conclusion.
In the fifth section (anuvāka), there are nineteen hymns (sūktas).
Among them, the first hymn, “apa svasuḥ,” is a long one (bahvṛca) dedicated to the Aśvins by Traidhātabha. It is enumerated as: “apa svasuḥ ṣaṭ.”
The application is concluded.
The sister departs from her brother at dawn; the dark one yields the path to the ruddy one.
We invoke you two, who bring wealth in horses and wealth in cattle; day and night, keep the archer away from us.

The sister, Dawn, does not yield her place; the dark one makes way for the ruddy one. O you who possess wealth in horses and wealth in cattle, we invoke you both; day and night, keep the arrow away from us. 1.

From her sister—that is, from Uṣas, who stands in the position of a sister—the Night (*nak*) departs, *apa jihīte*; that is to say, she withdraws of her own accord, making way for her. As it is said: "The sister has yielded the womb to her elder sister" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.124.8).

The dark-colored night (*kṛṣṇīḥ*) parts the path— the way for the ruddy one (*aruṣāya*), that is, for the shining day or for the Sun. Since this is so, because it is the time of your arrival, O you two who possess wealth in horses (*aśvamaghā*) and wealth in cattle (*gomaghā*),
meaning "O you two who are the givers of both."
Such as you two are, we invoke you; we praise you; we call upon you.
Day and night, at all times, keep the weapon—the destroyer—far away from us.
Come to the mortal who offers oblations, O Aśvins, bringing desirable wealth upon your chariot.
Drive away from us lack of food and disease; O lovers of sweetness, protect us by day and by night.

Come near to the mortal who offers oblations, O Aśvins, bringing with your chariot all that is desirable. Drive away from us exhaustion and disease; O lovers of sweetness, protect us by day and by night.
O Aśvins, you two have come near; you have approached in response to our invocation.
For what purpose?
For the sake of the donor, the sacrificer who offers oblations, bringing—by means of your chariot—the desirable wealth that is worthy of being won.
"From us"—separate yourselves from us;
what?
"Anirāma."
*Irām*:
that is, the absence of it; *amīvām*: and disease.
O ye two lovers of sweetness, full of honey, protect us—both by day and by night—at all times.
May the powerful ones, seeking favor, turn your chariot hither at the breaking of dawn for our well-being;
O Aśvins, with your immortal and enduring steeds, bring that chariot laden with wealth, its pole held fast by your hands.

May the bulls, seeking your favor, turn your chariot hither at the break of dawn; may they, desiring your grace, bring you with horses that seek the Truth and possess golden reins. O Aśvins, come hither, bringing with you wealth. 3.
When the dawn has arrived and is about to break, may your horses—well-yoked for your chariot, seeking your favor, and raining down blessings—bring you both hither.
O Aśvins, bring that chariot which has well-fashioned reins, beautiful rays, and is laden with wealth to be bestowed, by means of your water-seeking horses.
1. Kha-sūkta: the meaning is for Vasiṣṭha; Gha-sūkta: Vasiṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi). 2. Jha: Varṣakau.

O Lords of men, that chariot of yours which is the bearer, three-seated, rich in wealth, and having the oxen as its path—come to us with it, O Nāsatyas, when that one which brings all things desirable approaches you. That chariot of yours, O Lords of men, which is the bearer, three-seated, rich in wealth, and having the oxen as its path—come to us with it, O Nāsatyas, when that one which brings all things desirable approaches you. (4)

O Aśvins, you two are the protectors of men who perform sacrifices; that chariot of yours which is the carrier, which always remains present and ready for you—what is it like? It has three seats (trivandhura), provided with three places for the charioteer to stand, is rich in wealth (vasumān), and travels toward the setting of the sun (ustrayāmā).
Come hither to us, O Nāsatyas, Aśvins, with this very chariot. Whatever chariot of yours—whether it be that which is all-sustaining or that which is multiform—approaches and comes toward us;
so says another.
Since he who nourishes all and is most excellent approaches you and praises you, therefore come hither.

You two liberated Cyavāna from old age; you carried Pedu the swift horse; you rescued Atri from distress and darkness; and you placed Jāhuṣa within a secure refuge. You two liberated Cyavāna from old age; you brought down the swift horse for Pedu; you saved Atri from affliction and darkness; and you established Jāhuṣa within a place of rest.
O Aśvins, you two released Cyavāna from the decay of old age; you liberated him.
For it is said elsewhere: "O Aśvins, you made the aging Cyavāna young again" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.117.13).
Likewise, for the king named Pedu, you brought forth—that is, you delivered—a swift, fast-moving horse for battle.
The scriptural citation (*nigama*) is: "O you two, [you gave] the white [horse] to Pedu" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.118.9).
Likewise, you delivered the great seer Atri from distress, from the *ṛbīsa*—that is, from the fire—and from the darkness situated within the cave; [the citation is]:
"O you two, you made the *ṛbīsa* and that darkness a place of rest for Atri" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.39.9).
Likewise, you two placed Jāhuṣa back within his own loosened and weakened kingdom;
this is expressed in the hymn: "Jāhuṣa was besieged on all sides" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.20).

This is the thought, this is the song, O Aśvins; O Bulls, may you take pleasure in this well-fashioned hymn. May these prayers reach you both. Do you protect us always with your blessings. 6. The sixth [verse], "This is the inspired thought," has been explained.
The second hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "ā gomatā," is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is dedicated to the Aśvins.
It is enumerated thus: "ā gomatā pañca. Its application (viniyoga) has been stated for both the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina Śastra.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to the Aśvins, the first four verses serve as the invitatory and offering formulas (*yājyānuvākyā*).
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The four beginning with *ā gomatā nāsatyā rathena*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
Come, O Nāsatyas, on your chariot rich in cattle, rich in horses, and most resplendent;
all our teams attend upon you, as you shine with desirable beauty in your bodies.
1. *kha-ta³-na-bha-tadrathaḥ*; *gha-yat*; *śa-yadvāṃ*. 2. *kha-bha-naṣṭe*. *Ā*!
O Nāsatyas, come hither with your horse-drawn chariot, which is richly adorned. All our teams attend upon you, who shine with desirable splendor and beautify yourselves with your bodies. 1.
O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, [come] with that which is rich in cattle, yoked with cattle;
with that which abounds in horses, yoked with horses—that is to say, with horses capable of carrying you.
Or else:
"By one possessing cows" means by a giver of cows; "by one with many moons" means by one with abundant wealth— that is, by a giver of riches.
Come hither with such a chariot;
may all our many *niyuts*—our praises sent forth by us—attend and serve you both.
O you two who shine with a desirable splendor and a beautiful body!
Come to us with the gods, O Nāsatyas, you who are ever-joyful on your chariot;
for our friendship with you is ancestral, our kinship is common—be mindful of that.
Come hither to us with the gods, O Nāsatyas, on your well-gliding chariot; for our friendship with you is ancestral, and our kinship is common—be mindful of that. 2.
O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, you two, rejoicing together with the other gods, sharing common delight, come hither toward us on your chariot.
Regarding your arrival, he speaks of the excellence of kinship:
"The friendships between you two and us are ancestral, inherited from our fathers."
The meaning is that they do not now become attained through such conditions as praise and the like.
He says that very thing:
"Moreover (uta), the kinsman (bandhu)—that is, the binding ancestor—of both you two and of me is common (samāna), being one and the same."
"His wealth"—
here the genitive case is used in the sense of the object;
know him as the kinsman, or know that kinship as his wealth.
Vivasvān and Varuṇa were both born from Kaśyapa and Aditi; Vivasvān was the progenitor of the Aśvins, and Varuṇa [was the progenitor] of Vasiṣṭha—thus there is a common kinship.
And so it is stated in the Bṛhaddevatā: "Tvaṣṭṛ had a pair of children, Saramā and Triśiras, together.
That Saramā herself gave [her] to Vivasvān."
Then, when Saraṇyū had given birth to those twins, Yama and Yamī, from Vivasvat,
both of them were known as "the twins" (yamau), for Yamī was indeed the twin of Yama.
Having created a female horse possessing a beauty equal to her husband's while he was away, and having deposited his pair of children within her, she assumed the form of a mare and departed.
Because he was unaware of her, Vivasvān begot Manu upon her;
that royal sage Manu was like Vivasvān himself in his splendor.
Having realized that Saranyū, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, had departed assuming his own form,
he quickly pursued her, having become a horse endowed with the characteristic marks.
But Saramā, perceiving Vivasvat to be bodiless, nevertheless proceeded toward him for sexual union; and he mounted her.
Then, by the force of those two, that semen fell upon the ground;
and his own mare sniffed it, desiring its offspring.
"By the mere act of smelling it, that semen became two youths:
Nāsatya and Dakṣa, who are praised as the Aśvins" (Gṛhyasūtra 6.162–7.6).
The hymns of praise for the Aśvins have awakened; these divine prayers have been offered to you both.
Seeking to win over the two worlds, O wise ones, the inspired singer addresses you, O Nāsatyas.

The hymns of praise for the Aśvins have awakened; the kinship, the sacred prayers, and the goddesses of the morning worship have been stirred. Seeking to win over the two world-halves, the wise sage addresses these two divine ones, O Nāsatyas.

The hymns (*stomāsaḥ*, *stomāḥ*, *stuvāḥ*) have awakened (*abudhruan*), that is, they most excellently cause the two Aśvins to wake up.
*u* is a filler. *Vjāmi*:
this is a term for kinsman.
The Brahmins, who stand in the place of kinsmen, have been exalted; the deeds, which are divine and radiant, as well as the Dawns—
and by the word "and," the Aśvins too— have awakened.

The wise and intelligent Vasiṣṭha, desiring to serve the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins—who are worthy of praise as the two expansive worlds, heaven and earth, and who are worthy of being supported by the Dhiṣaṇā—addresses them directly and praises them.
When the dawns shine forth, O Aśvins, the poets bring their prayers to you;
the god Savitṛ has sent his light upward, and the priests chant loudly with kindled fuel.

And indeed, as the dawns shine forth, O Aśvins, the poets bring their prayers to you both. The god Savitṛ has extended his light on high; the singers praise him with kindled fuel like great clouds. 4.
The Aśvins [shine] at dawn; the dawns dispel the darkness, making it vanish—
*cet* being used here as a particle for emphasis (*pūraṇārtha*),
referring to what will be mentioned later in relation to the sun and so forth.
If there is no affliction through union [with you],
then, because of the connection with your praise, the *kāravaḥ*— the singers, the chanters— offer up (*prabharante*) the hymns (*stotrāṇi*) to the Brahman.
Savitṛ, the god, causes his light (*bhānum*), his brilliance, to rise upward.
The tawny ones, being kindled by the fuel—that is, by the act of enkindling—exult, that is, they are praised, in a manner that is lofty and exceedingly great.
‘Ā paścāttāt’: this is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal sacrifice to the Aśvins.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘Ā paścāttān nāsatyā purastād ā | goḥ |’
"O Nāsatyas, with your chariot... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
O Nāsatyas, come from behind; O Aśvins, come from the front, from below, and from above! Come from every side with wealth that belongs to all people. Do you ever protect us with your blessings.
O Nāsatyas, come from behind; O Aśvins, come from the front; come from below and from above; come from every side with wealth that benefits all people. Do you ever protect us with your blessings. 5.
O Aśvins, you who are true to your vows, come from the west— from the western region—

and likewise from the east— from the eastern region— and likewise from below— from the lower region— and from the south and from the north— from the northern region; in all these places, the connection is "come hither."
What need for more? Come from every direction, from all places, together with wealth that is beneficial to the people (*pāśvrjanya*), or even without it.
The four castes, with the Niṣādas as the fifth, are the "five peoples" (*pañcajanāḥ*).
The third hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “atāriṣma,” is the ṛṣi-seer Vasiṣṭha’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to the Aśvins.
The Anukramaṇikā states: “‘atāriṣma.
Its application is in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina Śastra.
We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness, offering our hymn of praise as seekers of the gods.
O Aśvins, you of many wondrous deeds, most ancient and immortal, the song calls upon you.

We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness. Bringing our hymn of praise, we call upon the Aśvins—the gods-loving, wonder-working, most abundant, ancient-born, and immortal ones—with our song. 1.

We have crossed over, we have reached the further shore, of that darkness—of ignorance and its effect, the suffering of saṃsāra characterized by birth and death—or, because it is the subject at hand, of the ignorance regarding the object of practice.
Doing what?
Being *devayantaḥ*, desiring the gods, [we have crossed] through *stoma*.
1. There is no [word] *āvivāsan* for the letters *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*.
2. Because of their perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*); those who are placing [their minds] upon praise, performing it among the gods.

O you two of many wondrous deeds (*purudaṃsā*), performers of many acts; O you two most excellent (*puruttamā*), most abundant ones; O you two ancient-born (*purājā*) and therefore immortal (*amartyā*), O Aśvins, the singer (*gīḥ*), the praiser Vasiṣṭha, praises, invokes, or calls upon you.
He, the beloved Hotṛ-priest of man, has sat down, O Nāsatyas, he who sacrifices and offers praise.
O Aśvins, drink the honeyed draught close at hand; I, rich in nourishment, call upon you both in the assemblies.

Om! The beloved human has sat down as the Hotṛ-priest for you, O Nāsatyas, he who offers oblations and pays homage. O Aśvins, [bring] the best of the honeyed draughts close at hand. I, rich in milk, call upon you both in the sacrificial assemblies. 2.

The beloved one, dear to you both—the human, born from Manu, or the priest who is the invoker of the gods and the praiser—has sat down; that is to say, he has taken his seat and is engaged in your service. O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, for him who performs the sacrifice, who offers praise, and who worships, drink this sweet Soma juice, which belongs to him; O Aśvins, drink it while remaining close at hand, even in our very presence.
"Drink"—this is the meaning.
At the *vidathas*, that is, the sacrifices, being rich in nourishment (*paryasvān*), I call upon you both. O Bulls (*vṛṣaṇā*), come hither with joy; accept this well-fashioned hymn (*suvṛkti*).
Like one sent forth with obedience, Vasiṣṭha, awakening you both, has praised you with hymns.

O Aśvins, choosing this hymn for yourselves, O Bulls, may you take pleasure in this well-fashioned praise. Like one sent forth with obedience, Vasiṣṭha has awakened for you with songs of praise as he chants. 3.

Performing a wide hymn of praise, we, the singers, shall carry forth—that is, increase—the sacrifice or the oblation which is the means for accomplishing it, for the sake of the gods who come along the paths of those that fly;
O two showerers (*vṛṣaṇā*), you who rain down desires, may you both enjoy this beautiful hymn (*suvṛkti*);
[we approach] you two with obedience, as it were.
*Śruṣṭi* is a name for speed;
[the horse] is like a messenger sent forth who goes quickly. *Vabodhi*:
it causes one to awaken, [signifying] that one must go swiftly.
Doing what?
Praising with hymns, extolling him repeatedly. Who? [The singer.]
"Vasiṣṭha, I have awakened.
Come hither, O two bearers, to our people; you who slay the Rākṣasas, come together with your strong-hoofed steeds.
The exhilarating juices have met together; do not neglect us, but come with auspiciousness.

Let those two bearers come hither; let them, the slayers of demons, enter our dwelling together. Let the strengthening draughts, rich in nourishment, reach us. Do not neglect us; come with your auspicious favor. 4.

May those two, the two carriers (*vahnī*), the bearers of our oblations (*haviṣāṃ voḍhārau*), come near to our people (*viśam*), our progeny, and our officiating priests (*ṛtvijam*). Of what sort are they?
They are slayers of demons (*rakṣohaṇā*), well-formed (*saṃbhṛtā*) with well-nourished limbs, and firm-handed (*vīḷupaṇī*).
Alternatively, this meaning should be explained as referring to horses;
in that case, its sense is: "Let those two strong-footed horses, the bearers of the chariot, approach the Aśvins."
O you two who are free from intoxication yet exhilarating, you have come together with the strengthening foods and the Soma juices that cause delight. Do not neglect us; do not harm us.
Rather, come hither together with auspicious and blessed wealth.
1. Kha reads *mānuṣasakāśāt*; Jha, Na, and Śa read *mānuṣo manuṣasakāśāt*. 2. Jha reads *kṣipraṃ gaṃtā*.

From behind, O Nāsatyas, from the front, from below, from above—O Aśvins, come! From every side, with wealth that wins the assembly, protect us always with your blessings. (5) The application and explanation of the fifth verse, beginning with "ā paścātāt," have already been given. The fourth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "imā u vām," is dedicated to the Aśvins and is the seer Vasiṣṭha’s composition. The first, third, and fifth verses are Bṛhatīs; the remaining verses are Satobṛhatīs. Thus it has been cataloged: "Imā u vām: six verses, in Pragātha form. This hymn is used in the Prātaranuvāka during the Āśvina Śastra in the Bārhata metre. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Imā u vām, ayam vām" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.15). In the Daśarātra sacrifice, on the fifth day, during the Prauga Śastra, "imā u vām" is the triplet for the Aśvins. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Imā u vām diviṣyaḥ, pibā sutasya rasinaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.12).

These people, longing for heaven, call upon you both, O Aśvins, like rays of light. I here invoke you for protection, O Lords of Power; for you go to every clan. These people, longing for heaven—meaning those who desire the celestial realm, including the subjects and even the officiating priests—O Aśvins, these "ustas" (rays or inhabitants) call upon you both. And I, Vasiṣṭha, also invoke you both, O Lords of Power (Śacīvasū)—those whose wealth is their skill—for our protection or for your own gratification. Why do both the subjects and I call upon you? To this he replies: because for that reason, you go toward every single clan, toward every person.

O Heroes, you two bestow wonderful wealth; impel it toward the one who offers true hymns of praise. With one mind, turn your chariot hither and bring it near; drink the sweet Soma juice. O Aśvins, you two possess wonderful wealth; you maintain that treasure. Bestow it upon the singer of true hymns. For his sake, being of one mind, direct your chariot toward us and draw it near; having done so, drink the sweet Soma juice associated with the Soma sacrifice.

Come hither, attend to us, and drink the sweet mead, O Aśvins! You have milked the milk, O bulls, possessors of noble wealth; do not neglect us, but come to us! 3. 1. *jha-ta2-1-dadhatur*; *na-śa-dadhathuḥ*. 2. *kha-jha-ta1-2-madhuraṃ rasam*; *śa-madhurasam*.
O Aśvins, you two, come hither!
Having arrived, be present nearby!
Drink the sweet soma-juice of the Maghavan!
And having drunk, O *vṛṣaṇā* (O showerers), O *jendyāvasū* (O you whose wealth is to be won)—
the meaning is that you have conquered wealth—
both of you have milked the *payaḥ* (water) of rain from the atmosphere.
Do not neglect us; do not harm us—for such a prayer itself constitutes harm. Come quickly! Come hither!
The horses that carry you to the house of the donor fly toward you, O Aśvins; bearing them, O Heroes, come hither quickly with these steeds, for as gods you must travel.
Horses! Those who fly toward the house of the donor, carrying you both—O Heroes, O Aśvins, come hither with them, for you are eager for food; come, O Gods, to the one who offers oblations! 4.
O Aśvins, those horses belonging to you two, which carry you to the house of the donor who offers oblations, fly there— meaning they cause you to go.
With these swift-moving, fleet-footed steeds, O leaders, O Aśvins, O gods, come hither to our sacrifice, desiring us.
O Aśvins, as you go on your way, may you bestow nourishing food like the sun;
O Nāsatyas, grant us enduring glory and a secure dwelling worthy of our praise.
O Aśvins, coming hither, bestow nourishments; may Sūrya grant them. May those two Nāsatyas bestow upon the liberal patrons enduring glory and a secure dwelling for us. 5.
And indeed, O Aśvins, the sacrificers who approach you with hymns of praise—those wise singers—enjoy abundant food, or they attain it.
O Nāsatyas, Aśvins, grant to us, the liberal patrons, enduring and unshakable glory, or rather, food that is itself glory, and a dwelling-home; bestow these upon us.
Those who go forth like yoked chariots, protectors of men;
they have flourished by their own inherent power and dwell in secure habitation.

Those who have gone forth, free from hostility, like chariots, are the protectors of men; indeed, by their own inherent power, these heroes have become renowned, and they dwell in a secure habitation. 6.

Those sacrificers who are harmless—meaning they do not seize the wealth of others—and who, among men, are protectors of men, that is, protectors of the officiating priests and kings, reach you both with oblations.
This is the illustration:
like chariots, just as chariots filled with rice and other grains reach the master’s house.
The word *uta* here depends on the subsequent sentence.
Moreover, those *naras*, the sacrificers, have *śūśuvuḥ*, they have increased, by their own *śavas*, by their own strength.
And furthermore, they *kṣiyanti*, they dwell in, that is, they go to and attain, *sukṣitim*, a good dwelling.
The fifth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with “dyuṣā āvaḥ,” is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Vasiṣṭha.
According to the Anukramaṇikā on the Ṛgveda: “dyuṣā [is] eight; it is indeed the sixty-fifth.”
Having said "tu vai," according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) beginning with "tuhya," these seven hymns beginning with *idam* have the Dawn (*Uṣas*) as their deity.

In the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*), in the *upastha* rite, they are used; in the *bhūmi* meter, in the *āśvina-śastra*, there are six hymns beginning with *vedam*. And thus it is enjoined: "The Dawn [is the deity] for desires... [1. jha-ta1-2-varṣakau].
2. *Jha*—harm (*hiṃsā*); *Śa*—non-harm (*ahiṃsā*).
3. *Śa*—substances and so forth (*dravyādi*).
4. *Jha*, *Ta* 1–2, *Anu*—the eight [limbs] of yoga (*aṣṭāṅga-yoga*).

"Ā vo divijāḥ" is a *pakti* verse in the *triṣṭubh* meter (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.14). The application (*viniyoga*) declared in the *Ṛgvidhāna* is written here: "One who, having risen with effort at the end of the night, being pure, should worship [the Dawn] with six hymns while joining his palms in reverence."
"He shall obtain gold, abundant wealth of various forms,
cows, horses, men, grain, women, garments, goats, and sheep" (Ṛgvidhāna 2.317–18).
"The Dawn, born of heaven, has come forth by the cosmic order (ṛta), manifesting her greatness."
He has awakened the most liberal milker, the most beloved, the most purified, from the earth.

Uṣas, born of heaven, has shone forth by the Eternal Law (ṛta); manifesting her majesty, she has arrived. She has driven away the evil, the darkness, and the loathsome; most radiant, she has awakened the earth.

This Dawn, born of heaven, having appeared in the divine mid-region, has shone forth; that is to say, she has made it manifest. Here, the prefix *vi-* in the verb *vyucchati* (to shine forth) carries the sense of "making to dwell" (*vasi-nivāsa*).

In the rule *chandasy api dṛśyate*, because the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* (is seen) serves to encompass other grammatical prescriptions, the augment *āT* occurs even for that which is not at the beginning (*anādi*).
Then, by the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ*, there is elision.
That very Dawn (*oṣāḥ*), manifesting her greatness—her own magnitude—through *ṛta* and splendor, has come; she has arrived.

And having come, he drives away—from us—the haters, the disagreeable, and the most unpleasant darkness; that is, he uncovers it. Furthermore, by means of the paths that are "most straight"—the word *arji* being derived from the root *arj* meaning "to go," thus *arjiṣṭhamāḥ* refers to the *aṅgirasas*, those who go most directly—he has awakened them; that is, he causes them to emerge.
The meaning is that it illuminates for the sake of the practical transactions of living beings.
