Awaken us today for great well-being; lead us forward toward great good fortune.
Bestow upon us, O Goddess among mortals, wondrous wealth that brings glory and human renown.

Be mindful of us today for our well-prepared libation, O Dawn; bestow upon us great good fortune. Grant us brilliant, glorious wealth; O divine and human goddess, grant us among mortals renown that brings us fame.

Today, for our great attainment of well-being—whether for the acquisition of happiness or for a pleasant journey—be mindful of us; become so. Furthermore, O Uṣas, bestow upon us great good fortune and prosperity.
Moreover, grant us and sustain within us wonderful, praiseworthy, and glorious wealth.
"O Mānuṣī, O goddess who benefits humanity, bestow upon us mortals a son who is glorious and possessed of food"—this is the syntactical connection.
These radiant, wonderful, immortal beams of the beautiful Dawn have arrived;
engendering divine ordinances and filling the mid-air, they have spread abroad.
These, those very rays of the beautiful Dawn, the bright and immortal ones, have come. Bringing forth divine ordinances, they have spread across the mid-air, filling it completely. 3.
Of the beautiful, lovely, and luminous Dawn, those well-known rays—wondrous, venerable, marvelous, immortal, deathless, and imperishable—which are seen before her, have come.
What are they doing?
They are generating and bringing forth the divine *vratas*, the actions pertaining to the gods.
Their status as producers [of rain] arises from their providing light conducive to that [rain].
Filling the intermediate spaces— that is, filling the atmospheres—
the single intermediate space itself is threefold due to the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of wind, clouds, and birds.
Therefore, the plural number is appropriate.
Acting in this way, the rays (*bhānavaḥ*) have stood apart; they stand in various ways; they move.
1. The manifestation of *kha* and *bha*. 2. Within *kha*, *jha*, *tā*, 1, 2, 3, *na*, *bha*, *śa*, and *matya*. 3. The manifold nature of *śa*. 4. *Jha*, *ta*, and *śa* spread forth.

Yoking herself from afar, she goes around the settlements of cattle in an instant; looking upon the wisdom of men, she is the daughter of Heaven, the mistress of the world. (4) She, that very Dawn, yoking herself while standing in a distant place, exerts herself for the sake of light and goes around the settlements of cattle—the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth—in an instant. What does she do? Looking upon the wisdom (*vayunā*) of living beings, she observes them as their witness. Of what nature is she? She is the daughter of Heaven, occupying the position of a daughter, and the mistress (*patnī*), the protectress, of the world—that is, of all created beings. "She goes around" is the syntactical connection. Possessing abundance, the wife of Sūrya, whose wealth is wondrous, rules over riches and treasures. Praised by seers, awakening [beings], the bountiful Dawn shines forth, extolled by the priests. (5) "Possessing abundance" (*vājinīvatī*): although this is a name for Dawn, since "whose wealth is wondrous" (*citramaghā*) is mentioned separately as another name for Dawn, one should understand here that one term is both etymological and conventional (*yogarūḍha*). She is the wife of Sūrya, whose wealth is wondrous—meaning her wealth consists of various rays—or rather, she rules over general riches (*rāyaḥ*) and over treasures (*vasūnām*) which are the support of all, including gods and humans. Alternatively, "treasures" refers to the rays that provide dwelling (*vasu*); she rules over those too. Praised by seers, awakening the multitude of living beings—that is, the Dawn, returning again and again, exhausts the lifespan of creatures—she is bountiful, possessing wealth, and shining forth, being extolled by the "bearers," the sacrificers who carry out the ritual, she makes the light manifest. The radiant horses of the shining Dawn have become visible, bringing her hither; they are wonderful to behold. The bright one, adorned with all forms, moves on her chariot; she bestows treasure upon the person who serves her. (6) Bringing the shining Dawn, the glowing, wonderful horses have become visible; they are beautiful to look upon. That Dawn, bright and blazing, moves everywhere on her chariot which is "adorned with all forms" (*viśvapiśā*). To the person who serves her, she bestows and gives delightful wealth. True with the true, great with the great, the goddess with the gods, worthy of sacrifice with those worthy of sacrifice—she breaks open the closed doors, giving away the cows of the barren ones; the cattle lowed toward the Dawn. (7) 1. *kha-vayunā vayunāni* | 2. *kha1-śa-dhanasvāviśiṣṭasya*; *ja-dhanasya viśiṣṭasya* | True, together with the true; great, together with the great; the goddess, together with the gods; worthy of sacrifice, together with those worthy of sacrifice—she breaks open the closed doors and gives away the cows belonging to the barren ones. The cattle lowed toward the Dawn. (7) 1. *kha-vayunā vayunāni* | 2. *kha1-śa-dhanasvāviśiṣṭasya*; *ja-dhanasya viśiṣṭasya* |

The goddess—who is true, free from blindness, great, worthy of worship, and increased by her virtues; who shines forth, and whose faults are removed through sacrifice; who is accompanied by the truthful, great, and divine gods who are worthy of sacrifice and possess auspicious marks, or by other gods such as the *kiras* who partake in the oblations—shatters and utterly destroys the firm and exceedingly stable darknesses.
This [word] "ustriyāṇām" is a name for cows.
Their etymology is "the enjoyments that flow forth" (*ustrāviṇa āsāṃ bhogā iti*). One gives for their movement;
by implication, the meaning is "for the sake of manifestation."
Or rather, he gives, he bestows cows upon his worshippers;
moreover, "cows" here is an elliptical expression [standing for all livestock].

All living beings, though obstructed by darkness, have indeed lowed together; they desire, that is, they long for [the dawn]. The mention of the cows specifically is because at daybreak they require the dawn for the purpose of roaming, and thus they are spoken of as the primary subjects.
Now, O Dawn, bring us wealth in cattle and long-lasting treasure, along with horses and much to enjoy.
Do not let our sacred grass be exposed to reproach among men; protect us always with your blessings.

Now, O Uṣas, bestow upon us wealth consisting of cattle, heroic sons, and horses—abundant nourishment for us. Let not our sacred grass be exposed to reproach among men. Do you all protect us always with blessings. 8.
O Uṣas, now bestow upon us wealth consisting of cattle, joined with many cows, accompanied by heroes—sons—and delightful treasures; grant us abundant nourishment and manifold riches.
(The repetition of "asme" [to us] is due to the metrical division of the verse.
Bestow these upon our sacred grass (*barhis*) and our sacrifice among men, amidst the multitude of human beings.
The meaning is "to those like us.
*Nide* means for the sake of censure; *mā vokaḥ* means do not do so.
The meaning is: do not act in such a way that they censure you.
The sixth hymn, beginning with “udu jyotiḥ,” consists of eleven verses; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is dedicated to Uṣas.
Thus it is enumerated: “udu sasa.
Its application (viniyoga) has been stated for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra.
Savitar, the god who belongs to all people, has extended the light of the stars, the immortal, for all mankind. By his wisdom, he was born as the eye of the gods; Dawn has revealed the entire world.

Up! Oṃ! Savitṛ, the divine lord of all people, has raised aloft the light, the immortal, common to all. Through his wisdom, he was born as the eye of the gods; Dawn has made manifest the entire world. 1.
The immortal, the bestower of immortality, the imperishable, or the light beneficial to all people (viśvajanya), the leader of all (viśvānara), the god Savitṛ, has raised up high;

he elevates [it] by means of the ritual action (kratu) of the gods—those who engage in worldly affairs or those who offer praise—or rather, for the sake of performing the sacrifice. This is the meaning.

For that purpose—or rather—the light of the gods (*devānāṃ cakṣuḥ*), which occupies the place of their eye, has been born and manifested through *kratu*, as the instrumental cause of their ritual action.
And having arisen, Uṣas has made manifest the entire world (*viśvaṃ bhuvanam*), the totality of created beings;
she has revealed the whole universe.
The god-traversing paths have become visible to me—unfailing, prepared by the Vasus.
The banner of the Dawn has appeared in the east; she has come forth from her lofty mansions toward us.

The paths leading to the gods have become visible to me; unobstructed, they have been prepared by the Vasus. The banner of the Dawn has appeared in the east; she has come hither from her lofty mansions, turning toward us.
1. Kha, śata, na, bha, śa, vā.

The paths leading to the gods—the ways that bring one to the gods—have been clearly revealed by me. Of what nature are these paths? They are *amardhantaḥ*, non-injurious; *vasubhiḥ*, with splendors; and *iṣkṛtāsaḥ*, well-prepared. In the east, in the eastern direction, the *ketu* of the dawn—the light that makes things known—has appeared; it is perceived. And she, moving westward, toward the western regions, has come from above the lofty places (*harmyebhyaḥ*). The word *harmya* indicates elevated regions. She approaches. Those days were many, O Dawn, which rose in the east before the sun, from which you appear like a lover approaching his mistress, and not like a woman who goes away never to return again. O Dawn, those very splendors of yours were indeed those many days, for the word "day" is conventionally used for the time endowed with the light of dawn. Having said "those," he asks "which ones? He says: those which, upon the rising of the sun, rise toward the eastern region of him; or rather, those which have risen repeatedly in the eastern region of the sun. O Dawn, by which splendors you are seen all around, you appear moving nearby like a lover toward his wife, or like a virtuous woman moving near her paramour at night—that is, moving toward the sun, the end of the night. Just as in the world a virtuous woman, though her husband may be wicked or prone to wandering, moves about without abandoning him, so too you move without forsaking him. You are not like a woman who goes away, leaving her husband and wandering about like an unchaste woman; you do not abandon the sun. The word "again" (*punar*) is used here to indicate a contrast. Thus, the connection is: those splendors by which you are seen surrounded are indeed those days. They alone were the companions in revelry of the gods; they were the truth-abiding sages of old. As fathers, they found the hidden light; with true hymns, they brought forth the Dawn. They alone were the *sadhamādaḥ* (companions in revelry) of the gods among the seers. They were the *ṛtavānaḥ* (truth-abiding), the *kavayaḥ* (sages), the *pūrvyāsaḥ* (ancient), the *pitaraḥ* (fathers). As protectors of all, the Aṅgirases found the hidden light—the solar splendor—by the power of their mantras. Being those whose hymns are true, they brought forth the Dawn. There are Vedic citations: "With the fourth Brahman, Atri found [the light]" (RV 5.40.6); "They found the light within the darkness" (RV 5.40.9). Here, the praise of the Aṅgirases should be understood as a praise of the Dawn itself. Gathered together in the same stall, they are of one mind; they do not strive against one another. They do not violate the laws of the gods, being non-injurious and striving with the Vasus. In the common stall, when the herd of cows was seized by the Paṇis and had to be recovered, they gathered together and became of one mind. They did not strive against each other. They do not violate the *vrata* (laws/vows) of the gods, being non-injurious (*amardhantaḥ*) and striving (*yardamānāḥ*) with the Vasus. (Note: The commentary notes various manuscript variants regarding the interpretation of certain words, such as *tava* being absent in some versions, or *patiṃ parityajya* being interpreted differently, but the core meaning remains as translated above.)
They strive together; that is to say, they perform their means of accomplishment in unison.
Those Aṅgirases do not violate—that is, they do not harm—the *vratas*, the ritual acts characterized by renunciation, of the gods.
But the meaning is that they protect;
what are they doing?
Not failing, not harming, with the *vasus*—the illuminating splendors of the dawns—moving along.

The Vasiṣṭhas, awakening at dawn, praise you with hymns, O fortunate one, having offered their laudations. Leader of the kine, mistress of booty, shine forth for us; O well-born Dawn, as the first, awaken us. 6. *Prati tvā stomair īḷate Vasiṣṭhā uparbudhaḥ subhage tuṣṭuvāṃsaḥ | gavāṃ netrī vājapatnī na ucchorṣaḥ sujāte prathamā jarasva || 6 ||* The Vasiṣṭhas, waking at dawn, praise you with hymns, O fortunate one, having offered their laudations. Leader of the kine, mistress of booty, shine forth for us; O well-born Dawn, as the first, awaken us. 6.
O fortunate goddess Dawn, the Vasiṣṭhas—awakening at daybreak and offering praise—extol you with hymns of praise.
You are the leader of the cows, the bringer [of them], and the mistress of booty;
that is to say, the giver of food.
Shine forth for us in such a manner;
O Uṣas, well-born one of auspicious birth, as the first among the other gods, awaken!

This leader of wealth and of pleasant truths, Dawn, shining forth, is praised by the Vasiṣṭhas—she who bestows upon us far-famed riches. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 7. This one; leader; of wealth; of pleasant truths; Dawn; shining forth; is praised; by the Vasiṣṭhas; far-famed; riches; upon us; bestowing; you; protect; with blessings; always; us. 7.
This Dawn, being the leader of wealth and of the singer’s pleasant praises, shining forth and driving away the darkness, is praised by the Vasiṣṭhas— those born of the Vasiṣṭha lineage—
as she bestows upon us wealth that is far-famed, heard of afar, and renowned everywhere.

The seventh hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "upo ruce," is the *uṣasya* (pertaining to the Dawn) seer-Vasiṣṭha’s composition. Thus it is enumerated: "upo ruce ṣaṭ. Its application (*viniyoga*) has been stated for the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*.

Like a youthful maiden for the sake of splendor, Agni has appeared, impelling all that lives to movement; he has become the kindler for men, a song of praise, a light that drives away the darkness. 1. *Upa*, *ruce*, *yuvatiḥ*, *na*, *yoṣā*, *viśvam*, *jīvam*, *prasuvantī*, *carāyai*, *abhūt*, *agniḥ*, *sam-idhe*, *mānuṣāṇām*, *arkaḥ*, *jyotiḥ*, *bādhamānā*, *tamāṃsi*. 1.
This Dawn shines in the very vicinity of the Sun for the sake of its splendor;
she is like a young woman, possessed of youth— a maiden who, like a wife, shines brightly in the presence of her husband with garments, ornaments, and the like.
What was she doing?
She was impelling and urging forth the entire living world, the multitude of living beings, for the sake of their movement.
Furthermore, Agni became the one to be kindled for the purpose of human beings; he became the fuel-kindler.
Having been kindled for the sake of his task,
he made the light— a mass of brilliance— that dispels, that is, drives away, the darknesses, the obscurities. Or alternatively:
The light of the dawn, dispelling the darknesses, has alone made them vanish.
Turning toward all things, far-extending, she has risen up, wearing this bright raiment;
golden-hued, beautiful to behold, the mother of the two cows and the leader of the days has shone forth.
1. kha-bha: those who praise;
2. jha: with hymns; tan-śa: with hymns.

Facing the entire world, the far-extending Dawn has risen; wearing a radiant garment, she has shone forth with brilliant light. Golden-hued, beautiful to behold, the mother and leader of the cows, I have shone. (2) Facing the entire world, facing toward it, the far-extending one has risen up, spreading out in every direction. And having risen, wearing a shining, bright, radiant garment—a mass of splendor—she increases. Golden-colored, endowed with a most pleasing hue, beautiful to behold—the term *saṃdṛk* means "that which shows"; she whose splendor is beautiful to see is such. The mother of the cows, or rather the mother of the rays of light—for at the time of dawn, the speech of men and others emerges, and because cattle also move about at that time, she is their progenitor—or else the creator of the rays. She has shone; she is the leader of the days, the bringer of the days. (3) The eye of the gods, the fortunate one, carrying [the sun], leading the white, beautiful horse, the Dawn has appeared, distinguished by her rays, possessing wonderful wealth, and spread out over the whole world. (3) The eye of the gods—the splendor standing in the place of the eye—carrying, holding; the fortunate one, possessing beautiful wealth; leading, bringing near the white, beautiful horse—the sun, who is ever-moving—she illuminates him, making him possessed of white color. What kind of Dawn? Distinguished by her own rays, she is seen; possessing wonderful wealth, she has spread out over the entire world for the sake of the worldly activities of all beings. (4) Near us is your treasure; drive the enemy far away. Make our pasture wide and free from fear. Ward off those who hate us; bring us riches and bestow bounty upon the singer, O wealthy one! (4) O Dawn, you whose treasure is near; shine upon us with your most excellent rays, O Goddess, prolonging our life. Bestowing nourishment upon us, O possessor of all boons, grant us wealth consisting of cattle, horses, and chariots! (5) O Dawn, O Goddess, shine upon us with your most excellent rays—splendors and lights—while increasing our lifespan. Granting us nourishment, O you who possess all desirable things, bestow wealth consisting of cattle, horses, and chariots! (5)
1. Gha, kṣa, ta, na: kurvantī; śa: karotī. 2. Śa: by means of its own rays (svakīyaiḥ kiraṇaiḥ). 3. Kha, kṣa, ta, na, bha, śa: "Bring the treasures" (avasūny āhara) is not present.
O Goddess, worthy of worship by all, shining forth for us—granting us food and wealth consisting of many cattle, accompanied by horses, and endowed with chariots—shine forth.

O Daughter of Heaven, O Uṣas, nobly born, you whom the Vasiṣṭhas magnify with their hymns—may you bestow upon us vast and abundant wealth. And may you all protect us evermore with your blessings. (6) O Daughter of Heaven, O Uṣas, nobly born, you whom the Vasiṣṭhas magnify with their hymns—may you bestow upon us, the Vasiṣṭhas, vast and abundant wealth. And may you all protect us evermore with your blessings. (6) O Daughter of Heaven, O Uṣas, nobly born, you whom the Vasiṣṭhas magnify with their hymns—may you bestow upon us, the Vasiṣṭhas, vast and abundant wealth. (24) The eighth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “Prati ketavaḥ,” is the seer’s own composition by Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to Uṣas. The Anukramaṇikā states: “Prati pañca. The application [of this hymn] has been explained.

The first heralds have appeared; her radiant rays spread upward. O Uṣas, with your great, luminous chariot, bring us desirable wealth from the near side. The first heralds—her rays that make things known—have become visible. Her radiant rays, which manifest all things, spread upward and extend everywhere. O Goddess Uṣas, with your great, vast, and brilliant chariot coming toward us, bring to us desirable wealth that is worthy of being sought.

The kindled fire crackles forth; the inspired singers praise it with their hymns. Dawn approaches, driving away all darkness and misfortunes, the goddess. The fire, being fully kindled, crackles and grows on every side. The inspired ones—the wise and the officiating priests—crackle [with joy] as they praise her with their thoughts and hymns. And the goddess Dawn approaches, moving upward, dispelling all darkness and our misfortunes with her light.

These very Dawns have appeared in the east, bestowing light as they shine forth. They have brought forth the sun, the sacrifice, and Agni; the wretched darkness has fled away. These—verily—those (Dawns) have become visible in the east, bestowing light, the shining Dawns. They have generated the sun, the sacrifice, and Agni; the loathsome darkness has gone away.
1. In manuscripts Kha, Jha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Śa, the word *gomat* does not appear.
2. In manuscripts Kha, Jha, Ta, Tha, Da, Na, Bha, and Śa, the phrase *rathavat rathair upetam* does not appear.
3. In manuscripts Kha, Jha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Rā, [the text] reads *sarvatrāyati*.
4. Kha, jha, ta, na, bha, śa, and dha are wealth for us;
*etā* and *u*—*u* is a filler.
These well-known dawns, shining brightly, fashioning their celestial chariots, bestowing light—that is, splendor—have become visible in the eastern direction.
Those dawns have brought forth the sun, the sacrifice, and the fire;
for since these arise immediately after the rising of the dawn, the dawn is figuratively described as their progenitor.
Furthermore, the *apācīna* (western) and *nīcīna* (downward) *ajuṣṭa* (unpleasant) darkness—
unpleasant because it obstructs the vision of all—
has gone away; that is, it has vanished.
The wealthy daughter of heaven shines; all behold the dawning Uṣas.
She has mounted her chariot, which is yoked by its own inherent power—the well-harnessed horses draw it forward.

She praises: the daughter of heaven, the bountiful one; all behold the dawning Uṣas. She has mounted her chariot, which is yoked by its own inherent power—the chariot which well-yoked horses draw. ||4||
The daughter of heaven, the bountiful Uṣas, rich in wealth, has become manifest; she is known by all. All living beings behold the dawning Uṣas as she shines forth.
Such a goddess has mounted her chariot, which is yoked by means of *svadhā*—that is, by food. She ascends it.
He has mounted that chariot which the well-yoked horses—horses of excellent harnessing—carry, bringing it to the desired destination.
May our liberal patrons and we ourselves awaken to you today with well-disposed minds as the dawns shine forth, making the world full of vitality; protect us always with your blessings.

Today our well-disposed kinsmen have awakened toward you; we ourselves, the liberal patrons, and [all] have awakened. O Dawns, as you shine forth with your radiant light, may you protect us evermore with your blessings. 5.
O Uṣas, today at this time, our men— our priests who possess good intentions, who offer excellent praise, and who are wealthy with oblations—
[invoke] you. Or rather,
"wealthy" (*maghavānaḥ*) may be an epithet of "we" (*vayam*).
We, possessing oblations, have awakened;
we have woken you up with hymns of praise.
O Dawns, as you shine forth and break through, may you make the world moist with fertile soil.
From the word *tilasneha*, [the suffix] *tilvi* is applied;
that which has a land (*bhūmi*) abounding in sesame oil is *tilvila*.
Make that so.
The remainder is clear.

The fifth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “dyubhir-ā vaḥ,” is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is addressed to Uṣas and is in the Triṣṭubh meter. The Anukramaṇikā states: “dyubhiḥ. Its application is prescribed for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina Śastra.
Dawn has awakened the people of the five human settlements upon the earth;
with well-kindled fires and stars, she has spread her light, and the sun has illumined heaven and earth with his vision.

Dawn has shone forth for the people of the broad earth, awakening the five human tribes. With her beautiful aspects, she has extended her luster through the stars; Sūrya has made the two worlds visible with his eye.

The Dawn, who is beneficial (*pathyā*)—that is, conducive to the welfare—on the path for all people (*janānām*, i.e., all living beings), has shone forth. Or rather, it should be construed as: "She has shone forth for the benefit of people."
What is she doing?
She is awakening the five human races—the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth—while being well-composed in such a manner. She is one who possesses beautiful forms, appearing in human shape.
*Saṃdṛk* is light (*tejas*), so called because it is seen or causes things to be seen. He attained radiance (*bhānu*) by means of the well-luminous, vigorous rays (*gobhiḥ*).
For the Śruti says: "The ruddy ones ran toward the race" (*aruṇeśā ājim adhāvat*, AiB 4.9).
"The cows of the dawns are ruddy" (Nirukta 1.15.7)—so says the Nirukta.
And Sūrya, by his vision—that is, by his light and splendor—unveils the two worlds, heaven and earth, which were enveloped in darkness.
It is manifested at the ends of heaven; like harnessed horses, the dawns strive together. Your rays turn back the darkness; they extend light, as Savitṛ extends his arms.

They anoint themselves at the ends of heaven with light; like people yoked for service, the dawns strive forward. Your rays roll back the darkness together and extend the light, as Savitṛ extends his arms.
The dawns manifest—the meaning is that they make clear—the radiant beams of heaven at the ends, that is, in the peripheral regions of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

Like tribes (*viśaḥ*) or like armies joined together with one another, they strive, that is, they exert themselves for the destruction of darkness or for proceeding here. Now follows a direct address:
O Uṣas, your rays—your cows—completely roll away, that is, destroy, the darkness and gloom; they extend, that is, bestow, light and splendor.
Savitṛ, the Sun, has extended his two arms.

The most Indra-like Dawn, the bountiful, has appeared; she has brought forth glories for our well-being. The daughter of Heaven, the goddess, best of the Aṅgirases, distributes treasures upon the one who performs good deeds.

She has appeared, the Dawn, most like Indra, the bountiful; she has brought forth glories for our well-being. The goddess, the daughter of Heaven, best of the Aṅgirases, distributes treasures to the doer of good deeds.
Most Indra-like, most sovereign over all, the bountiful one rich in wealth has become manifest; she has appeared.
For the sake of well-being, she has generated, that is, brought forth, glorious foods.
The meaning is that she has made them shine forth.
The daughter of heaven, the best of the Aṅgiras, the swiftest of those who come—
or rather,
she is called the "best of the Aṅgiras" because she arises even from the night along with the Bhāradvājas of the Aṅgiras lineage, and because the dawn is the very form of the night's conclusion.
The origin of the Bhāradvāja [lineage] together with Rātri is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Rātri, Kuśika, Saubhara; or Rātri is the daughter of Bhāradvāja" (Anu.
10. 127). Such a one bestows—that is, provides—the *vasūni*, riches, for the sacrificer who has performed good deeds.
Bestow upon us that wealth of yours, O Uṣas, as much as you have granted to those who praise you when you are lauded;
you whom they brought forth with the roar of the bull, you opened the doors of the enclosure with your stones.

So much, O Dawn, grant as bounty to us—as much as you, being praised, have dug out for those who laud you; you whom they brought forth with the roar of the bull, you opened wide the doors of the obstructing mountain. 4.
O granter of boons, you have previously bestowed such abundant wealth upon your praisers; now, being praised and extolled, grant us likewise that same wealth.
We call upon you with the roar of a bull—this is an elliptical simile.
The word "vṛṣabhasya" is used in the accusative sense (karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī).
Living beings recognize you by means of the roar of the bull— that is, by your very manifestation—
or alternatively, they recognize [you] or make [you] known by the sound of the roar of the "bull," that is, the exalted hymn of praise.
Of the firm, strong Vṛtra, you opened wide the doors—the gates that had been closed by the Paṇis after they had driven the cows inside—and you made them open.

Impelling the God of gods for our prosperity, and sending forth our hymns and truthful words, may she, shining forth, bestow upon us insights for our gain; and may you all protect us evermore with blessings.
Impelling every god toward abundance, sending forth our truthful words from us, shining forth, bestow upon us intentions for our prosperity. Do you all protect us always with blessings. 5.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the sixth [section] is explained.
In the seventh maṇḍala, ten hymns have been explained in the fifth anuvāka.
The eleventh hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "pratyu adarśi," is the ārṣa of Vasiṣṭha and has Upastha as its deity.
In the first [verse], the odd-numbered lines are *bṛhatī*s; in the second, the even-numbered lines are *satobṛhatī*s.
Thus it has been enumerated: "‘Pratyu adarśi,’ six verses, in the *pragātha* meter.
This hymn belongs to the *prātaranuvāka*, the *uṣasya* ritual, the *bārhata* *chandaḥ-sthā*, and the *āśvina-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The verse beginning with 'pratyu adarśi saha vāmena' belongs to the Bṛhatī metre" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.14).
The daughter of heaven, shining forth, has appeared;
she spreads the great waters for us to see and, as a noble lady, creates light to dispel the darkness.
She has been seen approaching, the daughter of Heaven, shining forth. She uncovers the great waters so that they may be seen; the noble lady creates light and dispels the darkness. 1.

Coming, approaching, shining forth, driving away the darkness, dispelling it—the daughter of Heaven (Dyaus) or of the Sun—such is Uṣas; she has been seen by all, she is visible to everyone. "U" is an expletive.
She, this very one, [drives away] the great, vast nocturnal darkness.
The compound of the two particles *apa* and *u* has the sense of "apart" (*apela*).
He opens (*apavṛṇoti*), that is, he uncovers.
For what purpose?
For the purpose of seeing— that is, for the sake of vision—
having acted thus, O Dawn, the noble one (*sūnarī*) who leads people well, makes the light, she creates illumination.
The sun, rising together with the radiant star, sends forth the bright cows.
O Dawn, at your dawning and that of the sun, may we partake together in the allotted portion.
The sun releases the ruddy cows together with him; when the radiant star has risen, O Dawn, may we indeed attain a share of the light of both you and the sun. 2.
The Sun, the impeller of all, the Āditya, simultaneously and at once emits and causes to rise the *usriyāḥ*, the rays.
Likewise, he makes the rising, shining, and appearing constellation—the planets, stars, and so forth visible in the sky—radiant with light;
for by the solar brilliance, the constellations such as the Moon shine during the night.
For there is a Vedic verse (*nigama*) stating: “The good son, the sun-rayed one, the moon, the Gandharva” (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 18.40).
This being so, O *uṣas*, goddess Dawn, when there is the dawning, the shining forth, and the manifestation of both you and the Sun, may we come together with food; that is, may we meet [with it].
The particle *it* is a filler (*pūraka*).
O Dawn, daughter of heaven, we have awakened you,
the swift one, who, O bountiful goddess, brings much that is desirable, like wealth, to the donor.
O Daughter of Heaven, O Dawn, we have awakened you, the swift one; you who, O bountiful lady, bring much that is desirable, like wealth, to the donor. 3.
O Daughter of Heaven, O Dawn born from the sky and the intermediate space, O Goddess Uṣas—we, the swift-acting ones, have awakened toward you; may we be those who wake at your arrival.
O possessor of desirable wealth! "Vananvatī" means she who possesses that which is to be desired—namely, worshipful wealth or the riches to be shared.
in that which possesses it

You who bring—that is, you cause to reach—the worshiper who has offered oblations a vast and much-desired wealth, like a delightful treasure (*ratna*) and joy (*maya*), even so do you bring it; to you, such as you are, we turn with praise. This is the connection. **Verse 4:** O Great Goddess, shining forth, you who by your greatness (*maṃhanā*) make the light visible for all to see; of you, the bestower of treasures, we beg for our share. May we be dear to you, like sons to a mother. **Verse 5:** O Dawn, bring that wonderful wealth which is most renowned from afar. O Daughter of Heaven, grant us that food of mortals which is yours; may we enjoy it. **Verse 6:** Grant fame to our patrons, immortal and full of riches; grant us strengths consisting of cattle. Driving on, O Dawn, rich in truth and inspiring the wealthy, shine forth and drive away our enemies. --- *Indrāvaruṇā*: This twelfth hymn, consisting of ten verses, is the work of Vasiṣṭha and is composed in the Jagatī meter. These first four hymns have Indra and Varuṇa as their deities. Thus it is stated: "Indrāvaruṇā... the Indra-Varuṇa [hymn] is indeed in Jagatī. This hymn is recited at the third pressing (*savana*) during the *ukthya* sacrifice. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Indrāvaruṇā... yuvamā vāṃ rājānau" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.1). (Note: The commentary provided above is a translation of the Sanskrit text embedded within the source material.)

O Indra and Varuṇa, you two grant great protection to our sacrifice, to our clan, and to our people. May we overcome the evil-minded enemies in battles who seek to harm those among us who perform long-continued sacrifices. O Indra and Varuṇa, you two grant great shelter—be it a home or happiness—to our people, that is, to our householders and to our offspring such as sons and grandsons, for the sake of the sacrifice. Furthermore, may we conquer those evil-intentioned enemies in the midst of battles who seek to destroy or injure our people who perform extensive and continuous sacrifices.

One of you is called the Universal Sovereign (*samrāj*), the other the Self-Ruling Lord (*svarāj*). O Indra and Varuṇa, you two are great and possessors of great wealth. All the gods in the highest heaven have bestowed vigor upon you both, O showers of blessings, and have endowed you with strength. The second foot of this verse is composed in the third person, while the remaining feet are in the second person. O Indra and Varuṇa, between you two, one—Varuṇa—is called the *samrāj*, meaning "the one who shines forth completely. This is celebrated in such passages as, "Those two universal sovereigns, to whom the clarified butter is offered" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 2.41.6). The other—Indra—is called the *svarāj*, meaning "the one who shines by himself, independent of others. This is celebrated in such passages as, "Indra is the self-ruling lord in his home" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.61.9). Such are you two, Indra and Varuṇa: great in your qualities and possessing great wealth. O showerers of desires, O Indra and Varuṇa, in the highest heaven, all the gods have bestowed *ojas* (vigor) upon you both for the sake of bodily firmness; that which has come into being is called *ojas*. As it is remembered: "Vigor (*ojas*) is the eighth stage [of life]. Likewise, they have bestowed *bala* (strength)—the capacity that serves as the cause for deeds such as the slaying of Vṛtra—upon you both.

With might you pierced the channels of the waters; you sent the Sun, the lord, up to heaven. O Indra and Varuṇa, in the exhilaration of this wondrous Soma, you caused the waterless rivers to swell; you made our prayers overflow with fulfillment. O Indra and Varuṇa, with your power you pierced the openings of the waters that had been blocked by Vṛtra; by the slaying of the obstructor Vṛtra, you removed the impediment to the rain. Likewise, you brought forth the Sun—the impeller of all, the pervasive lord—into the sky, the intermediate space; by his destruction, you caused the Sun, who was enveloped by his own darkness, to shine. O Indra and Varuṇa, when there is exhilaration from drinking this wise Soma, you caused the waterless rivers to swell, filling them with water. Thus it is recorded in the Nirukta: "In the exhilaration of this [Soma], O singer, Indra slew the unyielding [Vṛtra] and caused the waterless [rivers] to swell" (Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.25.1). Furthermore, you caused our prayers—the rites performed by us—to swell, fulfilling them with their fruits.

In battles and in many conflicts, we call upon you two; at the onset of peace, those with measured steps call upon you two. O Indra and Varuṇa, masters of both kinds of wealth, we poets, easy to invoke, call upon you. You two alone, in battles and in many conflicts—we, the many, call upon you two; at the onset of security, those of measured stride call upon you two. O Indra and Varuṇa, lords of both types of riches, we poets, who are easily invoked, call upon you.
O Indra and Varuṇa, the many officiating priests, the bearers of oblations or hymns, invoke you two alone for protection in battles and against hostile armies.
Even the Aṅgirases, with knees drawn up, invoke you two alone when the occasion for the production of security arises.

For this reason, O Indra and Varuṇa, we singers, the praisers, invoke you two alone—those who are the lords of both kinds of wealth, celestial and terrestrial, who are easy to invoke, and who are to be summoned with joy.

O Indra and Varuṇa, when you two created all these beings of the world by your might, Mitra honors Varuṇa with peace; the other, the fierce one, moves toward splendor with the Maruts. 5. O Indra and Varuṇa! When you two performed all these things, all the born beings of the world, by your greatness—with peace, Mitra serves Varuṇa; the formidable one, the other, goes toward glory with the Maruts. 5.

O Indra and Varuna, since you two have by your own power (*majmanā*) created all these visible beings (*viśvā jātāni*) belonging to the world (*bhuvanasya*), among those two, the god Mitra honors (*duvasyati*) one of them, Varuna, for the sake of security (*kṣemeṇa*).
For Mitra and Varuna have attained friendship with each other;
therefore, they are seen as companions.
Indra alone, being fierce with the Maruts— the hosts of Maruts— possesses formidable power and attains beautiful ornaments;
or alternatively, Indra, fierce and powerful together with the Maruts— the divine hosts stationed in the intermediate space— impels the beautiful water.

For the sake of the bride-price of Varuṇa, for his splendor, they two now measure their strength, since that which is his own is fixed. One [Varuṇa] overcomes the non-kinsman who is relaxing [the bond]; the other [Indra], with few [allies], prevails over the many. For the sake of the bride-price of Varuṇa, for his splendor, they two now measure their strength, since that which is his own is fixed. One [Varuṇa] overcomes the non-kinsman who is relaxing [the bond]; the other [Indra], with few [allies], prevails over the many.
This is an elliptical expression referring to Varuṇa [and Indra].

For the sake of the *tviṣ*, the splendor of both Indra and Varuṇa, the two wives of the sacrificer quickly (*nu*) fashion (*mimāte*), that is, produce through their hymn of praise, the *ojas*, the power.
For strength is born from praise.
For what purpose?
For great renown and for wealth.
For the sake of obtaining such wealth:
the construction is that he measures out *ojas*—that power which belongs to this Indra and Varuṇa, which is *dhruvam* (constant), eternal, and *svam* (their own), unique and exclusive to them.

Of those two, Indra and Varuṇa, the other one, Varuṇa, *atirat* (overcomes) the non-sacrificing worshipper who performs ritual acts while being a non-kinsman (*ajāmi*), one who is without kin (*abandhu*), one who causes fear, and one who does harm.
Indra alone, with few and small means, overcomes— that is, thoroughly obstructs and subdues— the many, that is, the greater number of enemies;
or alternatively, he elevates— that is, makes excellent and superior— the many, that is, the sacrificers.
Neither darkness, nor misfortunes, nor distress from any quarter shall overcome that mortal, O Indra and Varuṇa, to whom you two gods go and grant your favor; no mortal’s hostility can reach him.

Not [is there] for him, O Indra and Varuṇa, any double-dealing, nor any mortal [deceit]; from no side whatsoever can it overcome that man to whom you two, O gods, go and enjoy the sacrifice; no mortal’s treacherous plot reaches him. 7.
O Indra and Varuṇa, that mortal man whom evil does not afflict on any day,
nor do misfortunes— the difficult-to-traverse fruits of sin— reach him;
and from no cause whatsoever does he suffer the torment of penance.

O two gods, Indra and Varuṇa, endowed with qualities such as generosity, you who go to and reach the sacrifice (*adhvara*) of that mortal man, and whom you both enjoy and desire—affliction (*parihṛti*) or oppression does not reach that man; by the manner described, it does not affect him.
Come hither with divine protection; hear my call if you find it pleasing.
O Indra and Varuṇa, bestow upon us your friendship, your kinship, and your compassion.
Hitherward, O Heroes, come with divine protection; hear my call if you take pleasure in it. For the friendship and kinship that you possess, O Indra and Varuṇa, bestow your compassion upon us. 8.
O leaders, Indra and Varuṇa, come hither toward us with divine protection— that is, with protection pertaining to the gods—
and having arrived, hear my invocation, my hymn of praise,
if you two take pleasure in it.
The meaning is: "If there is affection for me, you two must come and listen to my hymn.

For indeed, O Indra and Varuṇa, bestow upon us both that friendship (*sakhyam*) which belongs to you two, and also that kinship (*āpyam*), that bond of relationship, and that compassion (*mārḍīkam*)—the means of attaining happiness (*mṛḍīka*). Grant these to us.
O Indra and Varuṇa, in every battle be our leaders of the host, overcoming the peoples with your might,
when both sides of men invoke you in the struggle for the acquisition of children and progeny.
O Indra and Varuṇa, in every battle, be our champions with the strength of the people, when both sides of men invoke you in the midst of the fray for the winning of offspring and descendants. 9.

O Indra and Varuṇa, you two whose vigor and strength draw away the power and force of enemies—be our front-line warriors in every battle. You both, whom the leaders of both kinds—the ancient and the present—invoke in the struggle for booty;
and furthermore, you both, whom they invoke on account of their offspring, their sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, who are to be cherished.
The grammatical connection is: "Therefore, you two become our vanguard warriors."
May Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman grant us glory and great, far-reaching protection.
O upholders of the Eternal Order (Ṛta), we meditate upon the blameless light of Aditi and the song of praise to the god Savitṛ.

May Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman grant us wealth, great protection that is far-reaching and blameless; may we meditate upon the light of Aditi and the hymn of the divine Savitṛ, who increase the cosmic order (Ṛta). 10.
May Indra and the other gods grant us, for our sake, *ghumnam*—shining wealth—and bestow it upon us.
Likewise, may they grant us *mahi*, great, and *saprathaḥ*, wide and extensive on all sides, as well as *śarma*, a dwelling.

Furthermore, [may] those who increase *ṛta*—the sacrificial rite—[bestow these]. (Note: The term *śaramatasya* appears to be a corruption; based on the context of the preceding *ṛtāvṛdhaḥ*, it is likely intended as *ṛtasya*.)
May the light and splendor of Aditi, the undepressed mother of the gods, be non-violent toward us. And may we know—
the meaning is that we perform— the hymn of praise for the divine Savitṛ, who is endowed with qualities such as generosity and is the impeller of all.
Or rather:
we meditate upon—that is, we beg for—the fame and glory to be granted to us by the divine Savitṛ.
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "yuvāṃ narā," is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Jāgata meter and is addressed to Indra and Varuṇa.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry: "yuvāṃ narā.
In the Ābhīvarta and Ukthya rites, when there is an increase in the Stoma, this hymn is used for the purpose of insertion (āvāpa) by the Praśāstṛ priest.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O two men, may I purify you both" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.9).
Beholding you two, O heroes, as their kin, they went forward with broad axes, whispering in secret.
Slay both the Dāsa and the Vṛtra-like enemies, and the Ārya foes; O Indra and Varuṇa, protect Sudās with your aid.
O Indra and Varuṇa, the edges of the earth—the borders and the heights—were devastated by the soldiers; they cried out together and were consumed by fire.
Likewise, a roar, the sound of the soldiers, ascended to the heavens in the celestial realm.
The enemies, the attackers of our people and our warriors, have surrounded me; they have come against me.
While this battle is thus proceeding, O Indra and Varuṇa, you who are ever-hearers of invocation, come toward us with protection and with aid.
O Indra and Varuṇa, growing strong and irresistible, you who conquer Bheda, protect Sudās.
Hear these prayers at his invocation; the priest of the Tṛtsus has become true.
O Indra and Varuṇa, growing strong, irresistible, and overcoming Bheda, you protected Sudās. You heard their prayers at the invocation; the Purohita of the Tṛtsus became true. 4.

O Indra and Varuṇa, you two who have grown great— having overcome with increasing weapons the enemy named Bheda who had not yet been reached, and having struck down that one named Sudās (the "Good Giver"), you two protected my sacrificer,
the king named Sudās, with preeminent care.
Hear, O Aśvins, the prayers and hymns of these Tr̥tsus who offer sacrifices for me;
when?
At the invocation.
A *havīman* is a battle, so called because people are summoned (*āhūyante*) therein for mutual combat.

In that [battle], because it was thus, this office of priest (*purohita*)— my consecration (*purodhāna*)— became true (*satyā*), that is, possessing the fruit of truth, for those who were eager for battle (*vṛtsūnām*), that is, for those who were designated by this name and were my sacrificers.
The meaning is that my office as their priest has become fruitful among them.
O Indra and Varuṇa, the hostilities of the enemy and the godless ones afflict me;
for you two rule over the wealth of both sides, so protect us on the decisive day.
O Indra and Varuṇa, the evils of the enemy oppress me; let the hostilities of the foe be warded off. For you two rule over both kinds of wealth; therefore, protect us on the decisive day. 5.
O Indra and Varuṇa, the weapons—the slaying arms—of the enemy, the adversary, burn me on all sides and press me from every direction.
Moreover, among the assailants who seek to harm me, the enemies who are ever-approaching torment me.
Indeed, you two rule over and possess both kinds of wealth: that which belongs to the earth and that which belongs to heaven.
O you whose action is sovereign power,
for this reason, protect us on that most noble day, the day of crossing, the day of battle in heaven.
Both sides invoke you two in the battles—Indra and Varuṇa—for the sake of winning the prize;
where, when Sudās was hard-pressed by the ten kings, you protected him together with the Tṛtsus.
Both sides invoke you two in the battles—Indra and Varuṇa—for the sake of gain. When Sudās was hard-pressed by the ten kings, you protected him along with the Tṛtsus.
The two kinds of people—the king named Sudās and his allies, the Tṛtsus—these twice-born folk invoke both Indra and Varuṇa in battles for booty; they call upon you two for what purpose?
For the sake of winning wealth, that is, for the purpose of its acquisition.

In those battles where Sudās was excessively oppressed (*nibādhitam*) by ten kings—ten in number—who were his enemies, you two, together with the Tṛtsus, protected him preeminently (*prāvavatam*). This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) with the phrase "in those battles."
1. When *kha*, *na*, *bha*, and *varta* occur;
2. *kha* is not reached; *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*, and *ra* are the *maprāsa*; *śa* is the *maprāti*.

May Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman grant us splendor, great protection, and excellent nourishment. May the unassailable light of Aditi and the hymn of the God who increases Truth be for our well-being; this we meditate upon. (10) This verse has been explained. As for the meaning of the syllables: may Indra and the others bestow upon us shining wealth, vast and great on all sides. Having increased the sacrifice, may the unimpaired radiance of the Divine Mother be non-obstructive to us. And we meditate upon—that is, we perform—the praise of the Impelling God. The fourteenth hymn, consisting of five verses, beginning with "ā vām," is by Vasiṣṭha, in the Triṣṭubh meter, addressed to Indra and Varuṇa. It is announced thus: "ā vām pañca. This hymn is used in the Maitrāvaruṇa recitation at the third pressing during the Ukthya sacrifice. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "ā vām rājānāvindrāvaruṇā madhumattamasya... is the Yājyā" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.1). 1. O Kings, Indra and Varuṇa, I would turn you both toward this sacrifice with oblations and with acts of homage. Holding the butter-sprinkling ladle in our arms, the sacrificial spoon, manifold in form, goes forth of its own accord around you both. O Kings, O radiant lords Indra and Varuṇa, I turn you both toward this sacrifice—which is free from injury—with offerings and with songs of praise. Furthermore, the *ghṛtācī* (the butter-dripping ladle), held in our hands, the *vipa-rūpā* (multiform)—*rūpa* here meaning the offering—is the *juhū* (sacrificial spoon) smeared with clarified butter; it goes forth by itself (*tmanā*) around you both. Or rather, *vipa-rūpā* may be understood as "of various forms," referring to you both. 2. The vast heaven promotes your kingdom, you two who bind the evildoers with straight-binding cords. May the wrath of the warding-off god Varuṇa avoid us; may Indra make for us a wide space. O Indra and Varuṇa, the vast (*bṛhat*) kingdom of you two, which is the heaven, nourishes all through rain. You two bind the doers of evil with straight-binding cords—meaning with bonds such as disease. May the wrath (*heḷaḥ*) of Varuṇa, the warding-off deity, avoid us; let it go elsewhere. And may Indra make for us a wide, spacious place. 3. Make our sacrifice dear in the assemblies; make our prayers praised among the wise. May wealth, impelled by the gods, come to us; extend us further with desirable aids. Make our sacrifice beautiful in the sacred gatherings; make our prayers lauded among the patrons. May wealth, sent by the gods, approach us; extend us forward with longings aids. (Note: Variants in manuscripts regarding the word "dhanaṃ" are noted in the source text.)
O Indra and Varuṇa, make our sacrifice—which is being performed in our homes for the sake of gaining wealth—excellent and endowed with fruit.
Likewise, make the *brahmāṇi* (prayers), the powerful hymns existing among us the singers, praised, most excellent, and partakers of the fruit.
Furthermore, let the chariot driven by you two gods come to us and bring us wealth.
Likewise, with your desirable *svāhā*-offerings and protective aids (*ūtayaḥ*), may you two cause us to prosper; that is, may you both increase us.
The prefix *pra-* combined with the root *tṛ* has the sense of "increasing."
O Indra and Varuṇa, bestow upon us wealth that contains all desirable things, abounding in riches and many cattle—
wealth which the Āditya, the hero, destroys falsehoods and distributes as unbounded treasures.

O Indra and Varuṇa, bestow upon us wealth that contains all boons, abounding in riches and many cattle—wealth which the Āditya destroys those who act untruthfully, while he, the unassailable hero, distributes treasures. 4.
O Indra and Varuṇa, bestow upon us (asme) a chariot and wealth (rathim dhanam).
Of what kind?

One that possesses all desirable things (viśvavāram)—to be sought after and honored by all—abounding in riches (vasumantam), providing a dwelling, and full of food (purukṣum), or rather, praised by many.
The son of Aditi, he who is Varuṇa, destroys—that is, he strikes down—the *anṛtā*, the unrealities that are devoid of truth.
The root is *mīñ* in the sense of "to injure.
That heroic Varuṇa, possessed of valor, bestows—gives to his worshippers—the *amitā*, the immeasurable and limitless *vasūni*, riches.
May this song of mine reach Indra and Varuṇa, providing strength for our children and progeny. May we go to the divine banquet with joyful play; do you all protect us always with your blessings.

May this song of mine reach Indra and Varuṇa; may it protect us, bestowing strength upon our children and progeny. May we, possessing excellent treasures, go to the feast of the gods. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 5.
May this song of praise, my own, reach Indra and Varuṇa;
thus impelled by me, may it protect us in regard to our children, sons, and grandsons.
And we, possessing excellent treasures, may we go to the feast of the gods—the sacrifice desired by the gods.
O Indra, Varuṇa, and all you gods, protect us always—throughout all time—with blessings that bring well-being.
The fifteenth hymn, consisting of fifteen verses each, beginning with "punīṣe vām," is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Indra and Varuṇa.
This is indicated by the introductory statement "punīṣe.
During the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) of the *ābhiplavika* days, this hymn serves as the insertion (*āvāpa*) for the *praśāstṛ* priest when the *stoma* and *pṛṣṭha* chants are performed.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O two heroes, I purify you both" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.9).
You purify our thought, free from demonic influence, as you offer the Soma to Indra and Varuṇa;
like the goddess Dawn whose face is bright with ghee, may those two be gracious toward our path in the encounter.

You purify for both [Indra and Varuṇa] a thought free from demons; offering Soma to Indra and Varuṇa, [I praise] her who has ghee as her face, like the goddess Uṣas. May those two protect us on our journey in the encounter. 1.
O Indra and Varuṇa, for you two—for your sake—I purify this *manīṣā*, a hymn of praise free from demons (*arakṣasaḥ*), unmixed with Rākṣasas. What am I doing?
Offering Soma to Indra and to Varuṇa, that is, with reference to Indra and Varuṇa.
1. [The calculation] ending in *kha-bha-śa* (20,850) is joined with the auspicious result; adding 330 to the moon (*soma*) results in *abhau*.
What kind of wisdom?
Divine, shining like the Dawn (Uṣas), with a face of clarified butter—that is, with radiant limbs.
The remainder [of the verse] is expressed in the third person.
May those two, Indra and Varuṇa, protect us—may they deliver us—in the encounter when the battle has arrived, whenever we go from station to station for the sake of combat.
Indeed, they vie with one another here in the calling of the gods, while the missiles fall upon those banners.
O Indra and Varuṇa, strike down those enemies with your arrow, driving them far away and scattering them in all directions.

They indeed vie with one another at the invocation of the gods; here, upon those banners where the missiles fall, O Indra and Varuṇa, do you two strike those enemies away with your arrow, scattering them in all directions. 2.
*Devahūya*:
Gods who desire victory, warriors, are summoned; they are mutually challenged for the sake of battle, thus it is a *devahūya*, a conflict.
In this [conflict].

*Hasvaḥ* (The Short One): He who, being possessed of reverence (*namasvān*), through reverence—that is, through homage or praise—serves you two who are endowed with power (*śavasā*), he, it is implied, is a doer of good deeds (*sukṛtuḥ*). Furthermore, he who, being possessed of oblations (*haviṣmān*), turns toward you two for the sake of protection or satisfaction (*avase*), that sacrificer, becoming possessed of food (*prayasvān*), shall surely exist (*asadit*) for the sake of a well-attained fruit (*suvitāya*). This song of mine has praised Indra and Varuṇa. May it protect us, bringing vigor to our children and grandchildren. May we, possessing beautiful jewels, go to the feast of the gods. Do you all protect us always with blessings. (5) *Vyākhyātā iyam* (This has been explained): My hymn has reached Indra and Varuṇa. Urged by me, may it protect us regarding sons and grandsons. May we, having excellent wealth, attain successive sacrifices. O gods, Indra, Varuṇa, and others, protect us always with auspicious things. (7) ‘*Dhīrā tv asya*’—this eight-verse sixteenth hymn is the seer Vasiṣṭha’s, composed in the *triṣṭubh* meter, and has Varuṇa as its deity. Thus it is announced: “*Dhīrāṣṭau vāruṇaṃ ha*” (Eight verses beginning with *dhīrā*, dedicated to Varuṇa). The application (*viniyoga*) is known. His greatness is indeed wise regarding his births—he who propped apart even the two wide worlds, heaven and earth. He pushed up the high, vast vault of heaven; twice he extended the star and spread out the earth. (1) *Asya varuṇasya janūṃṣi janmāni mahimā mahimnā tu kṣipraṃ dhīrā dhīrāṇi dhairyavanti bhavanti.* His births, through his majesty, quickly become wise and steadfast. That Varuṇa who propped apart even the two wide worlds, heaven and earth, established them in their respective places. And he who twice (*dvitā*) impels—the great sun and the visible star—sending the sun forth by day and the star by night; and who spread out the earth. Such is the connection: "of this Varuṇa. And with my own celestial body I salute [thee]. When indeed shall I be within Varuṇa? What offering of mine, not being angry, would he enjoy? When, being well-disposed, will he look upon us with mercy? (2) *Varuṇa, the seer desiring to go to heaven, reflects with this verse.* "Uta" is used in the sense of deliberation. Is it that I salute with my own body—my own physical form—or rather do I converse with him, Varuṇa? When indeed shall I be "within" Varuṇa, the god? That is, may I be accepted within Varuṇa’s heart. Furthermore, what offering of mine—be it a hymn or an oblation—would Varuṇa, not being angry (*ahaṇānaḥ*), enjoy? When, being well-disposed, will he look upon us with mercy? (2) (Note: 1. *Śa* reads "for the sake of protection"; 2. *Kha* and *Ma* read "by greatness"; 3. *Kha* and *Ma* read "impels"; *Śa* reads "he impels them thus").
468 Ṛgveda: [Aṣṭaka 5, Adhyāya 6,
Varga 8] For what reason (*kena hetunā*) would he *juṣeta*— that is, serve or enjoy?
Being *sumanaḥ*, one whose mind is auspicious, when (*kadā*)—at what time—shall I go toward (*abhi payeyam*) Varuṇa, the bestower of favor (*mṛḷīka*), to offer oblations (*havya*)?
I ask this of you, O Varuṇa; desiring to see, I come to question those who possess wisdom.
Even the sages speak of one common [fate] for me: that which Varuṇa holds against you.
I ask about that sin, O Varuṇa, desiring to see it; I approach you, the wise one, to inquire. Even the sages have told me this same thing: "This very Varuṇa is angry with you. 3.
O Varuṇa, I ask you about that sin; I inquire of you, desiring to see [it]. The elision of the *su* suffix is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Desiring to see [you], I have come near these wise people to ask various questions; tell me that sin by which cause I am bound with your snares when questioned. I have approached the learned ones to inquire in manifold ways.

Even those "seers" (*kavayaḥ*), people of far-reaching vision, have said to me, "It is the same," meaning it is indeed one and the same. As for what they said, that is what is being stated: "O singer, this very Varuṇa here is angry with you."
Therefore, abandoning your anger, release us from these bonds.
What offense have I committed, O Varuṇa, against the eldest [god], that you seek to strike down your own friend, the singer of praise?
Tell me that, O invincible one, O self-dependent lord; may I quickly go to you with this humble salutation, free from sin.

What was the greatest offense, O Varuṇa, that you seek to strike down the singer, your own friend? Tell me that, O invincible one, O self-dependent lord! May I, free from sin, quickly approach you with my homage. 4.
O Varuṇa, what was the most grievous offense, what transgression have I committed?
For by what sin do you wish to strike down your own friend, your worshiper?
O Varuṇa, difficult to deceive, invincible, self-sustaining, and radiant one, declare that offense to me!

This being the case, having performed an expiation for that [transgression], being "anenas" (sinless) and "turas" (hastening or swift), may I approach you with "namasā"—that is, through salutation or with an oblation.
Release us from the milk-drinking ancestors; release us from whatever we have committed with our own bodies.
O King, release Vasiṣṭha like a cattle-thief from his bonds, or like a calf from its tethering-rope.

O Aśvin, release us from the milk-drinking debt due to the ancestors; O Aśvin, release us from whatever we have committed with our own bodies. O King, like a thief who has satisfied himself with cattle, release Vasiṣṭha from his bond like a calf from its tether.
O Varuṇa, release—set free from us—the milked-out debts belonging to us which were inherited from our fathers, those acts of hostility that cause bondage;
separate yourself from us.
And whatever hostilities we have committed with our own bodies, release those as well.

O King, O Varuṇa who shines, release me—Vasiṣṭha—from this bond of sin, like a thief who has performed penance for his theft and at its conclusion satisfies the cattle with fodder and the like, or like a calf from its tethering rope. Release me from this bondage of evil.
1. *kha-kṣa-ta-na-bha-śa-āga* | 2. *kha-pitryāṇi*; *bha-pitryā pitryāṇi* | 3. *kha-hetūn* | 4. *kha-kṣa-ta-na-bha-śa-viśleṣaṇya ca*.
Not his own skill, O Varuṇa, is that steadfastness; it is wine, wrath, the vibhīdaka nut, and thoughtlessness.
There is an elder [who stands] over the younger; he is the one who stirs up the truth of the sun.

No, O Varuṇa; that is one's own skill, that is steadfastness, that is intoxication, wrath, the Vibhīdaka nut, or thoughtlessness. The elder is not [the cause] of the younger's transgression; even the sun itself does not dispel the darkness of falsehood.
O Varuṇa, that innate skill (*dakṣa*) of yours, which is the inherent power of a person, is not the cause for the engagement in sin.
What then? Firm resolve (*dhṛti*), established at the very moment of birth, is the cause; it is the course of destiny (*daivagati*).
The verbal root is *dhū*, meaning "to go" and "to be steady."
And that steadfastness (*dhṛti*) is of the nature that will be described hereafter.
*Surā* is intoxicating liquor; *manyu* is anger directed toward teachers and others, which is a cause for the production of passion;
and *vibhīdaka* is the die used as an instrument for gambling.
And that [fate], by inciting a person toward gambling, becomes a cause of misfortune.
Lack of reflection—meaning ignorance—is the cause of non-discrimination.
Therefore, such a destiny alone is the cause for a person's engagement in sinful activity.
Moreover, when a younger, inferior, and base person is about to engage in sin—that is, when such a tendency has approached him—the elder, superior Lord stands nearby as its restrainer;
it is He alone who impels him toward sin.
Thus it is declared in the scripture: "For it is He indeed who causes that man to perform evil deeds whom He intends to lead downward" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8).
This being the case, even one who asks his own question becomes a *prayoktṛ*—one who thoroughly mingles—the sin of falsehood.
The word "hence" (*itaḥ*) is a connective particle.
Since many sins arise even from actions performed in a dream, what need is there to mention that sins are produced by actions performed while awake?
Therefore, the sense is: "O Varuṇa, this transgression of mine has come about through destiny; it must be forgiven by you."
Like a servant for a bountiful master, I have performed much service for the God, even though I have committed sins.
The noble God has brought consciousness to the unconscious; the wiser Seer impels the skillful man toward wealth.
Like a servant, I shall perform many services for the bounteous god; being sinless, may the divine and noble one enlighten the ignorant. As a wiser seer, he impels the skillful man toward wealth. 7.

To Varuṇa—the one who has sprinkled, the showerer of desires, the sustainer of the vast world, the god endowed with qualities such as generosity—being sinless through his grace, may I perform sufficient service, enough and complete worship, like a servant properly attending to his master.
And may that noble lord, the god, awaken us who are unawakened; may he enlighten us and grant us understanding.
May the God, the more wise and the more skillful poet, impel and urge on the intelligent singer for the sake of wealth, that is, for the attainment of riches.
In the case of the Varuṇa animal sacrifice belonging to the Ekādaśinī set, "ayam" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "This [is] truly for you, O Varuṇa; O self-existent one, praise Varuṇa the Great" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.7).
O self-dependent Varuṇa, may this hymn of praise reach your heart;
may it be a blessing for us in rest and a blessing for us in exertion. Do you all protect us always with your blessings.
O self-dependent Varuṇa, may this hymn of praise rest within your heart. May it be well with us in peace, and may it be well for us in exertion. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 8.
O self-dependent Varuṇa, may this hymn consisting of this *sūkta*, being performed for your sake, be well-established, reached, and gathered within your heart.
The word *cit* is a filler.
May there be peace (*śam*) for us in security; may there be peace! (*ūm*).
May it be with us in yoga; do you all protect us always with blessings.

1. *i-sa-tara-4* is the divine state (*devagati*). 2. *kha-jha-ta-na-bha-śa* brings about joy (*pramodakāriṇī*). 3. *gha-ta³-śa* means "it should be endured" (*kṣantavyam*). 4. *kha-bha-t* consists of well-spoken words (*sūktātmakaḥ*).
Yoga is the attainment of what has not been attained; Kṣema is the preservation of what has been attained.
May there be *jha*—the pacification of calamities—in our *kṣema*, that is, in our protection.
And in our acquisition, O Varuṇa and other gods, let there be only the pacification of calamities; protect us always with blessings that bring no destruction.

The hymn beginning with “radatpathaḥ” consists of seven verses; it is the seventeenth hymn, composed by Vasiṣṭha, in the Triṣṭubh meter, and dedicated to Varuṇa. It is thus enumerated: “radatpathaḥ. Its ritual application (viniyoga) has been explained.

Varuṇa carved out paths for the sun; he made the waters of the rivers easy to traverse. Like a released flood, he, moving according to the *ṛta*, created the great channels for the days. radat | pathaḥ | varuṇaḥ | sūryāya | pra | arṇaॉṃsi | sudriyāṃ | nadīnām | sargaḥ | na | sṛṣṭaḥ | arvetīḥ | ṛtayan | cakāra | mahīḥ | avanīḥ | ahobhyaḥ || 1 ||
This god Varuṇa has spies;
"spies" (spaśaḥ) are so called because they "touch" or "observe" (spṛśanti).
The spies of the god Varuṇa are dispatched everywhere.
The word *sam* here functions in the sense of praise (*praśasti*) and assistance (*sahāyya*). [Thus, it means] "those whose movements are praiseworthy.
Or else:
Having been sent forth together,
they behold— survey from all sides— the two *rodasī*, heaven and earth, which are *sumeke*, meaning beautiful in their expanse or beautiful in form.
The meaning is that, abiding in both worlds, they look upon the people who perform meritorious and non-meritorious deeds.

Since this is so, therefore, out of compassion for them— those people who are *ṛtāvānaḥ* (possessors of truth), *karmavantaḥ* (performers of rites), *yajñadhīrāḥ* (wise in sacrifice), having their intellects fixed on sacrifices, *pracetasaḥ* (far-sighted), *kavayaḥ* (seers), and who *hṛyavanta* (bring) our *manmāni* (thoughts) or hymns of praise toward Varuṇa— that is, they cause them to reach him— they too behold [him]. Therefore, may they also release us, the singers, from *śaravaḥ* (evil).
Regarding the animal sacrifice to Varuṇa, "ava sindhum" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "ava sindhuṃ varuṇo dhauriva sthāpayat su tumyaṃ varuṇa svabhāvaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
Varuṇa has established the Sindhu like the sky; he is like a white, swift-footed deer, full of vigor. Of deep renown, the measurer of the mid-region, the ruler of good dominion, his son is the king.

Varuṇa has descended to the Sindhu like the sky standing firm; he is like a white drop, a vigorous wild beast. His word is profound, he is the measurer of the mid-air, and his dominion is easy to cross; the King has been born from this [ocean]. 6.
Like the sky and like the sun, he is radiant; Varuṇa, like the ocean, stands over the river and establishes it within its boundary.
The meaning is that he acts in such a way that it does not transgress the shore.
Of what nature is Varuṇa?

Like a drop, a swift-moving speckle; like a white water-drop, a bright-colored deer—this is an elliptical simile (luṣopama). Like a wild bull (*gauramṛga*), he is mighty, powerful, or grown great, and his proclamation is profound.
He whose praise and hymn of worship are profound and great is thus described.

The measurer or creator of the *rajas*—that is, of the waters—is Varuṇa, who possesses excellent power (*kṣatra*) for crossing over suffering, or whose strength and wealth are such that they effectively carry one across. He is the king and sovereign of this existing world.
May we be sinless before Varuṇa, who shows mercy even to one who has committed an offense; may we fulfill the ordinances of Aditi—do you all protect us always with your blessings.
May we be sinless before Varuṇa, who shows mercy even to one who has committed an offense; may we prosper according to the ordinances of Aditi. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. 7.

May we remain—indeed, become—sinless, that is, free from transgression, before that Varuṇa who shows mercy, who bestows compassion even upon the singer who has committed an offense, who has indeed performed a wrong.
What are we doing?
We are fulfilling, that is, accomplishing in due order, the *vratas*—the ritual acts—belonging to Aditi, the non-depressed Varuṇa.
O gods, Varuṇa and the others, may you always protect us with auspicious blessings.
The seventh hymn, the eighteenth [of the Maṇḍala], beginning with "pra śundhyuvam," is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Varuṇa.
It is introduced by the words "pra śundhyuvam.
Its ritual application (viniyoga) has been explained.
O Vasiṣṭha, present to Varuṇa, the purifier, a most excellent hymn to the bounteous one—
that which shall bring hither the worshipful, thousand-giving, mighty bull.
O Vasiṣṭha, bring forth a pure and most excellent hymn for Varuṇa, the bountiful giver—one who will turn toward us the worshipful, thousand-giving, mighty bull.
The seer, having made himself directly manifest, enjoins himself to the praise:
"O Vasiṣṭha, for Varuṇa—the bountiful showerer—bring forth, offer, and present this most beloved, pure, and reflective thought (*mati*), that is, such a hymn of praise;
[present it] to him, that Varuṇa who turns *īm* (this) Sūrya hitherward, toward us, making him appear in the mid-air. This is the syntactical connection.
Of what sort is the Sun?
He who is worthy of worship (*yajatra*), to be sacrificed to; who possesses a thousandfold wealth (*sahasrādha*); who is a showerer of desires (*vṛṣaṇa*); and who is vast (*bṛhantam*), great.
Now, having come into his presence, I shall contemplate the majesty of Varuṇa’s countenance;
for the Lord of the Sun has made the light visible, and they have led me toward that which he would bestow.

Now, having come into the very sight of him, I perceive the countenance of Agni; it belongs to Varuṇa. Since the Lord of the Stone has brought the light—the wondrous form—to be seen for me, even from the darkness. 2.
O Pathas, now behold the sight of the excellent Varuṇa; having quickly gone there, I shall praise the host—that is, the mass of flames—of Agni.
[I shall praise] that Varuṇa (this is the ellipsis).
When Varuṇa [beholds] the cattle, which are pleasant, situated upon the stone—that is, in the sense of "upon" or "in" the rock.

The meaning is "pressed. Such a composition (*pabandha*)—the Soma characterized as food—may be the "over-protector" (*adhipā*), that is, the superior drinker; the absence of the *ś* sound is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
"Pau" signifies inhalation (pūraka). At that time, "pamā" means "me" (mām), and "pavapuḥ" means "one's own body" (svakīyaṃ vapuḥ). "Vapuḥ" is a name for form (rūpa).
Or, he should direct his intention toward a praiseworthy form that is visible for the purpose of seeing it.
When Varuṇa and I board the ship and set it forth into the midst of the ocean,
when we move upon the waters with the songs of praise, then let us both go forward for the sake of glory.
When Varuṇa and I embark upon the ship, when we propel it forth into the midst of the ocean, and when we move over the ridges of the waters, then let us both urge it forward for the sake of glory. 3.
When Varuṇa was gracious, both I and Varuṇa prepared a boat made of wood as a means of crossing; we both mounted it.
And when we propelled that boat toward the middle of the ocean, we caused it to go forth with great speed.
And when we moved upon the surface of the waters, we traveled together with other boats that move by means of oars.
At that time, for the sake of beauty on the auspicious day for the animal sacrifice, we two shall mount the swing and carry it;
moving up and down upon those various elevations and depressions, let us sport together.
The word *pakama* means "filling."
Alternatively, it is an adverbial modifier;
the meaning is "in such a way that there is happiness (*kaṃ*)."
Varuṇa, the skillful worker, by his mighty powers made Vasiṣṭha a seer;
the sage made him his praiser on the auspicious days of the sun, so that he might run along the paths and extend his life.

Varuṇa placed Vasiṣṭha upon a ship; by his great deeds, the inspired sage made him a seer of noble works. He, the wise one, made the singer his own on the auspiciousness of the days, as he sped forth and crossed over the dawns. 4.
Thus, he shows what was done by Varuṇa for Vasiṣṭha, whom he himself had called forth. Verily, Varuṇa placed Vasiṣṭha upon his own ship;
likewise, Varuṇa made that seer *svapā*, one of beautiful deeds (*svapasa*), through his protections (*āvobhiḥ*).

Moreover, the wise Varuṇa, the master of the *pavi* (the thunderbolt or the sun), established the praiser among the *paḥ*—that is, within the days (*divasānām*)—in that state of being a *pasu-dina* (a "good day"), which is the fruitfulness of those days; this is the sense.
What was he doing?

He was swiftly spreading out, by means of his solar nature, the *pathāvaḥ* (the moving ones) as they go, the *pathāt* (those who go), and the *paupaḥ* (the nights characterized by the *upas*), as they move.
What have those friendships of ours become, since we were once companions in that which is free from harm?
O self-dependent Varuṇa, I have entered your great dwelling, your house with a thousand doors.

1. It was covered with stone slabs. 2. Those who were mounted on *kha*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*; we two have become mounted on *gha*. 3. On the swing of *kha*, *jhā*, *ma*, *ta*, *na*, and *bha*. 4. Establish *ta*, *1*, and *2*.

Where? To those [places]. For us. With a friend. We two have become together. That which is free from wolfishness. Even from of old. O Varuṇa, you who possess self-sovereignty (*svadhā*), I have gone to your lofty dwelling, your house with a thousand doors. 5.
O Varuṇa, where have those ancient friendships, those bonds of companionship between us two, gone?
That truth which is inviolable and eternal from of old—that we two shall surely maintain together.
*Cit* is a filler word.
Moreover, O Varuṇa, possessor of *svadhā* (nourishment), may I go to your house; "may I go" is used here in the sense of an imperative (*loṭ*). Of what sort is that house?
The vast, the great, the measure (*māna*).
It is called "measure" because all beings are measured within it;
the meaning is that it is the delimiting factor of the entire collection of beings.
It has a thousand doors and many gates.

O King Varuṇa, O Lord, may I not go to your house made of clay, fashioned from earth and other materials; rather, may I reach your beautiful home made of gold. Be gracious to me; O Ruler of noble dominion, have mercy and grant me happiness.

When I go, quivering as it were, like a blow from a heated thunderbolt, O wielder of the stone, have mercy, O Lord of good dominion; have mercy! When I go, trembling as it were with cold, like a blow from a heated thunderbolt, O wielder of the stone—have mercy, O Lord of good dominion; have mercy! O wielder of the stone, O Varuṇa, when I go, trembling as it were with cold, like a blow from a heated [iron] weapon, bound and filled with wind, then have mercy; grant me happiness. O Lord of good dominion, O possessor of excellent wealth, have mercy; grant me relief.

Through the weakness of my intellect, O pure one, I have gone against the prescribed course of action; O Lord of noble dominion, have mercy, have mercy! O *samaha*, endowed with all wealth, O *śuci*, naturally stainless Varuṇa, through the weakness (*dīnatā*) of my state—having failed in the performance of the rites (*kratvaḥ*) enjoined as duties according to the Śruti and Smṛti—I have gone (*jagama*) against the right path (*pratīpam*). Therefore, I have been bound by you. Such as I am, have mercy (*mṛḷa*), grant me happiness. The rest is as explained elsewhere.

Standing in the midst of the waters, thirst has found me, your singer. O you of good dominion, be gracious; have mercy! (4) Standing in the midst of the waters—that is, of the oceans—thirst has found me, your singer, even though I am one who stands there. Thirst—that is, the desire to drink—has seized me because it is impossible to drink the salt-heavy water of the ocean. Therefore, O you of good dominion, be gracious; comfort me. The rest is clear.
In the *devasuvām havīṃṣi* offerings, the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the oblation to Varuṇa is "yat kiṃ cedaṃ...
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "'yat kiṃ cedaṃ varuṇa daivye jana' and 'upa te stomān yaśupā ivākaram'—these two" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.11).

Whatever offense against the divine host we humans have committed here, O Varuṇa, or whatever of your laws we have violated through thoughtlessness—O God, do not harm us because of that sin. Whatever offense against the divine host we humans have committed here, O Varuṇa, or whatever of your laws we have violated through thoughtlessness—we have neglected your sustaining ordinances out of ignorance. O God, do not harm us because of that sin. 5.11.5.
