1. Formed from *gha*, *śa*, *mṛd* and so forth; formed from *jha*, *ta³*, *mṛd* and so forth; formed from *jha*, *mṛd* and so forth; formed from *tara⁴*, *na*, *mṛd* and so forth. 2. *kha-bha-mṛḍaya*. 3. *kha-ta³-bha-mṛḍaya* (be gracious) and *sukhaya* (make happy); *gha-mṛḍa*; *śa-mṛḍaya*.
4. Of the water of that ocean.
5. O Sky, be gracious; O Earth, be gracious; O Jha-ta-śa, be gracious and bring us happiness.
In this section (paḍha) and recitation (anuvāka), there are fifteen hymns (sūktas).
In this regard, the first hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "pra vīrayā," is the ṛṣi-seer Vasiṣṭha's composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is dedicated to Vāyu.
Among those verses, those containing dual forms from the fifth verse onward are dedicated to Indra and Vāyu.
Thus it has been enumerated: "Pra vīrayā consists of seven [verses]; it is dedicated to Vāyu, and those which are spoken in the dual form belong to Indra and Vāyu."
In the third *chandoma*, during the *prauga* recitation, there is the Vāyu hymn beginning with "pra vīrayā.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "pra vīrayā śucayo dadhire vāṃ te satyena manasā dīdhyānāḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.11).
Through heroic power, the pure pressed juices have bestowed your favor; they are mixed with milk and possess sweetness.
O Vāyu, harness your teams and come hither; drink of the pressed soma for exhilaration.

The pure pressed juices, accompanied by the Adhvaryus, have been offered to you both for the sake of heroic power; they are full of sweetness. O Vāyu, bring your teams of horses and come hither; drink of the pressed soma-juice for exhilaration. 1.
O Vāyu, [I offer] to you, the hero, who impels variously with heroic power;
the substitution of *yāj* for the dative case ending is according to the rule "supāṃ suluk... [Pāṇini 7.1.39]. [The form is] *vām te*.
The dual number is used by way of transposition.

For you, the Soma juices—pure, bright, and full of sweetness (*madhumantaḥ*), having been pressed (*sutāsaḥ*) by the *aitareyibhiḥ* (the priests of the Aitareya school) on this day during the *prauga* litany, are "presented" (*pradadhire*) by the *adhvaryubhiḥ*, the officiating priests who lead the sacrifice (*adhvarasya netṛbhiḥ*).
This is a form of the root *dad* (to give).
For this reason, O Vāyu, bring your chariot here with your unyoked mares;
and by that chariot, come hither—
approach our sacrifice.
And having approached, drink your own portion of the pressed juice— the soma characterized as *andhas*—
for the sake of exhilaration, that is, for the arising of intoxication.
At the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice, the *yājyā* for the oblation dedicated to Vāyu is "īśānāya.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "sa tvaṃ no deva manaseśānāya prahutiṃ yasta ānaṭ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.20).
This same verse serves as the *yājyā* for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) at the very sacrifice of the animal dedicated to Vāyu.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "He who has offered an oblation to Īśāna... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8), and "Make Vāyu, the yoker of the chariot, your leader... (Ṛgveda 7.92.1).
O Vāyu, you who drink the pure soma, for him who brings an offering to you, the Lord, you make him renowned among mortals; every son born to him becomes a hero through his power.
To Īśāna [be] the offering! He who has brought to you pure Soma, O drinker of the pure, him you make worthy of praise among mortals, O Vāyu; every son born of him is born a victor. 2.
O Vāyu, O Īśāna, O Īśvara— to you, for your sake, that sacrificer who has attained (ānaṭ)— that is, who offers— a most excellent oblation (prahuti) accomplished by means of the *caru*,

the *puroḍāśa*, and so forth; and likewise, O drinker of the pure (Soma), to you who drinks the pure Soma, he who presents the pure Soma among mortals— among men— you make that sacrificer praised, that is, preeminent.
And he, being born again and again, having appeared everywhere and become renowned, is "born" (ajāyate)—that is, he is deemed fit—for the attainment of "vājya," meaning wealth that is to be acquired;
the sense is that he obtains all wealth.

For the animal sacrifice dedicated to the deity Vāyu, who is distinguished by the quality of possessing a *niyuta* [of horses], the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is "rāye nu yam.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "rāye nu yaṃ jajñatū rodasīme pra vāyumacchā bṛhatī manīṣā" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
For wealth indeed these two worlds, Heaven and Earth, brought him forth; for wealth the divine Dhiṣaṇā establishes the god.
Then his teams attend upon Vāyu, and also the white one, the bestower of wealth, in his preeminence.
1. Of the pure one who is purified from the sky, and of the purified one who is pure;

2. for the attainment of heaven and earth—for wealth—verily, whom these two worlds, Heaven and Earth, brought forth. For wealth, the divine Dhiṣaṇā establishes the god Vāyu as his portion; may his own teams attend him, and the white treasure-holder in the highest place. 3.
These two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), have swiftly brought forth that Vāyu for the sake of wealth (*rāye*).
That god Vāyu, endowed with qualities such as generosity, the goddess *dhiṣaṇā*—the radiant hymn of praise—sustains for the sake of wealth;
that is to say, she impels him so that wealth may be obtained.
Now, even as the hymn of praise has begun, his own teams of yoke-mares, the carriers of the chariot, attend upon Vāyu; they follow him closely.
And moreover, he [is seen] with the white, brilliant-colored [steed] in the "nir-eka"—*nireka* being that which is utterly devoid (*reka*) of anything else.
The meaning is "poverty. When that [poverty] exists, they bring that Vāyu—the supporter and bestower of riches—to our sacrifice, being self-restrained; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In the second Chandoma, the Prauga-śastra.

Those who are lords, who bestow upon us heaven with cattle, with horses, with riches, and with gold—O Indra and Vāyu, those wise patrons, through their steeds and heroes, shall prevail in battles throughout their entire life. Those who are lords, who bestow upon us heaven with cattle, with horses, with riches, and with gold—O Indra and Vāyu, those wise patrons, through their steeds and heroes, shall prevail in battles throughout their entire life. O Indra and Vāyu, those who are lords—masters and powerful ones—who grant us heaven (*svaḥ*), that which is well-desirable, along with cattle, horses, riches (*vasubhiḥ*) meaning dwellings or treasures, and gold; or alternatively, *vasūni* meaning wealth other than gold, together with that gold—those wise patrons (*sūrayaḥ*), as givers, shall conquer the pervasive life-force (*viśvam āyuḥ*), whether it be food or the very existence belonging to the enemies, in battles (*pṛtanāsu*) by means of their steeds and heroic warriors. Or, in the third [interpretation], they shall overcome [the enemy] in assistance.

O Indra and Vāyu, according to the speed (*taraḥ*) of your two bodies, according to the impulse (*vegaḥ*), according to the vigor (*ojaḥ*), the strength (*balaṃ*), and according to the extent to which the men—the leaders of the rites and the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*)—are shining (*dīdhyānāḥ*) with their chests [of sacrifice] and with knowledge; O Indra and Vāyu, you who drink the pure Soma (*śucipā*), drink (*pātam*) this pure Soma belonging to us (*asme*).
And sit down (*āsadataṃ*) upon this sacrificial grass (*barhiḥ*) spread on the altar for the sake of drinking;
that is to say, sit down upon the *barhis*.
Harnessing your teams of horses that possess desirable heroes, O Indra and Vāyu, come hither on a single chariot;
for this foremost portion of the sweet soma has been presented to you, so being gratified, release [the teams] among us.

O Indrā-Vāyu, come hither with your team of steeds, those who are youthful, numerous, and possess desirable heroes; come with your beautiful chariot. For this first portion of the sweet soma has been presented to you both; now, being gratified, release [the horses] among us. 5.

O Indra and Vāyu, you who possess desirable heroes, drawing toward us your own teams of horses—those worthy of praise—yoking a single common chariot for both of you, come hither toward us. For this very portion of the sweet Soma, the first of the libations known as the *aindravāyava* cup, has been presented for you; it has been brought forward for the sake of the offering and led toward the high altar.
Now, therefore, after drinking such soma, being pleased—that is, taking delight—may you two release us from evil; that is, deliver us from it.
In the first *chandoma*, the *praüga* recitation for the cup dedicated to Indra and Vāyu consists of the third verse, "Then, your hundred... (*athā vām śatam*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'Then, your hundred teams, those which are a thousand'—these are the *atinyaḥ*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.9).
O Indra and Vāyu, those hundred teams and those thousand of yours that attend you, possessing all desirable things—
come hither with those most gracious ones, O heroes, to the presented honeyed draught.
Those hundred and those thousand teams of yours, O Indra and Vāyu, which follow you, possessing all boons—with them, being well-disposed, come hither; drink, O heroes, of the offered honeyed draught.

O Indra and Vāyu, those hundred teams of yours—those true ones numbering a hundred—which attend upon and serve you both; and those teams which are "all-desirable," numbering a thousand and worthy of being chosen by all—who attend upon you both; with these teams that bestow beautiful wealth, come hither toward us! Come!
O leaders, you two heroes, drink—drink such Soma as this, the sweet juice brought forward and led toward the high altar;
here the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
Drink such Soma!
Like those seeking renown, the Vasiṣṭhas, with well-sung hymns, beseech Indra and Vāyu. Striving for strength and for the light of heaven, we invoke you; do you ever protect us with your blessings.
Seeking glory like steeds, we Vasiṣṭhas, with excellent hymns, call upon Indra and Vāyu, desiring strength for the sake of the noble one. Do you protect us always with your blessings. 7.
This has been explained.

As for the literal meaning: like horses that carry oblations, we Vasiṣṭhas—those who possess excellent protection and who, desiring strength, make this request—invoke Indra and Vāyu with beautiful hymns.
1. In the manuscripts gha, ṇa, ma, and e, there is *ekaratham*.

2. In kha, jha, ta, ma, and śa, it is *nimistri-tavantau*; in ta₁, *niśrayantau*; in na, *nimiyantau*; in bha, *nimistri-tayantāv*; in śa, *miśrayantau*. 3. In kha, jha, ta, ma, and śa, the word *yāḥ* is absent.
The third hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "ā vāyo," is the work of Vasiṣṭha and is dedicated to Vāyu. It is thus catalogued:
"ā vāyo pañca."
At the Śunāsīrīya festival, for the sacrifice to Vāyu accompanied by his team of horses (*niyut*), the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) is "ā vāyo.

This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "ā vāyo bhūṣa śucipā upa naḥ pra yābhiryāsi dāśvāṃsamaccha" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.20). In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Vāyu with his team of horses, this same verse serves as the invitatory verse for the omentum offering (*vapā*). (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).
In the first *chandoma*, this same [verse] is the first of the triplet dedicated to Vāyu in the *prauga-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Samudrād ūrmibhiḥ*... and *Ā vāyo bhūṣa śucipāḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.9).
O Vāyu, drinker of the pure, come to us; yours are a thousand teams, O possessor of all boons.
I offer to you the intoxicating juice, of which, O God, you have made the first draught.

O Vāyu, drinker of the pure, come hither; a thousand teams of horses are yours, O possessor of all boons. To you this exhilarating soma-juice is offered, of which, O God, you have the first right to drink.
O Vāyu, drinker of the pure and purified Soma, come near to us; "bhūṣ" is the form of the root *bhū* meaning "to reach.
O Viśvavāra, one whose desirable things are universal, you possess a thousand *niyuts*—that is, a thousand mares—as your vehicles.
Since this is so, come quickly.
I offer to you today the exhilarating *soma*, characterized as the food (*andhas*) that causes intoxication (*madya*).
It was taken into the vessel for the *upayāma* rite.
O divine Vāyu, you possess—that is, you hold and maintain—the first drinking, the initial draught, of this Soma.

Since it is offered to Vāyu alone at the first *vaṣaṭ*-call during the *aindravāyava* libation, whereas it is offered to both Indra and Vāyu at the second, Vāyu’s drinking is the first. Such is that food (*andhas*) which I approach; this is the grammatical connection.
In the first *chandoma*, for the *prauga-śastra* dedicated to Indra and Vāyu, the verses beginning with “*pra sotā*” are used.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: “*pra sotā jīro adhvareṣvātsomamindrāya vāyave pibadhyai*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.9).
The active presser has brought forth the Soma at the sacrifices for Indra and Vāyu to drink,
when the god-seeking Adhvaryus with their skillful powers bring you the first portion of the honeyed juice.

Let the swift presser pour forth the Soma at the sacrifices for Indra and Vāyu to drink, when the Adhvaryus, seeking the gods, bring you the first portion of the honeyed mead with their skillful rites.
The swift-acting *adhvaryu* priest, the presser and the extractor, has brought forth the *soma* for Indra and Vāyu to drink at the sacrifices (*adhvareṣu*).
He has established it before the northern altar.

O Indra and Vāyu, in those sacrifices where the *adhvaryu*s, desiring the gods, bring forward and prepare your chariot with their skillful deeds—such as the pressing and other rites—of the first portion of the sweet *soma*.
The grammatical connection is with the word "in those sacrifices" (teṣvadhvareṣu).
At the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice, the verse beginning with “pra yābhiḥ” serves as the *yājyā* for the offering to Vāyu accompanied by the *niyuts*.

This is prescribed in the Sūtra: “‘pra yābhiryāsi dāśvāṃsamaccha sa tvaṃ no deva manasā’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.20). In the animal sacrifice dedicated to those same deities, this very verse is also the *anuvākyā* for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “With which [teams] you come toward the donor, with those hundredfold teams, come toward us” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
In the first Chandoma, this very verse is the second of the triplet dedicated to Vāyu in the Prauga-śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “O Vāyu, drinker of the pure, come hither to us; with which [teams] you come toward the donor” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.9).

With those teams by which you hasten toward the donor in his dwelling for the sake of abundance, O Vāyu— bestow upon us wealth that provides excellent nourishment, and grant us heroic sons and the gift of cattle and horses.
1. In the words *kha-sa-ta-na-bha-śa*, the sense of "near" (*upa samīpe*) is absent.
2. [The root] *kha-bha* means "to stand firmly" (*prātiṣṭhapat*); *na* means "did not stand" (*na pratiṣṭhat*). Ka 3-31.

With which teams you go toward the donor for the sake of sacrifice in his home, O Vāyu—with those [teams] come back to us. And having arrived, bestow upon us wealth rich in enjoyment; bestow upon us a heroic son and the gift consisting of both cattle and horses. In the first *Chandoma*, during the *Prauga-śastra*, this is the second verse of the triplet dedicated to Indra and Vāyu: "O Vāyus who gladden Indra... It is also prescribed in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (8.9): "O Vāyus who gladden Indra... those hundred teams of yours, those thousand..."

May those winds that exhilarate Indra, the divine ones who bestow gifts and are hostile to the enemy, slay the Vṛtras along with our patrons; may we, together with our heroes, be victorious in battle over our foes.
Those who exhilarate Indra for Vāyu.
O gods,
you who are bounteous toward the noble one.
Slaying the Vṛtras together with the patrons.
May we be victorious; may we be conquerors through battle.
With men, [subdue] the enemies.
May we, through our noble patrons (*sūri*) who are singers of praise, gladdening Indra with hymns and likewise satisfying Vāyu—
those who are godly, possessed of a *jāgata* nature, and thus the slayers of the enemy, the foe—
be those who strike down and destroy the *vṛtra*s, the adversaries.
Doing what? Overpowering—that is, subduing—the enemies who have become our foes through battles with our own men.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Vāyu Niyutvat, "ā no niyudbhiḥ" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the oblation.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "ā no niyudbhiḥ śatinībhir adhvaraṃ pīvo-aśvāṃ rayivṛdhaḥ sumedhāḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
In the first *Chandoma* day, this is the third verse of the triplet dedicated to Vāyu in the *Prauga-śastra*.
And it is stated in the scripture: "With your hundredfold teams come to our sacrifice; the swift presser has stood forth at the rites" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.9).

Come to our sacrifice with your teams of horses, by the hundreds and by the thousands, to this ritual. O Vāyu, rejoice in this libation! And may you all protect us evermore with blessings. O Vāyu, come to our *adhvara*—the sacrifice free from harm—with your teams (*niyut*) of mares numbering in the hundreds and in the thousands. Having arrived, thereafter, at this *savana*—the morning pressing—rejoice; be satisfied with the Soma. The rest is as before. The fourth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "śuci nu," is the work of Vasiṣṭha. It is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is dedicated to Indra and Agni. For it is listed thus: "śuci nu—aṣṭarcam; Aindrāgnam tu" (śuci nu is of eight verses; it belongs to Indra and Agni). The application of the hymn has been explained. Regarding the omentum-offering (*vapā*) for the animal sacrifice to Indra and Agni, this verse beginning with "śucim" is the *ājyā*. It is prescribed: "śuci nu stomam navajātam adya gīrbhir vapraḥ pramatim icchamānaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
1. Kha-bha-me-va-mu-bha-yā; 2. Ta-rā-yo; 3. Kha-bha-varṣa-kā; 4. Kha-bha-yud-dhaiḥ.

O Indra and Agni, slayers of Vṛtra, may you both take pleasure today in this pure, newly born, and formidable hymn of praise. For I invoke you both, who are easy to call upon; as such, you are most capable of bestowing strength instantly upon the one who desires it. O Indra and Agni, O slayers of Vṛtra—that is, destroyers of enemies—take pleasure (juṣethām) now (nu), at this very time (adya), in our hymn of praise (stomam), which is pure (śucim), faultless, and newly born (navajātam)—that is, produced just now. Indeed (hi), since you both (ubhā) are easy to invoke (suhavā), I call upon you repeatedly (johavīmi). Therefore, come and accept it. Furthermore, O you two such as these (tā), become the most generous givers (dheṣṭhā) of food (vājam)—whether as nourishment or strength—at once (sadyaḥ) to the sacrificer who desires it (uśate).

For you two have become winners of prizes, powerful through might, growing together, increasing by your strength; ruling over abundant wealth and fodder, bestow upon us the nourishment of enduring and bold food. O Indra and Agni, you two—such as you are, worthy of being honored by all, possessing power (*śavas*), indeed you have become those who devour enemies like their own strength. Being what? You who have grown together, increasing by your might; likewise, you who rule over vast wealth and abundant fodder. Such as you are, provide us with the nourishment of enduring and bold food—that is, of food which crushes the enemies. (The genitive case is used here in the sense of the dative, according to the rule that "the action itself may be taken as the recipient. Bestow such nourishing food upon us; grant it to us.

When the wise, seeking favor with their prayers, approach the assembly for the sake of the prize; like horses reaching the goal, those men who invoke Indra and Agni repeatedly—3. When the wise (*viprāḥ*), possessing strength (*vājinaḥ*) and offering oblations, desiring the supreme wisdom—the thought of Indra and Agni’s grace—for themselves, go toward the assembly (*vidatham*). "Assembly" (*vidatha*) is so called because they know it as the place of sacrifice where the gods are to be worshipped; they approach that [assembly] with prayers (*dhībhiḥ*), that is, with ritual acts or insights. The particle *u* is a filler. Those leaders of rites, like horses reaching the goal—that is, just as swift horses traverse the field of battle—they reach the sacrificial acts dedicated to Indra and Agni, and they call upon Indra and Agni again and again.
1. [The reading] *kha-bha-sukhena* [is found]; *gha-suṣṭhā*; *śa-suṣṭhumā*. 2.
[The reading] *jha-na-bha-śa-tadvat tadācarantau*; *śara-tatra tadācarantau*.
3. *gha-yojayataḥ*; *jha-ta-na-śa-svayojayataḥ*.
They obtain [the fruit] on the battle-ground of *kha-ta*; they obtain it on the battle-ground of *jha-na-bha*; they obtain it on the battle-ground of *śa*.
On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), "With songs" (*gīrbhiḥ*) is the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the oblation to Indra and Agni.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Indra and Agni, come with your protection; the sage, desiring your favor, [praises you] with songs" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.6).
The invitatory and offering verses for the cooked oblation dedicated to Indra and Agni are those of the *puroḍāśa* itself;
the *sūtra*, however, has already been cited.

The inspired sage, seeking wisdom with his hymns, implores Indra and Agni—the slayers of Vṛtra, wielders of the fair thunderbolt—for glorious wealth that grants precedence. With new protections, deliver us from our enemies.

The inspired singer, desiring wisdom, prays for glorious wealth that brings precedence. O Indra and Agni, slayers of Vṛtra, wielders of the fair thunderbolt, further us with new protections against those who hate us. 4.

Seeking your favor and benevolent mind, O Indra and Agni, the wise and inspired Vasiṣṭha praises you both with hymns of praise, aiming for wealth that is glorious, preeminent, and worthy of being honored from the very beginning. O slayers of Vṛtra, O Indra and Agni, wielders of the beautiful thunderbolt, further us with new, most excellent, and desirable riches. May you protect us!
When two great ones, contending and vying with each other, clash in their bodies for the sake of heroes;
then the godless man is struck down by the god-seeking people at the assembly, like a thread spun out by those who press the Soma.

When two great ones, clashing and contending, striving with radiant bodies in the battle for heroes, come together—then let the godless man be struck down by the god-seeking people who press the Soma and weave the thread of sacrifice. 5.

O you two great ones, O mighty ones, *v-mithatī*—either "crushing each other" or, since *methi* means the act of reviling, "reviling each other"—*v-spardhamāne*, "vying," competing with one another, *v-tanūrūcā*, "shining upon your bodies," *v-hatam*, "strike" or "harm. Likewise, *v-somasutā*, "you two who press the Soma," together with the *v-jana*, the assembly of sacrificers who press the Soma, *hiṃsatam*, "harm" the person who does not press the Soma. || 5 ||
Come hither, O Indra and Agni, to this very pressing of Soma for our goodwill;
for never indeed have we been encompassed by those who seek to harm us, but rather protected by you both with constant strengths.

To this well-pressed Soma, O Indra and Agni, come hither for our sake, for the sake of goodwill! For indeed, even now, for the sake of warding off those who seek to harm us, may we be encompassed by you both with ever-increasing strengths. 6.
O Indra and Agni, come well and graciously to this very Soma-pressing of ours for the sake of a benevolent disposition;
moreover, do not think of others at all, setting us aside—
regard only us always.
Since this is so, therefore I turn you two toward me with many, manifold, and excellent *vāja*s—foods—or indeed with various [powers].
Thus kindled today by this homage, may I address Mitra, Varuṇa, and Indra:
whatever offense we have committed against them, forgive that; may they loosen those bonds from us from the very beginning.
1. [The suffixes] *gha*, *jha*, *na*, *hi*, *saṃti*, and *au*; *ta*, *hi*, *saṃti*. [Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.6. Sūtra 94]. Fifth Book: 485.

*saḥ* | *agne* | *enā* | *namasā* | *samidhaḥ* | *accha* | *mitram* | *varuṇam* | *indram* | *voca* | *yat* | *sīm* | *āgaḥ* | *cukṛma* | *tat* | *su* | *mṛḷa* | *tat* | *aryamā* | *aditiḥ* | *śiśrayantu* ||7|| O Agni, with this homage, speak toward Mitra, Varuṇa, and Indra regarding the fuel-logs. Whatever sin we have committed, forgive that well; may Aryaman and Aditi cause that to be set aside. ||7||
O Agni, you, being kindled by this our homage and by this our oblation, being well-enkindled, speak to and address Mitra, Varuṇa, and Indra:
"This one of ours is to be protected"— declare this so that we may [be freed from] whatever offense or transgression we have committed.
*Sīm* is a word signifying the act of encompassing.

We have encompassed—that is, we have committed—this sin on all sides through speech, mind, and body; therefore, be gracious toward us and protect us well from that offense. May Aryaman, Aditi, Mitra, and Aryaman [the third] sever that offense from us.
May we, offering these foremost prayers together with the two youths, attain swift gains.
May Indra, Viṣṇu, and the Maruts not withhold wealth from us. Do you all protect us evermore with blessings.
These [are] for you two, O Agni, as we, aspiring, [perform] our sacrifices; together with you two, may we attain strengths. May Indra and Viṣṇu not [forsake] us.

O leaders, O Indra and Agni, do not deliver us to a state of wretchedness, nor to reproach; do not hand us over to the censurer. (3) O leaders, O Indra and Agni, do not deliver (*roradhat*) us to a state of wretchedness (*pāpatvāya*), that is, to a condition of degradation. Likewise, do not deliver us to reproach (*abhiśastaye*), that is, to the calumny inflicted by enemies. And likewise, do not deliver us to the censurer (*nide*), that is, do not place us under the power of a reviler. On the twenty-fourth day, at the morning pressing, this triplet beginning with "In Indra and Agni" (*indre agnā*) is used by the Acchāvāka priest; it is known as the *ṣaḍahastvipriya*. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "In Indra and Agni, the great homage... I invoke them as here... (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 7.2).

To Indra and Agni we offer great homage; with prayer and songs of praise, seeking aid, we approach them. ||4|| To Indra and Agni, homage, great; with well-fashioned hymns we come; with devotion and voices, seeking help. ||4||

[Maṇḍala 7, Anuvāka 6, Sūkta 95] Fifth Aṣṭaka, 487. O Indra and Agni, let not the violence (*dhūrti*) of any hostile man (*aruruṣaḥ*), of any malicious mortal (*martyasya*), reach us (*naḥ*). O Indra and Agni, grant us protection (*śarma*). O Indra and Agni, let the violence (*dhūrti*)—the injury—of any hostile man (*aruruṣaḥ*), of any malicious mortal (*martyasya*), never (*mā*) reach (*praṇak*) us (*naḥ*). O Indra and Agni, bestow (*yuñchatam*) protection (*śarma*) and happiness (*sukha*) upon us.

O Indra and Agni, may we obtain that wealth which, consisting of cattle, gold, and horses, we beg of you from others who possess such cattle. O Indra and Agni, through your grace, may we win and enjoy that wealth. O Indra and Agni, that wealth which is *gomat* (abounding in cattle), *hiraṇyavat* (endowed with gold), and *aśvavat* (accompanied by horses)—that wealth which we beg (*īmahe*) of you both, may we (*vanemahi*) win it through your favor. 9.

On the twenty-fourth day, at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the *ārambhaṇīyā* hymn "When Soma is pressed, O men" (*yatsoma ā sute*) is to be recited by the Acchāvāka in his *śastra*; and on the second and subsequent days of the multi-day soma-sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*), it is likewise to be recited at the morning pressing. As it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having recited the *ārambhaṇīyās*, [beginning with] 'When Soma is pressed, O men' (*yatsoma ā sute naraḥ*)," (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.2).

When the men, desiring to perform service, have called upon Indra and Agni while the Soma is being pressed—[the two] who possess excellent horses and are worthy of worship—then [come to us]. When the Soma is pressed, when it has been poured out for the sake of wealth, the men—the leaders of rites, the officiating priests—desiring to serve and possessing excellent horses, call upon Indra and Agni. When they thus invoke you, the ellipsis is: "then come hither."

By means of hymns, those two who are the greatest slayers of Vṛtra, who, being exhilarated by the song, seek to win [us] through their splendor—[those two] Indra and Agni, the greatest slayers of Vṛtras (obstructors), who, rejoicing and gladdened by the hymns and by the song, are sought after and served with praise; they who are sought after and served with the splendors of the *āghāra* offerings and other hymns—come to us! (This is the ellipsis). **Note:** *Vṛtra* refers to obstructors or enemies. *Mandānā* means rejoicing or being exhilarated. *Ākteḥ* refers to the splendors of the *āghāra* libations. The grammatical irregularity (*vyatyayena*) involves using a reflexive pronoun (*kartṛpratyaya*) in the sense of the object (*karman*). The final phrase "come to us" is supplied to complete the sense.

Slay that mortal of evil speech, the wicked-minded one, the demoniac; slay the consumer with your weapon, slay the surging one with your weapon. (12) O Indra and Agni, you two—slay that mortal enemy who is of evil speech (one who utters curses), who is wicked-minded (difficult to understand), who is demoniac (possessing great power), and who is a consumer (one who devours us by force). Slay him with your *hanman*—that is, with a weapon that is a means of striking. He confirms this very point by means of a simile: "the surging one" (*udadhim*). This is an elliptical comparison; it means "like a water-jar" (*udadhānam*). Just as a jar is broken without effort, so too do you two strike the enemy with your weapon without any exertion. (18)

The sixth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "pra kṣodasā," is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and has Sarasvatī as its deity. However, the third verse has Sarasvant as its deity.
This is indicated in the Anukramaṇī: "Pra kṣodasā—six verses; it belongs to Sarasvatī, but the third is for Sarasvant."
The Sūkta has been traversed:
1. *kha-ta3-na-śa-prayacchat*; 2. *kha-ma-tāvitta tāveva*; *gha-he indrāgnī tāvittī yuvām*.

The application (*viniyoga*) is as follows: in the *prauga-śastra* during the first *chandoma*, [the rule] states, "In the *prauga*, [one recites] 'pra kṣodasā dhāyasā śaṃsa eṣa' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.9).
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Sarasvatī, 'pra kṣodasā' is the *yājyā* for the omentum (*vapā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With a swelling, nourishing stream, this daughter of Pāvīru, of variegated life-span, has come forth" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
With her surging, nourishing flood, this Sarasvatī, the supporter of the Ārya, flows like a fortress;
pushing forward like a chariot, the river by her greatness surpasses all other waters.

With her swelling flood and nourishing stream, this Sarasvatī has become the supporter of the Ārya, a fortress. Like a chariot on its way, she flows onward; by her greatness, the river surpasses all other waters. 1.
This Sarasvatī is like a river;
this visible form of a river is Sarasvatī, who is made of iron (āyasī), like a fortress (pūḥ). [She is] the support (dharuṇam);
there is a change of gender [in the word].

6. *Dharuṇā*: supporting; 7. *dhāyasā*: by means of that which sustains; 8. *kṣodasā*: by means of water; 9. *pra*: forward; 10. *sasre*: she flows swiftly, she moves quickly; 11. *sindhuḥ*: the river, characterized by its flowing nature; 12. *anyāḥ*: other; 13. *viśvāḥ*: all; 14. *apaḥ*: the waters; 15. *āpagāḥ*: the rivers; 16. *mahinā*: by her greatness; 17. *prabābadhānā*: violently pressing against or obstructing; 18. *rathyeva prataulīva*: like a broad chariot-track, being wide, she *yāti*: she goes, she moves. Or alternatively: *Note: The provided Sanskrit fragments appear to be from a commentary on a Vedic verse (likely Ṛgveda 10.75.1–2). The translation reflects the technical meanings of these grammatical and exegetical terms.*
The meaning is that, just as a charioteer on a road crushes trees and other obstacles with his chariot, so too does he go along, crushing everything by means of his own speed.
In the sacrifice of the Sarasvatī animal itself, "ekā cetat" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "ekā cetsarasvatī nadīnām uta syā naḥ sarasvatī juṣāṇā" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
If Sarasvatī alone among rivers is pure, flowing from the mountains to the ocean,
she who perceives the wealth of the vast world has milked out clarified butter and milk for the sake of Nahuṣa.

Sarasvatī alone has taken notice—she who is pure among rivers, flowing from the mountains to the ocean. Perceiving the wealth of the vast world, she has yielded for the sake of Nahuṣa both clarified butter and milk.
A king named Nahuṣa, intending to perform a sacrifice lasting a thousand years according to the seasonal cycle, requested the river Sarasvatī.
She granted him milk and clarified butter sufficient for the duration of those thousand years.
This is the meaning set forth here.
1 Among other rivers, 2 the pure and purified 3 from the mountains, 4 hither 5 as far as the ocean—that is, reaching to the very limits of the sea—6 the 7 sole 8 river Sarasvatī 9 took notice;
she understood the prayer of Nahuṣa.

Likewise, 10 making known and bestowing 11 the abundant 12 riches 13 of the world—that is, of the multitude of living beings—for King Nahuṣa, 14 she 15 milked forth 16 both clarified butter and milk, sufficient for a thousand years, 17 like a milch-cow giving her yield.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Sarasvatī, "sa vāvṛdhe" is the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "sa vāvṛdhe naryo yoṣaṇāsu yasya vrataṃ paśavo yanti sarve" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).

He has grown strong among the maidens—the manly one, the bull, the youngling among those worthy of sacrifice. He bestows vigor upon the liberal patrons; let him cleanse his body for the sake of winning booty.

He has grown strong among the women, he who is manly; the bull, the youngling, among those worthy of sacrifice. He bestows vigor upon the liberal patrons; let him groom his body for the winning of booty.
1. In manuscript *jha* and *ta*, the phrase "of Sarasvatī" is absent. 2. In manuscripts *kha* and *bha*, it reads "by a thousand-year cycle.
Vāyu situated in the middle is Sarasvatī.

He who is beneficial to men (*nṛ*), the bull (*vṛṣā*) capable of procreation, the infant (*śiśu*) appearing in a state of non-existence at the time of his manifestation, the showerer (*vṛṣabha*)—such as he, Sarasvatī, has grown and continues to grow amidst the *yoṣaṇās*, the sacrificial waters (*yoṣaṇāsu yajñiyāsu apsu*) which are like wives to him and occupy the intermediate space. Such a Sarasvatī bestows upon the liberal patrons (*maghavadbhyaḥ*), the sacrificers possessing oblations, a powerful son (*vājinaṃ putraṃ*).

Likewise, for the sake of gain (*sātaye*), he "unfolds" (*tanvam*)— that is, he cleanses and prepares— their bodies (*teṣām śarīram*) for the purpose of profit. Although this is a praise of Sarasvatī, nevertheless, because that praise is for the purpose of pleasing Sarasvatī, its application (*viniyoga*) in the *chandomika* *sārasvata* *tūca* is not contradicted.
On the eighth day of the *daśarātra*, in the *prauga* [śastra], the seventh triplet is dedicated to Sarasvatī, beginning with "uta syā naḥ.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The *prauga* begins with 'uta syā naḥ sarasvatī juṣāṇā'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.10).
In the animal sacrifice to Sarasvatī, "uta syā naḥ" serves as the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "May Sarasvatī be pleased with us; lead us to greater prosperity through the [streams of] Sarasvatī" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).

And may that Sarasvatī, being well-pleased, listen graciously to us at this sacrifice—the auspicious one, who is approached by the gods who bow with knees firmly planted, and who, joined with wealth, is even superior to her friends. And may that Sarasvatī, being well-pleased (*juṣāṇā*), the auspicious (*subhagā*) one possessing beautiful wealth (*subhaga*), listen (*upa śravat*) to us (*naḥ*) at this (*asmin*) sacrifice (*yajñe*). May she hear our hymns of praise. Of what nature is she? She is approached (*iyānā*) by the gods (*namasyaiḥ*) who bow with knees firmly planted (*mitadrubhiḥ*). [The particle] *uta* has the sense of "and. She is accompanied by wealth (*rāyā*) that is ever-present (*yujā*), and she is superior (*uttarā*) to her friends (*sakhibhyaḥ*). Such a goddess, may she listen to our hymns—this is the syntactical connection. In the *Pavitreṣṭi*, "imā juhvānāḥ" is the *yājyā* for the oblation to Sarasvatī. It is also stated in the Sūtra: "imā juhvānāḥ... vadhikāṇṇe akāriṣam" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.12).

O Sarasvatī, accepting these oblations offered with our salutations, graciously accept our hymn of praise. Abiding in your most beloved protection, may we take refuge in you, as one seeks shelter under a tree. O Sarasvatī, we, offering these our oblations (*imā juhvānā*) to you with salutations (*namaḥbhiḥ*), [may we receive wealth] from you (*yuṣmat*). Accept (*juṣasva*) our hymn of praise (*stomam prati*). And we, being established in your most beloved (*priyatame*) protection (*śarman*), may we take refuge (*upa stheyāma*) in you, like a tree that provides shelter (*śaraṇaṃ na vṛkṣam*).

O auspicious Sarasvatī, these two doors of yours have been opened for Vasiṣṭha. O beautiful one, increase [our strength]; grant riches to the one who praises you. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. (6) 1. *yoṣaṇāsu* is not present in manuscript *ta*. 2. Manuscripts *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *na* do not contain *saḥ*. 3. Manuscript *jha* reads *sārasvataṃ*; manuscripts *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *dā* read *sārasvataṃ*. 4. Manuscript *tha* reads *namaskārye*. 5. Manuscript *jha* reads *pariveṣṭyāṃ*; manuscripts *ta*, *na* read *pariveṣṭyāṃ*. 6. Manuscripts *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *bha* read *tu padadviṣayeḥ*.

This one—*ūm*—to you, O Sarasvatī, Vasiṣṭha has opened wide the two doors of *ṛta*, O blessed one. Prosper, O radiant one; grant riches to the one who praises you. And may you all protect us always with blessings. 6.
O Subhage, O Sarasvatī of beautiful wealth, this Vasiṣṭha opens wide for you the eastern and western doors belonging to Ṛta, the sacrifice.
*U* is a filler.
O Śubhre, O goddess of auspicious color, grow, increase!
Thus, to Vasiṣṭha who praises you and performs the hymn of praise, grant and bestow strengths— that is, food—
and other things to be eaten.
The seventh hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "bṛhad u gāyiṣe," is the seerly composition (*ārṣam*) of Vasiṣṭha.
The first [verse] is a Bṛhatī, the second a Satobṛhatī, the third a Prastārapaṅkti, and the remaining three are Gāyatrīs.
The first triplet has Sarasvatī as its deity, and the other [triplets] also have Sarasvatī as their deity.
And thus it has been introduced: "The *bṛhat* is a *pragātha*, a *prastārapaṅkti*, and three *gāyatrīs* following [the verse] 'sarasvatī te'.
On the fifth day, the first *pragātha* in the *prauga-śastra* belongs to Sarasvatī.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'Bṛhadu gāyiṣe' is the *bārhatam praugam*; some [place it] at the *pragātha*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.12).
Sing forth a lofty word for the divine Sarasvatī, the foremost among rivers;
O Vasiṣṭha, honor her with well-fashioned hymns and songs of praise.
Great is the word you shall sing, "Ūm! Exalt Sarasvatī, the most divine among rivers, with well-fashioned hymns and praises, O Vasiṣṭha, and [exalt] both Heaven and Earth. 1.
Having thus addressed himself, he impels himself toward the praise of Sarasvatī:
"O Vasiṣṭha, you sing—that is, you chant—a great, indeed vast, hymn of praise. For what purpose?"
"Among rivers, [to] the Asuryā":
this is a substitution for the dative singular of the word *asura*.
[It means] "to Sarasvatī, who is powerful (*balavatī*), in the form of a river (*nadīrūpā*), [and] an Asurī."
The meaning is: "for the sake of pleasing her.

Likewise, [praise] Sarasvatī herself—who dwells in the two worlds, heaven and earth, residing predominantly in heaven in the form of a deity—with well-fashioned hymns (*suvṛktibhiḥ*), that is, with excellent praises (*stomaiḥ*) free from defects; honor her.
The sense is: always praise Sarasvatī alone, the goddess who shines forth.
When both great draughts of Soma, O radiant one, are poured upon you with majesty, be first to grant us your protection;
as one whose friend is the Marut host, impel the bounty of our patrons.

Both these [worlds], O radiant one, when they place the two draughts upon you by your greatness—be you first, our protector, with the Maruts as your friends; impel the bounty of the liberal patrons. 2.

O Śubhrā, of auspicious color, O Sarasvatī! Since by your greatness—that is, your majesty—the two kinds of food, both celestial and terrestrial (whether domestic or wild), humans who are to be nourished (*pūravaḥ*) partake of and attain, therefore, being our protectress and guardian, do you take heed of us; be aware of us. Moreover, you have the Maruts as your companions;
the Maruts are the divine hosts of the intermediate region.
O Friend, you who are such a speaker of the intermediate voice, impel—urge forward—the wealth of us, the patrons (maghavan) endowed with the riches characterized by sacrificial oblations.
May Indra and Sarasvatī, who possesses a single flood and is rich in prizes, bestow prosperity;
she is mindful when praised like Jamadagni and lauded like Vasiṣṭha.
Sing this auspicious word!

May Sarasvatī, who brings forth blessings, bestow what is good. She, the possessor of steeds, is mindful; she is praised like Jamadagni and like Vasiṣṭha, as she is extolled with the qualities of the singer. 3.
May Sarasvatī—the auspicious, the beautiful, the one worthy of worship—make for us that which is truly auspicious and indeed beautiful.
Likewise, may she whose movement is irreproachable, who possesses swift steeds, and who is rich in food, inspire us and grant us wisdom.
Or alternatively:
May he take note of my hymn;
likewise, being praised by me as by the ṛṣi Jamadagni, and as by Vasiṣṭha—
the suffix *vat* is used here in the sense of "worthy of" (*arha*).
O Vasiṣṭhāhī, be one who praises and is praised in a manner befitting the status of Vasiṣṭha.

For an animal sacrifice dedicated to Sarasvatī, there are three invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for the sacrificial cakes (*paśupuroḍāśa-havis*), to be used in sequence: "janīyanto nvagravaḥ" and so forth.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "‘janīyanto nvagravaḥ’—these three [verses] for the divine, fair-winged, great bird" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).

Desiring wives, indeed, like those without kin, desiring sons, we, the Sudārnava clan, invoke Sarasvant. Desiring wives, now, like those without kin, desiring sons, we, the Sudārnava clan, invoke Sarasvant.
Desiring offspring—
those who are called *janayaḥ* (procreators) because they give birth in their wombs—
and longing for wives, desiring sons, we, the givers of cattle, the bestowers of excellent gifts, the seekers of wealth, now invoke, praise, or call upon the god Pūṣan, who is rich in cattle.

O Sarasvatī, those waves of yours which are honey-sweet and dripping with clarified butter—with those, be our protector. 5. Those; yours; O Sarasvatī; waves; honey-sweet; dripping with clarified butter; with those; us; protector; be. 5.

O Sarasvatī, may your waters—your waves, those masses of water belonging to you—be rich in honey, full of flavor, and distilling clarified butter; they become the showers of ghee, that is, of rainwater. Through these three [streams], O Lord, be our purifier and our protector.
In the Anvārambhaṇīyā sacrifice, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the offering is "pīpivāṃsam.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "pīpivāṃsaṃ sarasvato divyaṃ suparṇaṃ vāyasaṃ bṛhantam" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.8).

May we enjoy the swelling breast of Sarasvatī, which is visible to all; may we obtain offspring and nourishment. (6) May we enjoy the swelling breast of Sarasvatī, which is visible to all; may we obtain offspring and nourishment. (6)
May we consume—that is, share and obtain—the swelling, overflowing breast of the divine Sarasvatī, which resounds like a cloud that is the common support for suckling calves.
This is the milk of her who is visible to all; she becomes visible, being beheld by everyone.
"That breast" means the cloud.
Likewise, by the grace of Sarasvatī, may we enjoy our progeny in the form of sons and others, as well as wealth and myself.

The eighth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “yajñe divaḥ,” is the seerly composition of Vasiṣṭha and is in the Triṣṭubh meter. The first verse is addressed to Indra; in the third and ninth verses, Indra and Bṛhaspati are the deities; in the tenth, Indra and Bṛhaspati; and for the remaining verses, Bṛhaspati alone is the deity. Thus it has been declared: “In the [hymn] beginning with ‘yajñe,’ from the tenth verse onward the deities are Bārhaspatya; the others are Aindra; and the third and ninth are addressed to Indra and Bṛhaspati.”

In the *ābhiplavika* sacrifices, at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), the *stomapṛṣṭha* hymns for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest consist of this and the following hymn for the purpose of insertion (*āvāpa*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*yajñe divaḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.9).

In the sacrifice, at the gathering-place of heaven and earth, where the god-seeking men rejoice for Indra, where all the libations are pressed for him who bestows wealth—therein lies the first vital strength.
1. *jña* becomes *bhavati*; 2. [the forms] *kha*, *na*, *bha*, *puroḍāśa*, and *haviṣām*;
3. *kṣa*, *śa*, *sarasvadeva*; *ghadeva*.

4. O Knower, may we enjoy [the fruits of] it; may we attain it. Under whose ordinance all cattle go, under whose ordinance the waters abide—whose ordinance nourishment enters—we shall invoke Sarasvatī for our protection.

At the sacrifice, at the seat of heaven and earth, where the men who seek the gods rejoice; where for Indra all libations are well-pressed, and the first choice-worthy draughts flow for exhilaration and for rapture. (Ṛgveda Khila 15.1)

In which sacrifice the leaders, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), desiring the gods (*devayavaḥ*), rejoice; in which the Soma juices to be pressed for Indra are extracted for Indra’s sake; in that sacrifice, which belongs to the earth and serves as the seat for men—the leaders—let him come first, before all the gods, from the heavenly world (*divaḥ*). For what purpose?
For the sake of exhilaration (*madāya*).
The meaning is "to drink the Soma.
Likewise, "the birds" refers to his horses; let them go, that is, let them come.

We choose for ourselves the divine aids; may Bṛhaspati come to our great [help], O friends! So that we may be sinless before the bounteous one, he who is our giver from afar like a father. We choose for ourselves the divine aids; may Bṛhaspati come to our great [help], O friends! So that we may be sinless before the bounteous one, he who is our giver from afar like a father.

We, his friends— those who share the same station, the singers— choose for ourselves, we appropriate, and pray for divine protections, those things pertaining to the gods. Bṛhaspati, the god who is the protector of the great, accepts our oblation for the sake of that magnificence.
He takes [it] for the uncooked [grain]. There is the elision of the *ta* suffix according to the rule "lopasta ātmanepadeṣu.

Just as Bṛhaspati, having brought grains from afar—from a distant place—becomes a giver to us, like a father to his sons; to that Bṛhaspati, the showerer (*mīḍhvuṣe*), may we be sinless, faultless, and without offense. O friends, the ellipsis is: "In such a way, you too should attend upon him."

I praise with reverence and oblations that most excellent and most gracious Brahmaṇaspati; may the great divine hymn attend upon Indra, who is the king of the sacred word (brahman) created by the gods. tam | ūm iti | jyeṣṭham | namasā | havirbhiḥ | suśevam | brahmaṇaḥ | patim | gṛṇīṣe | indram | ślokaḥ | mahi | daivyaḥ | siṣaktu | yaḥ | brahmaṇaḥ | devakṛtasya | rājā || 3 ||

I praise—that is, I extol—with reverence and with oblations such as cooked rice and sacrificial cakes, that very God known as Brahmaṇaspati, the protector of the sacred mantra, who is the eldest, most excellent, most gracious, and most blissful. Furthermore, may our divine hymn of praise, worthy of the gods, attend upon the great Indra.
"Of the non-Vedic prayer or of the mantra not composed by the gods—that which is made by the gods who are the praisers—Indra is the king, the lord, [of that] as well as of Brahmaṇaspati.
The connection is: "that Indra, that Brahmaṇaspati."

May he, Bṛhaspati, the most beloved and possessor of all boons, sit upon our place of origin. May he grant that desire for wealth consisting of heroic sons; may he carry us across the distress, keeping us uninjured and ever-prosperous. 4. May he, Bṛhaspati, the most beloved and possessor of all boons, who exists [as such], sit upon our place of origin. May he grant that desire for wealth consisting of heroic sons; may he carry us across the distress, keeping us uninjured and ever-prosperous. 4.
1. [In the versions] kha, gha, and śa, the word "nāṛtṛṇā" does not exist.
2. [In the version] śa, it is "abhijāmīmahe.

May Bṛhaspati, the most beloved (*preṣṭhaḥ*) and dearest (*priyatamaḥ*) dweller (*vasaḥ*), sit down (*ā sadatu*)—that is, having arrived, may he take his seat—at our *yoni*, the place characterized by the sacrificial altar (*vedi*).

Bṛhaspati, who is possessed of all boons (*viśvavāra*)—that is, he who is worthy of praise by all—and moreover, he who possesses wealth, fame, and excellent heroic power (*suvīrya*), let him grant us that desire which we have; let him bestow upon us that which is longed for. This is the meaning.
Likewise, having rendered us—though beset by calamities—unharmed and unassailed, he carries us across the mountains beyond our enemies.
The deathless ones born of old have established for us this hymn, acceptable to the Immortal;
we shall invoke Bṛhaspati, the pure-sounding, the worshipful one among the dwellings of prosperity, according to his own color.
To him—our hymn, acceptable to the Immortal—these immortals, born of old, have offered. We shall invoke Bṛhaspati, the pure-thundering, the holy one of prosperities, the peerless. 5.

That which is renowned everywhere as fit to be enjoyed, for the sake of *amṛta*—immortality and life—pleasing and sufficient, the *arka*, the food that is the means of worship: this the ancient-born ones, these immortal, deathless gods, by the command of Bṛhaspati, have bestowed (*ā dhāsuḥ*) upon us.
And we [offer] the pure-sounding one, the pure hymn of praise, for the *pastyas*. *Pastya* is a name for the house.
By that [name], those possessing it are indicated.

We should invoke—or praise—the sacrificer among householders, who is worthy of sacrifice, whose color is unchanging, who is unassailable by anyone, and who is Bṛhaspati, the protector of the great ones, the god.
The ruddy horses, carrying him together, bear Bṛhaspati;
they who dwell together, whose abode is dark-blue, clothe themselves in a form as bright as the sky.
The tawny, ruddy horses, carrying him together, bear Bṛhaspati; they, clothed in ruddy splendor, carry him whose dwelling is like the dark-blue cloud, and whose form is like the sky.
May the powerful, auspicious, and comfort-bestowing horses— whether capable or ruddy, shining, and carrying together as a team— carry that Bṛhaspati;
he whose strength is united with that of Bṛhaspati,
like the dark-blue [cloud].
The construction is as follows: he whose abode (*nilaya*)— that is, his dwelling (*nivāsa*)— is blue,
and whose shared place (*sadhastha*), that is, his common location (*sahasthāna*),
is likewise [blue], is Bṛhaspati.
What kind of horses?
Those wearing—that is, possessing—forms that are ruddy and shining like the sky or like the sun.
For he is pure, the hundred-winged; he is the radiant one with a golden axe, the vigorous bull.
Bṛhaspati is the sublime one who dwells within us, most skilled at providing nourishment for his many friends.

For he is pure, the hundred-leaved; he is radiant, with a golden axe, impetuous, the winner of light—Bṛhaspati. He is easy of access, sublime, and most effective in providing nourishment for his many friends. 7.
He indeed is Bṛhaspati, the pure, the cleansed, the hundred-leaved one who possesses many kinds of vehicles;
he alone is Śundhyu, the purifier of all, the wielder of the golden axe—
‘vāśī’ being a name for speech.
His speech is pleasant and delightful;
or else,
according to the Vedic citation, "With axes, fashion us [the wood]," (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.101.10), his weapon is an axe.
He whose weapons are made of gold;
he who is swift, a goer, or one to be sought after; the showerer of rain, or rather, the bestower of the waters that have the nature of flowing.
1. We shall praise with *kha-stūyema*; we shall praise with *jha-ta³-śa¹-stuvema*; we shall sound with *śara-cusuyema*. 2.

The blue dwelling is *kha-jha-na-bha-nīlaṃ nyalyo nivāsaḥ*; the blue dwelling is *gha-nīlaṃ nivāsaḥ*; the blue dwelling is *jha-ta¹-²-⁴-nīlanlayo nivāsaḥ*; the blue dwelling-like is *śa-nīlāntalyo nivāsavat*. 3.
Speech is exceedingly delightful when accompanied by *kha-jha-ta-na-bha-śa*.

He is Bṛhaspati himself, easy of access, providing a good dwelling, lofty, and beautiful to behold. Such a god, for his friends—the singers—shall I prepare an abundant draught; he becomes the most effective agent and the greatest giver.

The two goddesses, Rodasī, the parents of the god, have magnified Bṛhaspati by their greatness; O friends, provide skillful means for the one worthy of skill, making the path easy to traverse for him who acts with resolve.

The two goddesses, Heaven and Earth, the parents of the god, have magnified Bṛhaspati by their greatness. O friends, provide him with what is effective for his worthy task. For the sake of prayer, may he make the paths easy to cross and well-fording.

The two goddesses, Rodasī (Heaven and Earth), endowed with qualities such as generosity, who are the mothers (*janitrī*) of the god Bṛhaspati, have caused Bṛhaspati—possessed of a great roar (*mahirava*)—to grow; they have made him increase. O friends (*sakhāyaḥ*), you too [should act] for Dakṣāyya, who is to be strengthened;
here the dative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
Strengthen that Bṛhaspati; increase him with skill.
And may that Bṛhaspati, for the sake of the expansive, augmented, and abundant command, most effectively create waters that are "sutaraṇāni"—easy to cross—and "sugādhā"—easy to plunge into.
This well-fashioned hymn has been made for you both, O Brahmaṇaspati and Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Favour our prayers; protect our wise thoughts; destroy the hostilities of the rival who seeks to overcome us.

This well-fashioned hymn, O Brahmaṇaspati, has been made for you; a prayer has been fashioned for Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt. Protect our prayers, further our thoughts, and destroy the hostilities of the noble enemy who seeks to harm us. 9.
O Brahmaṇaspati, for you, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and for Indra, the possessor of the thunderbolt— to you both (the dative case is used here in the sense of "for the sake of")—
this well-composed hymn (*suvṛkti*), consisting of sacred mantras, has been performed; it has been composed by me.
O you two, protect our thoughts— that is, our ritual acts—
and likewise swallow up, that is, hear, our *purandhīs*, our manifold prayers of praise.
O noble ones, you who go against the enemies, destroy—bring to exhaustion—the hostilities, that is, the enemy armies, of us who are your devotees.
In the third *savana* of the *ukthya* sacrifice, the *ājya-śastra* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is "O Bṛhaspati, you two...
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "The *yājyā* is 'O Bṛhaspati, you two and Indra, [bestow] wealth... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.1).
In the Vājapeya, this same verse serves as the *paridhānīyā* for the additional *uktha*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The concluding verse is 'O Bṛhaspati and you, O Indra, [bestow] wealth' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.9)."
O Bṛhaspati and Indra, you two are the lords of the treasures of heaven and of the earth;
bestow wealth upon the singer who praises you, and protect us always with your blessings.

O Bṛhaspati and you, Indra, you two are the lords of celestial wealth and also of that which is terrestrial. Bestow riches upon the singer who praises you. May you always protect us with blessings. 10.
O Bṛhaspati and you, O Indra— both of you are the lords of divine wealth, that is, of the riches existing in heaven;
therefore, for the sake of the singer who performs praise—
this word "kīri" being a name for a praiser.
Bestow wealth and riches upon the singer; "cit" is a filler particle;
[you have] approached [him].
1. In manuscripts *kha*, *jha*, and *bha*, the reading is *sutarā sutarāṇi*; in *gha* there is no *asutarā sutaraṇāni*; in *na* it is *na-sutarāṇi*. 2.
In *kha*, *ta*, *jha*, and *śa* the reading is *upalakṣyata*; in *gha* it is *upalayata*; in *na* and *bha* it is *upalakṣaṇaṃ yata*.

The ninth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "O Adhvaryus," is the seerly composition (*ārṣa*) of Vasiṣṭha; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and addressed to Indra, while the seventh verse is addressed to Indra and Bṛhaspati.
And thus it has been enumerated: “The Adhvaryus [recite] the seven-verse hymn, with the last verse dedicated to the deity.
The application (viniyoga) is stated together with the preceding hymn.

O Adhvaryus, offer the red, milked stalk to the bull of the peoples. From the cow, Indra—the more perceptive one—goes down to the drinking-place; every day he goes seeking the pressed Soma. O Adhvaryus! The red, milked stalk! Offer it! To the bull of the peoples! From the cow, the more perceptive one! Down to the drinking-place! Indra! Every day! He goes! Seeking the pressed Soma! 1.
O Adhvaryus, leaders of the sacrifice, you priests—offer, offer the bright, shining, pressed stalk of Soma to Indra, the bull, the most excellent among the peoples and men!

Having approached the drinking-place, Indra—who is more learned than even the wild ox (*go*), being exceedingly wise—desiring and seeking the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma, goes indeed at all times, that is, every single day.
Therefore, the syntactical connection is: "Offer the Soma to that Indra."

For you have held as dear from of old that lovely food; day by day you desire its drinking. Rejoicing with heart and with mind, O Indra, desiring it, drink the Soma juices that have been set forth. yat | dadhiṣe | pradivi | cāru | annam | dive-dive | pītim | it | asya | vakṣi | uta | hṛdā | uta | manasā | juṣāṇaḥ | uśan | indra | pra-sthitān | pāhi | somān || 2 ||

O Indra, from of old—in days gone by, in former times—you have held (*dadhiṣe*) within your belly through drinking that food characterized by Soma which is lovely and beautiful; even now, day after day, you desire (*vakṣi*) the drinking of this very Soma. [This form *vakṣi* arises] from the root *vaś* (in the sense of "desire") with the suffix *sip*, after the elision of *śap* and the substitution of the *pluta* accent, resulting in this form. Moreover, O Indra, with your heart (*hṛdā*), [you desire it].
The word *uta* has the sense of *ca* (and).

For this reason, O Indra, you have filled the vast and wide mid-air with your own splendor;

Whether we face warriors who consider themselves great and challenge us directly with their arms, or men gathered in assembly who seek to overcome us— may we, through Indra’s protection, conquer those who would abandon our well-being.

When we must fight those who consider themselves great, may we overcome them face-to-face as they roar with their arms; or when, O Indra, surrounded by men, you must fight—may we, through you, win that glorious battle. 4.
O Indra, when you cause us to fight those numerous and powerful enemies who consider themselves great—

I shall proclaim the first deeds of Indra, and those recent ones which the Bounteous Lord has performed. When he overcame the godless illusions, then Soma became his own alone. I shall proclaim—the first, the most ancient—those heroic deeds performed by Indra; I declare them. Whatever wealth-inducing Indra has accomplished, both those which he did in the past and these which he performs now, ever-new ones—I shall proclaim them. As soon as he overcame and surpassed the godless, demonic illusions created by them, immediately thereafter, Soma became his alone, his exclusive possession.
The meaning is that from that time onwards, an exclusive relationship was established between Soma and Indra.

This entire universe around you, which you behold with the eye of the sun, belongs to you; O Indra, you alone are the lord of cattle. May we partake of the wealth that is offered to us by you. 6. "O Viṣṇu, increasing—that is, growing—by means of your immeasurable body which exists beyond all measure, no one attains to, nor pervades, your greatness; the meaning is that even by all people together, your majesty at the time of the three strides cannot be known. We perceive [thee] with our eyes and nothing else.

For the very same animal mentioned previously, "O Viṣṇu" (*na te viṣṇo*) is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*).

Neither being born, O Viṣṇu, nor already born, O God, has anyone reached the furthest limit of your greatness.

The sense is that for this very reason it is not known by all. He describes what that greatness is:
"The lofty," meaning beautiful to behold; "the vast," meaning great; "the *nāka*," meaning the heavenly world (*dyuloka*); "thou didst prop up," meaning thou didst support aloft.
So that it does not fall downward,

And likewise, another mantra says: "He who alone has supported the threefold earth and the sky, and all existing beings" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.154.4).

For you have become possessed of abundance and milk, dwelling in the sun, bestowing gifts upon mankind.

The meaning is that he made [the mountain] firm so that it would not move;

O Indra and Viṣṇu, for the sake of the sacrifice and the sacrificer, you two have indeed created a vast, expansive world known as heaven. What were you doing?
You were generating—that is, causing to appear once more—the Sun, the impeller of all; Uṣas, who removes darkness; and Agni, who was enveloped by the Asuras.

Those two leaders, Indra and Viṣṇu, you two slew the magical powers (*māyā*) of the Asura named Vṛśaśipra, that Dāsa who sought to destroy us, in the contests for booty, in the battles; you two destroyed them.
It is said that you two brought forth the sun and so forth.
O Indra and Viṣṇu, you shattered the ninety-nine strong fortresses of Śambara;
together you slew the hundred and thousand heroes of Varcin, the godless one.
O Indra and Viṣṇu, you shattered the ninety-nine strong fortresses of Śambara; together you struck down the hundred and thousand heroes of the irresistible Asura Varcin. 5.

The eleventh hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “nū martaḥ,” is the seer’s own composition by Vasiṣṭha; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and addressed to Viṣṇu.

Truly, no mortal who desires to gain will fail, if he should offer worship to Viṣṇu, the wide-striding;
he who, with a mind well-disposed toward protection, shall strive to win such a heroic one.
Now, the mortal who desires to win, who shall offer gifts to Viṣṇu, the wide-striding, and who shall worship with a well-directed mind—he shall strive to win such heroic power as this.
That mortal man, desiring to win—that is, wishing for wealth—quickly bestows it; he takes up wealth.
The root *day* should be understood here as having the sense of "to give" (with the prefix *ā*).
That man who would offer oblations to Viṣṇu, who is widely traversed—that is, worthy of praise by many.

And whoever, with a focused mind and through reflection and hymns of praise, should worship and honor Viṣṇu—him who is so great in extent, who is beneficial to men (*narya*)—and should serve him with prostrations and other acts of devotion for as long as this duration, that mortal shall be protected; such is the connection [of the verse].

Viṣṇu, the most powerful among the powerful, has stepped forth, for this is the name of that ancient one.

This god Viṣṇu, endowed with qualities such as generosity and the like,

Prosperity impels the self toward praise.
O Sage Vitiṣṭha, speak forth—utter—the threefold words consisting of Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, which are in the form of praise;
what kind of words? Those that possess light.
Those [vows] which have the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), luminous like light, as their foremost leader;
those words which yield honey—that is, the milk of water, the maker of rainwater—[toward] this uplifted cloud (*ūdhas*) visible in the sky.
Or else:
This [body] is like a vessel;
they milk it, as one milks a cloud that serves as the receptacle for milk, like a udder.
In the present indicative (*laṭ*) of the root *duh*, there is the elision of the *ta* suffix according to Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.41: *lopasta ātmanepadeṣu*.
The suffix *ruṭ* is used here by way of common usage (*bāhulaka*).
For it is Parjanya, being pleased by hymns of praise, who causes rain to fall through the clouds;
therefore, it is figuratively said that "they milk speech itself."
Alternatively,
"let him speak" (*vadet*) is the second person used by way of transposition;
"threefold" refers to the three types— fast, slow, and medium— or the three kinds of speech beginning with lightning, which he should utter.
Those words characterized by thundering milk this rain-bestowing cloud; they milk out its waters.

And such is Parjanya, making manifest—that is, bringing forth—the lightning-fire which dwells together with him as its calf, and making it the embryo of the plants, such as rice and others; being born—that is, having appeared—immediately and swiftly, he, the bull, the showerer, bellows—that is, he makes a loud sound.

He who causes the plants to grow, he who rules over the waters, he who is the God who lords it over all that moves—he, the threefold protector, may he grant us refuge and shelter; may he bestow upon us the threefold light for our well-being.

He who causes the plants to grow, he who [rules] over the waters, he who is the god who lords over all that moves—he, the threefold, may he grant us protection and refuge; may the threefold light, which is well-favored, be with us. 2.
Parjanya, who is the nourisher and increaser of the plants,
and who is the augmentor of the waters;
and that radiant god Parjanya who rules over the entire moving world.
The elision of *t* occurs by the rule *lopasta ātmanepadeṣu*.
The genitive case is used for the object when it is intended to be treated as a residual (*śeṣa*) factor, according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 2.3.52 (*adhīgartha...*).
Since the root is marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*), the *lasārvadhātuka* affixes are unaccented, and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.
The prohibition of the *nighāta* accent applies by the rule "yadvṛttānnityam.
May he, Parjanya, grant—that is, bestow upon us—the threefold refuge, the house consisting of the three worlds, as well as *śarma*, meaning happiness. This is the sense.
The augment *ḍa* is added after the final letter of the root *yam*.
The suffix *sip* is applied by the rule *sibbahulam*. The vowel *i* is elided by the rule *itaśca lopaḥ*.

Likewise, may he grant to us (*asme*) light and splendor (*jyotiś ca tejaś ca*) that is *trivartu*—existing preeminently throughout the three seasons. For it is heard in scripture: "There are indeed three splendors of the Sun: in the spring at dawn, in the summer at midday, and in the autumn in the afternoon" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.2.5). May such a one, who is *svabhiṣṭi*—one who is well-desired or who provides excellent aid—bestow this upon us.
The barren cow, though lowing, is pierced; he has indeed fashioned his body according to his own will.
The mother receives the milk of the father; by it the father prospers, and by it the son.
From you she becomes barren; from you she brings forth. As he desired, he fashioned his own body. The mother receives the milk of the father; by it the father prospers, and by it the son. || 3 ||
The word *tvat* ending in *t* is a synonym for "other," accented with the anudātta, and is listed among the pronouns (*sarvanāman*).
Of this Parjanya, *tvat* [the other] is the "barren cow" (*starīḥ*), a cow whose milk has ceased; just as she does not yield milk, so too he does not become manifest (*ūpaṃ na bhavati*).
The particle *u* is a filler (*pūrakaḥ*).
The second [meaning] is in the sense of the word *uśabda*. Like a cow (*dhenu*), it brings forth another form from you (*tvat*);
it causes waters to flow forth.
This Parjanya makes his own body, as he desires and according to his will, into both a covering and a cow;
moreover, from the father Heaven, the mother Earth receives the milk—the water of rain.
*Hramobhaṃḥ*.
1. *kha*-prakathaya; *na-bha*-prakasya | 2. *ta3*-ūddhatam | 3. *ta*-evam | 4. *kha-ta3-na-bha*-pravadeteti | 5. *jha-ta-na-bha*-vasate | Thus [is] the substitution of *bha*.
By that which has been accepted, having been transformed into the nature of the oblation (*havis*), the Father—the heavenly world (*dyuloka*)—increases.
By that very water, even the multitude of living beings born upon the earth prospers—
in which all worlds abide, the three heavens have been established in three ways with their forms;
the three vessels of the cask are sprinkled, and from them flows forth the abundant, roaring stream.
In which Parjanya all beings—all created things—stand;
that is to say, their existence depends upon him.
And in whom the heavens—the worlds beginning with Śubhrabhṛt—abide.
And because the waters have flowed in three ways—eastward, westward, and downward—from the Truth;
and because the three types of clouds—the eastern, the western, and the northern—which are the "upasercanās," meaning those that approach or serve, surround the vast Parjanya on all sides.
(The genitive case is used here in the sense of the object.)
They flow, they pour forth, they rain down honeyed water.

May this splendor be dear to Parjanya, the self-ruling one; may it find favor within his heart. May the rain-showers be sources of bliss for us, and may the plants, protected by the gods, bear fine fruit.

May this splendor be within the heart for Parjanya, the self-ruling lord; may he take pleasure in it. May there be life-giving rains for us, and may the plants, protected by the gods, bear good fruit. 5.
This speech, this hymn of praise, is offered to Parjanya, the self-ruling lord of heaven;
may it enter within his heart,
and may he graciously accept and enjoy this hymn.
The root *juṣ* is used in the senses of "pleasure" and "service. The augment *aṭ* is added as a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). The substitution of *il* for the suffix *śap* occurs.
May the rains, which bring about happiness, be for us through their grace;

likewise, may the plants, whose protector is the divine Parjanya, be rich in fine fruit for us. He is the seed-bestowing bull of all these eternal things; in him is the soul of all that moves and stands.
May that Truth protect me for a hundred autumns; may you always protect us with blessings. 6.

He is the seed-bestower, the bull of all eternal things; in him is the soul of everything moving and stationary. May that Truth protect me for a hundred autumns; may you always protect us with blessings. 6.
That Parjanya is the depositor (*retodhāḥ*)—the bestower and arranger—of the seed, that is, of the water which serves as the seed, for the many plants (*śaśvatīnām oṣadhīnām*).
"The bull" (*vṛṣabhaḥ*) is a simile;
just as a certain bull is the depositor of the embryos of many cows, so is he.
Therefore, in that Parjanya, the self—the body—of both the moving (jagataḥ) and the stationary (tasthuṣaḥ) exists.
May that *ṛta*, the water given by Parjanya, protect (pātu)—that is, preserve—me for a hundred autumns, for the sake of living a hundred years.
Regarding the word "mā," there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) and the shortening [of the vowel] according to the rule "ṛtyakaḥ."
The rest here is as follows:
1. Gha: three heavens; 2. Kha, Na, Bha, Śa: the Ordainer.
