O singers, sing forth a hymn of praise to the god Parjanya.
To what kind of one?
To the son of Dyaus, that is, of the intermediate space.
For it is there that Parjanya appears. To the bountiful showerer,
may that such Parjanya desire to grant us, for ourselves, fodder consisting of grass, herbs, and the like.
He who produces the embryo of plants, of cows, of horses, of mares, and of women—he is Parjanya. 2. He; the embryo; of plants; of cows; he makes; of horses; Parjanya; of women. 2.

That Parjanya who creates—the seed which is the cause of procreation—for the plants such as rice and the like, for cows, for horses, for mares, and for women; to that Parjanya—this is the connection with what follows later.

Therefore, offer into her mouth the most honey-sweet oblation; may she grant us nourishment that is well-restrained. 3. Therefore, indeed, into her mouth, offer the oblation, the most honey-sweet; may she make for us nourishment that is well-restrained. 3.
O officiating priests, offer—that is, pour—the most honeyed, most flavorful oblation into his very mouth, namely into Agni who has become the mouth of the gods;
and may that Parjanya grant us *iḷā*, food, in such a way that it is well-restrained, meaning properly gathered.
That is to say, may he give it.
The fourteenth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “saṃvatsaram,” is the ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha’s;
it is in the Triṣṭubh meter, though the first verse is in Anuṣṭubh.
Its deity is the frogs.
And thus it has been enumerated: "For a year, there are ten [verses] in praise of Parjanya; he praised the frogs; the first is an Anuṣṭubh.
This hymn is to be recited by one who desires rain.

Having lain dormant for a year, like Brahmins observing a vow, the frogs have uttered forth their voice, which has been quickened by Parjanya. *saṃvatsaram* (for a year), *śaśayānāḥ* (having lain down/slept), *brāhmaṇāḥ* (Brahmins), *vrata-cāriṇaḥ* (observers of vows), *vācam* (the voice), *parjanya-jinvitām* (quickened by Parjanya/the rain-god), *pra* (forth), *maṇḍūkāḥ* (the frogs), *avādiṣuḥ* (have spoken).

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: “Vasiṣṭha, desiring rain, praised Parjanya; the frogs rejoiced in him. Seeing them rejoicing, he praised them” (Nirukta 9.6). And: “Maṇḍūkāḥ [are so called] from *majj* (to sink), or from *mad* (to rejoice), or from *mand* (to be satisfied)—so say the grammarians—or because their abode (*oka*) is *maṇḍa*; or *maṇḍa* means intoxication. Of these, this [verse] occurs” (Nirukta 9.5). “*Vratacāriṇaḥ* refers to the *brāhmaṇas* who are performing the ritual (*vrata*) consisting of a year-long sacrificial session (*saṃvatsarasatra*).”
This is an elliptical simile (*luptopamā*).
Like such Brahmins who, for the sake of rain, lie down for a year—lying down for one year from autumn until the rains—the [Maruts] likewise lie down for a year.
They lie down for the purpose of raining.

1. *Kha-bha-gāyatraṃ*; the second [verse] is *pādanicṛt*. 2. *Kha-bha* (at the end)—*gāyatraṃ*; the second [verse] is *pādanicṛt*. These two [are for] Kumāra Āmeyopayajñasiddha or for those desiring rain. 3. *Kha-bha-jāpyam*.

When one of them repeats the speech of another, like a pupil learning from a master, all that is as a well-prospered joint among them; when they, eloquent of voice, increase [the hymn] over the waters.

O frogs, when among you one frog speaks, another frog repeats, echoes, and imitates it—just as a student learning learns the speech of a teacher who possesses power, so do you repeat it. And when you all, being of beautiful voice, float upon the waters, the rain-waters, speak out; utter your sound!
7. Then, all their joints and limbs become as if fully developed—indeed, fully developed and with no missing parts.
The word "as if" (iva) is used for emphasis.
The meaning is that frogs, having reached a state of softness during the rainy season, appear again with unimpaired limbs when the rains begin.
One is tawny, one is goat-like, one is speckled, and one of these is green;
bearing a common name, though diverse in form, they have fashioned their voices in many ways as they speak.
One bellows like a cow; one bellows like a goat. One is speckled; one is green. Bearing a common name, these diverse forms have fashioned their voices in many places as they speak.

Among these frogs, one frog has a sound like a jackal; that is, its sound (*māyu*) is like that of a jackal (*gomāyu*). Another frog has a sound like a goat; that is, its sound is like that of a goat (*aja*). One is *pṛśni*, meaning it is speckled in color.
One is another; green, meaning green-colored.

Thus, though diverse and of various forms, they bear and maintain the same single name, "frogs. Uttering sound—that is, making noise—in many places, in numerous regions, they have become manifest, that is, they appear; for the root *piś* means "to divide" or "to form parts."
From the word *pura*, the suffix *tra* is applied according to the rule beginning with "devamanuṣya" (Pāṇini 4.2.80).
Like Brahmins at the Atirātra Soma sacrifice, shouting all around like men by a full lake,
that day of the year has come for you, O frogs, which belongs to the rainy season.
Like Brahmins at the Atirātra sacrifice, they do not speak around the full vessel of Soma; that day of the year has come around, O frogs, which belongs to the rainy season. 7.
It is called *atirātra* because it proceeds having exceeded the night. In the *atirātra*, not in the *soma* [rite]—
just as in the *soma* sacrifice named *atirātra*, the Brāhmaṇas, that is, the priests, recite the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns by turn during the night, O frogs!

The second word *na* is used in the sense of "now. "Do not now" (*na saṃprati*). "Full lake" (*pūrṇa saraḥ*). "On all sides" (*abhitaḥ*) means everywhere. "Uttering" (*vadantaḥ*) means making noise at night. "On that day" (*tadahaḥ*) means on that particular day. "Be around" (*pari ṣṭha*) means be present everywhere. The meaning is: "Be present on all sides on that day which has become the rainy season (*prāvṛṣīṇam*), belonging to the rains (*prāvṛṣeṇyam*), and occurring during the monsoon (*prāvṛṣi*)."
The Soma-offering Brahmins have raised their voice, performing the sacred prayer that lasts throughout the year;
the Adhvaryu priests, sweating over the heated cauldron, emerge from their concealment like those who were previously hidden.

The Soma-offering Brahmins have raised their voices, performing the sacred prayer that lasts throughout the year. The Adhvaryu priests, heated by the cauldron and sweating, become manifest; none of them remain hidden. 8.
1. Of those [words] ending in *jha*, *ta*, *na*, and *ma*.
2. Like a jackal (*gomāyu*): *kha-jha-tara-śa-gomāyur-iva*; *gha-jha-ta-na-gomāyuḥ* [is] like a jackal.
3. *Jha*: "You, of the year."

"Sominaḥ" means those joined with Soma; "parivatsarīṇam" means that which pertains to a year, specifically the Gavām Ayana sacrifice; "brahma" refers to the collection consisting of Stotras and Śastras; "kṛṇvantaḥ" means performing;
"brāhmaṇāsaḥ" [is used here] as an elliptical simile (luptopama).
Like Brahmins, these frogs have raised their voices; they have made this sound.

Furthermore, like Adhvaryu priests performing the *gharma* rite with the *pravargya* vessel, sweating profusely, certain secret frogs—hidden in their burrows during the heat of the summer—now emerge and come forth when the rain has fallen.
The gods have indeed guarded his power; these men do not diminish his season.
When the rainy season has arrived after a year, the heated rays release their discharge for the sake of the sun-beam.

They have guarded the path beneficial to the gods; these men do not violate the season of the twelfth month. When the rainy season has arrived within the year, the heated vapors find release for the sun-beamed sky.
These leaders, these frogs, have guarded— that is, they protect— the "divine ordinance" (devahiti), the established rule made by the gods in the form of "this is the duty," at every proper time;
for this very reason, they do not violate— that is, they do not harm— the respective season of the twelve-month year, such as spring and the others.
The meaning is that through the rain-cloud’s approval, these become the causes for rain at their respective times.

When the year is complete and the rainy season has arrived, the creatures (*dharmāḥ*)—which were previously existing during the time of heat and afflicted by the scorching sun—now obtain release (*visargam*), that is, liberation from their burrows.
The jackal has given, the goat-eater has given; Pṛśni, being entreated, has given us riches. The frogs give hundreds of cows; they have extended our life by thousands.

The lowing cow has given; the bleating goat has given; the speckled one has given; the green one has given us riches. The frogs, giving hundreds of cattle at the thousandfold pressing, prolong our lives. 10.
The *gomāyu*: that frog whose cry (*māyu*) is like that of a cow (*go*); may he grant us (*naḥ*) riches (*vasūni*).
And may the *ajamāyu* grant them;
and may the green-colored (*harita*) one grant them.
May he who is speckled in color and possesses speckled marks grant [our desires].
Likewise, in the "thousand-fold pressing"— so called because a thousand kinds of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhayaḥ*) are produced or brought forth during the rainy season—
when that occurs, may all the frogs, giving us hundreds of cows— that is, immeasurable cattle— bestow them upon us and extend our life-span, increasing our vitality.
The hymn beginning with "indrāsomā," consisting of twenty-five verses, is a *pañcadaśa* (fifteen-verse) hymn; it is the *ṛṣi*-seer Vasiṣṭha’s composition.

Of these, the first six are *jagatī*s; the seventh is a *jagatī* or a *triṣṭubh*; the eighteenth, twenty-first, and twenty-third are *jagatī*s; the next [the nineteenth] is a *prati cakṣva* which is an *anuṣṭubh*; and the remaining fourteen are *triṣṭubh*s.

The ninth, twelfth, and thirteenth [verses] have Soma as their deity; the eleventh has the God (Indra) as its deity; the eighth and sixteenth have Indra as their deities; the seventeenth has the pressing-stones (grāvan) as its deity; the eighteenth has the Maruts as its deity; the tenth and fourteenth have Agni as their deities; the five verses beginning with "pra vartaya" have Indra as their deity;
and in the twenty-third verse, "mā no rakṣa," the first half-verse contains the prayer of Vasiṣṭha, and therefore it has him as its deity.
The latter half-verse has the Earth and the Intermediate Space as its deities;
for the remaining [verses], Indra and Soma are the deities who destroy the Rākṣasas.

And thus it is enumerated: “*indrāsomā* [is] with five; *abhike*, *indrāsomaṃ rakṣoghnam*, and that which consists mostly of curses and counter-curses [are] six or seven; [there are] twenty-one *jagatī*s; the eighteenth and the nineteenth are [in *triṣṭubh*]; the tenth and fourteenth are addressed to the Ādityas; the eleventh is divine; the ninth, twelfth, and thirteenth are *anuṣṭubh*s; the seventeenth is addressed to Soma; the eighth and sixteenth are addressed to Praṇa and Indra respectively; *pra vartaya* consists of five verses; and *mā no rakṣaḥ* is for the protection of oneself. (The variants *kha*, *na*, *bha* read *pūrṇe*.)
2. "Do not let the stubborn ones increase; O Maṇḍūki, speak forth as the rain has arrived! Four-footed [beings] have entered their own hiding places in the middle of the lake" (Ṛgveda-Laiṅga 16).
3. Jha-ta4: four [verses] addressed to Indra; Jha: four [verses] addressed to Indra; ta3-ma-śa: five [verses] addressed to Indra.
[Maṇḍala 7, Anuvāka 6, Sūkta 104] The fifth Aṣṭaka, page 509:
"The subsequent section has the Earth and the Intermediate Space as its deities.
Regarding this, it is enumerated in the *Bṛhaddevatā*: "For one year, however, [the hymn] beginning with 'maṇḍūkāḥ' is dedicated to Indra and Soma; but that which follows—"
Overwhelmed by grief for his son, he was like a seer;
then, enraged because his hundred sons had been slain by the Saudāsas, he was consumed by sorrow.
Thus, for the purpose of destroying demons, this hymn (*sūkta*) should be recited.
O Indra and Soma, burn up the Rakṣasas; crush them, O Bulls, and cast down those who thrive in darkness.
Strike down the senseless ones, burn them away, slay them, drive them off, and sharpen your weapons against the insatiable.

O Indra and Soma, burn up the *rakṣas*; crush it down; strike it low, O bulls! Destroy those who thrive in darkness; rend the senseless ones asunder; consume them; slay them; drive them away; sharpen your weapons against the thornless one! 1.
Regarding "he indrāsomā":
Indra and Soma are "Indra-Soma.
By the rule "devatādvandve ca," the [short] vowel of the preceding member is substituted.
The vocative case is udātta (accented on the first syllable);
the Rigveda.
O Indra and Soma, strike down the evil-doers, those who perform wicked deeds—the Rākṣasas—by casting them into the midst of the darkness, into the gloom that offers no support and no foothold.
Strike them so that not even a single one among them may rise up again from this darkness;
such is the meaning of "strike them down."

The augment *yaṅ* is added for the future tense (*eterlyaṅagamaḥ*). Then, by the rule "the elision of the *i*," there is the elision of the vowel *i*. Finally, the *guṇa* and *āy* substitutions take place.
May that well-known strength of yours two, full of passion and joined with wrath, be for the sake of overpowering the Rākṣasas.

O Indra and Soma, hurl down from heaven and from the earth your weapon, the crusher of the one who speaks evil. Carve it from the mountains with a thunderbolt, wherewith you burn up the waxing Rakṣas.
O Indra and Soma, hurl down from heaven and from the earth your deadly weapon; forge from the mountains a thunderbolt for the one who reviles us, wherewith you consume the waxing demon.
O Indra and Soma, from heaven, from the intermediate space, or from the celestial world, bring forth—that is, produce—the weapon that is the means of slaying.
From this earth as well, produce the destructive weapon for the sake of striking down the one who utters evil speech, the Rākṣasa who intends harm;
likewise, [produce] the heavenly [weapon] from the mountains, that is, from the cloud-masses possessed of mountain-like peaks.
The root *svṛ* means "to sound" and "to afflict. You have raised up— that is, you have extracted— the afflicting thunderbolt,
by which thunderbolt you two consume— that is, you strike down— the *rakṣas*, the demon, as it grows, increases, or has become fully developed.
The root *ju* means "to injure";
thus, the meaning is "he has carved out that thunderbolt."
O Indra and Soma, turn them back from heaven with these your swift-moving weapons;
with your unaging, heat-discharging bolts, strike down the devourers into the abyss so that they go forth voiceless.
O Indra and Soma, turn them back from heaven with your fire-darting, stone-hurling, heat-smiting, and ageless weapons! Strike down the devourers in the abyss; let them go forth voiceless. 5.
O Indra and Soma, from heaven and from the intermediate space, turn back and hurl forth your weapons on all sides.

You two, with those weapons that burn with heat, that strike with scorching blows, that are ageless and never-wearied, and that are made of iron—the product of stone—smite the Atriṇ, the Rākṣasa, in his flanks;
strike him down. And let those Rākṣasas go forth, departing silently and without a sound.
O Indra and Soma, may this prayer encompass you from every side, like two prize-winning horses urged by Kaśyapa;
quicken these sacred formulations and these priestly invocations which I present to you with wisdom, as if for a royal feast.

O Indra and Soma, may this prayer encompass you from every side; like two spirited horses urged on by a whip, quicken this hymn which I offer to you with wisdom—quicken these sacred words as two lords of men. 6.
O Indra and Soma, may this thought—the hymn of praise being composed by us—encompass you both from every side, O powerful ones, O possessors of strength.
Therein is an illustration:
just as a rope used for binding a horse encompasses the horse, so may it encompass you.
This sacrificial office (*hotrā*) and this speech which we offer to you both with wisdom— these prayers (*brahmāṇi*) are like two kings (*nṛpatī iva*).
May you two quicken us!
O Indra and Soma, may this thought—the hymn being composed by us—encompass you both from every side, O possessors of strength, O powerful ones.
As an illustration:
just as a rope used for binding a horse encompasses the horse, so may it encompass you.
May that sacrificial offering (*hotrā*) or speech (*vāk*) which [emerges] from you two through wisdom (*medhā*)— [let it] go forth, let it depart.
[The word *kakṣarbadhanī* is a variant.]
"I abandon" means "I impel";
this is the connection with the word "this thought.
Furthermore, "these"—meaning these hymns of praise (*brahmāṇi*) composed by us—"fill," that is, satisfy them with fruits, just as one fills [them] with wealth. "Jinvantam" means "filling."

Remember them both against the one who strikes down with his weapons; slay the malevolent Rākṣasas who are bent on destruction. O Indra and Soma, do not grant a path of ease to the evildoer; let him never again oppress us with his malice. prati | smarethām | tujaryad-bhiḥ | evaiḥ | hatam | duhaḥ | rakṣasaḥ | bhaṅgurāvataḥ | indrāsomā | duṣkṛte | mā | sugam | bhūya | yaḥ | naḥ | kadā | cit | abhidāsati | duhā || 7 ||
O Indra and Soma, with your swift, neighing, and rushing steeds that come hither, remember us and come toward us!
Here, by the force of the prefix *upa*, the root *smṛ* functions in a different sense;
as in the expressions *prasmaraṇa* (approaching) and *prasthāna* (setting out).
Having approached, O Indra and Soma, strike down the *rakṣas*, the malevolent ones who are full of malice, deceitful, and engaged in harmful actions.
O Indra and Soma, let there be no easy path for the evil-doing, sinful *rakṣas*.
The construction is as follows: "To that evil-doer who, joined with malice (*duh*), might at any time (*kadā cit*) seek to harm (*abhidāsati*) or strike us (*naḥ*)."

Whoever, with a simple mind, accuses me with false words while I am acting rightly—may he be like water caught in a net; may he be seized by his own falsehood, O Indra! 8. Whoever, with a simple mind, accuses me with false words while I am acting rightly—may he be like water caught in a net; may he be seized by his own falsehood, O Indra! 8.

O Indra, that Rākṣasa who, with words of falsehood and untruths, falsely accuses me—who am walking and acting with a mind that is ripened, matured, and pure, and who am a speaker of truth—may that speaker of untruth, that Rākṣasa, become non-existent; let him perish. Just as water held in a clenched fist is completely scattered, so may he vanish. May he cease to exist. This is the meaning.

Those who, by their ways, disrupt the one who speaks with simplicity, or those who, by their own nature, corrupt what is auspicious—let Soma deliver them to the serpent, or let him cast them into the lap of Destruction. 9. Those who, by their ways, disrupt the one who speaks with simplicity, or those who, by their own nature, corrupt what is auspicious—let Soma deliver them to the serpent, or let him cast them into the lap of Destruction. 9.

Those *rākṣasas* who, by means of these very [deeds] of their own—namely, these impetuous acts which have become the cause of their desire—sport with me, who am a speaker of truth and whose speech is mature (*pākaśaṃsa*), they especially carry me off and exhaust me;

that is to say, they revile me according to their pleasure. Or those who, endowed with their own powers (*svadhāmiḥ*), defile me—that is, make me wicked, though I am auspicious and of virtuous conduct—all of them, whether Soma or Agni, or even a traveling companion, let him deliver over to me.
May he place—that is, cast—the light into the lap, that is, the bosom, of *Nirṛti*, the goddess of evil.

1. *Gha*: "fill ye"; just as two kings, seen [in the world], fill [their domains], so too [here]. 2. *Janta*: those who hate. 3. *Jña*: those who speak untruth (*asatyavaktṛ*). 4. *Ta*: meaning "those who treat with contempt. 5. *Kha*, *Na*, *Bha*, *Śa*: existing prosperity (*kalyāṇa*). 512.
*Ṛgveda*:

O Agni, whoever seeks to harm our essence—whether that of our food, our eyes, our cattle, or our bodies—let that enemy, thief, and doer of mischief wander away; let him be utterly destroyed in his own body and in his offspring.

O Agni, whoever seeks to harm our essence after drinking, whoever is an enemy to our eyes, our cattle, or our bodies—may that thief, the stealer who commits theft, go to destruction; may he be utterly deprived of his own body and his offspring. 10.
O Agni, whatever Rākṣasa seeks to harm— that is, desires to strike down— the essence and strength of our food,
or seeks to harm the essence of our eyes, or seeks to harm the essence of our cattle.

And whoever seeks to injure the essence of our bodies—be he an enemy, an oppressor, a thief, a robber, or one who steals away wealth—let all such people encounter *dubhra*, that is, violence. Moreover, let that oppressor be deprived of his own body, his wife, and his offspring; let him be utterly ruined.
Let him be before us with his own body and his offspring; let all the three earths lie beneath him.
May the glory of that man wither away, O gods, who seeks to harm us by day and he who seeks to harm us by night.

Let him be before [us], let him be behind; let him be with his body and with his offspring. Let him be beneath the three earths, let him be below all things. O gods, may the glory of him who seeks to harm us by day and by night be dried up. 11.
That Rākṣasa, by means of his body (*tanvā*) and his offspring (*tanā*)—
the instrumental case here being used by way of transposition—
let him be far away, existing beyond the reach of both his own body and his progeny.
The meaning is: "May he be deprived of both.
May he be below the three pervasive worlds—the three worlds; that is, may he fall even from the three worlds. The meaning is: "May he be cast down."
O gods, let the glory, food, and fame of this enemy wither away.

Let the glory of that Rākṣasa who seeks to harm us by day, who desires to kill us during the day, and who also desires to kill us at night—let the glory of both these kinds of beings wither away; such is the connection of the words.
Easy to discern for the man who understands, truth and falsehood have contended for glory;
of these two, that which is true and more upright—Soma protects that very thing and strikes down the false.

It is difficult to discern for the man who possesses true insight. Both the existent and the non-existent strove together for glory. Of these two, that which is the truth, whichever is more upright—that indeed Soma protects; he strikes down the non-existent. 12.
Generally, with these initial verses, an oath is being made by the Ṛṣi against the Rākṣasa.
Regarding this, some say: "Having previously slain a hundred sons of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, you are either a Rākṣasa who has assumed the form of Vasiṣṭha, or [you are] Vasiṣṭha himself."
"I am Vasiṣṭha," the Rākṣasa said, desiring to kill him;
we have heard that at this point two further verses were seen by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus,
for the person who is observant and wise, this becomes easy to understand— that is, it is easy to comprehend.
What is that?

The true and the untrue, the real and the unreal— these two forms of speech, characterized by truth and untruth, contend with one another. Between those two, that which is the true, factual word, and whichever is more upright (*ṛjīyas*), most straight and free from crookedness— that very same non-crooked truthful speech Soma protects and preserves.
That which is contrary to what has been stated is "unreal" (asatya), and it "slays" or destroys [the speaker].
Thus, between these two—the true and the false—it is easily discerned by the wise who of them is the speaker of untruth; this is the meaning.
Indeed, Soma does not further the crooked man, nor the Kṣatriya who holds [his office] falsely.
He slays the Rakṣas, he slays the one who bites falsely; both lie ensnared by Indra.

The moon does not drive away the crooked; it does not slay the Kṣatriya who holds [his office] falsely. It slays the Rākṣasa; it slays the one who speaks untruth. Both lie within the grasp of Indra. ||13||
The god Soma does not indeed impel—that is, he does not drive forward—the crooked one who commits evil, the Rākṣasa;
he does not release him with the words, "Go you!
Likewise, [he does not impel] the Kṣatriya.

*Kṣatra* is power. It does not strike—that is, it does not release—a man who possesses it but who maintains *mithuyā*, that is, false speech; namely, a person who speaks untruth. Rather, it destroys him as a *rakṣas*, a demon.
He strikes down and destroys one who speaks what is non-existent and untrue.
Both of them—the Rākṣasa and the speaker of untruth—were slain by Soma and lie, bound, in the fetters belonging to Indra;
or rather:
In the phrase "indrasya," the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental;
[they were] bound by the Lord Indra with Soma.
The root *bīj* means "to bind."

The suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here in the sense of the object (*karmani*). According to the rule "the preceding *gati* [is unaccented]," regarding the *gati*: may Indra strike—that is, destroy—with his great, mature weapon, the thunderbolt (*vajra*), that two-fold kind of *rākṣasa*. [First: the *rākṣasa* who, while I am not a *rākṣasa*, addresses me with the vocatives "O ghātudhāna! or "O *rākṣasa*!"; [and second: the *rakṣas* or *rākṣasa* who says, "I am pure, I am clean; I am not a *rākṣasa*. May Indra slay both such types of *rākṣasa*.
And may he, being the lowest and most base among all living beings and all people, fall down.
She who comes forth at night like an owl, entering the house while concealing her body—may she fall down into the bottomless pits;
may the pressing-stones crush the demons with their loud sounds.
She who comes forth at night like an owl, entering the house while milking out injury—may she fall down; may the pressing-stones crush the demons with their loud sounds. 17.
The female demon (*rākṣasī*), joined with malice, who at night goes forth—advances like an owl (*khargalā*);
what is she doing?
Concealing her own body, yet revealing it, uncovering it.
May that Rākṣasī fall headlong, having gone to endless and boundless pits;
may the pressing-stones—the stones used for the extraction of Soma—slay the Rākṣasas with their *upabdas*, the sounds of the pressing.

Spread out, O Maruts; scatter them all! Seize the Rākṣasas and grind them to pieces—those who, having become birds, fly about at night, or those who have placed their hostility toward the gods during the sacrifice.

Stand apart, O Maruts! Seek out everyone! Seize the Rākṣasas and grind them to pieces—those who, having become birds, fly about at night, and those who have placed their treachery within the divine sacrifice. 18.
O Maruts, you all, spread yourselves among all creatures; stand forth in various ways.
There, desire to slay and seek out the hidden Rākṣasas. Immediately thereafter, seize and capture those Rākṣasas.
And having seized them, crush and grind them to powder!
Those Rākṣasas who, becoming birds, fly and come during the nights throughout the nights;
or those who have laid snares—that is, acts of violence—at the blazing sacrifice, the divine rite.
The syntactical connection is: "He crushes those Rākṣasas."
O Indra, hurl down the stone from heaven; O Maghavan, sharpen it with Soma and direct it.
From the front, from behind, from below, and from above, strike down the Rākṣasas with the mountain.
Cast down from heaven the stone, O Indra; sharpened by Soma, O Maghavan, direct it well. From the front, from behind, from below, and from above, strike down the demons with the mountain.
O Indra, from heaven and from the intermediate space, hurl forth the stone, the thunderbolt, to slay the Rākṣasas.
Likewise, O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, sharpen—that is, perfect—the sacrificer who has been whetted by Soma.
Furthermore, from the east, from the west, from below, from below, and from above—from every quarter—slay and destroy the Rākṣasas with the mountain-like thunderbolt.
1. Kha, gha, bha, and mā [represent] *mām* (me).
2. Jha, ta, ḷ, ḷh, and a represent *aśanam* (food); na represents *prāvāṇam* (the pressing-stone).

These very ones fly about like arrows; desiring to harm, they seek to injure Indra, the invincible. Śakra sharpens his weapon for the treacherous; he shall surely now hurl the thunderbolt at the sorcerers. These Rākṣasas, the *śaryātavaḥ*—those who strike with arrows (*śaraiḥ*) as their equipment, or those who move together with arrows—fly down or fall. Being desirous of harm (*dipsavaḥ*), they wish to injure (*dipsanti*) Indra, the one who cannot be harmed (*adābhya*). For those treacherous ones (*piśunebhyaḥ*), Śakra—the capable Indra—sharpens his weapon, the thunderbolt (*aśani*), to slay their deceitful guiles. Against the sorcerers, the Rākṣasas, he shall surely and swiftly hurl the thunderbolt for the purpose of destruction.

Indra has become the destroyer of the sorcerers, the crusher of those who plunder the oblations as they approach. Indeed, Śakra goes toward the Rākṣasas, shattering them like an axe felling a forest, or like a mallet breaking vessels. Indra has become the *parāśara*—the one who utterly crushes—the destroyer of the *yātus*, those harmful Rākṣasas who plunder the sacrificial offerings (*havirmathīnām*) as they come forward to seize them. Furthermore, this powerful Śakra approaches the Rākṣasas, striking them down like an axe (*paraśu*) cutting through a grove of trees, or like a mallet (*pātra*) smashing vessels; for the word *sata* is a synonym for *prāsa*, as Yāska states: "The term *tiraḥ sata* refers to a javelin" (*Nirukta* 3.20). Thus, he approaches, destroying and slaying the Rākṣasas with his darts. The particle *id* is used here as a filler.

Slay the owl-demon, slay the screech-owl demon, slay the śaryāta-demon, and the korka-demon; slay the eagle-demon and the vulture-demon; crush the *rakṣas*, O Indra, as with a millstone. 22 *Ulūkayātum* | *śuśulūkayātum* | *jahi* | *śaryātam* | *uta* | *korkayātum* | *suparṇayātum* | *uta* | *gṛdhrayātum* | *dṛṣadāiva* | *pra* | *mṛṇa* | *rakṣaḥ* | *indra* || 22 *Ulūkayātum*: He who torments (*yātayati*) or goes (*yāti*) along with owls as his attendants is an *ulūkayātu*; or rather, one who goes in the form of an owl is an *ulūkayātu*. O Indra, slay such a *rakṣas* for its destruction. Thus it is said in the *Bṛhaddevatā*: "O Indra, slay for me these *ulūkayātus*, those moving and unmoving beings of various forms, and the beasts of prey in male and female forms who desire to kill. This should be applied similarly to what follows. *Śuśulūkayātum*: Owls are of two kinds, large-owls (*bṛhadulkā*) and small-owls (*alpolkā*). Here, *ulūkayātu* is said with reference to the large-owl. A young owl is a *śuśulūka*; a *rakṣas* existing in that form is a *śuśulūkayātu*. *Saryātam*: A *rakṣas* existing in the form of a *śaryāta*. *Uta*: And also. *Korkayātum*: A *koka* is a ruddy goose (*cakravāka*); a *rakṣas* existing in that form. *Suparṇayātum*: A *suparṇa* is a hawk (*śyena*); a sorcerer (*yātudhāna*) having that appearance. *Uta*: And also. *Gṛdhrayātum*: A sorcerer in the form of a vulture. O Indra, slay all these forms. What need is there for more? Crush (*pra mṛṇa*), that is, kill, every *rakṣas* with the thunderbolt as if with a millstone (*dṛṣad*).
1. After [roots] ending in *jha*, *śa*, or *yā*, provided they contain *hi* or *sā*.
2. Of which kind are *kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, *śa*, and *kīdṛśī*?
3. [The forms] *śamathnātam*, *abhyāvivāsatām*, and *abhi*.

May the *rakṣas* not reach us; may it drive away the pairs of *yātumāvat* (tormenting) *kimīdin* demons. May the Earth protect us from earthly distress, and may the intermediate space protect us from celestial distress. May the *rakṣas*—the race of Rākṣasas—not reach (*abhi naṭ*) us; let there be no pervasion (*naśati*) of us by it. In the *luṅ* tense of the root *naś*, the suffix *cli* is elided by the rule "in mantras, [the suffix is elided] after *ghas* etc. There is no insertion of *aṭ* because of the connection with the prohibitive particle *mā*. Likewise, may it drive away (*apocchatu*) the pairs (*mithunā*), the couples consisting of male and female forms, of the *yātumāvat* Rākṣasas—those possessed of torment. May the Dawn (*uṣas*) also cause them to depart and cast them out. And as for those pairs which are *kimīdin*—existing with the intent to kill, asking "what is this? what is this?"—furthermore, may the Earth, the broad one, protect (*pātu*) us from earthly (*pārthivāt*) distress (*aṃhasaḥ*), that is, from sin related to the earth or the intermediate space. And may the intermediate space protect us from celestial (*divyāt*) distress, that is, from sin originating in heaven.

O Indra, slay the male sorcerer and also the female who exults in her magic. Let the foolish gods, their necks severed, perish; let them not behold the sun as it rises and moves across the sky. O Indra, kill the male *yātudhāna* (sorcerer/demon) who assumes a human form. And also kill the female demon who exults (*śāśadānām*) through her deceptive magic (*māyayā*). Furthermore, let the foolish gods (*mūradevāḥ*), those demons who delight in slaughter, perish with their necks severed (*vigrīvāsaḥ*). May such demons not see the sun (*sūryam*) as it rises and moves. This verse, "Prati cakṣva," is used for the *maṇḍala-homa* at the beginning and end of the *upākaraṇa* and *utsarjana* rites. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Yo naḥ svo araṇaḥ, prati cakṣva" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 3.5.7).

Look on! Look around! O Indra and Soma, stay awake! Cast forth your weapon against the Rākṣasas; hurl the thunderbolt at the sorcerers. O Soma, you and Indra, look upon each individual Rākṣasa; likewise, look around—look in every direction so that you may see how they might harm us. Both of you, remaining together, stay awake: be vigilant and intent upon the slaying of the Rākṣasas. Against the sorcerers, those who are full of violence, cast forth the weapon—the thunderbolt—in the form of a bolt; hurl it at the Rākṣasas. Thus ends the sixth Anuvāka of the seventh Maṇḍala. The seventh Maṇḍala is complete.
Oṃ.
Now begins the eighth maṇḍala.
In the eighth maṇḍala there are ten anuvākas.
In that [maṇḍala], in the first anuvāka there are five sūktas.
Among them, the first sūkta, consisting of twenty-four ṛcs, begins with "mā cid anyat."

In this regard, it is followed [by the tradition]: “Mācicca, Caturviṃśat, Medhātithi, and Medhātithi [composed] the Indra-hymn in the Bṛhatī meter, beginning with a Dvipragātha and ending with two Triṣṭubhs; the first two-verse section is a Pragātha. Now, Plāyogi’s son, Aṣṭaka—who, having been born a woman, became a man—having given a gift to Medhātithi, praised himself with the four verses beginning ‘Praise, praise! His wife, Śaśvatī, a descendant of Aṅgiras, having obtained a male child, was pleased and praised him with the final verse. This is its meaning.

The seers (ṛṣis) of this hymn are two named Medhātithi and Medhyātithi, both belonging to the Kaṇva lineage. Regarding the seer, the metre, and the lineage, it is stated by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "One who was previously a Mādhucchandasa is called a Kāṇva. However, the seer of the first two verses is a Kāṇva because, being the son of Ghora, he attained the status of being the son of his own brother, Kaṇva.
The seer (ṛṣi) is named Pragātha.

He was the son of King Playoga, a king called Āsaṅga, who, having experienced womanhood due to a divine curse, later became a man through the power of his asceticism and by the grace of Medhātithi. Having given much wealth to him, he praised his own sacrificial post—which had been given as a gift—with four verses beginning with "stuhi, stuhi" (praise, praise). Therefore, the seer of these [verses] is the king named Āsaṅga.

The wife of this Asaṅga, the son of Aṅgiras, named Śaśvatī, having obtained a male child from her husband, was delighted and praised her husband with the verse beginning, "Anvasya sthūram. Therefore, Śaśvatī is the seer (ṛṣikā) of that ṛc.
Of the other two verses, the second and fourth are Triṣṭubhs, while the remaining ones are Bṛhatīs.
Indra is the deity of the entire hymn (*sūkta*).
As for the verses beginning with "Praise! Praise!", they have him as their deity because the gift bestowed by him is being praised therein.
The deity of the verse beginning with "Anvasya" is the king named Āsaṅga.

According to the maxim, "That which is spoken by him is the deity," in the *Niṣkevalya* section of the *Mahāvrata*, there are twenty-nine days beginning from the first verse of the *Bārhatasāma-śastra*. Likewise, it is prescribed in the fifth *Āraṇyaka*: "‘Mā cid anyad hi śaṃsata’—with this one [verse], there are twenty-nine" (*Ai. Ā. 5.2.4*).

On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), the optional *stotriya* *pragātha* for the Maitrāvaruṇa is "mā cid anyat" and so forth. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *stotriya* and *anurūpa* are 'mā cid anyad dhi śaṃsata' and 'yaccid dhi tvā janā ime'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4). This [hymn] is also employed in the *prasthāna* chant.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “Come to us, O Indra, bringing splendor; do not praise anything else indeed” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.12).
Regarding the commencement and conclusion [of the study]: this same verse is used even for the *maṇḍala* and other [sections].
For it is enjoined: “Do not attend to anything else; come with the sweetest [hymn]” (Ṛgveda 8.93.28).
Praise nothing else at all, O friends; do not suffer harm.
Praise only Indra, the bull, together with the pressed juice; repeatedly recite your hymns of praise.
Do not praise anything else; O friends, do not suffer harm. Praise Indra alone, the bull, when the soma is pressed; repeatedly recite hymns of praise. 1.
O friends, you who share the same renown, O praisers, do not recite any hymn other than the hymn of praise to Indra; do not utter it.
Do not be harmed; do not become destroyers.
By reciting the praises of others, do not come to waste yourselves in vain.
When the Soma has been pressed, O Prastotṛ and others, praise together, in unison, Indra alone—the bull, the showerer of desires.
And you, O Praśāstṛ and others, recite repeatedly, again and again, the hymns (ukthas) and the liturgical chants (śastras) directed toward Indra.
Like an old bull that has been drawn away, like a cow that conquers the people,
[he is] a cause of hatred and a bringer of both [results], most mighty, fierce, and overcoming those who do not submit.

At the commencement and conclusion of the Vedic term, [we praise] him who has stepped forward, the bull, who is like one that does not age, like a cow that conquers the people, the one who causes enmity to turn back, the performer of both deeds, the most excellent giver, the possessor of both. 2.

Like a bull, like a bull that is "avakrakṣiṇam"—one who drags down, a destroyer of enemies—"ajuram"—undecaying or invincible—"gām na"—like a cow, like a bull—"carṣaṇīsaham"—the overcomer of *carṣaṇīs*, that is, of men who have become enemies—"vidveṣaṇam"—the one who causes hatred among enemies—"saṃvananam"—the one who brings about reconciliation, being properly honored by his praisers—"ubhayaṃkaram"—the performer of both, the agent of both restraint and favor—"maṃhiṣṭham"—most generous, the greatest of givers—"ubhayāvinam"—endowed with both kinds of wealth, characterized as both celestial and terrestrial.
Or rather:
it is endowed with two kinds of things to be protected, namely those that are stationary and those that are moving;
and furthermore, it is endowed with both types of people—those who offer praise and those who perform sacrifices.
The syntactical connection is: "Praise Indra who is of such a kind."
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing, the *anupapragātha* "ayacciddhi tvā" is for the *praśāstṛ*;
that has been stated in the Sūtra.

For although these people here invoke you in various ways for aid, O Indra, let this our prayer be your strength and your nourishment every day. (3) For although these people here invoke you in various ways for aid, O Indra, let this our prayer be your strength and your nourishment every day. (3)
All these people here who are visible, O Indra, though they invoke and praise you individually for protection, for preservation, or for satisfaction— *hi* being a particle of emphasis—
even so, may this *brahma*, this very hymn of ours, O Indra, be your *vardhana*, that is, your strengthener.
The meaning is that not only now, but indeed on all days—on every single day—may this very hymn of praise cause you to increase.

The inspired songs of the noble people, O Maghavan, are being spread abroad by those who perceive the truth. Step forward toward the one of many forms; bring us strength most near for our protection. vi tarturyante | maghavan | vipaścitaḥ | aryaḥ | vipaḥ | janānām | upa | kramasva | pururūpam | ā | bhara | vājam | nediṣṭham | ūtaye || 4 ||

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, those who take refuge in you—the wise ones, the singers of praise, the noble ones who advance against the people, the enemies, being stirrers of inspired hymns—they cross over and pass through their calamities most effectively. Such as you are, come toward us;
bring to us for our protection and satisfaction food of many forms, most near at hand.

O wielder of the stone, O wielder of the thunderbolt, even for a great price I would not give you away—not for a thousand, nor for ten thousand, nor for fifty hundred, O lord of a hundredfold wealth. || 5 ||
